#2. 5 Signs You’ve Graduated From Beginner Cyclist Status

“When did you first realize you weren’t a beginner anymore?”

It’s a question I posed to my coworkers at Bicycling, many of whom have been riding and racing for multiple decades, at elite levels, across staggering distances, possibly uphill both ways in the snow.

I expected my inbox to be flooded with inspiring anecdotes; tales of triumph and woe; or at the very least, smug hot takes on when it’s OK to start caring about insider stuff like embro and VO2 Max.

But such was not the case. “Oh, I still feel like a beginner almost every day,” was the almost universal, almost completely BS response.

While I admired the humility, based on how many times my colleagues have teased me about my sock height alone, I knew all that self-effacement was completely false. So I pushed back, and eventually they coughed up a few earnest responses.

In many ways, they’re right—it’s great to never lose that wide-eyed rookie sense of discovery and fun. But it’s also pretty cool to see those little glimpses of progress along the way.

If you’re anything like us, here’s how you might have guessed you were starting to get a handle on this whole bicycle-riding thing, no matter how much chain grease might be stamped across your calves.

#3. Nike Shoes Aren’t Just for the Elites. These Are the 10 Best Trainers Our Team Tested.

The Swoosh is known for innovation (Vaporfly 4%, anyone?). Here’s our list of the best Nike shoes on sale now.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Editor’s Note, October 19, 2026: In almost a month, the long-awaited Alphafly 4 is set for release on October 29. As we wait for the launch, the Alphafly 3 is still available.

Brownie points if you knew the waffle iron and Swoosh go a long way back. It was the early 1960s when University of Oregon track coach Bill Bowerman cofounded Blue Ribbon Sports (BRS) with one of his runners, Phil Knight. BRS was a proprietor of Onitsuka Tiger’s athletic shoes before manufacturing its own product. Depending on who you believe, Bowerman customized running shoes using a waffle iron either in the early 1960s, when he gave pairs to his athletes to compete in, or in 1971, the same year BRS was renamed Nike, after the Greek goddess of victory. And that’s how legends are born (and shoe awards are given).

You can read Knight’s side of the story by reading Shoe Dog, or watch Prefontaine or Without Limits for a more dramatic tale about one of the University of Oregon’s star athletes with Nike’s origin story in the background (the 1997 movie is the superior of the two, IMHO). Since the dawn of the Swoosh, the brand has rocked the running industry boat with its innovations. In the past 10 years, for instance, the Vaporfly 4% appeared on the scene, creating mass ripples of new World Athletics guidelines, academic studies on super shoes and running economy, and world records such as the late Kelvin Kiptum’s superhuman 2:00:35 at the 2023 Chicago Marathon.

Back in my early days at Runner’s World in 2018, the first Nike shoe I tested—and ran in—was the inimitable Vaporfly. The shoe left an impression, causing me to never turn back from racing marathons in carbon-fiber-plated trainers. But one thing that made me move on to other brands’ super shoe iterations was the narrow fit and unstable ride of Nike’s racers. All the more to show the brand’s ever-continuing evolution into being the best as well as more inclusive.

Battle of the Brands: The Best Brooks Running Shoes ● The Best Adidas Running Shoes ● The Best Mizuno Running Shoes

I’ve run and raced in several of the shoes on this list. As a Nike newb when I was hired at RW, I was schooled in the Swoosh’s indelible influence on the running industry—our magazine’s first issue came out six years after Nike’s renaming—and witnessed the dawn of the super shoe. All of the shoes on this list were tested by members of our 300-and-counting test team of local runners. They come from all walks of life, varying by gait pattern, arch height, and footstrike.

The Vomero 18 is the first Nike shoe I ran in that didn’t initially feel like a Nike trainer. The shoes fit wide. Its midfoot is broader than the narrow lasts I associate with the Swoosh. Running in the Vomero 18 for the first time, I noticed two things: this shoe is über-soft and doesn’t cause my ankles to turn inward.

This Vomero is the starting point of the brand’s other cushioned shoes, which also include this list’s Vomero Plus and soon-to-be-released Vomero Premium. The story behind this new fit is that Nike shoe development listened to women, applying their fit preferences to both the women’s and men’s versions. Turns out men like the new last too, according to a Nike rep I spoke with recently on the phone.

The Vomero 18 serves as a long-run trainer, daily trainer, and recovery shoe. The cushioning reminds me of Brooks’s Glycerin Max; it’s marshmallowy but responsive. The energy return is still there instead of being zapped like a sponge turning your runs into a slog.

“Hands down these are the best shoes I’ve tested!” said shoe tester Casey Green, a 7:00 pacer who previously tested the Pegasus Plus. “Despite all the extra cushioning the ride was incredibly smooth, responsive, and the shoe never felt weighed down despite the added padding. Every mile I ran in them felt great and slight accelerations or faster average paces were no problem.”

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com

The Winflo has always been a solid pick for beginners and high school runners. The price is an absolute steal well below the now-standard $170. But the shoe doesn’t feel cheap. Its plush cushioning, which Nike revved up with the twelfth iteration by adding even more Cushlon 3.0 foam underfoot, is fantastic for base building, long runs, or those jobs that require hours of standing.

A small knock is that Nike fit. Unlike the updated Vomero 18 and Structure 26, the Winflo 12 still has that classic Nike foot shape that’s too narrow for some. Sizing up will help alleviate the constriction. It’s worth it for the price and bouncy ride.

Shop Men’s nike.com | Shop Women’s nike.com

The Structure 26 has a few key updates that make it the stability shoe you shouldn’t sleep on. It’s me: I’m the one who slept on it. This is because Nike isn’t at the forefront of my mind when I recommend stability trainers. Lesson learned: the Structure 26 isn’t a shoe to forget. It provides reliable but subtle support for overpronators and neutral runners looking for more guidance, as well as a responsive ride. And it’s relatively cheap for a premium trainer.

The shoe now has ReactX foam, the same foam in the Pegasus 41 and Vomero 18. The foam delivers more rebound compared to the Structure 25’s Cushlon 3.0. An internal midfoot fit band—the triangular structure you can see on either side of the shoe—along with overlays brushed on the sides provide support. The Air Zoom bag was removed in the forefoot and replaced with blown rubber on the outsole to encourage smoother heel-toe transitions. Finally, the upper is cozier too. Nike padded up the collar and tongue for more cushioned touch points and a more secure fit.

Testers liked the shoe for its versatility and used it as their daily trainer for all kinds of workouts. “The shoe is an absolute do-it-all workhorse,” said tester Justin Brown. “I wore it for easy runs, and even progressed up to tempo paces and used it for some strides where I was close to sprinting and I feel like the shoe stood up to all of these really well. At the same time the stability nature of the shoe was honestly nailed, and I felt very secure in the shoe at all times even on wet pavement. The ride was smooth and felt cushioned, but there was enough energy return that I didn’t feel like I couldn’t go faster in it.”

Tester Rich Maier also highlighted the shoe’s support. “I was really impressed by the stability that I felt in both my feet and my legs,” he said. “I usually only experience that level of comfort and support with heavier shoes, but these managed to combine stability with a lighter weight shoe.”

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com

Even though the ACG Peg Trail isn’t intended for technical trails—that’s what the ACG Zegama Trail is for—our testers still praised the shoe for its capabilities on the unbeaten path.

“What I liked most about the shoe was its low-profile design that really hugged your foot on all the twists and turns out on the trail,” said tester Jeff Kilian. “Traction was exceptional as well. I feel this shoe is in a league all of its own. I would say the closest thing I can compare this Pegasus to is the Altra Timp, they’re both a lightweight shoe with not much cushioning in the sole.”

The lack of cushioning was a low point for some testers who wanted more support in the forefoot.

Despite the desire for more cushioning, they did appreciate the wider fit in the forefoot and toebox, which helped with stability on the trail.

“The fit has vastly improved,” said shoe tester Jessica Huber. “The width is perfect. There is plenty of space in the toes without feeling bulky.”

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com

The Nike shoe team wanted to make sure the next Pegasus was snappier and springier than the 41. The team added a full-length Air Zoom unit in the midsole, instead of separate units in previous models. This provides better compression throughout the shoe and improved energy return.

“What I like most is that it feels smooth, with a great rolling ride, but also supportive underfoot,” said tester Molly Sunderlin. “It feels easy to run quickly in, but also like I can do a two-hour long run without getting sore underfoot. I am not sure if this has to do with the shape of the heel which has sort of a ‘roll’ feature. It also wraps my foot so well, almost sock-like with cushion in the right spots. I like putting them on.”

Sunderlin is referring to the slightly curved toe of the shoe, which encourages smooth turnover. The shoe has a slightly modified foot shape to create a more accommodating fit in the midfoot and toe area. Still too tight for you? Not to worry; the Pegasus 42 is also available in extra wide.

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com

If you miss the Peg Turbo, get a load of the Peg Plus. The second iteration of the shoe is speedier and snappier thanks to an exposed Air unit, which we know signals “fast” in a Nike shoe. The unit functions as a carbon plate; it provides propulsion by compressing during forefoot impact. Its exposure gives it room to breathe; Nike reports this Peg Plus has 18 percent more energy return than the previous version.

Nike wanted to make sure this sensation was consistent with all sizes. The bigger the shoe size, the bigger the Air unit. Runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate liked the high rebound, but noted the shoe felt slightly heavy compared to other trainers in the speed category.

“That Air unit pushes back against you quickly, letting you feel snappy with your stride,” wrote Dengate in his review. “Sure, it’s heavy, but in that instance it doesn’t feel slow.”

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com

Nike’s mission with the Structure Plus was to change our perception of the stability trainer. Instead of a rigid, firm shoe, the brand wanted to make stability more palatable for all. The Structure Plus is lighter than its cousin, the Structure 26, and is more dynamic; instead of a full ReactX midsole, the Plus is dual-foamed with ReactX on the bottom and soft, energetic ZoomX PEBA foam on the top.

All this is housed in a 42mm stack height, which is 4mm taller than the Structure 26. Such a tall height would cause some to doubt the shoe’s support, but Nike widened the platform and implemented a convex flat sidewall with dense cushioning underneath the arch. The result: support for overpronators and neutral runners who want a little more pep in their stability trainer.

“What I liked most about the Nike Structure Plus was the strong sense of support it delivered on every run,” said tester Julian Caiazzo, an overpronator who averages 7:45 training pace. “The shoe felt stable and dependable without ever coming across as stiff or restrictive. It gave me the confidence to settle into my stride, and even with all that structure, the ride still felt smooth and enjoyable. It struck a great balance between guidance and comfort, which is exactly what I look for in a daily trainer.”

I wore the Structure Plus on a couple of long runs, including my 20-miler during my marathon buildup. Unlike the Vomero Plus, which had my feet roll inward on an 18-miler, the Structure Plus kept my form stable despite the growing fatigue in my weary, long-run legs.

Alternatively, runners who want a more grounded feel—and want to save—can opt for the Structure 26 ($145).

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com

This super trainer has next-level softness, from its thick—but breathable—cozy upper to its 43mm (heel) of plush, responsive foam underfoot. Its older sibling, the Vomero 18, has a dual-foam midsole with a top layer of ZoomX and bottom layer of ReactX. With the Vomero Plus, Nike went full PEBA, with the midsole using 100 percent ZoomX.

The shoe is lighter than the Vomero 18 and a smidge shorter (the heel on the Vomero 18 hits 44mm), but I honestly couldn’t detect a major difference in the ride. The Vomero Plus is bouncier, yet if you want to save $25, you could stick with the Vomero 18 (your legs will be none the wiser). But if you want to experience the powers of PEBA and can drop some extra cash, just listen to our testers who gave the Vomero Plus top marks. Our very own editorial assistant Michael McDonough will convince you that of the two Vomeros the Plus is the superior.

“The Nike Vomero Plus is one of, if not my favorite shoe that I’ve tested so far,” said McDonough. “The shoe lives up to the ‘plus’ in its name—I tested the Vomero 18s over the winter, and while I thought those were great as well, the Vomero Plus is an upgrade in several ways. Although they have the exact same amount of cushion, the switch from a mix of ReactX and ZoomX foam to purely ZoomX foam is an absolute game changer. The shoes feel lighter, cushier, and faster—and the fact that the shoe was able to improve all three factors at the same time was pretty remarkable.”

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com

It’s the shoe the late Kelvin Kiptum raced in during the 2023 Chicago Marathon, just 35 seconds short of officially breaking two hours. You could also say it’s structurally the most inclusive Nike racing shoe since the conception of the Vaporfly 4%.

Nike’s team made adjustments so the shoe would no longer feel catered to one type of runner (i.e., that guy who does laps around your block in short shorts, and the elites). The shoe has what you’d expect as a super shoe by Nike: a full-length carbon-fiber plate called a Flyplate, PEBA-based ZoomX foam, dual Zoom Air units, and a stack height just under the World Athletics limit of 40mm.

The changes made begin with a smoother transition. The heel is no longer decoupled; the midfoot and forefoot are now connected by foam. The midfoot has a wider fit with no rise in the sockliner, like there was in the previous version. This provides more stability in the hours when your form gets sloppy on a race course. Thirdly, Nike reduced the weight of the shoe, which is usually the goal when it comes to racing shoes: the lighter, the better—as long as the shoe maintains energy return, which our own testing confirms.

“Wow!” exclaimed overpronator and tester Helen Capparell. “This sneaker is a game changer! I usually wear Brooks but this shoe was significantly lighter, hugged my foot better, had an insane absorption of every stride and propelled me into a faster pace all while staying underfoot with a stable ride.”

As for my own personal story with the Alphafly 3: I raced in it in the 2024 Boston Marathon and bloodied up my toes. I don’t know what happened. Maybe the sizing was off; usually I need to size up in a Nike shoe, but I stuck with my usual size, which likely resulted in blister hell. There’s a lesson here, and it’s logging more dress rehearsals in a shoe before deciding to race in it the day before a ’thon. Rookie mistake.

Compare my experience with the rest of our testers: anomaly, here.

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com

Nike’s All Conditions Gear (ACG) has been around since 1989. This year, the brand introduced a new era of trail shoes under the ACG name. One of them is the ACG Zegama Trail, a shoe meant for tough all-terrain.

The shoe’s exterior makes it look unquestionably built for technical terrain. The ACG Zegama Trail has a durable cool mesh upper and an ankle cuff that functions as a gaiter, keeping debris out of your shoes. It was a favorite feature for our tester, Chris Fisher, who tested the ACG Zegama Trail last winter.

“Best thing about the Nike Zegama’s was getting into them,” he said. “They’ve got a modified gaiter collar design with a more traditional tongue that allows for easily slipping your feet in. The stretch collar does well at keeping debris out of the shoe which was nice with all the snow I was running in.”

A secure lacing system helps with stability on uneven, twisty trails, as does a broader base. The shoe has a wide forefoot and toebox to allow your toes to splay and lend support.

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com

To help runners pick and choose the soft ride they’re looking for, Nike has reworked its cushioning into three main categories:

Responsive Cushioning: Pegasus line, providing energy return for all-day wear.

Maximum Cushioning: Vomero line, offering ultimate plush comfort for longer runs.

Supportive Cushioning: Structure line, designed for stability and a supportive ride.

Cushlon: A descendent of Phylon foam, Cushlon is a proprietary EVA foam. It’s lighter than standard EVA midsoles, and provides support and springiness underfoot.

ReactX: Created using an injection process, this foam has more rebound than React foam.

ZoomX: Nike lightest and bounciest foam, it is primarily composed of PEBA.

Working in tandem with midsole foam, Zoom Air units are pouches on the shoe filled with air that help with propulsion. Upon landing, the units compress and absorb impact, then spring back to their original shape.

Should I race in the Alphafly or Vaporfly?

Nike’s premium marathon racing shoe is the Alphafly. It has all the bells and whistles, including PEBA, a Flyplate, and Zoom Air units. This means it’s made to withstand that high-mileage. While the Vaporfly can also be your shoe of choice for marathoning, it’s leaner, Zoom Air unit-free, and is built for racing distances as short as the mile.

During Vomero 18 development, the brand used women’s feedback to create “a better shoe for everyone.” Using these findings, the Nike team applied this to both the women’s and men’s models. According to a Nike rep RW spoke with, turns out men liked the adjustments inferred from women’s feedback too.

Amanda Furrer, Editor, Running Reviews, studied journalism at NYU and writing at Emerson College. She has reviewed gear and covered other topics in the running space for almost 10 years. Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon. She also has a master’s degree in gastronomy from Boston University and was formerly a professional baker for two years before hanging up her apron.

#5. Try Dana Linn Bailey’s Lateral Raise ‘Extended Set’ Trick for Broader Shoulders

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

If you’re tired of cranking out the same old reps, set after set, you may be ready to mix it up with something fresh. If that’s the case, 2013 Olympia Women’s Physique titlist Dana Linn Bailey has the shoulder workout for you. In a recent Instagram post, Bailey changed up the traditional dumbbell lateral raise with an “Extended Set.”

At the core of this session is the dumbbell lateral raise, an efficient isolation exercise that will add mass and definition to your shoulders by dialling in the lateral deltoid. As you lift the dumbbell up and away from the body, the lateral deltoid is activated, so taking this muscle to exhaustion will add width to your upper body while also building strength and posture.

There are many set protocols that you could use for lateral raises, ranging from 3 sets regular of 8 to 12 reps, through to drop sets or ascending sets, but Bailey has another option for obliterating your shoulders.

If the aim is to build tension and exhaust the shoulders so that they build back bigger, then this workout certainly delivers. You’ll start out with the banded dumbbell lateral raise. “Aim heavy enough to get about 10 reps,” explained the fit female for her two-million-plus IG followers. “The band adds extra tension as you raise up but also adds tension as you (resist on the) lower. So don’t let the band just pull you down.”

Next, drop the band and rep to failure. “You are keeping the same dumbbell weight, but you are getting rid of the band, so rep these out till failure,” advised the Olympia icon.

Finally, lose the dumbbells and pick the band back up so that you can make quarter reps or “pulses” to failure, making sure that you’ve squeezed every last drop of sweat out of this extended set. “These are a staple for me,” said Bailey of the quarter reps. “They may feel easy at first, because you are pulsing,” she added, but noted that they start to burn quick. Still, with a short pause, Bailey carries on to the conclusion. “Rest for five to 10 seconds and keep going,” she coached. “I get anywhere from 20 to 30 reps for these … Make them burn.”

Dana Linn Bailey enjoys these extended sets because they allow the workout to keep going beyond traditional reps. “And those final pulses may be a shorter range, but there’s no break in tension, just constant tension at peak contraction,” she said.

Bailey also shares that she uses the lightest band to lean into her extended sets. “These will burn but keep going through the burn. Your shoulders will thank me later.”

#6. Morning vs. Evening Runs: Which Is Better for Run Performance?

Experts help us unpack all the pros and cons of morning and evening runs.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Most races want you at the starting line early in the morning, making an a.m. run routine an obvious choice for mimicking race day conditions. But if you’re a night owl or have a jam-packed schedule, evenings might better suit your schedule.

Runners need to juggle sleep, hydration, nutrition, and training, all while making time for work, family, and a social life. So your unique lifestyle likely determines the time of day you run.

But could running when the sun comes up offer more benefits than heading out after work or vice versa?

To help you optimize your schedule, we spoke with exercise physiologists and run coaches to weigh the benefits and drawbacks of morning versus evening runs and help you choose which works best for your goals.

As mentioned, most runners race in the morning, says Greg McMillan, exercise physiologist and USATF-certified coach, so if you run in the morning consistently, you’ll be in the routine you need for race day. This allows you to practice how long it takes you to warm up, fuel properly, and head out the door on time.

Many coaches agree with McMillan, stressing the importance of simulating race day to eliminate any unknown variables. If you only ever run in the evenings but your race is in the morning, you just won’t be as prepared, says Janet Hamilton, CSCS, exercise physiologist and running coach with Running Strong in Atlanta.

She explains that morning runs can help you prevent any issues on race day by getting you used to eating an earlier breakfast, facing colder temperatures, and adjusting your sleep schedule so that you have enough energy when you wake up.

Kickstarting your day with just a 30-minute run may be all you need to feel more productive, according to research. A study published in 2019 in the British Journal of Sports Medicine examined a group of 67 sedentary, older men and women. The researchers had them perform 30 minutes of aerobic exercise on a treadmill in the morning along with three-minute walks every half an hour throughout the rest of the day.

Their findings suggest that starting your day with 30 minutes of moderate-intensity exercise may improve cognitive function related to memory and decision-making skills.

Exercising earlier in the day means you’re more likely to feel focused and productive right away, adds Kate Baird, CSCS, an exercise physiologist at the Hospital for Special Surgery in New York City. “This includes mood-boosting endorphins and neurotransmitters that help with focus and mental clarity,” she says.

Baird explains that you may also feel a sense of accomplishment from getting something done first thing in the morning, which can motivate you to keep going.

Running in the morning ensures that you start your workout with fresh legs, which is especially helpful if you know you’re going to spend all day on your feet, Hamilton says.

Hamilton explains this is especially helpful for runners who work long shifts at physically demanding jobs, as running in the morning ensures they get the most out of their muscles. Plus, walking can boost recovery after high-intensity exercise, so you can spend the rest of your day recovering after your morning workout and preparing for the next.

Your gut may not wake up when you do, says Hamilton. She explains that some people don’t empty out when they first get out of bed, and that generally, you won’t expect a bowel movement until about 10 a.m., which is probably later than an early morning run.

Meanwhile, research suggests it’s probably best to get things moving before your run so that you have more energy: A study published in 2023 in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition tested the exercise performances of 13 triathletes with two cycling time trials: one before defecating and one after.

The researchers found that pooping before their exercise led to enhanced performance, mainly because the brain received more oxygen and that decreased fatigue.

So, if you’re a person who needs time to move around, have breakfast, and use the bathroom first, then you might want to schedule your runs during afternoons and evenings.

In the mornings, your body needs time to properly warm up and acclimate to the temperatures outside. If you wake up feeling groggy and you’re pressed for time, it may be harder to give your body the time it needs to prepare for impact.

“The quality of the runs can be slightly lower in the morning because you’re still trying to wake up,” McMillan explains. “That can be a challenge for older runners. It can be challenging for runners that have injury issues, who need to warm up a little bit more,” he says.

If you’re somebody who spends time commuting into work early in the morning, or going to bed later at night, working out in the morning might require you to cut into your sleeping schedule, making it harder to feel refreshed in the morning.

The National Sleep Foundation recommends seven to nine hours of sleep per night for adults, and for runners, sleep is one of the most important factors for recovery.

Practically, if you work a 9-to-5 job, need time to get ready, commute, take kids to school, or walk your dog, you might have to start your day early in order to get in a morning run. This could look like getting out of bed around 5 a.m. and going to bed around 8 p.m., which might not be possible for some busy runners.

If you wait until the end of the day to work out, you might tap into some added benefits that can support your run performance. Research suggests that you’re more likely to run longer in the evening than in the morning.

A systematic review and meta-analysis published in 2023 in the Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research examined 31 studies on the effects of exercise on cardiorespiratory responses and endurance performance, and found a longer time to exhaustion when working out in the afternoon and evenings versus the morning.

Evening runs can help you unwind and relieve stress after a long day of work, McMillan says. You get a chance to let go of whatever happened during your day.

Research backs the benefits of exercise for stress relief: A 2023 survey published in Sports Physiology and Physical Performance examined the association between exercise frequency and stress among 3,440 Korean adults and found that higher-frequency exercise is linked to a lower perceived level of psychological stress.

This might be because running stimulates a part of your brain that regulates cognitive functions that help you deal with stress. A study published in 2018 in Scientific Reports, which examined 26 healthy runners, suggests 10 minutes of running can improve executive function, including memory, attention, self-control, and emotional response.

Running is a great way to care for your overall health, but it turns out the time of day you run can affect your metabolic health in particular.

A study published in Obesity examined 186 men and women who were overweight or had obesity and were diagnosed with at least one metabolic impairment, like high blood pressure or high cholesterol.

The researchers tracked their physical activity, what time of day they exercised, and their glucose levels over the course of two weeks. They found that those who did more than 50 percent of their exercise in the evening had significantly lower glucose levels compared to those who were sedentary, and better glucose regulation compared to those who mainly exercised in the mornings.

Additionally, a study published in 2022 supports these findings. Researchers gathered 775 active participants and assessed their blood sugar levels based on when they exercised. They found that those who performed moderate-to-vigorous activity in the evening had 25 percent lower insulin resistance than those who exercised in the morning.

If you run in the evening, you might not have enough energy left to devote to your training, which can leave you feeling unmotivated or struggling to run. Your job can affect your energy levels and leave you feeling fatigued at the end of the day, Hamilton explains.

This includes mental and physical exhaustion, McMillan points out. “Sometimes you’re not as fresh mentally or physically at the end of the day, particularly if you had a challenging day, and that can compromise your run,” he says.

Research supports McMillan’s point. A study published in 2023 in the International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance suggests that too many cognitively demanding tasks can have a significant effect on endurance.

Hamilton agrees, pointing out that whether you’re tired because you’re on your feet all day or because you’re under a lot of mental stress can affect how well you exercise after a day of work.

Hamilton explains that if you eat lunch around noon, and then start your run six or seven hours later, you need to have had a snack at some point so you have the energy to complete your miles.

“It might be a half a peanut butter and jelly sandwich, or a bagel, or some oatmeal—something to keep you from having hunger pangs while you’re out on your run,” she says. (For runs that are shorter than 90 minutes, though, runners can usually get away with just sipping on a sports drink or something light before taking off, Hamilton notes.)

This can get challenging for people that work, adds McMillan. He explains that if you have a busy day, or you’re working on a project and lose track of time, you might accidentally skip lunch, forget to hydrate properly, or might be eating later than you’d like. That certainly won’t lead to the best run in the evening.

If you wait to run in the evening, you might give yourself more time to talk yourself out of a workout. McMillan explains that your workouts, especially if you’re training for an upcoming race, should take priority in your schedule, and if you push them to the evenings, you may feel less motivated to get it done.

The most important thing is that you exercise at a time that works best for you. No matter if you’re waking up with the sun to run, or squeezing in a workout before you eat dinner, consistency is always king, says McMillan.

He adds that a consistent running schedule ensures you have an organized “stress-rest cycle,” where your body has enough time to recover between workouts, which can help prevent injury. To accomplish that, he suggests picking one time of day to run—mornings or evenings—and giving yourself 24 hours to recover between each workout.

It’s also crucial to note that no matter what time of day you run, you have to feel safe. You’re less likely to stay consistent with your training plan if you’re scared to run outdoors, so use your best judgment on where and when you run.

Kristine Kearns, a writer and avid runner, joined Runner’s World and Bicycling in July 2024. She previously coached high school girls cross country and currently competes in seasonal races, with more than six years of distance training and an affinity for weightlifting. You can find her wearing purple, baking cupcakes, and visiting her local farmers market.

#7. Choosing a Gravel Bike? These 12 Editor-Tested Models Deliver the Tire Clearance, Geometry, and Value That Matter

From bikepacking to gravel racing, these tested bikes cover every kind of dirt-road ride.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Instead of riding busy, congested city and suburban roads, many cyclists now head to lightly traveled gravel and unimproved roads. Gravel riding is a great way to see beautiful fall foliage, enjoy the fresh air, and avoid traffic. Most brands sell at least one gravel model; some offer multiple gravel platforms or bikes designed for particular gravel-riding niches. Whether you need a new bicycle for a big gravel fondo or race, a versatile bike for multi-surface rides, or a rig for bikepacking adventures, there’s a gravel bike for you.

The term “gravel riding” is very broad and doesn’t necessarily mean riding on gravel surfaces the entire ride. Gravel rides can include anything from hard-packed dirt roads (which you can often ride on a traditional road bike) to singletrack trails (typically associated with mountain bikes). Gravel riding also includes almost any other type of unimproved roadway; forest access roads, farm roads, jeep roads, rail trails, and canal paths are all commonly lumped under the gravel umbrella. And many of the best gravel routes and events incorporate a few of these surfaces.

Because they get ridden in such varied terrain, gravel bikes come in many shapes and sizes. They span the gamut of aero-optimized bikes that look similar to WorldTour road bikes to full suspension models that resemble mountain bikes with dropbars—But most gravel bikes fall somewhere in between these polar extremes. Most gravel bikes share a few key traits: Generous tire clearance, a more upright riding position, and geometry that prioritizes stability and confidence on rough surfaces.

Buying Tip: Don’t pass on a great gravel bike because you don’t like its tires. Focus on a bike’s tire clearance rather than the stock rubber’s tread or width. Brands usually equip gravel bikes with tires that work well in average conditions. If those tires don’t work for you, it’s a simple fix. Upgrading to tires that better suit your needs is often the best—and easiest—first change you can make, and it usually shaves weight.

The Canyon Grizl is a great all-arounder. It’s a gravel bike built for all sorts of adventures, whether it’s a casual after-work gravel spin, commuting around town, or a multi-day bikepacking trip. The SRAM Apex XPLR 1x12 drivetrain shifts quickly and has a wide gear range. The Grizl’s carbon frame also helps dampen the bumps on rougher roads and trails.

Since we tested the bike a few seasons ago, platform updates have improved its capability and appeal. The Grizl now features clearance for wider tires (up to 56mm), internal downtube storage, and an easily sourced UDH hanger. If this model doesn't speak to you, Canyon offers several Grizl options priced from $1,899 to $4,699.

If you don’t have thousands of dollars to spend but need a bike for riding actual gravel roads, your choices might seem limited. However, if you dig into brands’ websites and look for budget picks, you will find a few gems. The $1,300 Salsa Journeyer Essa is a good example; it stands out for its robust parts, wide tires, and size range.

Unlike some cheaper gravel bikes you may find on Amazon, the Journeyer’s aluminum frame comes in six sizes to fit riders from 4’8” to 6’5”. Additionally, it’s available through REI. This way, you’ll have warranty support if anything goes awry, and the bike is professionally assembled (if you choose in-store pickup).

For components, Salsa equips this Journeyer model with Shimano’s 1x8-speed Essa group (including Shimano mechanical disc brakes)—the parts aren’t fancy, but they’re robust. The only negative point of the Journeyer Essa is its standard QR dropouts, which make upgrading to lighter-weight or tubeless wheels slightly more difficult.

The Topstone 1 is Cannondale’s top-tier aluminum gravel bike. Designed for versatility and adventure, it’s equally at home on pavement or dirt, with a utilitarian setup that includes mounts for racks, bags, fenders, and extra bottles—perfect for long-haul rides. But don’t mistake utilitarian for boring; the Topstone still feels lively and efficient on the road, making it a great choice for days when your rides lean more toward pavement.

This model comes with 37mm tires, but the frame clears up to 45mm rubber. This allows you to choose tires for the terrain and rides you take. The Shimano GRX 2x11 drivetrain is another standout, offering a wide gear range for steep, rough climbs while keeping gear jumps tight—something you’ll appreciate when riding extended stretches of pavement.

Salsa practically invented the modern gravel bike with its Warbird, and the Minnesota-based brand remains as relevant as ever. Its recently launched Flyway C is a lightweight and responsive gravel bike for gravel racing or all-day rides. It features generous tire clearance (up to 57mm), a UDH dropout (for easy replacement or upgrades), and revised geometry (long reach and short stem) for improved control on rough terrain.

Several Flyway configurations are available (I tested the Force AXS XPLR model), and I think the Apex Eagle AXS model sits right in the sweet spot for many riders. As the name suggests, Salsa outfits this bike with a combination of SRAM’s Apex AXS and Eagle X1 AXS 1x electronic drivetrains to provide a superwide gear range. In addition to the great components, Salsa also equips this model with a flared carbon bar and a carbon seatpost. It’s an all-around great package for anyone looking to up their gravel game this season.

Trek’s Checkpoint ALR 5 is versatile, well-rounded, and a great pick for riders new to gravel cycling. In his review, Chabanov says, “The value sweet spot: modern geometry and feature set borrowed from the [Checkpoint] SL, delivered in a durable alloy package with smart mounts and standards—at a starting price that leaves room in the budget for meaningful upgrades. Because there are no proprietary parts, upgrading and swapping things like the handlebar, stem, and seatpost is super easy.”

Overall, the Checkpoint ALR gets far more right than it gets wrong. Sure, you can nitpick the stock wheels and tires—or wish for the carbon model’s downtube storage and IsoSpeed—but those trade-offs help keep the price in check while preserving what matters. This bike has confident handling, generous tire room, real-world durability, and an upgrade-friendly platform. The result is a thoroughly well-thought-out aluminum gravel bike that feels ready for anything from weeknight dirt spins to loaded weekend overnighters, or even that gravel race that’s on your bucket list.

If you’re a gravel racer on a budget, or simply like going fast and don’t have the money for bikes like the Specialized S-Works Crux or Colnago G5-X, Canyon’s new Grail should be on your short list. As my colleague Matt Phillips described in his review of the revised platform, “And “fast” was the word that stuck with me as I rode the Grail across singletrack, dirt roads, and paved roads. It feels fast. It made me feel like I was fast.”

Wide tire clearance is one of the latest Grail’s upgrade highlights. At 57mm, the frame and fork can fit the widest gravel tires and even 29 x 2.25-inch mountain bike rubber for rocky terrain or singletrack (or if you want a super comfortable feel). The entry-tier Grail CF SL models use a heavier carbon frame than the Grail CFR and CF SLX versions, but only 140 grams more than the high-end CFR bike (about the weight of a standard butyl inner tube). All models feature a carbon cockpit, seatpost, and wheels.

The Grail CF 7 Speed is a great bang-for-the-buck gravel racer. Canyon equips it with SRAM’s excellent Rival XPLR AXS 1x13 electronic shifting gravel groupset. Although Canyon doesn’t ship this model with a power meter, you can easily upgrade to a Rival power crank for under $200.

You’re not buying this bike for its tire clearance, gear-hauling options, or aerodynamics; plenty of other gravel bikes do those things better than the G5-X. You buy this bike because it’s a Colnago.

On fast gravel roads, double track, and even technical singletrack, Colnago’s superb geometry, fit, and ride comfort won me over. The G5-X feels super composed and planted when descending and over choppy gravel road sections. The bike is precise and refined—pick your line and take it. On climbs and rolling terrain, the G5-X is comfortable and efficient, and responds immediately to bursts of power.

Overall, Colnago’s latest bike is a beautifully fast gravel racer with sublime handling. However, while the G5-X has more tire clearance (53mm) than the brand’s previous gravel offerings, it falls a few millimeters shy of the clearance found on some new gravel models. This will matter to some, but many riders will seek out the G5-X for the name on the downtube and Colnago’s cycling legacy.

Inspired by the Tour Divide—America’s longest mountain bike race—this bike carries more and handles a wider range of terrain than almost any other gravel bike. It’s loaded with mounts for racks, camping gear, bike accessories, and water bottles.

Although it’s intended for burly rides, the Cutthroat features a carbon frame and fork, which helps to reduce weight. And Salsa’s Class 5 Vibration Reduction System absorbs uneven terrain for a more comfortable ride. The Cutthroat C GRX model also includes a Shimano GRX 1x12 mechanical, wide-range drivetrain and a dropper seatpost.

With its steel frame, bar-end shifters, and triple-chainring crankset, the Masi Giramondo is a throwback to a bygone era of bicycle design and construction. While the bike’s aesthetic and features might not appeal to athletes chasing fast finishing times in 200-mile gravel races, it’s perfect for riders who want to hit the gravel, dirt, or paved roads loaded down with gear for touring adventures.

Unlike most bikes sold for touring or bikepacking, the Giramondo comes stock with a front and rear rack. This means you won’t have to add them to your bike-buying budget. To make it slightly easier to pedal your fully laden bike up hills, Masi equips this model with a triple crankset. While triples aren’t as trendy as 1x drivetrains, they offer an extremely wide gear range: Its lowest gear is close to many mountain bikes, and the highest gear rivals many gravel race bikes.

While State labels this model “All-Road,” it’s very much a modern gravel bike. Starting at $2,400 for a complete bike, or $1,400 for the frameset, the All-Road Carbon checks all of the boxes without totally draining your bank account. It accommodates up to 2.2-inch tires (complete builds ship with 50mm Vittoria T50s), is UDH-compatible, and takes a T47 bottom bracket. The All-Road Carbon also features internal storage in the frame’s downtube with a Fidlock magnetic latch.

The Carbon All-Road’s frame isn’t super aero-shaped, and it doesn’t use funky proprietary parts—and that’s a good thing. This bike is made for riders who prioritize durability and functionality over flashy graphics, pro teams, and marketing hype. The All-Road’s geometry falls on the “race-inspired” end of the spectrum, compared with the more upright feel of adventure-style gravel bikes. The bike carries speed on hardpack dirt and gravel and feels adequately stiff when sprinting and out of corners. The ride quality is a little harsher than premium gravel offerings, but a complete Carbon All-Road costs less than most big-name brands’ frames.

The all-new Specialized Crux has shed its cyclocross roots and turned into a modern gravel racer. In his review of the fifth-generation platform, Test Editor Dan Chabanov says, “It is built around the demands of professional gravel racers, and around the idea that going fast off-road now means balancing low weight, aero efficiency, tire clearance, and stability rather than just chasing the lightest possible frame.” The result is an excellent gravel bike that, while optimized for racers, anyone who loves going fast can enjoy.

Senior Test Editor Matt Phillips rode the Crux 5 for several days on the gravel roads in Durango, Colorado, and walked away very impressed by the updated bike. “The Crux 5 leans more toward stability and predictability,” he said. “It’s fast, yes. Very fast. But it’s also composed. It lets you settle in. It doesn’t feel like it’s trying to prove something every second.”

That balance is a big part of what makes the Crux great for non-racers. “A lot of us don’t need a gravel bike that only makes sense at 300 watts,” Phillips said. “We need a bike that feels sharp when you want to go hard, but isn’t a pain in the ass the rest of the time.”

Of the five models in the Crux 5 lineup, the Crux 5 Comp stands out for its performance-to-price ratio. It features a slightly heavier carbon frame than the high-end S-Works variants, but it has the same great geometry, tire clearance, and aerodynamics. Specialized equips the Comp model with SRAM’s excellent Rival AXS XPLR 1x brakes and drivetrain, and the bike rolls on 26mm-wide inner diameter alloy wheels wrapped in 45mm-wide Pathfinder tubeless tires.

The bike used by two-time gravel World Champion Marianne Vos (🐐), the Áspero-5 is what happens when Cervélo combines aerodynamic principles of the Paris-Roubaix-winning S5 with a gravel race bike. This bike is eye-wateringly fast on smoother gravel and dirt roads. The Áspero-5 is fast enough that many riders will want to use it on paved roads too.

Much of this speed advantage comes from Cervélo’s aerodynamic tuning of the frame, fork, and bar; the 42mm-wide Vittoria Corsa Pro Control TLR rubber enhances it. An excellent road tire for broken pavement in narrow sizes, the Pro Control really shines in the 700x42c size on dirt and gravel surfaces.

With so many types and sub-niches of gravel bikes, it can seem overwhelming to pick the right one. My first advice: start by honestly evaluating the terrain you ride, then consider how you like to ride it. From there, narrow your choices to the bikes that meet your budget, personal tastes, and other factors.

Racing-oriented bikes typically feature an aggressive fit and handling with fewer mounts for bags or extra water bottles. At the other end of the spectrum are bikes built for long-distance, multi-day adventures, equipped with all the mounts you could want for gear and accessories. In between, there’s a wide range of subtle variations that can make a big difference.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#11. The Best Tune-Up Workouts to Help You Absolutely Crush This Year’s Turkey Trot

These two coach-approved tune-up sessions build 5K speed and sharpen your finishing kick.

Many runners sign up for a Turkey Trot 5K with no goal other than to enjoy the day and the company of their fellow trotters. Other runners take this annual race more seriously. Very seriously.

Either way, full support! But we have exactly what you need to rip a blazing-fast time this season, thanks to Jeff Gaudette, founder and head coach of RunnersConnect.

The key to running your fastest 5K? Structure the right workouts ahead of race day that will help you build and sharpen your speed. Gaudette shares the tune-up workouts that check both these boxes, plus he shares tips for racing your best Turkey Trot to date.

First, you’ll want to include a session that prepares you for what your goal 5K pace will feel like so you can maintain it through the finish. Next, as you get closer to race morning, you’ll benefit from some faster intervals that help sharpen the speed you’ll need to reel in competitors over the final stretch.

Why it works: When November begins, you’re close enough to race day to get a pretty good sense of the fitness you’ll bring to the starting line. To gauge exactly where you stand, Gaudette recommends a dose of 5K-specific training with what he calls a “speed endurance” session. Aim to do this workout about two to three weeks before your Turkey Trot.

The number of 400-meter repeats you complete will depend on your current weekly training volume, Gaudette says. Higher-mileage runners should shoot for 12 reps, while lower-volume runners will want to aim closer to eight. And if you’re still out of breath when it’s time to start the next interval, don’t worry—that’s exactly the point.

“The rest is short enough so you are not going to be fully recovered before you begin every single interval,” Gaudette explains. “This trains your aerobic system and will give you a pretty good gauge of whether you’ll be able to maintain this pace for a 5K race.”

Why it works: The second workout adds some running at speeds faster than your 5K goal pace. But rather than “speed endurance,” the goal of this effort is “speed sharpening,” which is what helps you prime a strong finishing kick. Aim to do this workout either just before or during the week of your Turkey Trot.

Unlike the first workout, you don’t want to skimp on rest between intervals. Make sure that you allow yourself a full recovery, says Gaudette. “The purpose of the long rest is so we’re not producing any type of soreness or fatigue. This workout is more about getting a sense of what these paces feel like.” For example, the 400-meter repeats help get your legs turning over faster and make your goal 5K pace feel a bit more comfortable by comparison.

Keep in mind that these workouts get more challenging as you progress through them. “Runners will usually find that the first third of the workout feels pretty easy. The middle third is hard but comfortable, and then the last third reaches that RPE of 8 or even 9,” Gaudette says.

A seasoned trotter, Gaudette toed the starting line of some of the largest and most famous Thanksgiving races, including the Manchester Road Race and the O’side Turkey Trot. The most common mistake he sees? Runners sprinting right out of the gate.

“Really focus on your pacing,” he says. “Going out too fast is the mistake most runners make, especially in turkey trots, because these races tend to draw less experienced runners. These runners don’t yet have that sense of pacing, and they don’t realize how hard the 5K can get in the second half.”

So, if you’re new to the 5K, don’t hammer with everything you’ve got right off the starting line. And if you’re an experienced runner, don’t get rattled if you find yourself farther back in the field during the first mile.

“A runner who typically finds themself in the top half of most of their races might end up in the back third initially since the entire field has gone out so fast,” Gaudette explains. “Just stay focused on your own internal pacing and make sure that first mile is within range: either at your 5K pace or maybe even a little bit slower.”

Why? Because that controlled start sets you up for a huge advantage in a 5K. Conserving your energy over the first mile or so allows you to race hard in the second half. “It’s a double-whammy,” says Gaudette. “You get the benefit of feeling strong, plus the extra motivation that comes from catching a ton of runners through the finish.”

Morgan is a gear editor who has been with Runner’s World since 2017. She started as an intern ghostwriting The Warmup, a bygone version of the daily RW newsletter. Now, she tests and reviews anything you might find on runners’ feet-from crew socks and compression boots to carbon-plated super shoes.

A lifelong runner and shoe geek, Morgan has been chasing the perfect pair of kicks since she joined her grade school cross-country team. Since then, she ran as a Division I walk-on for the cross-country and track & field teams at the University of Delaware, where she studied English and Biology. She has one full marathon under her belt, and has raced more halfs and 5Ks than she can count.

#12. Is Cycling Good Cardio? Here's How It Compares to Running and Swimming

Learn how cycling compares to other cardio activities like walking, running, and swimming.

Riding a bike is as good a workout as it is a ton of fun. Hop on a bike—any kind—and your heart rate will pick up, your breathing rate will increase, and you’ll break a sweat. Whether you choose to fly over asphalt on a road bike, cruise back roads on a gravel setup, or push pedals in an indoor studio, you’re doing your mind and body big favors when you hop in the saddle.

One of the biggest payoffs? Cardio benefits. Read on for how cycling boosts your cardio fitness and how it stacks up to other forms of cardiovascular exercise, like running and using an elliptical.

Cardio exercise is any exercise that increases your heart rate and respiration (breathing rate). Cardio exercise can be aerobic or anaerobic. Broadly, what makes cardio aerobic or anaerobic is the intensity level of the exercise (and physiologically, the source of energy for that exercise).

Aerobic exercise, defined by the American College of Sports Medicine, is a rhythmic activity that uses large muscle groups and can be maintained continuously. This is also called steady-state exercise, and it can include running, walking, cycling, rowing, using the elliptical or stair-stepper, swimming, and hiking.

Anaerobic cardio exercise is high-intensity, and true anaerobic activity can only be performed for short periods of time; sprinting is a good example of anaerobic cardio exercise. Activities like jumping rope and mountain biking—and any of the aforementioned activities performed in high-intensity spurts—can also fit into this cardio category.

In any case, “cardio exercise often consists of extended periods of time with an elevated heart rate and an increase in oxygen demand,” says Alexander Rothstein, ACSM-certified exercise physiologist, strength and conditioning coach, and coordinator for the exercise science program at New York Institute of Technology.

“Performing cardio exercise will stress the cardiovascular system, which will signal the need for adaptation and cause improvements in the body’s ability to supply and utilize oxygen,” he explains.

The goal of cardio exercise is to increase the efficiency of your heart, lungs, and circulatory system, thereby improving your overall fitness and endurance.

“Cardiorespiratory fitness reflects the ability of the cardiovascular and respiratory systems to supply oxygen-rich blood to skeletal muscles during sustained physical activity,” says Joe Scarrella, triathlon coach and certified personal trainer at Life Time Chanhassen in Minnesota.

This type of fitness “is vitally important to health and wellness, especially to the ability of engaging in normal activities of daily living without excessive fatigue,” he says. “Because of its heart-strengthening and overall health benefits, cardio training should always be near the top of priorities when allocating time to a fitness program.”

Yes, cycling is cardio exercise—an excellent form of it, in fact. Cycling requires continuous movement that increases your heart rate. When you pedal, your heart works harder to pump blood to your muscles. This steady effort challenges your cardiovascular system, helping it become more efficient over time.

A cycling habit brings about a lot of benefits, including:

While cycling is a fantastic form of cardio, it’s not your only option. Here’s a look at how it measures up to other popular forms of cardio exercise.

Cycling burns more calories per hour than walking, according to the Compendium of Physical Activity. Cycling at a leisurely pace (less than 10 mph) can burn about 330 calories per hour for a 180-pound person. Walking at a leisurely pace (2.5 mph) burns about 246 calories per hour for a person of the same weight.

Both cycling and walking are low-impact exercises, making them ideal for those with joint pain or arthritis. Cycling allows more room for increasing speed or resistance without changing joint impact, which offers a more intense cardio workout for individuals with joint concerns.

On the flip side, walking is a weight-bearing form of exercise, while cycling is not, so walking could be the better choice for individuals with bone density concerns.

Walking is more accessible because it requires no equipment beyond a good pair of shoes. Cycling, on the other hand, requires much more gear: a bike and helmet, at minimum, plus safe space to ride outdoors. An indoor stationary bike or bike trainer is required for cycling inside, and while there are budget options, it’s still an investment.

If you're looking for a simple, accessible form of low-intensity cardio, walking might be the best option. However, for a more intense workout that’s still easy on the joints, cycling is the way to go.

Running tends to burn more calories than cycling, because it’s more difficult for many individuals to achieve the increase in heart rate that they may get from running, Rothstein says. It may take longer to burn as many calories as one would while running.

According to data from the Compendium of Physical Activity, cycling at a “self-selected moderate pace” burns about 573 calories in one hour for a 180-pound person. That same person may burn about 615 calories “jogging at a self-selected pace,” according to the Compendium.

Running is a high-impact exercise, which can place stress on your joints, especially your knees and ankles. Cycling, in contrast, is low-impact, making it a better option for people with joint issues or those recovering from injuries.

Both running and cycling primarily work your lower body, including your quadriceps, hamstrings, glutes, and calves. During cycling, your core and back muscles may be recruited more to maintain posture on the bike, depending on the style of your bike. When running, your core, back, and arms all work to maintain posture and stability.

If joint health is a concern or you prefer a lower-impact workout, cycling is the better choice. Running is a viable option for people who can handle the joint impact and/or don’t have the means to invest in a bike or stationary bike.

Swimming and cycling burn similar amounts of calories, depending on intensity. According to the Compendium of Physical Activity, swimming freestyle at a vigorous pace for one hour burns about 800 calories for a 180-pound person. The same person would burn about 818 calories cycling at 14 to 16 mph, which may be a moderate or vigorous effort depending on your fitness level.

Swimming has virtually no impact on joints because the water supports your body, making it an ideal option for those with joint pain, injuries, or mobility issues.

Cycling is also low-impact but not quite as easy on the body as swimming. Depending on the type of bike, some individuals may struggle with mobility when cycling. (For example, on a road bike with drop bars, it can strain the neck and back to reach them. In such a case, a bike with an upright frame might be a better choice.)

Swimming is a full-body workout, engaging both your upper and lower body, as well as your core. You’ll recruit more muscles in the arms and shoulders while swimming, compared to cycling, which primarily targets the lower body.

If you want a no-impact, full-body workout, swimming might be your best option. Keep in mind that sticking to a swimming plan requires having access to a lap pool, which isn’t feasible for everyone. Even though a bike can be a big investment, it may be the more accessible option in this case.

Cycling burns more calories than elliptical training at the same effort level. For a 180-pound person, cycling at a moderate pace (12 to 14 mph) burns around 654 calories in 60 minutes, while a moderate 60-minute session on the elliptical burns about 409 calories.

Both are low-impact exercises, making them suitable for people with joint concerns. The elliptical may provide an advantage for people who struggle with mobility, because you remain in an upright position and don’t have to significantly flex the spine like on the bike.

Elliptical machines engage both the upper and lower body, while cycling primarily focuses on your lower body, though the upper body and core are still engaged to some extent while riding a bike.

If you prefer a workout that engages your whole body, the elliptical may be the better choice. However, if you like the idea of getting outside and/or exercising with a community, cycling offers a more dynamic experience in that sense.

Overall, “all forms of cardio are similar in their cardiovascular health and weight loss benefits,” says Rothstein. “The increased oxygen demand and overall cardiovascular stress will result in improved health and well-being. The ability to burn calories is also similar even if the rate might be different between types of cardio.”

Adaptations in stamina are where the most significant differences lie, says Rothstein. “We adapt based on the specific training stimulus, so in cyclists, stamina improvements will mostly be shown in cycling performance. For example, if you train cycling, you will not improve your running unless you also train as a runner. This is because even though both have cardiovascular adaptation benefits, the muscular adaptations will be specific to the type of training.”

In other words: Train what you want to be good at doing.
