#61. 13 Yoga Poses That Strengthen Your Upper Back

You hear a lot about yoga to stretch your back. But what about strengthening your back? In particular, yoga to strengthen the upper back, which tends to be overlooked compared to the lower back. Yoga teacher and certified trainer Amber Sayer explores the research and the poses that help you support your upper back muscles.

When you think about practicing yoga for your back, you probably think of seeking release from kinks near your neck and shoulders or finding relief from stiffness in your lower back. And there is no shortage of poses that support each of those. Yet there’s an equally essential approach that is talked about far less, and that’s practicing yoga to strengthen the upper back muscles.

Holding an isometric contraction in the upper back, as one does in many yoga poses when the muscles are engaged in a static position, is a fantastic way to not only to build strength but also endurance in ways that promote healthy posture. These muscles include the upper, middle, and lower trapezius (positioned from the neck to the shoulder blades) as well as the rhomboids (found beneath the trapezoids and between the shoulder blade and spine), and the erector spinae (running along the spine).

And there’s no shortage of research that suggests yoga can strengthen the upper back. A recent study found that yoga poses resulted in a more diverse array of concurrent muscle activation in the upper back and shoulders compared to traditional gym exercises. In one instance, Downward-Facing Dog and the version of Bridge with the hands interlaced behind the back were shown to be significantly effective at activating the muscles of the upper back muscles.

Another study found that long-term, consistent yoga practice correlated with improved posture and curvature of the spine, including fewer instances of thoracic kyphosis (rounding of the upper back) and lumbar lordosis (swayback). Participants had been practicing yoga an average of three times a week for anywhere from 1 to 15 years. The results were supported by another study that found a 6-month yoga program could significantly improve upper back strength.

Ultimately, the improvements found from enhancing upper back strength resulted in more ease and less struggle as participants navigated everyday life.

Following are the yoga poses that target and strengthen the overlooked muscles of the upper back. Most of them do so by holding your body in isometric contraction against gravity. And the best news? All you need is your body and your yoga mat; no fancy gym equipment or weights required.

One of the most beginner-friendly yoga poses for upper back strength is Sphinx Pose (Salamba Bhujangasana). It’s a modest backbend that, thanks to your forearms resting on the mat and propping up your chest, is typically quite passive. But press through your forearms and actively lift your chest and you’ll activate the erector spinae muscles. Then draw your shoulder blades together and away from your ears to engage your posterior deltoids (back of the shoulders), rhomboids, and trapezius. Consider it a backbend with training wheels.

Think of this as a progression from Sphinx Pose. Start by resting your palms on the mat beneath your shoulders as you engage your upper back muscles and lift your chest off the mat in Cobra Pose (Bhujangasana). That ensures you create the shape by enlisting the erector spinae muscles. To maximize muscle activation, lift your chest farther away from the mat or, even better, float your hands off the mat.

This dynamic movement between the two shapes asks you to flex and extend the spine, improving mobility over time. Rather than just go through the motions, take your time and make certain you exaggerate the shape of the upper back as you transition between Cat and Cow. Inhale as you arch your back and lower your belly toward the mat, exhale as you round your back.

It’s easy to focus on the challenge passed along to the arms and shoulders in Downward-Facing Dog (Adho Mukha Svanasana), but the upper back plays a strong role in holding your body stable. Focus on drawing your shoulders away from your ears and pressing your hips toward the ceiling behind you to maximize engagement of the lower trapezius.

Dolphin Pose has a similar shape and effect as Downward-Facing Dog but with your forearms on the mat. This lessens the strain on the wrists and transfers more of the work to the shoulders and upper back. Be certain to press your forearms down as you lift your shoulders up and away from the mat.

This cousin of the more common Plank Pose is typically overlooked. And that’s a shame because Reverse or Upward Plank (Purvottanasana) challenges you to engage your upper body muscles as you support a significant portion of your body weight against gravity. It strengthens all the muscles of the upper back as well as the triceps and shoulders (particularly the rear deltoids and rotator cuff muscles).

As with Plank, it’s important to squeeze your glutes to enlist these strong muscles in supporting the body in safe alignment.

Practicing Plank on your forearms is commonly considered a core-strengthening exercise—and it is. But it also strengthens the upper back muscles as you stabilize your shoulder blades along the back of your rib cage while keeping your body in alignment. Focus on not allowing your shoulders to roll forward. A strap tied around your upper arms can help keep the upper arms from turning outward.

This is one of those fantastic full-body yoga poses that challenges and strengthens most major muscle groups. Warrior 3 (Virabhadrasana III) can also be a powerful activator of the upper back and shoulder muscles when you reach your arms straight ahead and hold them in alignment against gravity.

As your shoulders and upper back muscles start to fatigue, imagine helium balloons attached to each arm, helping them remain aloft and parallel to the floor.

This balancing pose is typically appreciated for its emphasis on strengthening the lower body, although it also demands significant upper body integration. Try engaging the muscles between your shoulder blades to actively roll your top shoulder slightly back (but without letting your arm fall behind you) in Half Moon Pose (Ardha Chandrasana). Imagine pinching and holding a pencil between your shoulder blades to fully engage your upper back muscles. You want your shoulders stacked and expansion across your chest. Feel the difference?

Rather than press your palms into the mat to lift and hold your upper body aloft in Locust Pose (Salabhasana), let your upper back do the work. You can float your hands off the mat, reach them alongside your legs, interlace your fingers behind your back and reach your knuckles toward the wall behind you, or reach your arms forward like Superman to engage your triceps, posterior deltoids, levator scapulae, rhomboids, rotator cuff muscles, traps, and various spinal extensors.

Research that explored muscular activity in the upper back during various yoga poses found that Locust Pose with the arms extended overhead most efficiently targets the trapezius (upper back muscles).

Remember to squeeze your glutes to reduce the workload on your lower back muscles.

It’s not the lifting of your hips that activates your upper body in Bridge Pose (Setu Bandha Sarvangasana). There’s a hidden benefit in interlacing your fingers behind your back, rolling your upper arms slightly underneath you, drawing the shoulder blades away from your ears, and actively pressing your upper arms, forearms, and the pinky sides of your fingers into the mat. That’s what activates the muscles you’re intending to target.

This shape might look simple. After all, you’re just sitting. But it can be surprisingly difficult to sit upright with flawless posture in Staff Pose (Dandasana). Pressing your hands into the mat further engages the spinal stabilizers and postural muscles.

You can take it one step further and maximize the isometric contractions of your shoulders and upper back by practicing the shape with your back against a wall. Actively press your shoulders and backs of your arms into the support behind you. You can also bend your elbows 90 degrees and bring your arms into a cactus position so your upper arms are straight out to the sides, fingers pointing toward the ceiling, palms facing forward. If your lower back arches, draw it closer toward the wall.

An intense backbend, Bow Pose (Dhanurasana) should only be practiced after warming up your body with increasingly intense backbends, including some of the earlier ones in this list as well as Upward-Facing Dog (Urdhva Mukha Svanasana), Dancer (Natarajasana), or Camel (Ustrasana). Also, avoid this pose if you experience back pain or have other contraindications for exaggerated backbending.

As you lift your upper body off the mat, squeeze the glutes and let these powerful muscles do most of the work rather than forcing your smaller, weaker back muscles to overcompensate. Also, come into the pose slowly, relying on intention rather than momentum. Once you’re in the shape, actively draw your upper arms slightly back to open across your chest, which engages the back muscles (namely, the trapezius and rhomboids). You can also work your way up to Bow Pose by practicing one side at a time.

#62. Stop Cramming Bikes in Your Car. These 10 Editor-Tested Hitch Racks Make Hauling Easier and More Secure

Our editors hauled bikes for thousands of miles to find the easiest, sturdiest hitch racks.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Cramming your bike into your car or SUV gets old quickly. Removing wheels and getting mud or grease all over your interior is no fun, and transporting your bike inside your car also leaves less room for passengers, luggage, or gear. Hitch-mount racks are the easiest, most secure way to carry your bike to your riding destination without mess or hassle. They’re ideal for heading to your local mountain bike trails, taking a road trip with friends, or going for weekend rides with your kids.

Hitch racks mount to the receiver on your vehicle’s bumper, making hitch racks easier to load than roof racks—hoisting a heavy bike onto an SUV’s roof after a long ride is never fun. Plus, you don’t need to remove your front wheel. Unlike roof racks, you can also drive into parking garages and drive-thrus with bikes on a hitch rack. And importantly, in an era of sky-high fuel prices, hitch racks typically impact your gas mileage less than roof-mounted options.

While hitch racks usually cost more than simple, low-cost trunk-mount racks, they can last for many years with proper care and maintenance. Hitch-mount carriers can also carry heavier bikes, like electric bikes or full suspension rigs, than trunk racks and are more stable at highway speeds.

Our editors and test team evaluated dozens of hitch racks to see which ones perform best. Our staff has used some of these racks on their own vehicles for years, safely transporting bikes over tens of thousands of miles. Our picks for the best hitch-mounted bike racks vary in features like position, trunk access functionality, bike capacity, and price—but all are dependable options for your next cycling trip.

Based on price, weight capacity, and ease of use, Thule’s Outpace ranks as our current Best Overall pick. The Outpace is lighter and more compact than most hitch racks, which makes it easy to install and remove. At only 28 pounds, it’s light enough to carry across the garage and slide into the receiver tube. Setup takes less than a minute, so you can mount it on the car when you need to haul your bikes (rather than it semi-permanently living on your bumper).

The rack can accommodate a wider range of bike wheel sizes, making it great for families. The rack adapts easily to any size bicycle in either position. The tradeoff for this versatility is that it takes a bit longer to load than bulkier racks with cinch-style clamps. But for something that can carry all of our bikes, and is so quick to install or remove that it never has to be a permanent fixture, that’s a small price to pay.

Our tester noted the Outpace’s receiver arm is on the short side. It fit snugly against the bumper with about two inches to spare, but on another vehicle, it wouldn’t fit without a hitch extender.

The Trail Rider is a great, lower-cost alternative to premium racks. It holds two bikes in fixed wheel mounts, secured with a single ratcheting arm that clamps down over the frame. The upright beam (which holds the frame holders) folds back and out of the way for trunk access; it’s also handy for loading up two bikes. We could fold it down, set a bike on the rack closest to the car without lifting it up and over the arm, then lift the arm back into place and position the second bike.

The trade-off for the Trail Rider’s low price isn’t stability or strength, but adjustability: The bikes are positioned in a fixed location. You have limited ability to separate them if two bikes don’t fit well together. That said, you can stagger the wheel cradles so the bars and saddles don’t interfere.

The Swagman XTC2 is one of the most affordable 2-bike racks we recommend. This no-frills rack is a solid choice for budget-conscious riders. It fits both 1¼-inch and 2-inch receiver tubes, and it accommodates wheel sizes from 20 to 29 inches. However, with a total weight capacity of 70 pounds (35 pounds per bike), it’s not suitable for e-bikes.

As expected at this price, the rack has some trade-offs. The wheel hoops are adjustable, but not as smoothly or precisely as on more premium racks. The rack doesn’t tilt away from the vehicle when loaded, limiting access to tailgates or liftgates. Lastly, you must remove the center support bar to load a bike on the inside tray.

Yet, the XTC2 is lightweight, durable, and very reasonably priced. If you’re willing to trade a bit of convenience for significant savings, the Swagman XTC2 is a reliable and practical option.

The Piston Pro X is our runner-up for Best Overall hitch rack; its construction, features, and style make it a standout pick in the category. Aside from the high price, the Piston Pro X is almost the perfect hitch rack for most users.

With the Piston Pro X, Küat elevated the rack from something purely utilitarian to a desirable piece of gear that’s easier to use than other racks. The rack includes smart features (such as integrated brake and turn-signal lights) and can carry more wheel sizes (and more weight) than almost any other rack on the market.

The top-end Pro X model costs more than almost any other hitch-mount rack, but it has proven extremely durable and maintains its good looks. It's also available in 3- and 4-bike models. Küat also offers a slightly cheaper Piston Pro variant, which ditches the Kashima coating on the pistons and the integrated brake lights and turn signals.

If you like the Küat racks but $1,600 is out of your price range, the brand offers several other hitch-style racks that could meet your needs. One great option is the Sherpa 2.0 model.

While the Sherpa doesn’t have the features or carrying capacity of Küat’s more expensive racks, it has two big upsides—color options and low weight. The Sherpa weighs only 32 pounds (claimed) in the 2-inch hitch configuration (1.25-in. also available). Küat offers the Sherpa in three colors: black metallic (with a silver accent), grey metallic (with orange), and pearl white (with silver).

The Sherpa carries two bicycles weighing up to 40 pounds per tray. So it’s ideal for non-electric road, gravel, and mountain bikes. It has an integrated cable lock to secure your bikes during rest stops or meal breaks, and it features a foot-operated lever to lower the rack into position for loading bikes.

It’s often difficult to carry e-bikes that are equipped with racks and fenders on traditional hitch racks. That’s because many hitch racks secure the bike with extending arms that clamp one or both wheels. However, Thule’s EasyFold XT model holds your bike by its frame.

Another feature that makes the EasyFold ideal for e-bike owners is the included ramp. This makes loading or removing your bikes much easier; no more wrestling with heavy bikes or front wheels or handlebars flopping as you load them onto the rack. And the ramp attaches to the rack when you’re finished.

Thanks to the rack’s 45-pound weight, it’s easy to remove it from your vehicle when you’re not using it. It folds down and features casters (which make moving it around your garage easier). The EasyFold XT’s biggest drawback is that Thule only rates it to 65 pounds per bike. While that will accommodate many e-bikes, some fat tire models may weigh too much.

When Thule debuted the T2 over a decade ago, it raised the bar for what cyclists expect from a hitch-mounted bike rack. Over the years, Thule updated the rack to accommodate wider tires and different wheel sizes. It also improved the T2’s look and made it easier to operate. One of the best recent upgrades is a wide-trigger handle that allows you to raise and lower the rack (and dip it out of the way for access to rear hatches) with one hand.

Integrated cable locks help keep your bikes secure for quick stops, and each tray can hold a bicycle up to 60 pounds and tires up to 5 inches wide. This makes the T2 a good option for all but the heaviest e-bikes. The T2 Pro’s arms have wide, comfortable grips that slide easily to secure the front wheel. Instead of using a bolt, the rack secures to your hitch receiver with an expansion wedge that tightens with a locking knob. The system makes installing and removing the T2 easier (though it weighs 52 pounds), but it’s not foolproof.

Yakima’s StageTwo two-bike rack goes head-to-head with premium offerings from Küat and Thule at a lower price. In about 2,500 miles of on-car testing, the StageTwo impressed us with its ease of use and flex-free performance. This rack is only rated up to 35 pounds per tray, so it’s not made for transporting e-bikes. However, it’s one of only two racks on this list that accommodates wheels as small as 16 inches.

The StageTwo’s trays are offset, which means less chance of contact when carrying two similarly sized bikes (however, bikes sit more widely apart, so watch those tight parking spaces). The rack includes two SKS locking cables (they don’t auto-retract, so tuck them back in when not in use). The StageTwo also includes an integrated lock loop for extra security when parked or locking your rack off the vehicle.

The rack is offered in 1.25- and 2-inch sizes. The 2-inch variant can accommodate four bikes with an add-on kit. Also, check Yakima’s fit guide before buying—One of our testers experienced a hardware fitment issue.

If you travel to mountain resort towns (or have been around trailheads or bike parks lately), you’ve probably seen behemoth racks like these on the back of vans and trucks. Since modern mountain bikes are bulky, racks like Thule’s ReVert make sense if you’re hauling a full load with a single vehicle.

The ReVert holds six bikes, loads quickly, and sticks out no farther than a standard 2-bike horizontal rack. Its carrying capacity makes it ideal for large families, race teams, or ride groups.

At over 87 pounds, the ReVert is undeniably heavy. However, a few smart features make the rack manageable. Dual hydraulic dampers assist with lowering the rack when it’s fully loaded, so you don’t have to wrestle with it. Once in the lowered position, even shorter riders and kids can lift their bikes high enough to slot them into the baskets. Individual bikes are spaced 11 inches apart, giving you plenty of room to carry any combination—flat bar, drop bar, even cruisers.

1UP USA has built a cult-like following with its industrial-looking racks that take a simplistic approach to securing your bike. This model features two ratcheting arms that clamp down on your wheels—no hooks or straps necessary.

The Equip-D’s pivot mechanism is smooth and reliable even after years of abuse (although an occasional shot of WD-40 White Lithium Grease Spray goes a long way in keeping the release mechanism running smoothly). A T-handle release positioned at the end of the hitch bar means you don’t need to reach through the rack to fold it up. Tiered trays position bikes closer together, and the rack rides out of the way of most exhaust pipes. 1Up also offers the Equip in a single-bike version for a sleeker look.

Hitch racks are bicycle carriers that attach to your vehicle’s hitch receiver. Popular models carry one to four bikes, but some hanging-style hitch racks can haul up to six bikes.

A hitch is a standard feature on most trucks and many SUVs. However, if you have a car or wagon, a hitch can often be added. If your vehicle doesn’t already have a receiver, it’s easy to have one installed. (U-Haul is a reliable and affordable option for installation.)Receivers come in two sizes: 1¼-inch and 2-inch (measured across the inside of the square opening). Most trucks and SUVs use a 2-inch receiver. Many racks are available in both sizes, but heavier-duty racks—and racks that carry three or more bikes—often require the larger 2-inch receiver for added strength and stability. Racks rated to carry heavyweight e-bikes also typically require a 2-inch receiver.

If the rack will live on your vehicle year-round or see frequent use, invest in the most durable model your budget allows. While all racks listed here secure bikes effectively, higher-priced options tend to have sturdier moving parts—ratchets, straps, buckles, and locks—that stand up better to long-term use.

Not all hitch racks are rated for the extra weight of e-bikes. Those that aren’t suited for heavier bikes are clearly noted in our reviews.

Some racks are quite heavy, which contributes to their strength but can be inconvenient if you plan to remove and reinstall the rack frequently.

For most vehicles—aside from sedans—accessing the trunk or tailgate is restricted when the rack is in use or folded up. Many of our top picks offer tilt-down designs that allow you to open the back of your vehicle even with bikes loaded. For full access, swing-away adapters like the Küat Pivot v2 Swing-Away allow the entire rack to pivot 90 degrees, completely clearing the rear of your car or truck.

Need more clearance? Sometimes a simple hitch extender can do the trick. For added stability and peace of mind, we also recommend using an anti-rattle clamp with any rack you choose.

Pros: Hitch racks strike the perfect balance between the ease of access of a trunk rack and the security of a quality roof rack. They slot into your car’s hitch receiver, relying on no flimsy straps or sketchy hooks. They’re also positioned behind your car, which is great for gas mileage and roof-collision prevention (low standing height). Better yet, many are modular, allowing you to add extra trays, locks, and even bottle openers for more personalized functionality.

Cons: These racks are the most consistently expensive out there—quality materials and a confidence-inspiring construction unquestionably affect their price. Furthermore, they can be a pain to remove, as most options weigh well over 40 pounds and need tools to detach. Furthermore, with bikes on the rack, they add significant length to your vehicle, which could prove tricky if you need to parallel park. And most critically, not every car has a hitch, which means you’ll either need to install one yourself or forego this style entirely.

Our editors drove hundreds (and in some cases, thousands) of miles with their bikes on these racks. We hauled road bikes, mountain bikes, e-bikes, and city bikes. We carried bikes with disc brakes, big wheels, and fat tires. Our test team used these racks for months, in various environments and conditions. We tested them in the salty winters of Pennsylvania, the high mountains of Colorado, and the gritty Arizona desert.

These racks in this story stand out for their ease of installation and use, lack of play in key areas, manageable weight, and bike capacity. We also looked for sharp prices and deals.

Whether you’re a roadie on the way to your next fondo, a mountain biker heading to the trailhead, or loading up the family for a weekend adventure, our rack picks will cover whatever needs you and your riding crew may have.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

Though GLP-1 agonists can be beneficial for weight loss, it’s important to keep in mind that there is limited research on the long-term effects of these medications.

Additionally, research from 2022 suggests that weight regain is likely once you stop taking GLP-1 agonists.

Therefore, it’s best to pair GLP-1 agonists with modifications to your diet and lifestyle. A healthcare professional, such as a doctor or registered dietitian, can also provide ongoing guidance and support to promote long-term weight loss.

GLP-1 agonists are currently approved for three conditions: type 2 diabetes, obesity, and heart disease.

Keep in mind that these medications should be used alongside other lifestyle modifications, including changes to your diet and regular physical activity.

A doctor or other trusted healthcare professional can help determine whether a GLP-1 agonist may be beneficial for you, depending on your health concerns and goals.

Though GLP-1 agonists may support weight loss and help manage blood sugar levels, it’s important to be aware of the possible side effects, such as vomiting, stomach pain, fatigue, constipation or diarrhea, mood changes, and more.

Less common but more severe side effects include:

Because of the risk of side effects, it’s important to check in regularly with a healthcare professional. Additionally, it’s important to discuss any concerns you have about potential side effects with your doctor or other healthcare professional to make sure the medication is right for you.

When you lose a lot of weight quickly, your body loses fat, but it also loses lean mass, including muscle and bone density. This is problematic because muscle is the “engine” of your metabolism, helping you burn energy even when you are resting.

Research shows that people taking GLP-1 medications can lose a significant amount of muscle alongside fat. For example, in studies, about 15% to 40% of the total weight lost was lean mass. Exercise, such as strength training, can help preserve and build muscle while the medication helps you lose fat.

Exercise is also vital for bone health. Rapid weight loss is often linked to a reduction in bone mineral density, which can make bones weaker and more prone to fractures later in life.

A 2024 analysis of a randomized clinical trial found that people using the GLP-1 liraglutide without exercising lost weight but had decreased bone density in the hips and spine. People who combined liraglutide with regular exercise experienced the best weight loss and preserved their bone mineral density.

Exercise also has a lot of other benefits that GLP-1 medications can’t provide, like:

When used along with a balanced diet and exercise, Mounjaro can be an effective off-label treatment for weight loss and long-term weight management. How quickly the drug starts to work and the amount of weight loss can vary between people.

To learn more about what to expect when using Mounjaro for weight loss, talk with your doctor. They can tell you how soon you may see results and help determine what a safe weight-loss goal is for you based on your specific health factors.

#66. Is it too late to start strength training at 70? (No. Here’s what happens when you do.)

People in their 70s, 80s, and 90s get meaningfully stronger when they start strength training, and beginners tend to see the biggest response to training.

You also need far less than you’d guess: 30 to 60 minutes of lifting spread across a week is a great starting point.

Here’s the science, three ways to begin, and a client who started at 57 and is still going at 77.

A reader wrote me this week. Her whole email was one sentence:

That hits deep. That fear of: have I missed my window?

I want to share with you what I shared with her, because the science behind this is actually super cool and empowering.

People in their 70s, 80s, and 90s still get stronger when they start lifting. And it meaningfully improves how they move through their lives.

And if you’re someone who hasn’t trained before, or hasn’t trained in a while, I have even better news.

As a beginner, your body is even more sensitive to training. Translation: you get even more reward for your effort!

In the first few weeks, most people feel stronger before they look any different.

That’s because a lot of early strength is actually your muscles and brain learning to coordinate. The movement gets smoother. Standing up from a chair feels a little easier. Etc.

Over a few months, muscle starts to build.

Your bones respond to the load too (strength training is one of the best-supported ways to support bone health as we age.)

You’ll start to feel some muscle in your arms that you didn’t notice there before, like this reader who’s been doing workouts 3x/week and kicking butt with it:

Is every body different? Yes. Does it also depend on sleep, nutrition, and what else life is throwing at you? Also yes.

But the direction is the same for everyone. No matter your age, you can make a meaningful impact in your overall health, fitness, and quality of life!

1) Don’t start with workouts. Start with practice.

Take a few minutes each day to learn and practice a couple of strength moves.

You’re not training yet. You’re getting acquainted.

Try some push-ups off of the wall or the countertop. ​ Sit down in a chair, slow and controlled, and practice keeping your weight evenly spread across your feet (that’s a squat right there!)

Grab a gallon jug, some light dumbbells or canned goods or whatever you have on hand, and practice a one-arm row. See if you can feel it in your upper back as you pull the weight up.

Work within whatever your ability level is, what feels safe and approachable to start.

You’re collecting information about what your body is ready for, and learning exercises like you’re learning a new skill.

30-60 minutes of strength training in TOTAL across the week goes a surprisingly long way.

You can break that up however works best for you. A short 5-10min session most days of the week, inserting some “movement snacks” throughout the day, or a couple of longer sessions 2x/week, etc.

It doesn’t require hours of your day to make serious progress.

3) It’s easier to level up than to cut down

Because your body is more sensitive to strength training, you’ll likely feel more sore in the beginning.

So in general, I recommend you err on the side of less is more.

If you do a few short sessions during the week, and wake up the next day feeling great with little to no soreness, great! You can add a bit more the next week.

Mentally, I’ve also just found it’s way easier to be “leveling up” than having to cut back, which really helps with building that early momentum.

Becky, a Nerd Fitness coaching client, is someone I immediately thought of when I read that initial email. She’s 77, and didn’t start going to the gym until she was 57. Here’s what she had to say:

I couldn’t have said it any better myself, Becky. 😊

No matter your age or where you’re starting from…YOU GOT THIS! 💪

Whenever you’re ready, here are more ways we can help

1) Here’s an article with a bunch of different bodyweight exercises and progressions you can do at home.

2) Our coaches build programs specific to you and your needs. Here’s the exact system we use.

Nerd Fitness cuts through the fitness B.S. to help people get stronger, healthier, and more confident – all with a fun, no-nonsense approach.

Humans featured are exceptional examples and do not guarantee individual success. Your experience and results may vary.

#68. The 5 Best Outdoor Saunas for Getting Your Sweat On in 2025

Experts explain how hot and cold wellness therapies could improve health. These outdoor saunas help you get these potential benefits at home.

Written by Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC × The Expert Panel is a network of specialized health and fitness professionals who help ensure we present the most accurate information to our readers. This includes physicians, certified trainers, elite-level coaches, and more. Learn more about our experts. expert-verified Stephen Sheehan, CPT Last updated on Mar 4, 2025

Sauna bathing is an age-old Nordic tradition that can have huge benefits for your overall wellness.

There are a variety of sauna styles available, from the traditional barrels to more modern cube designs with electric heaters, infrared heaters, or wood-burning stoves. Some newer models have high-tech features like surround-sound speakers, added LED light therapy, and charging docks for your electronics. However, all you need to reap the potential benefits of your sauna experience is a high-quality product you’ll actually use.

We found six of the best outdoor saunas and included a comprehensive guide for picking the right sauna for you. We also tapped Saloni Sharma, M.D., Medhat Mikhael, M.D., and Earric Lee, a postdoctoral researcher studying exercise science and Sport and Health Sciences faculty member at the University of Jyväskylä, Finland (a.k.a., sauna central), to help us understand how sauna use can benefit athletes during training.

This content is meant to be informative, but should not be taken as medical advice. It is not intended for use as diagnosis, prevention, or treatment of health problems. Always speak with your doctor before starting any new supplement or exercise regimen.

If you’re seeking a more technology-forward sauna experience, Sun Home’s Luminar outdoor infrared sauna is an excellent model to invest in. This five-person model uses an infrared heating system, which you can control through your phone via a mobile app. Indoor saunas often have infrared heat, but Sun Home claims its Luminar model is more than 12.5 times more powerful at 500 watts than competitors. This sauna includes Bluetooth speakers and soothing LED chromotherapy, making sitting in a hot room more enticing to beginner bathers. Yes, it’s a pricey model, but it has ample features and floor-to-ceiling windows for a panoramic view of the outdoors.

According to SweatTent, you can set up the SweatTent Outdoor Sauna in about three minutes. It is somewhat portable because it is simple to put up and take down. The material is durable, insulated, and weather-proof, so you can leave the sauna outdoors indefinitely.

A wood-fired stove heats the SweatTent and comes with 20 pounds of sauna rocks, a fire poker, and heat-resistant gloves to feed the fire safely. The SweatTent is our favorite option for a complete sauna kit. It’s easy to set up, comparatively inexpensive, portable, and works well.

The Sun Home Luminar Sauna is a cube sauna with a carbonized wood exterior and dura-glass windows built to withstand any climate conditions. Luminar has a compact footprint compared to other two-person cube saunas. It uses a combination of infrared and full-spectrum heaters positioned to maintain optimum heat regardless of exterior conditions.

The choice of grade-A carbonized red cedar wood and thick double-pane glass throughout the sauna ensures durability and insulation. With nine heaters, including three far-infrared heaters under the bench and six full-spectrum heaters surrounding the cabin, the Luminar Outdoor Sauna guarantees an efficient and effective sauna session. Sun Home places these heaters strategically to envelop the users in 3D healing wavelengths from all angles.

You can control the Luminar temperature from an app to start heating your sauna before you get home. It has Bluetooth surround-sound speakers and a panoramic view through the dura-glass windows.

The Redwood Outdoors Barrel Sauna is a traditional barrel sauna made with Thermowood. It has all the features you need with nothing extra. We appreciate that you can customize several parts of this dry sauna, from the heating mechanism (you can go the Finnish sauna route with a Harvia electric heater or a wood-burning stove) to add-ons like a weather-resistant shingled roof and even a cold plunge tub. It has a spa-like sauna scent and dry heat, and comfortably fits four to six people.

One benefit of a Thermowood sauna is its durability and resistance to the elements. Redwood Outdoors says that, when properly cared for, this sauna should have an outdoor lifespan of 20 years.

The Redwood Outdoors Thermowood Cabin Sauna is our best outdoor sauna for cold climates because of its robust, weather-resistant construction. This sauna has a traditional Scandinavian design with Scandinavian softwood treated with intense heat to provide exceptional insulation. This design enhances its longevity and contributes to its energy efficiency, ensuring even heat distribution throughout the interior.

The Thermowood Cabin Sauna package includes a Harvia electric heater, wooden heater guard, water bucket and ladle, sauna rocks, and interior seating benches, providing all the necessary components for an authentic sauna experience.

If you’ve spent quality time in the locker room sauna, you’re committed to the wellness practice, and you live somewhere with outdoor space, a sauna might be an excellent investment for your health. “Researchers have found several possible health benefits from sauna use; most importantly, they have shown to help cardiovascular diseases—particularly high blood pressure and heart diseases—as well as acute and chronic pain and neurological diseases,” Mikhael says.

Putting a sauna inside can create some logistical challenges, though, from installation to insulation and more. An outdoor sauna might be easier to install, and it gets you closer to nature, as many of them have spacious windows. “One big bonus of outdoor saunas specifically is they exist outdoors,” Sharma says. “There is a problem in our society labeled Nature Deficit Disorder, which means we aren’t spending enough time outside. There are many proven benefits of being outdoors, and these saunas allow you to combine them with the potential benefits of heat therapy.”

Depending on your model, once your outdoor sauna is installed and ready to go, you can set the temperature via a manual dial, Bluetooth-enabled app, or touchscreen. The heat comes from sauna heaters or wood-burning stoves. Some outdoor saunas allow you to set the timer up to 36 hours in advance. From there, all you need to do is open the door, climb in, and relax.

As for timing, “Two to three 15- to 25-minute sessions per week are ideal,” says Mikhael. “After 15 to 25 minutes, people can benefit the most without feeling like they’re getting dehydrated or dizzy.”

Bring a book, crank up your music, or bring a friend to sweat it out with you—and remember to stay hydrated.

“You want to ensure you’re hydrated before and after,” says Sharma. “A sauna induces a lot of sweating, so you can get dehydrated very easily.” We recommend an electrolyte powder after use if you sweat a lot.

Ideally, you should be heading to your sauna soon as part of your post-workout routine, Lee says. “We found not only is a combination of exercise and sauna bathing stronger in its effects, but many cardiovascular benefits, like lower blood pressure, were sustained for a longer period afterward.”

Most saunas use electricity to run the lights and heaters. Low-tech wood stove-heated saunas might not need any power if there are no lights. There are some solar-powered saunas, too, if you want less strain on the environment (and your electric bill). You’ll just need to make sure you have a battery as a backup.

Given their size and weight, saunas are not very portable. So we’d recommend buying an outdoor sauna once you’re living in a permanent residence rather than an apartment or rental. But even then, life happens, and sometimes you need to move. You can move a constructed outdoor sauna, but it would likely need professional equipment to hoist it into a truck bed. There are very portable tent saunas—much more affordable than the outdoor ones on our list.

The outdoor saunas we recommend cost between $1,599 and $9,799. Based on our research, the lower end of the spectrum offers plenty of heat but fewer bells and whistles. The more pricey saunas can typically seat more people, have more temperature adjustments, provide more comfortable accommodations, and are made with higher-quality materials.

Many outdoor saunas on this list offer additional accessories a la carte. While these aren’t integral to your new sauna routine, they might make it more fun, luxe, and/or comfortable. Some standard accessories we noticed are outdoor showers, cold plunge tubs such as the Plunge, and wooden recliners. Nothing’s stopping you from DIY-ing those accessories, though.

Many wellness fads are short-lived trends (and even potentially harmful). But saunas have been staples in Scandinavian life for centuries, showing significant promise in improving your well-being. Our experts say regular sauna use can improve muscle soreness and even chronic pain.

If you’ve dabbled in heat therapy in the past and want to make it more of a long-term lifestyle (and you have the budget to match), an outdoor sauna can be a valuable and beneficial tool. But, like any significant investment in your health, our experts say you should always consult your doctor before purchasing an outdoor sauna or starting a sauna routine—especially if you have severe cardiovascular or lung issues.

The cost of an outdoor sauna depends on several factors, including capacity, heat source, extra features, integrated technology, and materials. We found saunas at around $1,599 and others at up to $9,799, depending on your budget and needs.

Yes, outdoor saunas typically come with features and accessories to help weatherproof them (like shingles) and keep them dry and ventilated during winter.

When investing in an outdoor sauna, you have to consider its costs, including the electricity used by electric heaters, lighting, and more. When purchasing an outdoor sauna, look for the wattage and amount of electricity it needs to run; it doesn’t hurt to crunch the numbers to estimate your electric bill with a sauna in the mix.
