All of the Different Types of Bikes—Explained

10 Trail-Ready Hardtail Mountain Bikes, Tested

#87. 13 Black Women Share How They Found the Strength to Survive—and Thrive—With Breast Cancer

When it comes to Black women’s breast health, the statistics rarely tell a hopeful story. Black women are diagnosed with breast cancer at a younger median age (60, compared with 62 for white women) and are 38% more likely to die from the disease. They have the lowest survival rate for every known stage of breast cancer. And about one in five Black women with breast cancer are diagnosed with hard-to-treat triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), more than any other racial or ethnic group.

But here’s what the numbers will never capture: the phone calls at 3 a.m., the head-shaving parties, the therapy sessions that cracked something open, the moment a woman looks at her daughter or granddaughter and decides they are reason enough to fight. Black women have always been more than a data point, and perhaps nowhere is that truer than in the way they face, survive, and remake their lives after a breast cancer diagnosis.

The stories below belong to 13 Black women who refused to be reduced to a statistic. They are individuals with careers, children, humor, faith, rage, and joy whose experiences with breast cancer changed them in ways both devastating and profound. In finding their own paths through treatment and beyond, they’ve built something the data can’t quantify: community, purpose, and a hard-won blueprint for survival they’re passing on to every woman who comes after them.

Monique Bass, 53, had always been proactive about her health. A single mother of twin sons and grandmother of four, she started getting annual mammograms at 40. But it was a self-exam at 47 while lying in bed one night that changed everything. She found a lump that didn’t feel right.

What followed were three tissue biopsies of the lump over three years, each coming back benign. Doctors wanted to keep monitoring. Bass pushed back. The lump was growing, and she knew her body well enough to realize something was wrong. She insisted they remove the lump (a procedure called a lumpectomy) and test it. The diagnosis: stage 1 invasive ductal carcinoma that was aggressive enough to require immediate chemotherapy.

Bass got the call while sitting in a car wash. “I felt like I was in The Twilight Zone,” she says. “Not in a million years did I think I would ever hear the words, ‘You have cancer.’” The timing made everything harder. It was 2020, the height of the pandemic, so she navigated much of her journey alone. Adding “another emotional layer,” she was also going through a divorce. Treatment included four rounds of doxorubicin, four rounds of paclitaxel, and 21 radiation treatments. Losing her hair hit the hardest. “But the silver lining is that it grew back even more beautifully after treatment,” Bass says.

Throughout it all her faith anchored her. “I’m not a deeply religious person, but I believe in God, and I knew he had me in the palm of his hand,” Bass says. On the other side of treatment, she founded What’s Behind the Bra?, a New Jersey nonprofit that distributes comfort care packages to breast cancer patients year-round and hosts a weekly podcast of the same name every Sunday at 7:30 p.m. ET.

Jaqueline Beale, 64, comes from a family with a long history of cancer, including her mother, who had breast cancer. That’s why it wasn’t a huge surprise when, at 40, she found a lump during a breast self-exam. Even though a sonogram and mammogram came back clear, it was obvious that something wasn’t right, so Beale got a biopsy.

When the radiologist called with her result—stage 1 breast cancer, which means the cancer hadn’t spread beyond where the abnormal cells had developed—she could hear a lot of noise in the background. He said, “I’m in New York trying to hail a cab, but you have breast cancer. You need to find a breast surgeon.” Despite the bluntness, Beale says she couldn’t help but find the humor in the situation, which is something she carried with her through treatment.

“I made sure that I surrounded myself with laughter and love,” she says, “and I told my family that I knew they loved me, but I also needed a lot of laughter to get through it.”

She recalls one incident in an elevator after her sister had taken her to a chemo treatment. “I had been sick as a dog after, and a woman got in and asked if I was okay. My sister said, ‘Oh, she’s fine. She’s just got a little bit of cancer.’ The woman looked horrified, but I laughed. My family knew that their sense of humor is what I needed.”

Annita White, 51, was five months late for her mammogram. As a single mother of two boys, a higher education administrator, and a first-year PhD student, she always had something more pressing. When she finally went, she expected the usual letter in the mail saying everything was fine. Instead, she got a call. There was a mass that hadn’t been there before.

By the time the biopsy came back, she already knew. A technician had commented on how hard the mass was, and White felt the diagnosis in her spirit before the words were ever spoken. The confirmation came the next day. “When I got the call, I fell to the floor and cried tears of desperation,” she says. “My first thought was, ‘Lord, I can’t do this.’”

What followed was hard in every way: chemotherapy, losing her breasts, losing her hair, which had always been full. “Being bald left me feeling vulnerable and insecure,” White says. “Physically, losing my breasts and going through chemotherapy made me feel like my body was no longer my own.” Through it all the fear that drove her was running out of time—time to see her sons become men and to meet her grandchildren someday.

Her faith, which she’d been privately wrestling with for years, met her exactly where she was. She’d been asking God to truly show up in her life. “He did,” she says. “In the middle of one of the hardest seasons of my life, he carried me through.”

Three years later White is cancer-free, her hair is back, and she recently finished her PhD. She now walks in her purpose as Dr. Nita, a member of the African American Breast Cancer Alliance survivor network, sharing her story and those of others facing the disease. “What once felt like the end became the beginning of something greater,” she says.

Marylande Regis, 38, had been in her new Georgia home for four months when everything changed. A registered nurse, realtor, wife, and mother of three, she had just stopped breastfeeding her nine-month-old when she found the lump. Her baby had never latched well on that side. When she messaged her provider, the on-call response was that it was probably a clogged milk duct and that she was too young to worry about it being something more serious. Regis didn’t accept that. She called back and left a message, insisting that something was wrong. “Another ob-gyn saw the message and encouraged me to make an office appointment immediately,” she says. Within two weeks she had a diagnosis: aggressive stage 2B, BRCA1-positive breast cancer. Within two more weeks what had been one tumor and one impacted lymph node had become three tumors and four impacted lymph nodes. Regis was 36.

“I was relieved that I advocated for myself,” she says. “I was proud that fear didn’t factor into my decision.”

What followed was relentless. Regis went through six months of chemotherapy, a bilateral mastectomy, six weeks of radiation, a total hysterectomy (to eliminate her body’s main source of estrogen), and breast reconstruction, all over a span of roughly 18 months. She lost friends to cancer along the way, as well as a cousin diagnosed around the same time. Her faith was, as Regis describes it, “shaken and stirred and flipped every way possible.” She wrote the important letters. She wrote her own obituary. She was practical about it. “I wanted to be positive, but I am also very realistic,” Regis says.

The hardest part wasn’t any single treatment—it was losing control. As her family’s go-to planner for everything from doctor’s appointments to vacations, she found it foreign to ask for help. But when she told her parents, her mother showed up and never left. “We joke, but my mom never went home,” Regis says. “This is her house now.” Her husband, Kory, came to every appointment and held steady even through both of them losing their jobs. “He deserves a trophy,” she says.

As the daughter of Haitian immigrants, raised to be everything her parents couldn’t be, Regis says the fight was never just medical. Today strength looks different than it did before cancer. It looks like making it to the bus stop with her son, who has autism. It looks like seeing her oldest finish nursing school and work toward becoming an ob-gyn. It looks like watching her youngest hit milestones like learning to talk. “I would have missed that if I didn’t fight,” she says. “The clouds are moving. The sun has decided to show itself. I can’t wait to soak it all in.”

Illness had always been an afterthought for 75-year-old Judy Fambrough-Billingsley. Why would it cross her mind? She walked three miles every day, swam laps all summer, took Zumba classes, and played soccer for 30 years. Judy Fambrough-Billingsley had never smoked or drank, and she didn’t even need to take medication. Being healthy wasn’t something she worked at; it was just who she was. A naturalized American citizen born in Germany, she traveled back to her home country regularly to visit family. Her life was full and active.

So when she felt a lump—and then another six months later—she ignored them. After all, she’d had a clean mammogram earlier that year. But when she noticed them growing and multiplying, she went back to her doctor. The results were not what she expected.

“I was shocked,” Fambrough-Billingsley says. She suddenly found herself navigating an entirely new set of experiences: prescription bottles, hospital procedures, lab processes—the whole medical system. “Being a part of a world where sickness exists had never been my world until now,” she says.

What carried her through was far older than her diagnosis. She grew up during the Civil Rights Era, the daughter of a successful Black entrepreneur who built his business during tumultuous years in US history. Both her parents were lifetime members of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP). She was president of the NAACP Youth Council and an active member of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee. Fambrough-Billingsley knows something about fighting for your life in systems that weren’t built for you.

“Growing up during the Civil Rights Era contributed to this era of fighting,” she says. “Never giving up.” That same spirit—the one her parents modeled, the one she fell into during her work as a community organizer and across decades of a life fully lived—is the one she’s bringing to this too. She may still be on her breast cancer journey, but this is not her first fight.

Taylor Johnson was nearly 30 when she found the lump on her left breast. A mom and content creator who loves trying new things and staying active, she went to her primary care doctor, who referred her for an ultrasound and a mammogram. Johnson was denied a mammogram—she was told she was too young. She pushed anyway, got a biopsy (in lieu of the mammogram), and days later, had a diagnosis: stage 2 triple-negative breast cancer.

“My reaction was a very deep pause, trying to process what my doctor had told me,” Johnson says. “It then hit me, and all I could do was cry.”

She’s in the middle of her treatment plan, which includes six months of chemotherapy, followed by surgery and three weeks of radiation. After finishing chemo Johnson felt confident that would be the hardest part of her journey, both physically and emotionally. But her own health wasn’t her only concern: She knew her five-year-old was watching her every move, and she wanted to stay stable for her daughter. “I was so used to always being the strong one,” Johnson says. “This definitely tested that.” She held it together not because it came easily, but because she understood what her daughter was absorbing.

She is grateful for the community that rallied around her while she waited. Weekly prayer calls, rotating visits from family and friends, and a medical team at Mayo Clinic in Arizona that went above and beyond carried her through.

Though Johnson hasn’t finished treatment yet, completing chemo clarified something for her. “It has reassured me how strong I truly am,” she says. Strength, she’s learned, isn’t just physical. The emotional and mental muscle it takes to keep going counts just as much.

Jessica Ncube, 41, built her life around caring for others. A licensed clinical social worker, the co-owner of a mental health practice, and a mom, she was always in motion. Her life revolved around showing up for others and helping them navigate their hardest moments. “Looking back I do not know that I was always receiving,” she says.

Her diagnosis came quietly. A routine mammogram caught it; nothing in her body had felt amiss. That silence, Ncube says, is exactly why early detection matters. When she got the news she went into survival mode. “You hear the words, but it takes time for them to land,” she says.

Ncube’s journey started with a lumpectomy. When her margins came back unclear, meaning the pathologist could not determine whether all the cancerous cells were removed, she made the decision to move forward with a double mastectomy with reconstructive surgery. “Losing a part of your body, even when it is lifesaving, is still a loss,” she says. “The hardest part was learning how to sit in both gratitude and grief at the same time.”

As someone professionally wired to be strong for others, letting that tendency go was its own kind of work. “Strength became less about holding everything in and more about being honest about what I needed,” Ncube says. Her faith grounded her, and her community showed up, but she also had to unlearn something deeply familiar. “As a Black woman there is a resilience that is almost ingrained in us,” she says. “I had to learn how to balance that resilience with softness.”

After completing treatment Ncube has become more present and deliberate. Her definition of strength has changed entirely. “Strength today is softness. It is honesty. It is allowing myself to receive, to rest, and to not have all the answers,” she says.

Ameiko Newman, 40, didn’t learn of her diagnosis through a routine screening. She was rushed to the hospital for abdominal pain, and that’s when she learned she had breast cancer. Life before her diagnosis had been stressful, uncertain, a season of not quite knowing where she was headed. In a strange way, cancer gave her direction.

“For me, cancer saved me,” she says. “It made me a better person. It made me fight harder, push through the hard times and know what I want in life.”

Newman is still in treatment, receiving chemotherapy and immunotherapy every week, and she is honest about what that looks like: There are good days and bad days. She goes to church faithfully, prays every day, and tries to stay positive through it all.

What has surprised her most is that in the middle of fighting for her own life, she found her purpose: helping others fight for theirs. Newman rebranded her business entirely around that mission and started designing scarves with chemo patients in mind. “I started making them mainly for my Black women because you know we love having style,” she says. But a wide variety of women from all over have since bought them.

She wakes up every day, gets her kids ready, works out, and moves through life. Faith, she says, is what makes that possible. Her message to any Black woman who’s just gotten diagnosed is both simple and hard-won: “Cancer doesn’t define you. You define you. Even though you’re fighting for your life, help someone else fight for theirs.”

Charlotte Connor, 38, had just undergone a breast augmentation when she felt a lump in her breast. “When I saw my doctor, they weren’t concerned, in part because of my young age,” says Connor, who was 30 years old at the time. She had a mammogram and ultrasound to check for signs of cancer, but no MRI. “Looking back now I wish I would have asked for that MRI,” she says.

At the first checkup six months later, they told her she was fine. At the second—one year after the original lump was found—the lump had tripled in size. Her doctor ordered a biopsy, and her diagnosis was confirmed: stage 2A ductal carcinoma, which means the cancer was growing but contained to the breast and surrounding lymph nodes.

“When they told me I had cancer, I was calm,” she says. Her mindset immediately shifted from a sinking feeling to being optimistic about the future. “I focused on getting healthy again,” says Connor, who started fantasizing about what she would do after treatment.

She remembers thinking, I may be feeling sick and throwing up from chemotherapy, but what restaurants am I going to go to after all this is over? It’s an outlook that didn’t necessarily come naturally to her, either. “I’m not even overly optimistic in life—I think I’m a realist—but in this situation, I shifted to being overly optimistic.”

Part of that mindset shift was for her young daughter. “I couldn’t be pessimistic; I had to be strong for her,” she says. “And I knew that how I acted in this situation was how she was going to mirror things and react to stressful situations when she got older.”

Connor’s other pillar of support came from a tight-knit circle of friends and family, who threw her a head-shaving party before she lost her hair due to chemo. “Making things fun and lighthearted like that got me through my darkest, saddest moments,” she says.

It was 1999, and Donna Culmer had just received a clean mammogram. A few months later she felt a stone-size bump on her right side, so she went back to her ob-gyn to get it checked out. They redid the mammogram on both breasts, and while what she’d felt was actually a fibrocystic lump, the imaging found a small, not palpable spot on her left side that turned out to be a stage 1 cancer. “I was stunned,” Culmer says. “I didn’t even know what questions to ask.” She drove back to work in a daze and told her boss what had happened.

At 46 she was serving in the Navy as an instructor and trainer to personnel who were working alongside the Marines. She was married to a Marine and raising three children. There was no good moment for this. There never is.

Four months of chemotherapy followed, with nausea and exhaustion that never quite let up. Her doctors were concerned that the chemo might not work, so she had a mastectomy. Through it all her community refused to let her go through it alone. Her father drove her to every session and sat with her. Her church came to her, literally; services were held at her house.

Twenty-seven years later, Culmer, now 73, has had time to reflect. “As Black women, we have been through challenges our whole lives,” she says. “This is just one more.” Her advice is practical and clear. “Don’t panic and ask questions, even if you have to write them down,” Culmer says. “The treatments available now are so much better than what I had.”

One morning, Patricia Fox, 38, woke up with a lump in her right breast that wasn’t there the night before—she was just 26 years old at the time. Fox scheduled an appointment with her ob-gyn that day. “They told me that I was a young Black woman and had dense breasts, and it was likely a cyst,” she says. “They were ready to turn me away.”

The lump, which was a little smaller than a golf ball, seemed strange to Fox. Thankfully, she listened to her intuition. “There was something telling me to get it checked out,” she says, so her doctor did a biopsy just to be sure.

Her results came back as estrogen receptor-positive stage 2A breast cancer, meaning her cancer had estrogen receptors that would respond to hormone therapy drugs. Fox says she’ll never forget her doctor’s words: “Patricia, you’ll be a breast cancer survivor.” That sentiment set the tone for her mindset as a fighter. “It made me think that I could face this and survive this,” she says.

Still, cancer treatments quickly overwhelmed Fox, and soon she faced her lowest point: crying on the floor for hours, feeling like having cancer at such a young age was a punishment for being a “bad person.” But she pulled herself out of it with hard work in therapy.

“I found that talking to a therapist helped me process my diagnosis and examine the areas of my life—certain people and my own behavior patterns—that were cancerous for me that I needed to do something about,” she says. “While therapy didn’t make the pain go away, it did make how I coped with it much better.”

In the Black community, therapy is often taboo, says Fox, but it’s become her mission to dispel that belief. “Therapy fortified me to get through cancer,” she says, “and I tell everyone that they don’t have to suffer in silence.”

Annette Colden, 63, was sitting at her sister’s bedside during the last days of her final battle with breast cancer when the conversation turned to screenings. Her sister had been through cervical cancer and two bouts of breast cancer before passing away from the disease. “She made me promise I’d get my mammograms,” Colden says.

Colden’s first two yearly mammograms were clear. On the third there was a spot, but she was told by her doctor that things looked okay and it wasn’t cancer—she just had lumpy breasts.

“There’s this inner feeling you have,” she says. “Something was inside me saying, That’s not right.” Her sister’s doctor had told her the exact same thing, but Colden was so happy to hear she didn’t have cancer that she didn’t follow up.

A year later she went back for a mammogram, and that’s when her doctors found it: stage 0 breast cancer, meaning only abnormal cells had been found. She was 42. “Now, looking back, I always tell women that if something doesn’t feel right, get a second opinion.”

Despite the diagnosis Colden remained calm. “I’m a religious person,” she says. “In my prayer I said, ‘Lord, if you will be my pilot on this journey, I’ll be your copilot.’” She immediately felt a sense of peace.

After her recovery she decided to share that calming presence with other women going through breast cancer at a support group through Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center, where she had treatment. “I say, ‘It’s going to be a long road. If you don’t want to travel it alone, I’m right there with you.’”

And she means it. Sometimes that involves talking with someone at 3 a.m. when the pain from chemotherapy hits. Other times it means sending food delivery boxes to the homes of people with breast cancer who can’t muster the strength to leave. “My sister did a lot of support work before she got really sick,” she says. “This is her vision.”

Ricki Fairley, 69, was in the security line at the airport for a work trip when she got a call from her doctor. They’d found a peanut-like lump under her nipple that turned out to be cancer.

Fairley, who was 55 at the time, said, “I don’t have time for this right now. I’ll call you when I get to my destination.” A couple days later she found out she had stage 3A TNBC, and it was really aggressive. Compared with other breast cancers, TNBC has fewer targeted-therapy treatment options, often spreads beyond the breasts, and is more likely to recur. Black women have nearly three times the risk of developing triple-negative breast cancer.

Her diagnosis woke her up. “It made me realize that I needed to get all of the ‘cancers’ out of my life,” Fairley says. During treatment that first year which involved a double mastectomy, aggressive chemotherapy, and radiation, she quit her job and started her own company. Then she filed for divorce and later sold her house. “I quit my life and started a new one, and changed everything,” she says. “I had to learn that my peace is nonnegotiable. I really think that stress caused my breast cancer.”

A year later her life changed again. Fairley was diagnosed with metastatic breast cancer and told she had two years to live. After finding out her current doctor had only treated two previous cases of TNBC and both women had died in eight months, she found a new doctor, who was well-versed in current research and treatments for the disease. She beat cancer a second time. “I remember sitting at my daughter’s graduation thinking, Okay, I made it. What’s next for me?” Fairley says. The answer: helping others. In the years that followed, Fairley cofounded The Black Breast Cancer Alliance, which works to reduce the mortality rate for Black women.

#88. How to Organize Your Shoe Collection Without Losing Your Mind

From marathon trainers to stilettos, here’s a system that works even when your closet (and your patience) is at capacity.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

I’m a gear tester for Runner’s World, which means I regularly swim through an ocean of sneakers, and also, I work inside the Hearst Tower, surrounded by people who can pull off Céline loafers at 9:15 a.m. with the same ease I pull off neon race-day trainers. At any given time, I have well over 30 pairs of running shoes, plus a collection of heels, sleek work shoes, and (because we are all human) maybe two pairs of oh-no-is-she-leaving-the-house Crocs.

Translation: My shoe collection is massive, wild, and constantly threatening to collapse in on itself like a very expensive Jenga tower. You are in safe hands. Let’s organize your chaos. Fair warning: I am also autistic as heck (thanks, Mom!), and organization is one of my special interests. Alas, I also have ADHD (thanks, Dad!), so keeping it up is hard. These tips may seem hyper-specific, but trust me, they work.

If you’re serious about organizing your sneaker collection, the first step may seem counterintuitive: You need to touch every single pair. Line them up—your marathon-ready carbon-plate racers, your limited-edition Jordans, that thrifted pair you swore you’d “beat” but never wore outside—and assess. Not “do they spark joy,” but do you actually wear them, or are they taking up space you could dedicate to sneakers you truly love? From there, sort them: running shoes, daily beaters, hype pairs, and sneakers you keep telling yourself you’ll donate “eventually.”

Other footwear—boots, loafers, heels—are best stored separately from your sneaker setup. If you’ve got work boots or muck boots, for example, they should live in your mudroom or garage, well away from your sneakers.

We love this one because after a year with my son, it’s still in fantastic shape. His shoes? Gross. His room? There’s a reason there’s no photo from our house. He’s 18, so there’s a ton of gaming clutter and papers and deodorant and things all over it. But the point is that we clean it all the time with Lysol wipes, bleach wipes, and we’ve even hosed it out when he spilled root beer on it before school and didn’t notice. You simply cannot kill this locker, it looks amazing, and it stores 30 pairs of shoes and then some.

If you’re short on storage (I get it, I live in NYC), this is a good solution. Sturdy, wooden boxes on wheels that slide under the bed for invisible and convenient storage. Bonus? You can store anything in these.

How did I pick them? Ten thousand years of organizing both my and my mother’s shoe closets packed with excessive sneakers, work shoes, and the hideous slip-ons I try to hide in my mother’s closet so she can’t find them and wear them in public.

It’s affordable, durable, and doesn’t wobble when fully loaded with carbon-plated sneakers. You can adjust the height of the rack to each shoe type, and even add a traditional shoe rack on a shelf.

This is both surprisingly sturdy and easy to put together. The whole thing is slim enough to fit in an entryway or beside a door, but has enough space for plenty of your favorite trainers.

If you want something that doesn't hit your eyeline, a low, wide shelf like this is your BFF. I also like this one for your trail runners to hang in the garage. Stick your gunkiest shoes on the bottom.

As someone who lives in NYC, I get the need for multifunctional spaces. Having a place to sit to lace up and store your sneakers is a great, space-saving idea. And hey, this one looks pretty darn good.

Clear, protective, and stackable—shockingly chic if lined up and LED-lit. Easy to open, and oddly great for other things (like art supplies or purses!).

These are fab for your everyday casual and work shoes. They can be stored on a steel rack for additional space, and they’re just the right fit. I caution against the type that only has a bar or pair of bars as the base, as heels tend to fall through.

This is what I use in the front hall of my home. I have it set up for daily trainers and whatever shoes I wear that day. I covered the glass in stained glass contact paper and it’s really pretty.

This is absurdly sturdy for the price. It holds at least a dozen pairs of shoes, and it’s also great for displaying flowers, photos, and more.

No collapsed calves, no creases. Just standing tall with dignity. Thigh highs? Pool noodles are your friend. BUT, these are also good for high tops, hiking boots, and shoes you want to store off their soles.

Charcoal bags like these not only deodorize but they also pull the moisture out of the shoes.

Bonus points if your closet is also cedar-lined. It will smell even better than your shoes after using these.

These are the best that I’ve tried. And they work. My feet, of course, smell like roses, but my teen? Sigh.

You can toss them into a hanging organizer or a bin, because they’re immortal and require zero dignity.

Over-the-door organizers are your best friend. Or embrace the chaos—it reads “artsy.”

Cedar inserts or sneaker balls. Or just accept that some runs are too heroic for your shoes not to smell like triumph and sorrow.

#90. The Best Compact Rowing Machines for Small Spaces in 2025

A smaller footprint doesn’t mean you have to miss out. Here are the best compact rowing machines for a top-notch workout.

Written by Stephen Sheehan, CPT × The Expert Panel is a network of specialized health and fitness professionals who help ensure we present the most accurate information to our readers. This includes physicians, certified trainers, elite-level coaches, and more. Learn more about our experts. expert-verified Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC Last updated on Mar 4, 2025

expert-verified Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC

If you’re limited on space, don’t let the length of a rowing machine deter you. While there are many great rowing machines on the market, there are also some awesome compact alternatives that offer all the same tech features you’ll find in other cardio machines.

During our search for the best compact rowing machine, we found an array of excellent standalone options and options that fit in well with other top-rated home gym equipment. We considered the overall footprint and other key features, and scoured the reviews to see what users had to say about each product. Below is our list of the best compact home rowing machines available.

The rowing machines included in this list were carefully selected based on what most users would want out of a rowing machine, keeping in mind that they needed to have a smaller footprint and folding or upright storage options. We evaluated each choice based on size, portability, cost, high-tech features, versatility, and durability. We also scoured the reviews to see what users had to say about each rowing machine.

On the Hydrow website, the Hydrow Wave is rated 4.6/5 stars with over 9,000 reviews at the time of writing. It’s the brand’s compact, budget-friendly option for those who want to elevate their at-home workout routine. The length is just 80 inches, which is the shortest on this list, and the overall size is 30 percent shorter than the original Hydrow Rower. You cannot fold it, but there is the option to store it upright using The Hydrow Wave Vertical Anchor. This is a wall-mounted strap that holds the rower upright. It costs an additional $190, which is a bit on the pricey side.

The frame is made of aluminum and steel. It has a flat anthracite polymer body, which is a durable and lightweight material. The handle has an ergonomic design for a low-stress grip, and the strap is made from water- and rot-resistant polyester webbing. It also has a patented electromagnetic drag system that mimics the experience of rowing on open water.

Overall, the reviews on the Hydrow website are positive, and many mention how quiet the machine is and how much they like the small footprint. One review says, “The machine is such great quality. It’s quiet and sleek looking.” The critical reviews make up 3 percent of the overall reviews and state issues like non-working parts being delivered. However, Hydrow has responded to each review to resolve any issues.

The NordicTrack RW700 has a 10-inch HD touchscreen you can tilt and pivot to follow along with an iFIT workout led by your favorite trainer on or off the rower. An iFIT subscription is $39 per month, and you’ll have access to live and on-demand classes. Membership to the fitness app is not required to use the rower; however, you won’t have access to trainer-led classes without it.

A trainer-led rowing workout gives you the option to row on the open water for a more scenic experience, and there are also studio sessions. The resistance is adjusted automatically among 26 resistance levels during each class, so you don’t need to worry about stopping to make changes. The oversized foot pedals have adjustable nylon foot straps with quick release, which is excellent for those who want to incorporate movements off the rower into their workout.

The rail is 87 inches long and made from durable steel. It has an inertia-enhanced flywheel, so it should maintain a smooth rotation. If you have a shared space, the NordicTrack RW700 rower has a magnetic resistance system that creates tension against the flywheel without touching, making it a quieter option. After your workout, this magnetic rowing machine can be moved using the front wheels, but it can’t be folded.

The flywheel has been designed to maintain inertia and rotate smoothly, and the steel rail is oversized to help keep you stable. The large, pivoting foot pedals with adjustable nylon straps keep your feet in place, and the seat is molded with comfort in mind.

If you like to incorporate other movements into your rowing workout or train off of the rower, the Echelon Row-s has a 22-inch HD touchscreen that can be flipped 180 degrees. While an Echelon Fit subscription is not required, the extra $35/month workout app gives you access to over 40 live classes and more than 1,000 on-demand workouts from its library, including rowing, biking, running, and functional training classes.

The ergonomic design of the seat and the ability to adjust the foot platforms to a comfortable position help you maintain proper posture and alignment. If you’re short on space, the length goes from 84 inches long to just 41 inches long when folded. On the Echelon website, this rower is rated 4.6/5 stars. “The machine looks great, operates very quietly, and gives a great workout no matter your level,” says reviewer Brett P.

Dimensions: 87.02" L x 22.0" W x 47.24" H

Storage: Folds in half for vertical storage

Available programming: Live and on-demand workouts, scenic rows

The NordicTrack RW600 balances great tech features and an accessible price, making it a great value. The 10-inch screen is an excellent option for those who want to take instructor-led classes using an iFIT membership. NordicTrack’s patented Silent Magnetic Resistance can be adjusted up to 26 levels automatically in an iFIT class or manually as needed.

The pivoting foot pedals are oversized, and the nylon straps keep your feet secure. The handlebar has a soft grip, and the molded seat is designed to help you feel comfortable. When your workout is finished, the NordicTrack RW600 can be folded and stored out of the way.

What factors should you consider before you pull the trigger on a rower? Here’s what we’d recommend you take into account as you ponder your purchase decision:

Once you’ve decided on your rower location, it’s a good idea to measure the length, width, and height of your space to determine what size machine works best. You’ll want to measure height to see if you have enough clearance for rowers to be stored upright.

After measuring, think about how much you’re willing to spend. Take into consideration any additional costs such as a monthly subscription. Some rowers also have add-ons for purchase, such as a lumbar support system or seat upgrade.

Ask yourself: How many levels of resistance do I need? Am I looking for an HD touchscreen with trainer-led classes or do I prefer a more simplistic display? Other features such as a magnetic resistance system may be important if you’re in a shared space and need a quieter machine. The rower’s maximum height and/or weight capacity may also play a role in your decision as well.

Rowing allows you to implement low-impact, cardio-based training, and you can adjust the resistance for a strength-focused session. It’s a full-body workout that uses 86 percent of your muscles. With each stroke, you’re using your core and legs for the initial pull and finishing the rowing movement by using your upper body. Since you’re in a seated position, there’s less pressure on your knee and ankle joints.

Getting all four types of exercise (endurance, strength, balance, and flexibility) has benefits, according to The National Institute of Health (NIH). A rowing machine can be utilized for two types: endurance and strength. Many rowing machines have built-in programs or subscriptions that offer classes geared toward building strength and endurance.

Rowing is a great way to build strength and endurance while working various muscle groups. There are choices to suit a variety of budgets with different storage options and sizes. Figuring out how much space you have, your price range and the features you’d like will help you choose the best compact rowing machine for you.

The machines on this list range from just over $700 to around $2,000. You can find a rower in your price range, but if you opt for a rower under, say, $200, you may be compromising quality.

Typically, rowing machine length ranges between six to nine feet with more compact options at six or seven feet long.

The level of resistance that’s best for you depends on your fitness level, experience, and goals. Overall, you don’t want your workout to be too easy or so challenging you don’t accomplish the goal of your training session.

Compact rowing machines usually have air or magnetic resistance, and some options implement both.

#91. What I Learned from Finishing a Triathlon When Everything Goes Wrong

Before the start of her second attempt at the Cowichan Challenge, Anna Rea had high hopes of besting her time from the previous year. (Photo: Courtesy Anna Rea)

For this article, a novice age-group triathlete shared, in her own words, her experience racing the Olympic-distance Cowichan Challenge Triathlon. Despite multiple setbacks, she received encouragement from volunteers and fellow racers to keep going, and has tried to apply that same perseverance to other areas of her life.

It was a perfect early summer morning. The forecast wasn’t too hot, the water was warm, and there was no hint of wind. I had fueled and hydrated the day before. I was well rested and ready. I had done the exact same race one year earlier, which was my first ever triathlon.

This time, I assumed I would be faster. I had to be. Any other outcome would feel like failure.

But within a few minutes of the race start, the rest of the swimmers were barely visible. I had recently done two private lessons with a swimming coach, during which I learned that my technique was broken. There was no time to properly address it before the race.

The swim took 53 minutes, so I was eager to make up some time on the ride. But after five minutes on my bike, just as I was finding my rhythm, my derailleur seized up, and I couldn’t move the pedals. This was defeat.

I tearfully walked my bike back toward transition. I assumed there was no helping this situation. I hadn’t taken my bike for a tune-up before the race. I had failed.

After 25 minutes of walking, a race volunteer spotted me and ran over. He tinkered with my bike for a couple minutes, and I secretly hoped he would confirm my fears – that the bike was broken and it was time to give up. An easy out.

But when he fixed my bike with a couple turns of an Allen key, my guts twisted with dread. He encouraged me to get back on the bike. I told him I had given up, but he told me I might as well keep going since there were still a couple hours until the cut-off time. I had already spent the money, trained, and showed up to the race — I had nothing to lose.

I was alone for most of the ride. I kept apologizing to the volunteers along the race course because I felt guilty that they had to wait for me. I didn’t think I would even start the run, but I kept my focus on the moment, on each corner and hill, until I was back at transition.

My sister, who had completed the sprint distance and was already finished, was waiting for me. I updated her on my situation and asked if she and my mom were OK with waiting until I finished. She said yes and encouraged me.

Then a race worker advised me that the race cut-off was in 52 minutes. He said there was no way I would make it in time and suggested I drop out. I told him I wanted to try, and I accepted that I would complete part of the run without support.

I started the run before I could change my mind. I had a hard time seeing the direction markers on the course. After a couple wrong turns, I was overwhelmed with the urge to give up. I cursed out loud, turned on my heel, and started walking back toward transition. But I immediately met the eyes of an athlete walking back to his vehicle, finisher medal hanging from his neck. He told me to keep going. I told him about my broken bike, the bad swim, not making the cut-off time, and running in the wrong direction. He encouraged me to go anyway, so I did.

I did most of the trail run alone. The race volunteers were supportive and stayed past the cut-off even though they didn’t have to. I was overwhelmed with gratitude, and this time saying thank you was easier than saying sorry.

I shouted curses on the run, stumbling over tree roots in my fatigue, fueled by frustration and determination. When I was 1 kilometer from the end, I almost passed out at a hydration station. I regrouped and kept moving.

Four hours and 15 minutes that felt like an eternity were suddenly coming to an end. I saw the finish line arch. I heard the applause as by now the awards ceremony was well underway. My sister saw me approaching, turned to a group of people behind her, and told them I was coming. And finally, after hours of exhaustion and frustration, wanting to give up the whole time, I crossed the finish line in front of a cheering crowd. And it was all worth it. I wouldn’t change a thing.

I’m not good at this. I don’t feel like I’m good at much. Genetic vision loss has greatly impacted the last few years of my life. I’m struggling to start a new career while managing chronic mental health issues and an acquired disability.

My confidence has taken a hit, and I think about giving up all the time. Things could be a lot worse – I have a support system and free healthcare in Canada. I am privileged with a great quality of life and generally good health aside from my eye disease.

But I feel behind. And by challenging myself to do things like triathlon, I expose myself to people who are incredibly fit. Self-criticism and body dysmorphia usually tag along.

The three months that have passed since that race have been difficult, and I feel out of touch with the person who persevered that day. I’m trying to let some light in and keep going – keep adapting to vision loss, keep building my career, and keep pushing myself.

I used to care a lot more about being good at things. Now I care about following through. Life is hard, and persisting when you don’t feel like enough is a feat of strength. I faced my fear of being slow that day and finished to a crowd of cheers. Of course I want to be faster. I want to finish in the pack. I want to be good at triathlon. But we can learn so much by being bad at things and doing them anyway.

Walking my bike back to the car, finisher medal around my neck, I turned to my sister and said, “Winning is cool, but losing is where it’s at.”

Do things you’re bad at. Challenge yourself. It’s OK if you don’t feel like a triathlete. How many things would you do if you weren’t afraid of failure?

#92. How to use fitness trackers to enhance performance and wellbeing—without losing touch with yourself

Today, if you’re curious enough, you can measure your heart rate, your step count, your exercise intensity, and your sleep quality—sometimes all on one sleek device.

In the best cases, these devices offer a bridge between what you subjectively feel and what you can objectively measure.

This is generally a really cool and amazing thing.

Our subjective feelings and assessments matter, but they’re not always the most reliable. Us humans just aren’t particularly skilled at quantifying our experiences and behaviors with cold precision.

Take, for example, a colleague of mine. He believed he was eating within a narrow caloric window, but after careful tracking, he learned that he was putting away a bonus 500 Calories a day—in barbecue sauce.

That said, some of us are better than others.

Ben Johnson, the Canadian sprinter, was reported to have been able to call out his 100 metre time within a tenth of a second of the stopwatch readout.1

That’s outlier performance, to be clear, but it still makes you wonder:

And, how can you improve your accuracy through the wise use of technology—like fitness trackers—to help you make better decisions about your health?

In the following article, we’ll tackle the above, plus we’ll address:

Some brands produce better products than others. This is not just hardware but also the quality of their software and datasets.

Beyond that, not all things are equally easy to quantity.

For example, heart rate and step-count data are generally reliable,2 but many other types of outputs—from calories burned to movement velocity—have substantial margins for error.

The below chart shows the reliability of various tracking devices.

(If you’re curious, we cover the accuracy of various progress indicators in more detail here: Are Fitness Trackers Worth It?)

The good: Tracking devices offer us more data about our behaviors and bodies than ever before.

The bad: Tracking devices offer us more data about our behaviors and bodies than ever before.

“What’s really remarkable,” says Samantha Kleinberg, a computer scientist who studies decision-making, “is that even a tiny amount of surplus information has a big negative effect on our decision-making.”3

That’s the paradox of tracking: Too little detail makes it tough to make the right decision, but so does too much.

This can be expressed as an inverted U, with the sweet spot at the top of the curve.

Consider the analysis paralysis you feel after scanning hundreds of reviews from the various taco places in your neighborhood. (All you wanted was a decent el pastor, but now you don’t know which taqueria to pick!)

Finding just enough information to make good decisions is an art form—especially in the world of health and fitness, where it seems like everyone is trying to outdo each other when it comes to providing more science, more customization, and more complexity.

But when all that information starts to blur together with no clear path forward, what should you do?

For starters, you can ask yourself a simple question:

Does tracking increase my wellbeing and performance?

If the answer is a clear yes or no, you know what to do. (Either continue tracking as you were, or drop the gadget and walk away.)

If you’re a little fuzzy, here are three signs to watch for to help you determine if tracking is helpful—or not.

When Zak’s coach raved about the benefits of zone 2 cardio, it sounded logical. But when the rubber on his running shoes hit the road, Zak second-guessed everything. Zak prided himself on his ability to grind, and simply didn’t trust that something that felt easy could also be effective.

Yet, the data didn’t lie. As the weeks went by, Zak watched his resting heart rate drop—along with his recovery time from hard runs. With that reassurance, Zak began to relax about the process—and his resting heart rate dropped further.

Zak hadn’t trusted his feelings, but he did trust the data from his heart rate monitor.

Using a tracking device enabled Zak to calibrate his own perceptions so they were more accurate and realistic.

If you’re a coach who has a client like Zak who’s high performing but doesn’t know it, tracking can help build confidence and reduce the anxiety that they’re “not good enough.”

Here, you empower them by shining a spotlight on existing performance. Expert assurance can go a long way but can also be bolstered by reliable data.

(Recently, many people have begun using continuous glucose monitors, or CGMs, in order to “optimize” their blood sugar levels. This can help “validate” certain food choices… but it can also be a waste of time. Read more: Should people without diabetes use CGMs?)

Sometimes, data can stress you out without any upside—like when you receive poor scores about things beyond your control.

Take the new parent of a newborn who gets a poor sleep quality score.

Tracking has a time and a place. When scores are beyond your control or your priorities lie elsewhere, tracking can create unnecessary stress and is counterproductive.

You can always revisit tracking when circumstances or priorities change.

For a behaviour to take place, you need three things4:

Fitness trackers shine when you’ve got plenty of motivation and ability—and just lack the prompt.

Take my client, Margaret. She used to have a glass of wine most nights, believing it helped her sleep better. Once she started wearing a sleep tracker though, she saw that her sleep quality was much poorer the nights she imbibed. Once she received this prompt—her sleep score—she adjusted her behavior.

When you highlight important data, the right choices become clearer.

When it comes to changing behaviours, sometimes all it takes is one key piece of data. As they say, “Once you see it, you can’t un-see it.”

(PN’s CEO Tim Jones used the feedback he got from various lifestyle trackers to finally reduce his genetically high cholesterol levels—and built a richer, more meaningful life in the process. Read more: How This Guy Cut His Cholesterol in Half Without Drugs)

When Jan, an avid recreational cyclist, found out he could view—then demolish—the records set on local biking trails, he set to work. But as those records were destroyed, so too was his ability to ride for enjoyment. His focus on speed left him under-recovered and eventually led to burnout.

If workouts have become more about the numbers and less about technique, experience, or even enjoyment, tracking is likely no longer helpful.

The harder you work, the better your results.

This belief tends to get grinders like Zak into trouble because they think they’re making progress—but really they’re just getting in their own way, even inhibiting performance and recovery.

Meanwhile, there are also many people who chronically underestimate their effort and capacity, and would benefit from turning up the heat. Here, data can help us more accurately understand our own potential.

Let’s look at high-intensity interval training (HIIT) as an example. HIIT workouts alternate fixed periods of intense effort with fixed periods of rest. However, these fixed periods of rest are just estimates of recovery times.

Heart rate data can create a more individualized picture of actual recovery needs, which may be faster or slower than you expect.

Sometimes, the mind says yes but the heart says not quite yet.

A good coach does more than just simply ask for more. They also help keep clients out of the unproductive “junk volume” zone, where fatigue accumulates but performance doesn’t improve (and maybe even worsens).

By looking at real-time metrics of output, fatigue, and recovery, you can better understand yourself and your clients, and help keep everyone training and recovering efficiently.

When you become overly reliant on data, you risk losing touch with your own sense of how you feel, whether that’s hunger and fullness levels, energy and fatigue, or something else.

A relevant example is “The Great My Fitness Pal Blackout.”

When the app wouldn’t load, I recognized the mild panic I felt was unhelpful. My overreliance on the app had disconnected me from my own internal signals, and without it, I felt adrift. Since then, I’ve shifted my focus to how energetic I feel. I also consult one of the oldest tracking technologies available: the mirror.

(If you feel like you’re lost without your besties—your phone and your apps—there’s a name for that. There are also ways to develop a healthier relationship with your tech. Read more: What is nomophobia?)

Before we get to how to do the above, let’s talk about why assessing things by feel can be so important.

Whether it’s body fat percentage or movement speed, even supremely motivated and capable clients will experience diminishing objective results from their training.

The scale stops dropping, the number of plates you’re able to load on the bar plateaus, or—gasp—your race time even regresses.

Motivation based purely on progress or other extrinsic goals6 will fall away during these times.

However, exercisers who focus on feelings of mindfulness7, mastery, meaning8, and success9 develop a more resilient practice. They also enjoy the process more, whether that’s the process of running, lifting, winding down for a good night’s sleep, or just enjoying a meal.

So, although objective data can provide essential feedback and guidance, you’ll only reap the full benefits of your practice—that is, enjoyment and results—if you maintain connection with your felt experience.

And good news: You can actually use fitness trackers to calibrate and even improve your ability to accurately sense what’s happening in your body.

Can you imagine asking someone how their vacation was and then waiting for them to look at their photos to be able to answer? That’s what it’s like when you rely purely on external data about your own experience.

Whatever the metric—how far you biked, how many calories you consumed, or how fast your heart was beating—the simplest way to work mindfully with tracker data is to pause, breathe, and then tune into the powerful (if not always accurate) prediction-making powers of your brain.

Once you’ve checked in with yourself, you can calibrate your self-assessment by comparing the detailed (if not always accurate) outputs of your fitness tracker.

Over time, you may be able to narrow the gap between two.

(Note: Don’t forget to regularly update your app. Algorithms and data sets are regularly adjusted for better predictive accuracy.)

The coaches I work with regularly ask people to estimate the boundaries of their strength (such as how many reps they can do at a given weight until failure).

Novices are often terrible at estimating this—and regularly off the mark by five or more reps. However, the use of objective trackers can help calibrate their understanding, and most people can reduce their margin of error dramatically.

In theory, you might use fancy tools like accelerometers or blood lactate measurements, but our coaches just ask, “For a million dollars a rep, how many more reps do you think you could do?”

Though there’s nothing objective about this question, most clients are able to use the prompt as a kind of shortcut to understand maximal effort. (After all, that last rep may be worth seven figures!)

The question also leverages the rate of perceived exertion (RPE)—your perception of how hard you’re working—which is one of the most validated sensory-driven approaches.

Not everyone is automatically good at estimating RPE, but most people can improve their skills by mapping their felt experience with occasional calibration with objective data.

Trackers have components like accelerometers, GPS, and gyroscopes to sense data about speed, distance, and more.

You have access to an incredibly rich network of sensory information—something that technology cannot begin to touch.

All of this information is fed into the powerful pattern-recognition machine of your nervous system.

To continue honing your ability to use this rich network of sensory information, regularly check in with what and how you’re feeling.

When you learn to calibrate your own senses with objective data, you can leverage all the cool advances in wearable tech—while still keeping your own experience front and centre.

#94. Forging Resilience: Ryan Del Grosso’s Journey Through the Air Force, Harvard and Overcoming Cancer

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

From growing up in Saudi Arabia during a tense geopolitical era to graduating from the Air Force Academy, commanding special tactics teams across the globe, and navigating a grueling battle with stage 3 lymphoma, Ryan Del Grosso’s life is defined by a relentless pursuit of purpose and growth. Whether he is lifting others up through his various efforts, working with the U.S. Olympic and Paralympic Committee (USOPC), or building businesses aligned with authentic human values, Del Grosso embodies the true spirit of resilience, and he credits fitness and training in part for that.

“Fitness gives you something to draw on when life gets difficult: the experience of having worked through hard things before.”

Del Grosso’s journey into the military lifestyle began with deep-seated roots. Being raised in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia by parents who previously served in the Air Force, he was in fifth grade at the time of the events of September 11th, 2001, which he said played a part in his entry into service. He also cited being inspired by films such as Black Hawk Down, Annapolis, and Into the Wild, which made him want to go out west. Del Grosso pursued and eventually found his way to the Air Force Academy. Coming from a rural Ohio school with no prior service academy connections, he relied heavily on the support of prior-enlisted peers from day one.

He recalled, “Some of my classmates had already served, and I really admired the maturity and confidence they brought. I learned a lot by following their lead and working alongside them. That respect for the experience other people bring to a team has stayed with me.”

His journey soon led him to the elite special tactics career field, where he gutted out a grueling two-and-a-half-year training pipeline. Operating as a class leader and officer candidate, Del Grosso learned early on how to forge team cohesion under intense physical and mental pressure. When looking back at his military career, his proudest moments aren’t tied to tactical execution, but to leadership and legacy.

“For me, the pipeline was an education in how people become a team. I was learning to recognize individual strengths, help people develop, and bring those strengths together to accomplish something difficult. I was learning how to help the team succeed while working through the same challenges myself.”

Operating within the special tactics career field, Del Grosso served across multiple high-stakes regions, including Afghanistan, Eastern Europe, and Southeast Asia. He later commanded teams across three distinct deployments and participated in critical Joint Special Operation Command (JSOC) exercises.

Like any true leader, Del Grosso feels his best accomplishments were for others, such as writing and advocating for the upgrade of two Silver Star medals for a fellow operator over a multi-year process and mentoring a younger team member through rigorous planning to successfully lead a large, combined force operation.

“Those moments meant a lot to me. I could help a teammate get the recognition they’d earned or help someone prepare to lead and then see them succeed. That’s work I’m proud of.”

Many service members believe that the oath they take has no expiration date, and they find ways to continue to serve others after they leave the military. Del Grosso is no exception, which is why the Harvard Business School grad has gone on to make differences both in the private sector and with multiple charities such as Huts for Vets, a non-profit organization based in Colorado that provides no-cost wilderness therapy retreats for U.S. military veterans and active-duty service members. Del Grosso served on their board and was even chairman at one time before stepping down as a way to elevate others and bring new members into the fold. He confirmed that his time with Huts for Vets did something for him as well.

“Huts for Vets helped me heal, too. Being part of that community gave me a different understanding of how I could support other veterans and continue to serve.”

Del Grosso also co-founded and is a partner of IMPCT Group, an agency and strategic advisory firm focused on blending commercial innovation, social impact, and brand growth. The concept behind IMPCT was a unique one, but it has also proved to be successful thus far.

“I wanted my work to reflect what I actually cared about. IMPCT grew out of that same belief: a business’s purpose should shape both what it sets out to achieve and how it goes about achieving it.”

He also worked with the USOPC as an MBA Fellowship during my time at HBS. After sports like distance running, wrestling, and training during his time in the military having served him so well, he wanted to do something to return that favor.

“Sports gave me a way to connect with people and find my place in a community. I was drawn to the competition, too—the chance to stand out, see how I measured up, and push myself to get stronger and faster.”

He continued, “Sports changed the course of my life. It opened doors that might otherwise have stayed closed and gave me a platform for so much of what I went on to do. When I thought about how much that had given me, I wanted to help create those possibilities for other people. That’s what drew me to the fellowship with the U.S. Olympic and Paralympic Committee.”

In March 2026, Del Grosso was diagnosed with stage 3 non-Hodgkin lymphoma. He underwent surgery, a port placement, and chemotherapy. Throughout his process, Del Grosso did his best to maintain training with support from a group called Be Fit, Be Well, which gave him access to a community, trainers, and tracked progress when he needed fitness to be a part of his cancer journey. He feels that thanks to their help, he was in a better position to overcome the adversity he was faced with; even if he admittedly may not have been in the best of moods some days.

“They were patient with me, even on the days I showed up frustrated, which seemed to be most days. Sometimes I just needed to push a sled and work some of that out. They understood that and created the space for me to find peace.”

One month following completion of chemo, Del Grosso chose to test his fitness by climbing a 14,000-foot mountain in Colorado. He would pass that test and felt proud of what he had done and was glad that his fitness continued to serve him.

Del Grosso stated, “That climb was about feeling like my body was mine again. It wasn’t easy or pretty. It took me forever, and there were moments I wanted to quit. But I had chosen that challenge, and finding my way through it helped me reclaim a sense of agency. I needed that to begin moving forward from cancer and chemo and feel that I could shape what came next.”

The husband and father is grateful but not satisfied. Del Grosso is forward-focused and is looking ahead to more challenges and doing what he can to make a difference. That is why he is involved in the upcoming Military World Games, set to take place in the summer of 2027. He sees this monumental event as an opportunity to amplify stories of strength and show the world how veterans are still able to serve and be a positive force.

Del Grosso can serve as a positive example of the capabilities veterans have. He advised that they don’t need to pressure themselves into having everything figured out immediately. Instead, he suggests veterans start by finding something they are passionate about and find a way to integrate that into their everyday lives.

“Take some time to think about what you want your life to be about. What do you care about? Where would you like to make a contribution? Then find people doing things you believe in and get involved. You bring a lot with you from the military, and that experience can be valuable in places you might never have considered. Give yourself the chance to find work and a community that means something to you.”

M&F Senior Military Editor Rob Wilkins contributed to this Fit to Serve article.

#95. The Three Most Common and Costly Things People Miss When Buying a Used Bike

Before buying a secondhand bike, inspect these potentially costly trouble spots first.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

The customer came in right before a race because there was an issue with their shifting on the training ride. Yes, there was an issue with cable tension, but that wasn’t the biggest problem. The missing chip of carbon where the top tube met the seat tube overshadowed anything going on with the rear derailleur. When I asked the customer if he knew the chip was there, he said, “I bought the bike used and the seller said it was just a chip in the paint.”

Unfortunately, I’ve been on that end of the conversation with a lot of customers who brought in used bikes over the years. I get why someone would buy a used bike. Even when I ran shops, I would suggest used bikes as a way people could save money on a new (to them) bike. But there were too many times someone brought a used bike in for us to run through and we would find things like frame damage or wheels that needed to be replaced. Prices of new bikes have gone up dramatically over the last few years. Used bikes have their place for so many riders, but be aware of what you’re buying. Sometimes between the price of the used bike and then the parts and labor needed to make it ride-ready, you’ll be toeing the price of a new bike. Many of those new bikes also come with things like one free service or warranties from the manufacturer.

If you’re in the market for your next bike, it does make sense to consider used options. There are plenty of deals to be had on the used bike market. Here, I’ll give you the three most common mistakes I see people make when going the used route and give you my best practices when considering that used bike.

The biggest mistake I’ve seen people make is missing damage on the frame. I’ve had customers bring in used bikes where the frame had chips or cracks in the carbon or irreparable damage to aluminum frames. While there are shops that offer carbon repair, there are not a lot of reliable options for frame repair.

Let’s compare some pricing—an entry-level road bike is around $1,200 depending on the brand. Many times this will include some type of warranty, at least one free service or check on the bike, and at a minimum a free floor fit for you on the bike.

If the used bike’s frame needs to be replaced, then step one will be finding a frame compatible with as many existing components as possible. Many times parts like cables and housing, bottom brackets, and handlebar tape will need to be replaced when swapping to a new frame. Once a new frame is found, the parts listed above are added, and service gets put on the ticket, you are at or above the price of what that new bike would have cost.

This can be avoided by doing a thorough inspection of the frame when looking at a used bike. Do a thorough check of the frame—even the hard to get to parts like where the tires hide and under the frame. If I were buying a used bike I would bring a shop rag to wipe any dirty spots to do my due diligence. I wouldn’t recommend buying a damaged frame, unless you like it for wall art.

Wheels can be the second biggest money pit on a used road, gravel, or hybrid bike. When I was a service manager, we had to replace many wheels on newly purchased used bikes because the existing wheels were either damaged beyond repair or because the parts and labor to repair them outweighed the price of a new wheel.

The pricing was always surprising to people. Most shops I’ve worked in priced wheel builds around $100. If we were going to pull the hub (center of the wheel) and other components from the old wheel to install on a new wheel, there was a small, but additional charge. For people getting a used entry-level road, mountain, or hybrid bike, the labor of a wheel build, not including parts, could outprice the cost of a new wheel.

Reasons we would need to rebuild or replace a wheel were things like cracks in the rim at the spoke nipples, severe knocking in the hub (where the wheel develops too much lateral movement), or when the wheel was significantly out of true. Wheels can sometimes be straightened out (truing a wheel), but there are points where it can’t be brought back.

When looking at a used bike, there is a relatively easy way to check all of these wheel issues. First, look at the base of the spokes where they meet the rim. If you see cracks on the rim at any of these points, the wheel will need to get replaced. Once you check the base of the spokes, then hold the frame in one hand and the top of the wheel or tire in the other. Test for lateral movement in the wheel by holding the frame still and trying to move the wheel side-to-side. If it doesn’t move laterally, that’s another box checked.

Finally, spin the wheel while it is on the bike. Sometimes it can be hard to tell if the wheel is straight if the used bike has a flat tire. Try using your thumb as a guide. Hold your thumb a set distance from the rim surface (at least an inch). This technique will allow you to see if there is a severe wobble in the rim. Remember to keep your fingers far enough away from the wheel to not get them stuck in the spokes of the wheel as it spins. A small wobble can usually be fixed for under $50 at most shops.

This can be the hardest thing to see on a used bike because it can be really hard to tell how worn a drivetrain (chain, cassette or gears, and chainrings or crank) is with the naked eye. When someone is committed to buying a bike, a chain checker is one of the tools that can save you hundreds of dollars in the long run. A chain checker is a small, relatively inexpensive tool that checks how worn a chain is. By checking how worn a chain is, you can tell what other parts will need to be replaced. Many shops will recommend replacing an 11, 12, or 13 speed chain when a chain checker reads over 50 percent worn, replacing a chain and cassette or freewheel (gears on the back wheel) over 75 percent worn, and replacing chain, cassette or freewheel, and chainrings or crank (gears in the front near the pedals) over 100 percent worn.

If you don’t have the tool there are ways to check visually too. Sometimes you can see wear on the gears on the rear wheel (called the cassette or freewheel). When the teeth on the gears on the front or back start to become uneven and resemble shark teeth that is another quick visual check.

One fairly reliable trick to see if the chain is stretched is to try to pull the chain straight up and away from the gears by the pedals (called the chainrings). If it easily lifts up and away, and especially if there is a significant gap between the chain and chainring, there is likely a significant level of wear in the system. Having the chain checker is an easy way to tell just how much.

Pricing to get this fixed can easily exceed a few hundred dollars when all three components of the drivetrain (chain, cassette, and chainrings) need to be replaced. If the bike needs any additional labor that price can climb quicker than people expect.

When I ran a shop, I would always suggest customers get at a minimum a safety check or base-level tune-up on a used bike. This allows an experienced bicycle technician to inspect the bike, torque all the bolts and parts on the bike, and adjust things like shifting, brakes, and tire pressure. Even if the bike is a new bike that the seller said they just never rode, you never know who built it initially. I’ve had bikes in the stand that were in this category and the handlebar spun around with the slightest bit of pressure.

If you don’t want to take it to a shop, then consider options like local bike clubs, local bicycle nonprofits (our local example is the Coalition for Appropriate Transportation), or even an experienced cycling friend. Anyone who can run through the bike with an experienced set of eyes can help get you on the right path.

I used to suggest having the seller meet the potential buyer at my shop. This would allow both parties to be there when a service technician or adviser inspects the bike for an impartial assessment of the condition of the bike. Before using your local shop as the meet-up, give them a call to see if this is something they can offer.

This list includes the most common mistakes I would see specifically in the road, gravel, and hybrid categories of bikes. It does not touch on mountain bikes because that is an entire list in and of itself. Parts like suspension forks, rear shocks, dropper posts and pivot bearings are all things to be cautious about with used mountain bikes. If you have any other tips for buying a used bike let me know in the comments below.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures.
