#141. 3 Signs You’re Getting Faster—and When to Push Your Pace

Use these coach-backed cues to know if it’s time to adjust your workout targets.

Progress often presents itself in the margins of a training log: You finish a quality workout feeling strong instead of spent. The final interval of a workout comes with control rather than desperation. An easy run actually feels…easy.

Subtle signals like these can tempt you to speed up every run. But before you change your targets, you need to establish a clear pattern of progress. For example, your body may adapt to a hard workout within seven to 14 days, but noticeable pace and performance gains often take eight to 12 weeks, Laura Norris, an RRCA-certified run coach and exercise scientist, previously told Runner’s World.

But taking note of progress ahead of those longer-term speed gains acts as the ultimate motivator and can help inform even smarter training. So coaches share the signs you’re progressing your fitness and when to push the pace without sacrificing recovery.

The first sign you’re improving is when a familiar workout stops feeling like a desperate fight to get through. Your breathing never gets out of control, you hit your targets without straining for each split, and your form stays strong rather than falling apart.

Use this signal as a testament to smart training, rather than a directive to push pace even faster. Jon Mott, a three-time U.S. Olympic Marathon Trials qualifier and founding coach of Runnersfix, previously told Runner’s World that he wants runners to complete two or three speed sessions week after week—and recover well from them—before changing their pace targets.

The opposite signal matters, too. If a prescribed tempo pace suddenly feels like a race effort, don’t force it. This mismatch can point toward overtraining or inadequate recovery, Sam Renikoff, an RRCA- and USATF-certified run coach, previously told Runner’s World.

Fitness doesn’t only show up during a hard effort. It also shows up in the days after.

When training clicks, you may experience less lingering soreness, steadier energy on easy runs, and more confidence heading into your next workout. Peak weeks can leave you tired, but Norris notes that runners should generally return to feeling normal around three days after a hard session.

Mott uses easy runs after speed sessions as a barometer for progress. If a runner drags through those runs, he holds off on a pace increase—even if the speed workout itself went well.

Before you increase paces, ask yourself: Can I regularly complete hard sessions, recover from them, and still run my easy days easily? If not, hold your current targets.

Some runners don’t recognize the full payoff from a training block until race day actually arrives.

A strong run isn’t just a confidence-booster, it’s a collection of useful data. Maybe you held a faster pace than expected without a heart-rate spike, raced with control through the final miles, or recovered better than usual afterward. Renikoff says experiencing the payoff of your training during your race—without seeing its effects during your build—perfectly reflects the long-term nature of physiological adaptations.

Plus, a strong race can offer a useful new baseline for your next training block.

During your training cycle, when the above signs of progress show you’re getting faster—and you maintain those signs of progress for a few weeks, not just one workout—adjust one hard-workout pace at a time. Mott recommends a general increase of five to 10 seconds per mile for tougher sessions, including tempo runs, intervals, or VO2 max work.

Keep easy efforts easy, though. Mott notes that easy paces may barely change, even as a runner builds top-end speed, because those runs should emphasize recovery and not push intensity boundaries.

Give your new pace target a trial run before you commit. If you can only hold it for about half a workout the first time around, don’t panic; try again next week and gradually extend how much of the session you complete at that pace, Kai Ng, a New York City-based RRCA- and USATF-certified run coach, previously told Runner’s World. If you can only manage a few reps before falling apart again, that’s a sign your pace may have jumped too far.

Above all, don’t stack changes. Faster intervals and added mileage should not happen at the same time, Norris says. Let your new paces settle in for a few weeks, and stay alert for rising fatigue, pain, or an easy-day effort that feels too hard before progressing your mileage.

As Ng explains, your training should feel challenging enough to spark adaptation: not so hard that every workout leaves you completely wrecked and not so easy that every workout is a breeze. The right pace bump should also feel almost boring, because it’s controlled enough to repeat, small enough to recover from, but challenging enough to pull you forward.

Matt Rudisill is an Associate Service Editor who has been with Runner's World since 2025. A Nittany Lion through-and-through, Matt graduated from Penn State in 2022 with a degree in journalism and worked in communications for the university's athletic department for three years as the main contact and photographer for its nationally-ranked cross country and track & field teams. Matt was also heavily involved in communications efforts for Penn State football, men's basketball, and women's gymnastics. In his role with Runner's World, Matt has interviewed Olympians, world champions, and countless experts in the field to create service content that helps runners of all ages and experience levels train smarter and race faster. When he’s not out jogging, Matt can be found tweeting bad takes about the Phillies or watching movies.

#142. Is there a Best Time of Day to Work Out? Science May Have Figured Out Whether Timing Matters

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

The fitness industry has a remarkable ability to take something simple and futz with it until you need a spreadsheet. Apparently, just going to the gym wasn’t complicated enough. Now we have optimal meal timing, optimal sleep timing, optimal supplement timing, optimal carbohydrate timing and, of course, optimal training timing. Your biological clock must be consulted before squats. God forbid you train legs at 10:30 a.m. when your circadian rhythm had you scheduled for 4 p.m.

Well, some researchers actually put this one to the test, and they did it considerably better than the usual exercise study involving eleven college kids and a leg-extension machine. A randomized controlled trial published Sept. 25 in the Journal of Cachexia, Sarcopenia and Muscle took 108 men and women between 60 and 80 years old and first figured out when each person was actually strongest. They tested them at 8 a.m., noon, 4 p.m. and 8 p.m. on separate days. Then they assigned them to train either around their personal strongest time, their weakest time, or not train at all.

That’s a pretty clever setup because people really did have stronger and weaker times. On average, strength varied about 11 percent during the day, although individuals ranged from almost no difference to a whopping 34 percent. Peak strength showed up most often in the afternoon and evening. So the premise wasn’t stupid. You’re probably stronger at certain times of day, and the researchers proved it.

Then came the part Instagram optimization gurus aren’t going to like.

After 12 weeks, training when the subjects were naturally strongest produced no clear advantage in strength or lean-mass gains over training when they were naturally weakest. The researchers also compared people training at the various fixed times and couldn’t find a consistent superior time there either. Basically, your body may perform somewhat better at 4 p.m. than 8 a.m., but that didn’t translate into noticeably more muscle or strength over the course of the study.

Now, don’t run wild with this. These were healthy older adults, average age 67, not 25-year-old competitive bodybuilders on 8,000 calories a day and enough gear to make a racehorse nervous. Ninety-three participants made it into the final analysis. They resistance-trained twice a week with five exercises, three sets each, plus one moderate cycling session. So we can’t automatically declare that time of day never matters for anybody under any training circumstance. Science doesn’t give you that license.

But this study does reinforce something people who have trained for a long time already know. The best time to train is very often the time you can actually keep training.

The adherence numbers were over 90 percent in both training groups. That’s the part I find more interesting than whether someone’s quads possess a circadian sweet spot. A perfect program you miss twice a week isn’t a perfect program. A theoretically inferior workout you do religiously for ten years is going to kick its ass.

There’s also an important distinction between performance and adaptation. You may very well feel stronger later in the day. The subjects frequently were stronger later in the day. If you’re attempting a one-rep max, competing in powerlifting or trying to produce your absolute best performance at a particular hour, that could matter. What this study says is that being temporarily stronger when you train didn’t result in better long-term muscular adaptation in this particular population. That’s not the same question.

Which brings us back to the guy setting his alarm for 4:17 because somebody on a podcast told him testosterone, cortisol and Jupiter’s gravitational field make that the anabolic window.

Train when your life allows you to train hard and consistently. Eat correctly. Recover. Add weight or reps when you can. Keep doing it.

We’ve spent 50 years trying to discover the secret time to lift weights.

Turns out the important part may still be lifting the weights.

#144. These Are the Three Accessories You Need for a New Bike—And the One You Don’t

The right accessories can make your first rides safer, smoother, and more fun.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

During my time working in bike shops, I have sold hundreds, if not over a thousand, bikes, and significantly more accessories. I’ve seen some people buy every accessory under the sun while they get their new bike, and others opt out of any accessories other than a bottle cage. A bottle cage is a good start, but there are a few other accessories to make sure you have the best possible first ride.

New bike day is a big day. The price of a new bike from a name brand manufacturer can be a big expense, so it’s understandable to hesitate when having to buy more. However, I’ve seen too many bikes become a clothes rack in a basement because someone didn’t have the experience they were hoping for on those first crucial rides. Getting the right gear from day one can change those initial impressions from negative to positive, but be aware you don’t need to buy all the things at once.

Here we’ll talk about the three accessories I recommend on day one, the one accessory I’ve steered a lot of riders away from when getting a new bike, and a few honorable mentions to consider as you ride more. Whether you’re a seasoned rider or just looking for tips on your first bike purchase, this story is for you.

Assuming you’re buying a bike that comes with pedals, helmets have always been the first piece of gear I suggest to riders buying a new bike. While helmets are not foolproof, they are a significant line of defense in keeping you safe as a rider. I’ve personally broken five helmets over the years, one of those times the doctor told me it likely saved my life. Keep in mind you don’t need to spend hundreds of dollars on a great helmet. When considering a new helmet, Virginia Tech Helmet Rating is the go-to resource on helmet safety testing.

Tara Seplavy, deputy editor at Bicycling, recently published a story on some of the Bicycling team’s favorite picks from the top-rated Virginia Tech helmets. One of the highest value helmets from the top ten on the Virginia Tech list is the P2R A20 Mips. This helmet comes in at only $60. “With its excellent safety rating, great adjustability, and budget-friendly price, the A20 Mips outperforms many helmets that cost three, four, or even five times its price,” says Seplavy.

If you’re buying your fifth bike and think you don’t need a new helmet, consider this—most of the major helmet manufacturers recommend replacing a helmet every three to five years. This is due to things like sun exposure, normal use, and even repetitive small impacts over time. For riders looking for a higher level of performance out of a budget helmet, then consider the aero helmet from P2R. It’s priced at $100 and as our resident tester Tom Messina said, “it has no business being this good.”

I know, I know—a flat kit consists of multiple accessories. Typically my basic flat kit for people getting a new bike consists of: some type of inflation, tire levers, a multitool, the correct tube for the new bike, and something to carry it in. Some brands sell a flat pack that consists of all the above. If your new bike has internal storage and you plan on putting your flat kit in there, just be sure to make sure it all fits before your first ride.

Even for riders that have multiple bikes I suggest a new flat kit. Bikes have different requirements for tube sizes and valve types and lengths for different rims. There’s nothing worse than getting a flat and taking everything apart just to realize you have the wrong size tube or your valve isn’t long enough (let alone if your spare tube has a Schrader valve, but you need a presta).

If you have multiple bikes keeping a flat kit on each one also makes sense because when you’re taking a bike out you don’t have to switch around the flat kit. This means you’re less likely to forget something, and it takes away a hurdle from you getting out the door.

There are plenty of options to go with when considering inflation. I typically carry one to two CO2 cartridges and a CO2 inflator in a flat pack or frame storage because they take up such little room and can (sometimes) reset a bead on a tubeless tire. I also carry a frame-mounted hand pump on longer rides, because I’ve been stranded after running out of CO2 in the past. Mini electric inflators have been gaining steam in the past few years, and the convenience of them is hard to pass up.

A lot of bikes these days have more than one place to put a bottle cage, so if your new bike allows I suggest going with two bottle cages. Current full-suspension mountain bikes typically only fit one (I’m not a fan of a bottle on the down tube of a mountain bike), so that’s an exception to the suggestion.

I typically suggest recommending bottle cages to people getting a new bike over something like a hydration pack. The most impactful reason is because when you use a hydration pack it puts more weight on your sit bones when you ride. Water is one of the heaviest things you’ll carry on the bike, but you need it as you ride. Since you have to bring it, put that weight on the bike instead of having the weight sit on your sit bones.

There are two honorable mentions worth talking about—one has to do with safety and the other has to do with comfort. The first is a taillight. I didn’t mention it above because it’s less of a necessity if you’re strictly trail riding off road.

One of the things I would always hear about in the shop was, “but I’m not riding at night so I don’t need a tail light.” Daytime running lights have that name for a reason—you run them day or night. These lights help increase visibility of cyclists as we share the road with vehicles. Drivers can more easily spot riders thanks to varying strobe patterns of the light and some even have radar and cameras built in like the Garmin Varia series of lights. The radar in the Varia detects cars coming from behind and gives you a heads up on your phone, watch, or head unit. I couldn’t imagine riding on the road without a radar taillight at this point.

The second honorable mention is a pair of cycling shorts—specifically bike shorts that have a built-in chamois pad. These shorts help improve comfort like few other things when riding a bike. It took me years to convince my wife to try them, but now she won’t ride without a pair. I’ve tried a lot of bike shorts and I’ve learned that the bib style stay in place better throughout a ride compared to the standard shorts.

Another essential piece of advice when picking the right chamois is you get what you pay for. I’ve tried a $20 Amazon pair and I’m currently testing the Dottore Clima Bib Shorts from Q36.5. The Q36.5 bibs are by far the most comfortable bike shorts I have ever tried whether I’m doing shorter lunch rides or doing 100 mile gravel days. The flip side is they are also by far the most expensive pair of bike shorts I’ve ever tried, but there is a significant level of comfort no matter how many hours I’m in the saddle.

At this point it is safe to say that many of us have a smartphone. There are always exceptions, but throughout my time working in a shop I’ve come across a small handful of folks still using a flip phone. In addition to smartphones becoming an ingrained part of society, smartwatches are seen more and more on people’s wrists. If you have either of those things you don’t need a bike computer—especially to get into riding.

Bike computers are nice to have for training purposes and navigating a new area or route. But most of those things can be done on a phone or smart watch these days. I have used watches from Apple, COROS, and Garmin for tracking rides, navigation, and as a guide for training on a ride with success. If you’re a new rider and have a smartphone I typically suggest downloading Strava because it’s easy to track rides, the navigation tool is fairly user-friendly, and it’s easy to see your progress the more you ride.

Don’t get me wrong—I love my bike computer. It pools data from my heart-rate sensor, CORE body temperature sensor, cadence and power from my power meters, and even my sweat data through my Nix sensor. I can see every metric I can think of and most head units allow you to customize the layout on the screen. But the reality is that a worthwhile head unit is typically a few hundred dollars. Conversely the phone mount that I typically suggest costs less than $30 and is fairly universal. Bike computers make sense for some riders, but don’t start here if you’re prioritizing certain accessories over others for your new bike.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

#145. Solveig Løvseth Shares How She Kept Going After Calamitous Kona Collapse

With just a kilometer to go, Solveig Løvseth (NOR) looked like she had the 2026 Ironman World Championship win in the bag. For nearly eight and a half hours, she had seemed calm, even happy, out on the brutally hot and humid course, methodically working her way through the field on the bike and surging past Taylor Knibb with five miles left on the run to move into the lead. Now, with over a minute and a half gap, she was less than five minutes away from becoming the first woman to defend her title since all-time great Daniella Ryf in 2018.

That is, until seemingly out of nowhere she started to weave back and forth across the road before finally stumbling to the ground.

“I really wanted to stop,” Løvseth told Triathlete with a giant smile on her face. “I’ve been saying in a lot of interviews that I’m not that competitive. But I guess I am a little bit competitive since I didn’t want to DNF, but I still did prioritize my health because I did lay down.”

After that first moment meeting with the pavement, Løvseth found the strength to get back up. But after a few more steps, she was back on the tarmac. She waved off medical, trying to regroup to make it to the finish line despite watching her competitors stream past her.

At the pre-race press conference, Løvseth said she didn’t really have a race plan and would just see what happens. Collapsing so close to the finish line is certainly something you can never plan for.

Her will to continue resulted in an eighth-place finish, 25 minutes and 39 seconds after Knibb broke the tape. Making it to the line ensured Løvseth also stayed in the Pro Series hunt, ultimately placing second behind Laura Philipp, who took second at the 2026 Ironman World Championship.

Not winning the race cost her $182,000 in prize money between the championship title and the Ironman Pro Series title — not to mention multiples more in sponsorship bonuses and future contracts. But speaking with Løvseth at the finish line, it’s clear she doesn’t do triathlon for the money. You’ll be hard pressed to find a competitor more gracious in defeat.

#146. 6 Signs Your Skin Needs Medical Attention, Stat

Your skin is your most visible organ, so it’s easy to notice when something seems off. It’s normal to experience some skin issues from time to time, like itchiness, breakouts, or ingrown hairs. But when these skin symptoms stick around, it could be a sign that something more serious is going on.

Many of these skin issues get better with the right at-home remedies or changes in your skin care routine. For example, if dryness pops up when Old Man Winter comes along, slathering on a more intense moisturizer may help.

But if skin symptoms don’t go away with a little self-care — or they return frequently — a chronic skin condition might be the culprit. However, just because you have a lasting symptom or two doesn’t necessarily mean you have a chronic health issue.

Here are the symptoms you should watch for and what they might mean. And if they don’t improve, consider checking in with a dermatologist for a proper diagnosis and a plan of action.

If you wish you had cat claws to satisfy your skin itch, you could be dealing with eczema. Eczema is an umbrella term for several conditions that impact the skin, with atopic dermatitis being the most common.

With most forms of eczema, your skin may show signs of inflammation, such as:

These symptoms may flare up occasionally and then go into periods of remission, where your skin isn’t as irritated.

Allergies can also lead to itchiness. For example, if you’re allergic to a skin care ingredient, a fabric type, a pet, or another allergen, your skin might react as a way to tell you to avoid this trigger.

Ongoing or regular periods of itchiness are a reason to see a dermatologist.

A rash can affect the skin in various ways, including:

A one-off or temporary rash might result from friction or chafing from a new outfit item. It could also be a heat rash when sweat gets trapped in skinfolds or bodily creases.

A persistent rash could be a sign of eczema or allergies. However, different types of rashes can be a sign of other things. For example, a butterfly-shaped (malar) rash across the face is a common sign of an autoimmune disease known as lupus.

If you frequently experience skin rashes, talk with a dermatologist to help you get to the bottom of the issue.

Dry skin can be just that — dry skin. Common causes include:

But if your skin is so dry it makes you want to bathe in a vat of thick moisturizer, it could be a sign of psoriasis.

Psoriasis is an inflammatory skin condition potentially caused by an overactive immune system. It can lead to dry, cracked, or scaling skin. In fact, psoriasis often involves a buildup of scales or plaques on areas like the elbows or knees — though they can occur anywhere.

Psoriasis and eczema are different conditions, but they have overlapping symptoms that mimic each other. So if you experience these symptoms, it’s important to see a dermatologist to identify and treat the underlying cause.

Changes in skin color — including red, brown, gray, or purple patches of skin — can be a sign of various skin issues, including eczema, psoriasis, or allergies. But it can also be a sign of rosacea.

Rosacea typically involves persistent redness that looks like a sunburn or blushing. It may also lead to skin thickening.

The good news? Rosacea is highly treatable. So working with a dermatologist can help you address it.

No one is immune from developing the occasional pimple or ingrown hair. But sometimes, skin bumps can be a sign that something else is going on.

Acne is one of the most common skin conditions that could bring skin bumps like pimples.

Hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is another condition that causes painful, boil-like lumps to form underneath the skin. These bumps can turn into pus-filled pockets that may connect via tunnels. HS typically shows up in areas of high friction or where skin meets skin, such as the armpits or groin.

Other types of skin bumps may include ingrown hairs, which can get infected and turn into folliculitis.

Talk with a dermatologist to help you address any bothersome skin bumps you may experience.

Common moles are growths that develop when pigment cells (melanocytes) grow in clusters. The average adult has between 10 to 40 common moles.

An irregular mole, also known as a dysplastic nevus, is a type of mole that looks different from your common moles. If you have a dysplastic nevus (or several), schedule regular skin checks with a dermatologist to look for anything suspicious. Be sure to mention any changes in:

These types of changes could be a sign of a form of skin cancer such as melanoma, which occurs in melanocytes. Melanoma can develop anywhere, including on normal-looking skin, a common mole, or a dysplastic nevus.

Skin symptoms — like rashes, bumps, discoloration, dryness, or itchiness — may come and go. But if symptoms stick around or return frequently, consider seeing a dermatologist for an evaluation. Your skin may be telling you that there’s an underlying issue that needs to be addressed.

A dermatologist can provide a proper diagnosis and treatment plan to help reduce, or, in some cases, resolve your skin symptoms. If you don’t currently have a dermatologist, your primary care physician or nurse practitioner can refer you to one.

#147. It’s Nia Long’s Moment—Again

There is a specific kind of vertigo that comes with leaving a movie theater in the middle of the day. The world is suddenly too bright, too loud, and slightly unreal. You have, after all, been inside someone else’s carefully constructed reality for two hours. And then you’re back outside, blinking into the afternoon light, not quite returned to yourself, the movie still clinging to you like perfume. It’s in this particular state that I meet Nia Long for an early lunch in a quiet corner at the Chateau Marmont.

I have just seen Michael (the new Michael Jackson biopic) a month ahead of its April release. I’m still thinking about the film when Long, who plays Jackson family matriarch Katherine Jackson, arrives looking chic but low-key in an oversized blazer, wide-leg jeans, and a Miu Miu baseball cap pulled low. As we ease ourselves into the conversation, I’m struck by the strange doubling effect of the movie vertigo: the woman before me and the woman I have just watched, layered like two transparencies held up to the light.

On screen, Long plays Katherine Jackson with a studied stillness. The first time we see her, watching her boys rehearse, the frame holds on her loving face for just a few beats. She says almost nothing. She doesn’t have to. Juxtaposed to Colman Domingo’s blustering portrayal of Joe Jackson and Jaafar Jackson’s uncanny performance as his late uncle Michael, Long has found a way to make silence load-bearing. Restraint is the most visible thing in any scene she occupies.

In person she seems the opposite of restrained. She is blunt but also quite warm, with a dry sense of humor and a deep well of emotional intelligence. She is very much a Scorpio. She notices everything. And, in playing Mrs. Jackson (who is still with us at the age of 95), Long has tapped into the part of herself that knows how to let silence do the work. The word she reaches for when she talks about the experience of playing the matriarch—a word she will return to several times during our conversation—is grace.

“There have been moments in my life where I’ve been required to be more graceful than I’ve ever had to be in the past,” she says. “And that requires a sense of really being able to dig deep into some sort of self-examination. Like, what do I stand for? What’s important to me, ultimately, regardless of Hollywood, the noise? And number one, for me personally, my children come before anything. And so I think when you look at Michael’s journey, and you look at Katherine’s journey, the only way you thrive and survive is through a tremendous amount of grace.” She pauses. “What I think I learned from her is that sometimes grace is really quiet.”

Long occupies a place in our cultural memory that few actors do. She is, for a certain generation, the platonic ideal of ’90s Fine, a phrase that’s not only about beauty or aesthetic but also about a certain feeling. Watching her as Nina in Love Jones or Jordan in The Best Man or Lisa in The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air, you conjure up a place and time and attitude that feels synonymous with Long. Of course, there is the image, and then there is the human sitting across from me, eating her go-to order of salmon with a side of mustard. And as she does, I ask what she thinks about the iconography and the nostalgia that surrounds her.

“My commitment to work is not for accolades or attention, or even to be famous, quite honestly,” she says. “But I do think because of my commitment to truth and purpose, there is a thing, and I don’t know what that thing is, that people see in my work. And it makes them feel good. It makes them feel inspired. It makes them feel like they know me.”

In a fickle Hollywood landscape that’s even more fickle when it comes to Black actors, Long doesn’t take the longevity and love she’s cultivated for granted. “There's highs and lows,” Long admits. “I’m having a great year, but I don’t know what’s happening next year.”

Long has starred in several iconic Black films, and she’s always been intentional about how she plays her characters. Much like with the Katherine Jackson role, she creates a version of the person that feels, to her, like something true.

“The only strategy I have in this game is my bank account. Let’s strategize how we’re going to make money and create generational wealth. That is where I’m strategic.” She laughs, scratches her palm. “My hand just started itching the minute I said money. That’s a good thing. Maybe something’s happening. Something’s coming.”

Once she’s in it, though, the work becomes something more personal. “I work hard to make sure that when I represent us, it’s not just someone putting their agenda on me. Whether it’s my hair, my makeup, my wardrobe, my lines.”

Now that her eldest son is in his 20s and her youngest son, 14, is old enough to stay home by himself, the actor feels ready to expand in all directions. She wants to continue to produce more films, craft new stories both behind and in front of the camera. She tells me about a new film she’s just wrapped shooting in New York, Don’t Ever Wonder, a romantic dramedy (“If that even exists anymore”) three years in the making. It will feature her onscreen reunion with Love Jones leading man Larenz Tate. Directed by Eugene Ashe and featuring an ensemble that includes Blair Underwood, Susan Kelechi Watson, and Algee Smith, the film is all about second acts.

“This is not a continuation of Love Jones,” she emphasizes. “This is a continuation of love, and of what happens once you’ve had your kids, they’re off to college, and you’re empty nesters. And that’s kind of where the story begins. There’s a lot of funny and there’s a lot of heartbreak, and I think it’s a really honest story.”

In talking to Long, I get the sense that honesty and truth is what she values most in the stories she tells. It’s what she values in life as well. Perhaps that’s what compels me, somewhere in the middle of our lunch, to unmask. I mention that I am conducting the interview a little out of sorts, having just ended a 12-year relationship.

“Okay, but when was it really over?” she asks.

"You didn’t have to gag me like that!" I say.

She laughs. I tell her that I am trying to imagine what life will look like—what I will look like—on the other side of this break-up. That’s when the idea of grace comes up again.

In 2022, Long went through that peculiar part of fame where something private becomes public overnight: her partner’s cheating scandal that resulted in the end of their 13-year relationship. She doesn’t have to go too deep into it if she doesn’t want to, I assure her, but the actor doesn’t shy away. On the other side of the experience with her ex, with whom she now has a healthy coparenting relationship, she has an unflinching clarity about the whole ordeal.

“The amount of pouring into myself that I’ve done is strong and mighty and intentional. I’ve now identified the things that I need to work on and the things that I need to heal. But I have also identified what is intolerable.”

That clarity has been hard-won. When the cheating scandal happened, there was a groundswell of support from fans, a protectiveness over Long as a woman and as a cultural touchstone. But in the instances that she’s talked publicly about it, including in our conversation, I’m struck by how her gratitude for the support is always tempered with nuance.

“I’m proud of myself for giving so much grace. For being able to say people make mistakes and things happen. It’s life. When the stakes are high, the news is big. I can’t do anything about that, but I don’t have to protect my ego in any of this.” She says all this very matter-of-factly, which is the only way she seems capable of saying things.

In the same straightforward tone she suggests I write out everything I need to say to my ex without sending it, because ultimately “it’s not about another person’s behavior. It’s about your bottom line and the magnitude in which you’re committed to self-love,” she says. “I don’t think it's healthy to hold onto things because then you’re just walking around with this burdensome energy. It could be writing it down. It could be meditation. It could be prayer. There’s a lot of ways to manage the noise. But you don’t have to respond to the noise with the undercurrent of your own trauma.”

I write down this last sentence because it is useful, but also because it is the key to something I’ve been watching Long do across the whole of our conversation: find the lesson in whatever she is given.

Long is working on her first memoir, a process she describes as one of the “biggest, bravest, challenging” things she’s ever done. It’s been a two-year process, a constant negotiation with her own relationship to letting go.

“I can read something I wrote two years ago and go: ‘Oh no, that’s not actually how I feel about that now.’” Long’s father, Doughtry Long Jr., a poet who died in 2020, told her the hardest thing about writing is knowing when to stop. “And I’m like: When is that going to happen? Because I haven’t gotten there yet.”

The memoir takes her back to Iowa City, where she spent six years of her childhood while her mother attended university. She was born in Brooklyn, in a Trinidadian household where everyone on the block was Black. Living in the Midwest during her formative years, she encountered few other Black girls, which disoriented her relationship to race.

“In writing this memoir, I realized the impact that experience had on my own view of beauty,” she says. “And my own self-acceptance of being a pretty brown-skinned little girl growing up in Iowa. I thought I was beautiful because my mother said it and my family said it, but the world told me something different.” She lets that sit. “So to now be a face for Estée Lauder, it’s kind of ironic, because I didn’t feel beautiful until Black Hollywood said I was beautiful.”

That an entire generation of Black women found a reflection of Black beauty in Nia Long while Long herself was still waiting to see it tells us something about how beauty standards work, and how much labor goes into transforming them. Nineties Fine, after all, did not emerge from a vacuum. It was a corrective, Black Hollywood’s answer to a century of the larger industry rendering Black women invisible or, worse, making us visible in ways that were wholly out of our control. Long’s most iconic characters—and indeed, Long herself—reflected a new idea of beauty, of the Black leading lady, expansive in some ways and still restrictive in others. Now, some 30 years on, Long embodies a new facet of being a Black woman in Hollywood.

“Black don’t crack” gets lobbed at Black women constantly, ostensibly as a compliment, but one that sometimes erases the very real pressure that comes with aging—especially aging on a public stage, especially when people have a particular image of you stored in amber.

But Long is not interested in pretending that the body is not a thing that transforms. “I’m 55. I got hormonal stuff going. Your body shifts, changes. It’s a whole new body.” She is not wistful about this. She also ate the truffle parmesan fries and does not appear remotely conflicted about it. She mentions the coming press tour for Michael, how she wants to be in beautiful gowns but she also wants French fries.

“I don’t deprive myself of anything that I want,” she says. “I find the balance.”

Beauty was never her primary currency, she says. It had to be something else, other inheritances: her father’s curiosity, her mother’s fierce self-possession. Tattooed and free-spirited, her mother wore leg warmers in the middle of summer because they matched her outfit, and she did not care for one second what anyone thought about that. Embarrassed, Long would beg her mother to take them off. She never did. As an adult, Long sees the power and freedom in that.

Our plates are carted away. Long has to leave soon for a pizza party at home with her youngest son and his friends. Before she goes, I ask her what freedom, at this point, is to her.

“Being able to do what you want to do when you want to do it, because it serves your spirit, not what everyone else thinks you need to be or should be,” she says. That type of freedom, Long adds, doesn’t require an audience.“You don’t have to have anyone else’s permission to do what you love. And it doesn’t have to be on the big stage. It could be in your kitchen. I know I have freedom right now to make a pizza. I’m going to do it.”

#148. Exactly What to Do During Your Marathon Taper, According to Experts

Experts share a research-backed protocol for reducing mileage and fueling well in the weeks before race day.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Tapering is one of the most important parts of any marathon training plan, but in many cases, it’s also one of the hardest to implement. Many runners start to feel antsy, restless, or anxious during this period of reduced training—some refer to it as the “taper crazies” or “taper tantrums.” Others often fear cutting back on mileage during the marathon taper, because they believe too much rest will undo all their progress right before their big race.

The truth is, though, that reducing mileage is important not only to allow for full recovery before your race, but also to allow you to reach peak performance.

To help you make the most of your marathon taper, here’s everything to know about this part of your training, including the benefits you can expect and exactly how to adjust your mileage and intensity as you approach race day.

Most marathon plans include a three-week taper, meaning you will run less and recover more during the final 21 days between your last long run and the start of the marathon.

If you skip the taper, you can miss the opportunity to tap into your true potential on race day. You may also set yourself up for injuries and delayed postrace recovery.

“So many runners train hard right up to the day of the marathon because they’re desperately afraid of losing fitness if they don’t,” Patti Finke, a retired run coach, exercise physiologist, and coauthor of Marathoning, Start to Finish, tells Runner’s World. “What they don’t realize is that in those last few weeks, it’s the rest more than the work that makes you strong. And you don’t lose fitness in three weeks of tapering. In fact, studies show that your aerobic capacity, the best gauge of fitness, doesn’t change at all.”

Giving your body time to recover before race day not only means your legs will feel fresher, but also stronger—which could pay off in better performance.

Research backs this up. A study published in Frontiers in Sports and Active Living reported that strict tapers, which progressively decrease training in the weeks leading up to race day, are distinctly effective. The researchers analyzed the training plans of more than 158,000 recreational marathon runners and found an association between a strict taper of up to three weeks long and better performance.

Specifically, it could improve average finish times by about five minutes, compared with a minimal, relaxed taper.

You might think that because you’re running less, you should eat less, too. But that’s not the case. Continue eating carbs to get ready for race day, but also make sure you’re eating enough protein.

Protein helps “to aid in the repair and recovery of muscle tissue damaged during the high-mileage phase of marathon training,” says Alan Titchenal, PhD, a retired sports nutrition professor at the University of Hawaii and marathoner.

If you don’t eat meat, fill up on protein from eggs, beans, dairy, and soy products.

To strengthen your immune defenses and possibly prevent a cold or flu, load up on vitamin C. Kiwis, orange juice, red bell peppers, broccoli, and strawberries are some potent food sources. (Make sure you’re getting enough micronutrients of other types, too!)

The following plan explains how to modify your running and eating in the crucial weeks before your race.

The first tapering week begins the day after your last long run (around 20 miles), three weeks before the marathon. The taper starts gradually, because this training still “counts,” and a dramatic drop in workload isn’t necessary yet.

The week before you start your taper should be your highest-mileage week. The first week of the taper, stick with the same basic running schedule you’ve been following, just decrease your total mileage from last week by at least 20 percent.

You should also avoid running extremely hilly courses or hill workouts, which can cause the kind of muscle tissue damage you want to minimize during your taper.

Your shorter weekday runs shouldn’t be much different than the previous week’s, but shave a mile or two off your longer midweek runs. Generally, weekday training should consist of one medium-long run of eight to 10 miles, one marathon goal pace run of four to six miles, one nonrunning day, and two runs of three to five miles.

Your weekend long run in the first week of your taper (two weeks before the marathon) should be a 12- to 14-miler at the same pace—not faster—as the previous week’s 20-miler.

Except for your run at marathon goal pace, all running this week should be at a relaxed pace of one and a half to two minutes slower per mile than your marathon goal pace.

This week is a transitional period. You’re halfway between your last 20-miler and the starting line of your marathon. Rest truly replaces training as the most important element of your race preparations, and race strategizing takes on increasing importance.

Your mileage this week should be about one-half to two-thirds the amount you ran during your highest-mileage week. Almost all your running should be slow—about one and a half to two minutes slower than marathon goal pace—except for two miles run at marathon goal pace in the middle of a midweek four-miler.

“Even this small amount of goal-pace running is important because it physically and mentally reinforces the pace you want to run on race day,” says Finke. “This follows the rule of specificity—simulating as closely as possible what you hope to do in competition.” It’s also fine to throw in a few 100-meter strides after one or two workouts just to help you stay smooth and loose.

Your weekday short runs should not exceed four miles, and your longest weekday run should be between six and 10 miles. Your weekend long run—one week before the marathon—should be eight to 10 miles. Any longer and your muscles may not be able to fully rebound before the race. Additionally, you’ll want to stop any strength training during this week.

While your mileage may be dwindling, you need to keep those calories coming in. Your body still needs to repair tissue damaged during your mileage buildup. “This is no time to diet,” says Titchenal.

Even though you’re running less, resist the temptation to cut way back on fat. A reasonable proportion of dietary fat (30 percent of your daily calories) is beneficial because it can be accessed as a backup energy source when stored carbs are used up.

Fat reserves can therefore postpone or prevent a race-day collision with the notorious “wall.” Just look for foods that are high in unsaturated fat, such as nuts or fish cooked in canola oil. Limit foods that are high in saturated fat and trans fats.

Beginning on Monday, avoid running longer than four miles. And when you do head out, remember that these jaunts are more for your head than your body, because training has little effect this week.

Almost all running should be done at one and a half to two minutes per mile slower than marathon goal pace—except, for example, a Tuesday two-miler at marathon goal pace, sandwiched by one-mile jogs. Again, if you want, throw in some quick 100-meter strides after one or two of your runs. This helps fight off the sluggish feeling that can occur during your taper.

Three days before the race, run just two to three miles easy. Then, two days before the race, don’t run at all. On the day before the race, jog about two miles—this is known as your shakeout run—to take the edge off your pent-up energy so you’ll sleep better that night.

For nutrition help, follow our guide on how exactly you should carb-load before a big race.

Wash all those carbs down with fluids so your energy and hydration levels are high on race morning. Alcoholic beverages don’t count toward your fluid totals, however, and you’ll need to make up for their diuretic effect by drinking extra fluids. You’ll know you’re adequately hydrated if your urine is pale yellow in color.

Don’t restrict salt from your diet either. Low-sodium intake combined with excessive hydration can lead to hyponatremia, a rare but dangerous condition that can afflict marathoners. Drinking sports drinks and snacking on salted popcorn and pretzels will help keep your sodium levels up.

A running veteran for more than a decade, Movold is a licensed strength and running coach for Runner’s World+ members and at the Mile High Run Club in New York City. When she’s not motivating class-goers through grueling treadmill workouts, you’ll likely find her zig-zagging boroughs on bridges throughout Brooklyn and Manhattan or training for her next marathon . She’s ready to push you to your next running goal as she chases her own—running a marathon in under 3 hours.

#150. How to Use Jojoba Oil for Hair: Expert Tips for Stunning Results

Jojoba oil is a must-have for moisturizing shampoos and skincare products.

The slippery oil is squeezed out of jojoba plant seeds. These plants are shrubs that pop up around the desert-y spots ofArizona, southern California, and Mexico.

Though it’s been used as a natural remedy for centuries, jojoba oil is having a major hair moment right now.

Keep reading to learn how to use it for strong, shiny hair and a healthy scalp.

“Jojoba oil is incredibly nourishing,” says Mayara Macedo, a hairstylist and scalp specialist in NYC. “It’s a natural oil that closely resembles the sebum our skin and scalp produce,” Macedo explains.

Because of this, Macedo says it’s super compatible with our bodies and works great as a balancing treatment — whether you have an oily or dry scalp.

While its proven benefits mainly revolve around its help with scalp health, jojoba oil can also strengthen and moisturize hair. However, it’s not the go-to pick for improving hair loss (that’s usually minoxidil).

If you’re dealing with dryness, jojoba oil is fantastic for adding moisture to your scalp,” Macedo says.

“Its natural hydrating properties help restore balance, leaving everything healthier and more manageable.”

“Jojoba oil has been known for its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties in addition to its conditioning and emollient properties,” says Kseniya Kobets, MD, board-certified dermatologist and Director of Cosmetics Dermatology at Montefiore Einstein Advanced Care.

These properties help out with dry, irritating dandruff.

This also explains jojoba oil‘s Mexican Indian history as a treatment for sores, which eventually caused researchers to flag its potential for improving skin conditions like acne and psoriasis (but please see a dermatologist for proven treatment options).

Though many say that jojoba oil grows hair, this claim is probably tossed around because it helps moisturize hair follicles — which can keep dryness at bay.

A dry environment can be a breeding ground for breakage, hair loss, and dandruff.

Also, your split ends say hello — jojoba oil can help by restoring hair health overall.

“If your scalp gets oily quickly after washing,” Macedo says, “It could be because your scalp is overcompensating, thinking it doesn’t have enough moisture and needs to produce more oil.”

She says adding jojoba oil helps signal to your scalp that it has enough, which can slow down excess oil production.

Although you can apply jojoba oil to the length and tips of your hair, Macedo says she prefers to use it only for the scalp, saying that other oils, like argan oil, will work better for the length.

Here;s how Macedo recommends using jojoba oil:

You can also buy shampoos or conditions that already have it!

Macedo says you can apply jojoba oil to wet or dry hair, depending on your goal.

“If you want to lock in moisture and add shine, you can try applying it to damp hair.” However, she doesn’t recommend this because it’s easy to accidentally apply too much or distribute it unevenly on wet hair, which she says can leave your hair feeling heavy and greasy.

“Applying it to dry hair reduces frizz and adds a light shine to styled hair,” she suggests.

Kobets recommends using oils overnight for extended exposure. However, she points out this can get messy (RIP pillowcases), so you can always apply them for a few hours and wash them off before bed.

Macedo also suggests being mindful of the amount you use — too much can make your hair look greasy, especially true for fine hair. “For a lightweight finish, start with a small amount and focus on the ends of your hair. But again, I’d recommend jojoba oil for the scalp and argan oil for the hair,” Macedo adds.

“If you’re using jojoba oil as a pre-wash treatment to balance scalp oil or as a deep conditioner, apply it before washing,” Macedo explains. “If you’re using it as a leave-in conditioner or frizz-tamer, you can apply it to freshly washed hair — careful not to apply too much.”

Kobets suggests washing the scalp after using oils, noting that her patients don’t always prefer to use them because they can reduce hair volume for some.

Kobets says that someone with a dehydrated scalp and coarse hair may want to leave the oil in to hydrate the scalp better. “People with fine or oily scalps usually want to wash the oils out,” she adds.

Jojoba oil is a natural moisturizing ingredient known for improving scalp health. It can also add shine and help strengthen your locks.

It’s not the move for improving hair loss, however.

Do a patch test to make sure you aren’t allergic first! Then you’re good to glow.

#151. ‘Starting Strength’ Remains a Time-Tested Program for All Lifters To Get Bigger and Stronger

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Today you’ll find no shortage of complicated ways to get strong. Apps track your every move, algorithms determine your training split, and a fancy watch tells you the rest. But the Starting Strength program takes a different approach: learn the big barbell lifts, perform them well, recover, add a little weight, and repeat.

Starting Strength centers on the big barbell lifts. You perform these lifts through a full range of motion, with small weight increases driving progress from workout to workout.

That’s why Starting Strength is still relevant—and why it’s worth reviewing here.

Strength training knowledge has evolved, but the core idea of doing the basics well and progressively asking your body to do a little more never goes out of style. So, does this old-school strength method still deliver, or has modern-day programming passed it by?

Starting Strength is the brainchild of Mark Rippetoe, a competitive powerlifter turned strength coach who began coaching at the Wichita Falls Athletic Club in Texas during the 1980s. Decades of teaching people to lift convinced Rippetoe that beginners didn’t need complicated programming, but only needed the basics to get stronger.

That philosophy became the book Starting Strength: Basic Barbell Training. But the title is misleading because Starting Strength isn’t only for beginners. It’s a system for teaching and developing strength that still applies, no matter how much lifting experience you have.

The programming centers on a simple idea: Apply enough stress to disrupt homeostasis, recover, and come back stronger. Beginners are better positioned to take advantage because they don’t need a massive training stimulus to improve.

That’s the engine behind Starting Strength’s famous novice linear progression. Instead of worrying about complicated blocks or peaking cycles, beginners focus on adding small amounts of weight from workout to workout. 1.25- and 2.5-pound plates become valuable tools for progression.

It’s old-school programming at its simplest.

Rippetoe emphasizes a small number of compound barbell lifts that use lots of muscle mass through a large range of motion, training three days per week.

But exercise selection is only part of the equation. Consistency and progressive overload make the method work. Beginners repeatedly practice the squat, bench press, overhead press, deadlift, and power clean. Once form is down with appropriate load, the goal is to make small weight progressions each workout.

That’s the method’s beauty—and eventual limitation. Beginners can get stronger quickly because even small doses of training move the needle. But you cannot keep adding weight to the bar every workout forever. Starting Strength uses that rapid adaptation window for as long as possible before more complex programming becomes necessary.

For a novice lifter, that’s a feature, not a bug.

Rippetoe has some very specific ideas about how these lifts should be performed and why they are in his program.

Rippetoe favors the low-bar back squat performed through a full range of motion, meaning the hip crease ends below the top of the knee. In his system, the low-bar position maximizes muscle involvement over a large range of motion.

Bar path is another big deal. The bar should stay over the midfoot throughout the rep because a straight vertical line is the most efficient path between two points. Rippetoe also coaches driving the knees out, which increases hip external rotation and helps maintain the desired lower-back position at the bottom of the squat.

One distinctive Rippetoe coaching point is to shrug at the top of the press, which places the shoulder blades in a better position to support the bar overhead. Don’t obsess over keeping the wrist perfectly straight, either. Rippetoe considers roughly 10 to 15 degrees of wrist extension normal during the overhead press.

Rippetoe’s setup again centers on the midfoot: The bar starts over the middle of the foot, touching the shins, with the shoulders slightly in front of the bar. Pushing the knees out also helps engage the glutes in the pull. There’s even attention to where you hold the bar. Rather than burying it deep in the palm and letting it roll down during the pull, he recommends placing it between the creases near the base of the fingers to help reduce callus formation.

The bench press gets the same nuts-and-bolts treatment. Rippetoe recommends looking just past the bar while lying on the bench and suggests a grip of about 22 to 28 inches between the index fingers, which should give most lifters vertical forearms. The bar rests toward the heel of the palm, with the fingers and thumb wrapped around it.

You’ll alternate between the power clean and the deadlift later on in the program. Although it’s an explosive exercise, you perform it at the end of the workout instead of the beginning because Rippetoe focuses on strength, not power. It adds an explosive element while sticking to his core philosophy.

You establish your working weight, perform your reps with good technique, recover, and—if everything goes according to plan—add a little more weight next time.

You don’t walk into the gym, slap plates on the bar, and hope your joints got the memo. Rippetoe recommends ramp-up sets to work toward your working weight gradually. These sets prepare you for the heavier work without creating unnecessary fatigue.

For beginners, Starting Strength’s bread and butter is 3 sets of 5 working reps on the primary lifts. The deadlift is the exception, where the program calls for only one working set of five. The program aims to provide enough training stress to build strength without burying a novice in volume.

When you finish your working sets, plan on increasing the load for the next workout. Rinse and repeat. But Rippetoe recommends against big weight jumps, and that’s where smaller plates become your friend. Those little plates may not look impressive, but adding 2.5-5 pounds adds up over time.

He recommends two minutes of rest between sets for beginners, with intermediate and advanced lifters extending rest periods to between three and five minutes. Rest long enough to maintain technique and produce the effort required for the next heavy set.

As long as the lifter can train, recover, adapt, and return capable of doing slightly more, there’s little reason to complicate the process. That’s Starting Strength progression in four words: Do five, add weight.

It begins with an A/B setup built around three exercises per workout. The order matters. Squat first, press second, and deadlift last, so you can tackle the squat while fresh before moving from upper-body pressing to the session’s heaviest pull.

Train three nonconsecutive days per week, alternating Workout A and Workout B. For example, you’d perform A/B/A during Week 1 and B/A/B during Week 2.

You squat every session, alternate the two major presses, and pull from the floor. The simplicity lets beginners focus their energy on learning the lifts and getting stronger. Rippetoe suggests running this for 3 weeks, but you can run it until you fail the same weight across multiple sessions despite adequate sleep, food, and rest, or progress stalls. This often happens because recovery suffers from squatting and pulling heavy three times per week.

The program begins introducing power cleans and assistance exercises while maintaining the three-day schedule and squatting every workout. Deadlifts begin alternating with power cleans instead of being performed every session.

Here’s what a two-week sequence looks like.

Power cleans take some of the pulling workload off deadlifts, while chin-ups and other assistance exercises start filling gaps left by the initial program.

Next, we’ll dig into those other assistance exercises with programming suggestions.

Two of Rippetoe’s favorites are chin-ups and heavy EZ-bar lying triceps extensions. Chin-ups provide plenty of upper-back, lat, and biceps work to balance all that pressing. Once you can knock out around 12 to 15 bodyweight reps, he recommends adding weight. For lying triceps extensions, he prefers lowering the bar behind the head rather than a skull crusher, for 10 to 15 reps.

But those aren’t the only tools in the Starting Strength toolbox. Here are a few assistance exercises that he suggests.

Halting Deadlift: Strengthens the lower back and reinforces position during the first part of the pull, using roughly 70–85% of deadlift 1RM for 5–8 reps.

Rack Pull: Overloads the upper portion of the deadlift and targets lockout strength. Sets of 5 work.

Pause Squat and Press: Removes some momentum and forces you to produce force from a dead stop or paused position. He recommends 50–60% of 1RM for sets of five.

RDL and Stiff-Legged Deadlift: Adds posterior-chain work with 65–75% of deadlift 1RM for sets of 5–10.

Good Morning: Another posterior-chain option, performed for 8–10 reps with no more than 35% of squat 1RM.

Dips: Rippetoe favors full ROM, lowering the shoulders below the elbows, and prefers dips to decline pressing for lower-chest work.

Pendlay(Barbell) Row: Adds back volume and is generally performed for 5–10 reps.

Back Extension and GHR: Posterior-chain work for 3 sets of 10–15 reps.

The incline bench press and push press are also options.

Choose assistance work because it solves a problem, not because you’re bored. There’s no cap on how many assistance exercises you should include, but Rippetoe includes only one or two.

If you want to try this program, you’ve got to love the barbell. Starting Strength isn’t designed to accommodate every training preference. It teaches a specific approach to getting stronger, with the barbell as the star.

No program is perfect because each is designed for a specific goal that might not be yours. Keep that in mind as you review these pros and cons.

Simplicity: Beginners often get distracted, and Starting Strength clears away that noise. Learn the lifts, perform your work sets, recover, and try to lift a little more next time.

Frequent practice: Squatting every workout and regularly benching, pressing, and pulling gives a beginner plenty of opportunities to develop skill with the major lifts.

Efficiency: Three main exercises can produce plenty of stimulus without burying you under junk volume. Assistance work can gradually enter the picture, but it remains secondary to the lifts responsible for most of the program’s progress.

Builds Strength: It can take anywhere from 3- 9 months to exhaust the linear progression in Starting Strength. In that time, you’ll get brutally strong.

Expiration date:  Workout-to-workout linear progression has an expiration date. As the weights get heavier, recovery gets harder, and adding another five pounds won’t work.

High Recovery Demand: Squatting three times per week works well when the weights are manageable, but as the load increases, recovery demands rise. Accumulated fatigue can make it harder for some lifters to recover between sessions.

Restrictive exercise selection: Rippetoe has strong opinions on which lifts to perform and how to perform them. The low-bar squat is a good example. He prefers it and provides detailed reasoning for its use, but that doesn’t mean every lifter must low-bar squat to become strong.

Not for muscle: You’ll undoubtedly gain muscle while getting stronger, especially as a beginner, but someone whose number-one goal is hypertrophy may benefit from greater exercise variety and targeted volume.

The pros and cons stem from the same place: Starting Strength knows exactly what it wants to be. That’s fantastic when its goals align with yours and less useful when they don’t.

Starting Strength may be old-school, but old doesn’t mean outdated. Barbells are still awesome, gravity hasn’t released an update, and beginners still need to learn how to squat, press, and pull while getting stronger.

It gives novice lifters a clear mission: learn a handful of big lifts, perform them consistently, recover between sessions, and gradually add weight—few distractions and nowhere for program-hopping to hide.

I also appreciate that there’s more beneath the surface than the program’s reputation for “just doing 3×5.” Rippetoe gets into the weeds on technique, bar position, breathing, exercise order, assistance work, and introducing exercises such as power cleans as the lifter progresses.

But Starting Strength should be viewed for what it is: a starting point. Eventually, the easy workout-to-workout gains disappear. Recovery takes longer, weaknesses become obvious, and programming needs to become more customized.

That’s not Starting Strength failing. That’s the lifter succeeding.

Starting Strength still offers something rare in fitness: a straightforward plan that teaches you to stop majoring in the minors and to start getting stronger.

Upper and lower abs aren’t separate muscles; exercise choice can bias the work, but not isolate either region.

Your grip position may be the missing piece when a lift feels uncomfortable, unstable, or weaker than it should.

There’s a workout sweet spot between intensity and recovery. Finding it is the challenge.

#152. 5 Useful Tips to Consider When Hosting a Yoga Retreat

Calin Van Paris is a YJ editor. Here, she talks to yoga teacher Dusty Swehla, who has led 16 yoga retreats around the world, about what to keep in mind if you’re planning to host. When you’re ready to explore more retreat and wellness travel options, we have destinations.

If you teach yoga classes, hosting a yoga retreat can feel like a normal—even expected—next step. Retreats seem to be everywhere these days. According to BookRetreats.com’s 2026 State of Retreats Report, which is comprised a survey of more than 1,000 U.S. travelers along of the site’s own learnings, searches for yoga retreats are up 15% year over year. Additionally, nearly 80% of those polled are interested in partaking in a yoga retreat within the next year.

The trend is ubiquitous within the yoga industry, with resorts, studios, influencers, and teachers all students to explore their practice in a beautiful place. Retreats also invite participants to approach on their yoga in a new, focused way, without the distractions of everyday life.

But getting a group together in any capacity, even to do something as healing as yoga, comes with its own challenges and learning curves. Weather patterns, travel realities (think flight delays, illness, lost luggage, etc.), proper planning, and personalities all play a part in the success of a yoga retreat. And although not all of these variables are within your control, certain elements are.

“I actually have a questionnaire, and then I meet with everybody, whether it be on Zoom or in person, just to see if we mesh,” says Iowa-based yoga teacher Dusty Swehla, who has hosted 16 retreats around the world. On one of her recent gatherings at Vista Celestial in Uvita, Costa Rica, she walked me through some of the most important things she’s learned along the way. And much of it comes down to something quite simple. “It’s just figuring out what works and what doesn’t,” she says.

Whether you’re planning a retreat, are attending a trip, or are just interested in the ins and outs of hosting, these considerations take some of the guesswork out of the process.

Patience is an important part of hosting retreats. As with building any business, it takes time and experience to learn the ropes, develop a rapport with resorts and students, and curate an event with seeming ease. If you feel called to do so, keep putting yourself out there.

Surprise: you don’t have to host a retreat across the world for it to be a meaningful experience. Swehla hosts retreats in locations including Costa Rica and Peru, but her initial offerings were much closer to her home state.

“I started with smaller, single-day retreats,” she explains. “Just a one-day immersion, or maybe a weekend in places like Wisconsin or near Chicago in the Midwest.”

Deciding to begin with an experience that’s more intimate and closer to home allows you to learn the ins and outs of hosting without the inevitable snags that come with international travel.

This option also gives you a low-stakes opportunity to build trust with your community of students. After enjoying a few shorter experiences with you, the option to buy a plane ticket to practice under your guidance might make a little more sense.

If you’re getting into the retreat game for the money, you might be disappointed to learn that there often isn’t much takeaway for the teacher. As for attendees, there’s a reason that partaking in a retreat often comes with a steep price tag.

Some resorts and retreat centers offer packages, often based on head count for hosting teachers—especially as you develop a working relationship with a destination. But most simply provide room, board, and practice spaces. The rest is up to you. Be sure to calculate all of the costs.

Alternatively, if you host your own retreat at an Airbnb or other rental, everything—including the rental fee, meals, goodie bags, transportation, and any additional services or experiences—fall on you. For her part, Swehla typically hires at least one helper who also enjoys free access to the retreat.

Finally, allow yourself the permission to determine how much your own time and teaching is worth and price your retreat accordingly.

Marketing is an essential part of any yoga retreat. After all, how can anyone sign up if they’re not aware of the option? More often than not, all of the publicity is your job.

“Some places will put your retreat on their website, but not unless you ask them,” says Swehla. “I really rely on my own marketing and reach.” To that end, Swehla likes to tie each of her retreats to a theme (such as self-love) that helps personalize the journey and focus the promotional material. Flyers, studio announcements, and of course social media are all crucial tools for generating interest.

As you cultivate a reputation as a retreat host, filling those retreat slots will likely become a more natural feat. But at the beginning, it’s all about believing in yourself enough to spread the word on your own behalf.

Leading a yoga retreat requires that you go with the flow, wear many hats, and get comfortable with shifting plans and personalities.

“You have tons of balls in the air at one time,” says Swehla. “You need to be able to pivot and stay flexible, whether it be issues with the food, people complaining—and yes—people getting sick.”

For this reason, Swehla doubles down on her suggestion of starting things small. Not only do simpler retreats allow you to observe how people interact in these kind of containers, they also enable you to observe how you handle unexpected snafus.

The best way to figure out how to host your yoga retreat? Participate in those led by others.

“Go on a couple retreats and take note on what works, what doesn’t, what do you like, and what don’t you like,” says Swehla, who suggests looking to your dharma, or your life’s purpose, to determine what you really want. “What brings you happiness and joy?”

Ultimately, your yoga retreat is a reflection of you. Taking the time to get clear about your why can help you figure out what makes sense for your facilitated experiences, allowing you to say no to the rest.
