#153. For Some Women, Weight Loss Drugs Are a Secret They Keep From Their Partners

The first time Caroline went on Wegovy, it wasn’t a secret: She told her boyfriend, mother, and close friends. Over the course of six months, they watched as she shed 30 pounds, going from 130 back to what she calls her “healthy original weight” of 100 pounds. Even still, her loved ones worried about the extent of her weight loss and didn’t want her to lose even more.

“I had tried every way under the sun to lose weight,” Caroline tells SELF. The 34-year-old, who lives in Montreal, asked to use only her first name to protect her privacy. “I was really tired of trying.” At five feet four inches, she wasn’t obese and didn’t think her primary doctor would approve a prescription.

So she went online and found a doctor who prescribed the medication over the phone, unaware of how much Caroline actually weighed. Immediately after starting Wegovy, she says, “the weight started coming off incredibly fast.” After six months she decided she wanted to stop. But as soon as she got off Wegovy, the weight came back: She gained 10 pounds in a month. “I realized, I can’t stop,” Caroline says.

So for the past six months, she has been taking Wegovy again, this time at a maintenance-level dosage. But there’s one big difference: This time, she’s keeping it a secret from her boyfriend and family. “Now that we’re talking about kids, he’s seen all the impacts [of the drug] and he’s done with it,” she says. Since she lives alone, hiding her medication from him is relatively easy—she stashes it in the back of the fridge, since it needs to be kept cold. But she’s still worried he’ll see it, and when they travel together, she has to hide the medication in the hotel room fridge—or, if they’re visiting his parents, in their refrigerator. “So imagine, I’m hiding stuff in my parents-in-laws’ fridge, hoping they won’t see them,” she says. “It’s super awkward.”

Caroline isn’t the only woman going to great lengths to keep her GLP-1 use a secret. On a recent thread on the r/GLP1microdosing subreddit, women shared their tips and tricks for hiding medication from their partners. One stashes them in a tomato paste box. Another uses a play food container from a child’s pretend kitchen. Still others have turned to an opaque feta cheese container, butter stick box, anchovy paste box, empty bottles of women’s probiotics and Alani Nu supplements, a plastic to-go container, a metal water bottle, a box of wine, and a baking soda box in the back of the fridge—all to conceal the weight loss medication.

“It’s a real thing,” Kia Mitchell, MD, who specializes in family and obesity medicine, tells SELF. She has seen numerous women in her Jacksonville, Florida, practice go to similar efforts to hide their medication from their partners. The first time she heard about this pattern, it was from a patient who “just didn’t want to turn this into a debate at home,” she says. “She just wanted to have the option” to take the medication. “A lot of my patients are similar,” Dr. Mitchell adds. “There’s this loss of control with the gaining of the weight, but being able to control the narrative around weight loss has been empowering and exciting” for her patients. “Because now they can reveal it on their own terms. That’s where the control comes back.”

The reasons women want to reveal their weight loss medications on their own terms are palpable in that subreddit thread. “If my husband found out, it would just be a series of lectures,” wrote a user called Vivid-Act-6442. “Just don’t want to hear any negative or critical opinions,” wrote another user called [deleted]. “After 52 years of marriage, one knows one’s mate.” One woman chimed in to say she was hiding her meds from her teens—because she didn’t want them telling her ex-husband. “I just don’t feel like the questions,” she wrote.

Dr. Mitchell has mixed feelings about this type of secrecy. Anyone on a health journey benefits from having a “network that’s really cheering for you,” Dr. Mitchell says. “Dealing with something like this, I want people to have community.” But, she continues, it’s “empowering and protective” for women to get to decide who knows about their weight loss drugs—even if, ideally, “you really want to be in a relationship with someone you trust completely.”

From a medical standpoint, there are some potential pitfalls to hiding GLP-1s from a significant other. For one, it’s easier to get pregnant while taking them—Mitchell says she has “several GLP-1 babies” in her practice. There are also the drugs’ potential side effects, and hiding medication can make it more difficult for a patient to turn to her partner if she’s struggling. And more generally, secrecy can cause stress. “When someone is trying to lose weight, we want their stress hormones to be as low as possible,” Dr. Mitchell says. “If you’re trying to hide [medication], we’ll be fighting an uphill battle if you’re stressed about that.”

The bigger issue is hiding GLP-1 medications from your regular doctor, something that has become much easier thanks to the rise in telehealth companies like Hers and Ro. That’s a problem Caroline is having: She didn’t tell her doctor both times she went on Wegovy and still doesn’t want to, even though she’s concerned about how the drug may interact with the Accutane and Ritalin she takes. The idea of admitting her GLP-1 use to her doctor makes her anxious, since she doesn’t want to break their trust. But her annual physical is coming up, and her doctor will see that she’s lost a lot of weight.

“I use ChatGPT as my doctor at this point since I can’t be honest with my own doctor,” she says. “I say, ‘Hey, this is my actual weight, what type of dosage is okay to take with other drugs?’” Admittedly, she adds, this is “probably not the best option.”

Caroline got her Wegovy prescription through Hers. During the process she was only asked for basic bloodwork and received no counseling, just “documentation to read.”

Craig Primack, MD, the head of weight loss at Hers, tells SELF that the company’s prescribing doctors “do ask [patients] to talk with their primary care doctor about the care they’re getting.” He acknowledges that the company doesn’t do much in the way of direct counseling but says that “we ask about mental health and anxiety and stresses.” The Hers app contains what Primack terms “psychologist-built information” about topics such as sleep management and eating personas.

Dr. Primack is “absolutely” aware that some patients hide their medication from their partners. He says that some don’t want to say anything until they’ve proven they can lose weight; some don’t want to say anything because of the medication’s cost; some worry about how it could change the way they and their partner see each other. “Your weight and persona set up a dynamic in your couple,” Dr. Primack says. “When you start changing that, sometimes spouses get very jealous—‘Oh my god, you’re becoming potentially more attractive.’ Not that weight is directly linked to that, but that’s what I hear them say.”

And then, of course, there’s the more general stigma associated with weight and weight loss. “One benefit of telemedicine is it takes the bias and stigma away,” Dr. Primack says. “One reason we are here is because people are uncomfortable going to talk to their primary care doctor about it.”

Whether or not Caroline decides to tell her doctor about her medication, she still will have to grapple with the larger issues that her Wegovy use, and her secrecy around it, have raised. “It’s very stressful,” she says. “The fact that not only can I not talk about it, but I’m also unable to get off of it. I don’t love the idea of taking medicine like that forever, but I’m kind of stuck with it.” She doesn’t want to gain weight, she explains. “But I wonder to which extent I’m too harsh with my criticism of my body. Maybe my goals are too intense.”

Given the incredible degree of vulnerability and sensitivity tied up with weight loss, the dilemma about whether to tell people about a GLP-1 medication is all too understandable. But how to tell people can make it easier, says Rachel Goldman, PhD, a clinical assistant professor in the department of psychiatry at NYU Grossman School of Medicine and a clinical psychologist whose areas of expertise include weight management and disordered eating, tells SELF. “Framing it around their own experience and needs can make the conversation feel more manageable and less like something they have to defend,” she says.

Since deciding whether to have this conversation isn’t easy, Dr. Goldman would first encourage a patient to “think about their why,” she says. “What led them to this decision? What does this treatment mean for their health and wellbeing?” Once someone feels more grounded and confident in their reasoning, “it becomes easier to communicate it with that confidence.”

Dr. Goldman also suggests coming up with some sample scripts before having the conversation. “I would suggest that they lead with their own personal experience and not think about others and why/how others are using it,” she says. “I would encourage them to use ‘I’ statements.”

It’s also helpful to think ahead of time about a partner’s potential reaction and to have a plan in place for different scenarios. Thinking about what you want from a partner is likewise helpful—is it support, understanding, “or simply space to make their own health decisions without judgement?” Dr. Goldman asks. She adds that it’s important to remember that a partner’s initial reaction might not be their final reaction—it can take time for someone to process a conversation and to work through their own biases and misconceptions.

“Ultimately,” she says, “the goal isn’t to have a perfect conversation, but it’s to open the door to more honesty, connection, and support over time.”

But if that fails, there’s always a box of anchovy paste.

#154. Can Your Road Bike Handle a Cyclocross Race?

A 33mm tire may fit, but mud clearance, gearing, and frame durability still matter.

A decade ago, it was still common to see Tour pros racing on 23mm tires, with 25mm considered progressive. Views on tire width have shifted. At this year’s Tour de France, most riders were on tires labeled 28mm to 30mm; mounted and inflated, many measured 30mm to 32.5mm. The widest setups measured in the paddock were more than 33mm—above the UCI cyclocross limit.

Road bikes with room for 32mm tires are increasingly common. Some clear rubber as wide as 40mm. So you might be wondering: Can I install a pair of 33mm cyclocross tires on my road bike and race the local ’cross?

As these photos show, I mounted 33mm cyclocross tires on Trek’s Madone 8 road bike. And there was even a bit of clearance, even though Trek states the Madone’s maximum tire clearance is 32mm.

But just because you can doesn’t mean you should. There’s more to racing cyclocross on a road bike than stuffing knobbies into any frame that clears them.

CX race bikes are designed to take a 33mm knobby tire with generous mud clearance. A road bike’s stated maximum tire width leaves room for some debris around a slick tread, but not for peanut-butter mud.

Then there is all the other stuff you will find on a cyclocross course: sand, ruts, off-camber turns, barriers, and sharp corners.

You’ll dismount, shoulder the bike, pound into bumps and holes, and crash.

Your road frame wasn’t built with all of cyclocross’s many charms in mind. The engineers I’ve asked about this point to the seatstays as particularly vulnerable to damage in cyclocross.

There is precedent, though. Toon Aerts won the 2025 European Cyclocross Championships on an Orbea Orca OMX road frame fitted with a fork from the Orbea Terra Race gravel bike. That’s a pro-level workaround for a sponsored athlete, not a green light for every road bike.

Your road bike’s gearing is probably too high for a ‘cross course, which is likely to feature steep, slippery climbs and slow technical sections. Road gearing can mean more dismounts; an easier gear can help keep you riding instead of getting off to push.

If you want to race ‘cross without buying a cyclocross bike, a gravel bike is a better place to start. It usually has lower gearing and is built for bigger impacts and rougher use. A gravel bike definitely has room for a 33mm tire. If it’s a modern model built for 50mm-plus tires, it’ll have heaps of mud clearance—so much that a 33mm CX tire might look a little lost in there.

And if you use your gravel bike, you can also use wider gravel tires. The UCI caps CX tire width at 33mm, but that only applies to races they sanction.

Your local CX series is probably not UCI-sanctioned.

Local rules vary, so check before you line up. If wider tires are allowed, a wider gravel tire may offer more comfort and grip—and could even be faster, depending on the course.

There’s a handling trade-off. CX bikes are made to whip through tight, slower-speed corners; gravel bikes usually favor stability. So a gravel bike might feel too long, too stable, and the steering too slow, on a tight ‘cross course. But you might actually prefer a more placid-handling gravel bike in the anaerobic blur of a cyclocross race.

So, can you ‘cross your road bike? Technically, yes—if a 33mm tire clears without rubbing, the course is dry, and your gearing suits the terrain. But just because you can doesn’t mean you should. If you already have a gravel bike, start there. Check the rules, fit the tires, and go have a race.

A gear editor for his entire career, Matt’s journey to becoming a leading cycling tech journalist started in 1995, and he’s been at it ever since; likely riding more cycling equipment than anyone on the planet along the way. Previous to his time with Bicycling, Matt worked in bike shops as a service manager, mechanic, and sales person. Based in Durango, Colorado, he enjoys riding and testing any and all kinds of bikes, so you’re just as likely to see him on a road bike dressed in Lycra at a Tuesday night worlds ride as you are to find him dressed in a full face helmet and pads riding a bike park on an enduro bike. He doesn’t race often, but he’s game for anything; having entered road races, criteriums, trials competitions, dual slalom, downhill races, enduros, stage races, short track, time trials, and gran fondos. Next up on his to-do list: a multi day bikepacking trip, and an e-bike race.

#156. ‘A New Challenge’: Courtney Dauwalter Is Chasing a 2:37 Marathon—and a Spot at the 2028 Olympic Trials

The ultrarunning star is also considering an Ironman in 2027.

Renowned ultrarunner Courtney Dauwalter hasn’t decided which trail races she’ll run in 2027, but she will be back to chasing a new marathon PR and a U.S. Olympic Trials qualifying mark this fall. And she might have an Ironman triathlon on her schedule next year.

It’s all part of a quest to keep pushing her perceived limits and pushing through what she calls “the pain cave” in different endurance pursuits.

While the Colorado-based runner has achieved most of her success in 100- to 250-mile races, she switched things up last fall and ran two road marathons that saw her lower her personal best to 2:49:54 at the Twin Cities Marathon last October and then down to 2:38:55 at the California International Marathon in early December.

She was so inspired and intrigued by her experience running CIM with a pack of fast women who were chasing the U.S. Olympic Trials qualifying standard of 2:37:00 that she’s heading back to do it again on December 6. She was on pace to hit 2:37 in the first half of CIM last year (1:18:33), but slowed slightly in the second half (1:20:22) and missed the qualifying mark by less than two minutes.

“That was such a fun side road to take last year, and I knew when I finished CIM that I for sure would be wanting to take another road marathon side road like that,” Dauwalter said. “CIM was a great fit. I also loved just the momentum of that women's pack going for the OTQ. I've never run in a pack like that, and being part of it last year was really, really beautiful. It's insane what you can do in a pack like that versus what you could do by yourself. If you can hold onto the momentum of all that positive forward motion, it's amazing how much faster you can run. It’s super inspiring.”

Dauwalter, 41, spent part of last week training in Kailua-Kona, Hawaii, before the Ironman World Championship on October 10. She wasn’t there on a tropical vacation, but instead was there on behalf of her main sponsor, Salomon, which is taking over as the title sponsor of the race in 2027.

She said it’s very likely that she’ll try an Ironman next year, even though the thought of doing a 2.4-mile swim, a 112-mile bike ride, and running a 26.2-mile marathon in one fell swoop is still a bit daunting. She knows she can handle the distance on the bike and the run, but she admits the open-water swim makes her a little nervous.

“I’m 100 percent curious about trying an Ironman, I just have to practice the swimming quite a bit,” she said with a self-effacing chuckle while looking over Kailua Bay.

While she might start dabbling in triathlons next spring, for now, her sights are firmly set on making a serious run at the U.S. Olympic Trials qualifying mark in the marathon. She said she’s been able to pick up her training where she left off last fall, even though she spent another summer competing in ultradistance races.

After placing second in the Cocodona 250 in Arizona in May and winning the Hardrock 100 in Silverton, Colorado, for the fourth time in July, Dauwalter entered the 107-mile Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc in Chamonix, France, in late August with eyes on winning that race for the fourth time. She started strong and was leading the women’s race early through the first two climbing sections, but she eventually slowed and dropped out at the 50-mile mark because of lingering fatigue.

But five weeks removed from that, she’s already back into marathon training with high-volume training weeks and some faster workouts on the roads.

"After running well at Twin Cities last year, we kind of said, ‘Well, heck, someone already made this time of 2:37 as a goal, so why don't we just put that out there as like the thing we're striving to get towards?,’ And so that was the pace I was always trying to work towards holding at CIM last year,’” Dauwalter said. “And last year I didn't quite get it, so part of the chase of going back to CIM again will be to see if I can hold and stick an OTQ because that would be a fun target to aim for.”

Dauwalter said last year’s marathon training was mostly a fun endeavor and a learning process—learning how to run faster, learning how to ingest gels running at fast paces, and learning how to maneuver through aid stations without losing contact with a pack of women.

Even though she had to run much faster in training last fall than she ever had, covering the marathon distance wasn’t a challenge because of many years of running ultradistance races.

“I actually remember during the road marathons last fall getting to certain mileages and feeling like it was like the home stretch. But those mileages were like mile 13, and I was excited and like, ‘Oh, last 13 miles, Let's go!" And that felt like a really lucky perspective to have because that's not actually the home stretch. For me it’s just trying to get to that fast pace and being able to hold it versus someone who can run a faster pace but needs to learn how to run it for 26 miles. For me, I’ve got the 26 miles, but now I've got to figure out how to get them in much faster.”

Last year, Dauwalter primarily trained at high altitude in Leadville, Colorado, which is situated at 10,000 feet above sea level. But she and her husband, Kevin, moved down the Arkansas River Valley to Buena Vista last winter, which sits at about 7,900 feet.

She admits it's harder to run faster paces at higher altitudes, so she might consider dropping to lower elevations for some of her training this fall.

“I think one of the key pieces of switching and doing some marathon stuff last year was just the mental refresh and reset of something new,” she said. “A new challenge, a new area where I had a lot of room to grow, a lot of things to soak up, a lot of room in my sponge to be a full rookie and really just take everything in. And I think the change-up of routines, the change up of routes, the change up of paces was mentally really helpful leading into another ultra season in the spring.”

If she runs a sub-2:37 at CIM, Dauwalter would be able to line up at the 2028 U.S. Olympic Trials Marathon in St. Louis 17 months from now. The top three women at the Trials with appropriate qualifying times will earn spots on the U.S. Olympic team for the Los Angeles Olympics later that summer.

“If I have the opportunity to take part in the Olympic Trials, I mean, of course I would want to be there,” she said. “Because what a cool thing it would be to be surrounded by these women who all worked for that same goal to stand on that same start line and just take part in that specific race. That's pretty special.”

Brian Metzler is a Boulder, Colorado, writer and editor whose work has appeared in Runner’s World, Sports Illustrated, ESPN, Outside, Trail Runner, The Chicago Tribune, and Red Bulletin. He’s a former walk-on college middle-distance runner who has transitioned to trail running and pack burro racing in Colorado.

#157. Kona Mechanics’ View of the Ironman World Championship

On the Thursday before the 2026 Ironman World Championship, I was cruising down Aliʻi Drive around Kaliua-Kona, Hawaii, after a delicious lunch at Clover and Mug Coffee when it struck me that there weren’t many triathletes out biking and running. Over the next six miles, I saw a total of only 15 athletes (two of whom may have just been locals on an afternoon run).

Then I turned onto Palani Rd. and was greeted by the sight of around 30 athletes with pink, turquoise, and a few neon yellow wristbands wheeling their bikes up and down the hill. As I pulled into the parking lot, I quickly learned where all the Ironman athletes were – at Bike Works Kona, our town’s one and only dedicated triathlon shop.

After finding a parking spot, I tried to fight my way through the stream of jittery athletes and into the shop. I settled in to chat with Taylor Bushong, a traveling race mechanic who had a pop-up work stand on the shop’s lanai, about the crazy things he’d seen during the week of the 2026 Ironman World Championship.

It begins with the absurdly catastrophic: “Someone brought in a bike for us to build and it had two front wheels. How do you leave home with two front wheels? I blame it on taper brain,” said Bushong, speaking from personal experience as an Ironman Wisconsin 2025 finisher.

“Someone else brought in a bike with two rear wheels,” added Ivey Langley, a globe-trotting race mechanic. Could the two athletes combine their taper half brains to form one complete brain and one complete bike? Not quite, but fortunately, there happened to be a few wheels available for rent from the shop.

“Then there was the guy who needed us to fix his front derailleur. He insisted it would only take five minutes,” Bushong said. Like many of the repairs that the traveling mechanics and employees of Bike Works Kona tackle during race week, fixing the derailleur was not as simple as turning a screw or two. “I had to drill his frame and rivet something back into it. That’s really the hardest part of Ironman week – managing athletes’ timeline expectations. Managing the unrealistic ‘can you just’ requests. The understanding of the level of the request seems to be outside the scope of recognition.”

When time is of the essence, changing tires is a reasonable request but new chains are tricky, especially at 3 p.m. on Friday, three hours before the bike check-in cut-off. That’s when one athlete chose to seek help with a chain that was skipping after they replaced the old one.

“They failed to realize that if the old cassette is heavily worn, you’ll need a new cassette and a new chain because the new chain won’t sit properly in the worn grooves of the old cassette. When you pedal hard, the chain will skip over the teeth,” Langley said.

Replacing a chain can be tricky when there’s a tight deadline, but changing out wheels is a nightmare. And it often starts with a seemingly bright idea: Give your older, 11-speed bike an upgrade by borrowing Zipp wheels from a friend. If the friend rides a brand new, 12-speed Cervélo, however, you could run into trouble.

“One person came in on Friday [the day before race start] because their gears weren’t working after they changed out their race wheels,” Langley said. “ I had to explain that they had a 12-speed cassette on an 11-speed drivetrain and their gears were jumping because the spacing between cogs, the chain width, and the shifter indexing on an 11-speed drivetrain don’t match a 12-speed setup.”

The consensus among everyone I spoke to at Bike Works Kona was that Friday was the most chaotic day of Ironman week, demanding that the staff act as both professional mechanics and temporary therapists.

“There was one athlete who was on their way to check in his bike when the back tire just went flat. The tube he was putting on was not working so he came back in here. He was so worried that he wouldn’t make it to bike check-in that he started crying. I had to calm him down,” Bike Works’ Marc Grande told me once I finally made it through the shop’s door to the sales counter. “Sometimes they need new tubes or valve extenders. Other times, they just need someone to look at their bike and tell them that their bike is OK and there’s nothing to worry about.”

“But sometimes they need new bike computers,” added my husband, Patrick Stover, who helped at least three triathletes whose computers had popped off while they were on training rides during race week. “Often, it isn’t enough to click it into the mount. If you don’t want to buy a new Garmin the day before Ironman, use a tether or find another way to secure your bike computer.”

The most common issue that arose during race week was with tubeless tires. Triathlon has largely been moving toward tubeless tires and the appeal feels like a no-brainer: Tubeless tires with sealant are far less prone to flats than tubular tires — and you can run them at lower pressures for lower rolling resistance and increased comfort. But you have to know how to properly put sealant in those tires.

Or you can head to a bike shop in a panic before your race, like hundreds (literally, hundreds) of athletes did this year during Ironman World Championship week. There were tubeless tires that were bone dry. Somehow there were both tires lazily hanging off their rims, while others obstinately clung to their rims. It wasn’t pretty. And it wouldn’t happen if more of us learned how to add sealant to our tires and test out our tubeless repair kits earlier in the season.

Another common yet preventable problem? Gear that was lost or damaged because of poor packing practices. If you’re packing your bike yourself, don’t forget to take the CO2 cartridges out. If you do forget, the TSA is going to go through your bike case and “help” you repack. Spoiler alert: It rarely goes well.

“We’ve heard firsthand from athletes whose cases were opened by TSA. One lost a shoe. The other lost a wheel. Save yourself the headache and buy your CO2 canisters once you get to Kona,” said high-performance technical director at Breakthrough Sports and lead mechanic for neutral support for pro athletes at the T100 Series Anthony Foy, who was on hand to help the Bike Works staff and traveling mechanics. “We’ve also seen shifters broken on the front end because people forget to remove the handlebar extensions when they pack their bikes.”

A handful of athletes visited the shop for help replacing their gear after their luggage was lost, including their race kit. You can’t control these things, but it helps to pack your goggles, race kit, bike and run shoes, and helmet in your carry-on. You really don’t want to be rushing around trying to replace those familiar touchpoints once you get to Kona for ostensibly the biggest race of your year (or life).

“One stressful situation involved a bike that came in just a few days before race day with several issues to sort out. We had to do quite a bit of troubleshooting to figure out what was going on. We ended up replacing several pinched wires in the aero bars and seat tube, and found that the Di2 battery had failed. … The damage looked consistent with an assembly issue, and we believe the customer assembled the bicycle themselves,” said Alex Flores, Bike Works’ service manager.

Other telltale signs of an athlete-assembled bike are loose aero bars and incorrectly mounted derailleurs and chains. “It’s a good reminder to have your bike assembled or checked by a mechanic well before [Ironman World Championship]. When your bike is essential to your race, a little preparation can help prevent stressful and costly surprises close to race day.”

But despite some forehead-slapping moments and unseen eye rolls, there’s something special about the triathlon world descending upon one place in time at a bike shop in the middle of the Pacific Ocean. There’s a universality to the experience, even if triathletes are speaking different languages. Fortunately, the Bike Works team during race week included mechanics who speak Spanish, Filipino, Japanese, and Swiss German, making the shop feel like a U.N. camp for those seeking mechanical refuge.

“It’s fun to see bikes and racing bring together people from so many different cultures,” added Stover.

And there can be perks: Last year, a triathlete left five carbon fiber wheels at the thrift shop by the Kona Transfer Station (ostensibly the town’s dump), which Stover bought for a grand total of $50. “The Zipp 808 front wheel alone was worth $500. It’s interesting to learn about where the athletes come from. It’s equally as interesting to see what they leave behind.”

#159. Benjamin Lee Explains Why “Normal” Blood Work Isn’t Always Optimal

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Being told that your blood work is “normal” can be reassuring, unless you still feel terrible.

For people experiencing persistent fatigue, unexplained weight changes, brain fog, low motivation, or other symptoms, hearing that “everything looks fine” can be frustrating. It may leave you wondering why you don’t feel like yourself when your test results appear to be within the expected range.

That experience is more common than many people realize. According to a CDC study published in 2025, 76.4% (representing 194 million) of US adults reported 1 or more chronic conditions in 2023, and 51.4% (representing 130 million) of US adults reported two or more. With that many people living with ongoing health concerns, understanding what your lab results do and don’t reveal has never been more important.

Benjamin Lee, whose work focuses on health information and wellness, says part of the issue may come down to the difference between what is considered normal and what may be relevant to an individual’s circumstances.

Laboratory reference ranges are useful for identifying results that fall outside the expected range of a population. However, being within a reference range does not necessarily explain how someone feels or provide a complete picture of their overall health.

A result being “normal” does not automatically mean that it explains every symptom a person is experiencing. Symptoms, personal history, lifestyle, medications, age, and other biomarkers can all provide additional context when laboratory results are being considered.

That does not mean standard reference ranges are wrong. They serve an important purpose. Rather, they are one part of a larger picture.

Thyroid testing provides one example of why looking beyond a single number can sometimes be useful.

A TSH level of 4.0 may fall within the reference range used by a particular laboratory. However, some practitioners who focus on health optimization may consider narrower target ranges when evaluating thyroid function, particularly when symptoms are also present.

The same concept can apply to other biomarkers.

For example, testosterone around 350 ng/dL may fall within a commonly used adult reference range, while whether that level is appropriate for an individual depends on factors such as age, symptoms, other hormone measurements, and personal health history.

Vitamin D provides another example. A result around 30 ng/mL may meet certain definitions of sufficiency, while some practitioners may consider different target levels depending on the individual’s circumstances.

These examples do not establish universal definitions of “optimal” health. Reference ranges and clinical targets can vary by laboratory, test, practitioner, and individual. The broader point is that a single number rarely provides the full context.

Thyroid health also illustrates why symptoms and multiple laboratory markers may need to be considered together.

TSH is commonly used to evaluate thyroid function, but a more comprehensive assessment may include Free T3, Free T4, and thyroid antibodies such as TPO and TG antibodies. In some situations, practitioners may also consider Reverse T3 alongside other information.

This can be particularly relevant when someone experiences symptoms such as fatigue, hair loss, sensitivity to cold, weight changes, or mood changes. Those symptoms can have many possible causes, so looking at the broader picture may help identify what questions are worth exploring.

This can be particularly relevant when someone experiences symptoms such as fatigue, hair loss, sensitivity to cold, weight changes, or mood changes. Because these symptoms can have many possible causes, they should not automatically be attributed to thyroid function. Instead, they can be part of a broader conversation with a qualified healthcare professional.

The importance of understanding your own health information became particularly personal during a six-month health crisis experienced by Benjamin Lee.

Following the extraction of two impacted wisdom teeth, severe jaw pain was initially suspected to be related to dry sockets. The situation eventually became much more serious. Diverticulitis led to partial colectomy surgery, followed by three separate small bowel obstructions that required an NG tube to relieve pressure.

The experience was particularly unexpected because, before the crisis, he maintained approximately 7% body fat year-round at around 205–210 pounds and had spent decades focused on wellness. He also had four physicians in his immediate family, an established medical team, and considerably more access to health information than most people.

Yet he still found himself struggling to advocate for himself.

That experience prompted a difficult question: if someone with extensive health knowledge and significant resources could find it challenging to navigate a complicated health situation, how difficult must it be for someone with little familiarity with medical terminology or laboratory testing?

The experience later influenced his work with 4BPM and LEAP, where he focuses on helping people better understand health information.

The lesson isn’t that everyone needs to chase narrower laboratory ranges or assume that something has been missed.

Searching online can be a useful starting point, but information found online should not replace professional medical advice. Instead, it can help people prepare for a more informed conversation with their healthcare provider.

If you continue to feel unwell despite being told that your results are normal, consider asking:

Most importantly, don’t treat an “optimal range” found online as a diagnosis or a universal standard. Laboratory results should always be understood in the context of the individual and their overall circumstances.

Benjamin Lee’s experience illustrates why understanding health information can be valuable, particularly when symptoms and laboratory results don’t seem to tell the same story. Knowing what your results measure, what they don’t tell you, and which questions to ask can help you have more informed conversations about your health.

#160. How Taking a GLP-1 Could Affect Your Bone Health

When it comes to treating obesity, type 2 diabetes, and other chronic health conditions, GLP-1 agonist drugs—such as Ozempic, Zepbound, and Wegovy—have been a game changer for literally millions of Americans.

But as with any medication, these drugs can deliver unwelcome side effects. And a recent study that just garnered a bunch of attention raised the possibility of new ones.

The research, which was presented at the 2026 American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons annual meeting in March and has not yet been peer-reviewed, found a link between GLP-1 use and increased risk of bone issues, including osteoporosis (weak, brittle bones) and osteomalacia (soft bones). The study also found a link between GLP-1 use and heightened risk of gout, a type of arthritis that causes pain and swelling in the joints.

The lead study author said he became interested in whether GLP-1s might affect bone and other connective tissue after some of his patients “developed serious tendon tears following relatively minor injuries,” according to NBC News. After analyzing five years of medical records from nearly 147,000 adults with type 2 diabetes and obesity, the study authors concluded that GLP-1 use was associated with a “significantly increased” risk of osteoporosis, osteomalacia, and gout.

Of course, this news is likely unsettling for anyone on these medications. But should we be legit worried about these findings? And how exactly could GLP-1s harm bone health in the first place? We tapped two experts for answers, along with practical tips for protecting bone health while taking GLP-1s.

First, some relieving news: As of now, there is “no sound scientific evidence” that suggests GLP-1s directly increase the risk of osteoporosis or osteomalacia, Marci Laudenslager, MD, an obesity medicine physician with The Johns Hopkins Healthful Eating, Activity & Weight Program, tells SELF. (Same goes for gout, she adds.)

Dr. Laudenslager, who was not involved in the study, points out that it was observational in nature, meaning it looked at correlation…not causation. “While well-conducted observational studies can reveal a potential relationship between a medication and a clinical outcome, they cannot determine whether a medication directly causes that clinical outcome,” she explains.

Another limitation of the study is that it relied on medical records alone, which means it assumed that all patients who were prescribed GLP-1s, as noted in their medical records, were actually taking the drug. In reality, many patients who are prescribed GLP-1s are unable to take them because of cost or medication shortages, Dr. Laudenslager says. Moreover, people who do start taking don’t always continue due to insurance, cost, or problems tolerating the drug, she adds.

Beyond that, the study didn’t take into account factors that commonly impact bone health, like exercise habits, nutritional habits, and other lifestyle factors, Kelyssa Hall, an exercise physiologist and certified strength and conditioning specialist at Hospital for Special Surgery, tells SELF. “These factors can play a huge role in bone health with or without the addition of GLP-1s.” The study also didn’t account for certain endocrine conditions, cancers, alcohol use, family history, and steroid use–all of which can also play a role in bone health, Dr. Laudenslager adds. And the study didn’t note which specific GLP-1 drug people used and the dosage, she adds.

Lastly, the study findings have not yet been peer reviewed–a step that Dr. Laudenslager describes it as “essential” in the scientific process. As Hall puts it: The study “highlights the need for more research on these topics.”

Okay, so that particular study has its limitations. But other research supports the notion that these drugs may be linked with declining bone health. So…is there actual cause for concern?

According to Dr. Laudenslager and Hall, taking GLP1-s can indeed decrease bone density for some people. But that’s likely due to the volume and rate at which people lose weight while on these drugs—and not anything specific to the medication itself, Dr. Laudenslager says.

“When you take GLP-1s, there can be rapid weight loss which means there is less load being carried around on the skeleton,” Hall says. “Bone formation or strengthening is improved with load to the skeletal system,” she explains, “so losing weight decreases the regular load on the bones overall.”

Over time, this decrease in loading can translate to a decrease in bone density, Dr. Laudenslager says. But, again, this isn’t unique to GLP-1s: “Significant weight loss through any mechanism—lifestyle change, medications, or surgery—can impact metabolism as a whole and bone metabolism, in particular,” she says. Basically, whenever you lose a bunch of weight—regardless of how you lost those pounds—there’s always a risk of bone loss.

In short, while it’s true that some people taking GLP-1s have had changes to their bone health, these changes seem to “be driven primarily by magnitude of weight loss rather than a direct, negative consequence of the medications themselves,” Dr. Laudenslager says. That said, the use of GLP-1s and bone health “is an active area of study,” she adds. More research is needed to fully understand the impact of GLP-1s on bone density.

Resistance training is important for pretty much everyone—and that includes folks on GLP-1s. One of its many benefits is that it’s been shown to improve bone density, Hall says. That means it can be a helpful strategy to bolster bone health when you’re on a GLP-1. Plus, strength training can help guard against muscle loss that can happen when you’re losing weight. “Retaining muscle mass is important for strength and stability,” she says. And it can also help support your overall metabolism, she adds, which can help your body sustain weight loss results for the long haul.

If you’re new to strength training, Dr. Laudenslager recommends gradually building up to a routine of two to three sessions a week, with at least a day off in between each workout to allow your muscles the time they need to recover. Before getting started though, make sure to check with your doctor or other medical provider so they can advise what type of workouts are safe and recommended for you.

A common side effect of GLP-1s is appetite suppression, which can sometimes lead people to follow a really low calorie diet. Calorie restriction can suppress bone growth and increase the risk of fractures, according to research, which is one of the reasons you want to make sure you’re still eating enough to support your overall health while on a GLP-1. “Hunger is an essential hormonal cue we all need in order to sustain health,” Dr. Laudenslager says. The ideal amount of calories is highly individualized, but if you’re unsure that you’re getting what you need, bring it up with your doctor or another qualified expert, such as a registered dietitian.

Protein is often touted for its muscle-building benefits, but it’s also vital for bone health, as it helps to build bone mass. The recommended dietary allowance for adults is 0.8 grams of protein per kilograms of bodyweight a day—a general guideline that Dr. Laudenslager also suggests for people taking GLP-1s. She suggests a slightly higher intake for people at greater risk of bone health issues (such as older adults and postmenopausal women) and lesser amounts in people with kidney disease. Just make sure that as you prioritize protein, you don’t skimp on important components of a well-rounded diet, including fiber, water, healthy fats, and essential vitamins, minerals, and nutrients, she adds.

Rapid weight loss can be harmful for bone health, so to mitigate this risk, strive for a more gradual reduction in pounds. The recommended rate of weight loss depends on your starting weight, but as a general guideline, Dr. Laudenslager recommends losing 5% to 10% of your total weight over the course of about six months. This translates to an average of about 0.5 to 2 pounds lost a week. So if you notice that taking a GLP-1 is causing you to lose weight at a faster pace, bring it up with your doctor. They may want to adjust your medication dosing to help slow your weight loss rate into a more ideal, gradual range.

Bone loss isn’t an overnight thing. In fact, clinically significant bone loss typically happens over the course of years, Dr. Laudenslager says. “This means there are a wealth of opportunities throughout a person’s weight loss journey to prevent and treat bone loss early on if it’s detected through surveillance.” So if you have any bone health concerns, mention them to your doctor (though hopefully your provider is proactively thinking about this too).

On that note, Dr. Laudenslager strongly encourages people interested in obesity treatment to seek care from a board-certified obesity medicine physician. She recommends the American Board of Obesity Medicine and the Obesity Action Coalition websites as resources for finding a board-certified provider.

GLP-1s can be a true game-changer for people struggling with chronic health conditions. Unfortunately, there’s still a lot of societal stigma and misunderstanding surrounding obesity, including the misconception that “anti-obesity medications are dangerous and should be avoided,” Dr. Laudenslager says. In truth, though? “The medication side effects are quite manageable when prescribed by providers who are well-versed in current practice guidelines,” she says.

#161. Jeff Galloway Spent Decades Making Running More Accessible. 8 Months After His Death, NYRR Is Honoring Him.

The late Olympian and run/walk pioneer will be named the 2026 recipient of the Abebe Bikila Award at an October 30 ceremony.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Jeff Galloway spent much of his life making distance running feel possible for people who didn’t necessarily see themselves as distance runners. Eight months after his death, New York Road Runners is honoring just how much that changed the sport.

Galloway has been named the 2026 recipient of the Abebe Bikila Award, which NYRR presents annually to someone who has made a major contribution to distance running. He will receive the honor posthumously, during the New York City Marathon Opening Ceremony on October 30, shortly before this year’s NYRR Hall of Fame class is inducted.

The award carries some serious marathon history of its own. Abebe Bikila won Olympic gold for Ethiopia in Rome in 1960, famously racing barefoot, before defending his title four years later in Tokyo. That second victory made him the first athlete ever to win two Olympic marathons.

Galloway’s own résumé could have kept the conversation focused on fast times. He represented the United States in the 10,000 meters at the 1972 Olympics, placed fifth at the Boston Marathon the following year, and eventually ran 2:18:29 for the marathon. He also helped create Atlanta’s Peachtree Road Race and won its inaugural edition in 1970.

One of the more memorable stories from his elite career had less to do with a result than what he gave up. Already bound for the 1972 Olympics in the 10,000 meters, Galloway raced the marathon trial a week later alongside friend and training partner Jack Bacheler. The two reached the finish fighting for the last spot on the U.S. Olympic marathon team, and Galloway stepped aside so Bacheler could have it.

The interesting contradiction of Galloway’s career is that a guy who once trained as much as 140 miles per week ultimately became famous for telling runners they didn’t have to run every single step. His run/walk method built planned walking breaks into running and racing, opening longer distances to people who might otherwise never have considered them.

And he kept finding new audiences for that message for more than 50 years, whether he was coaching runners, writing books, building training programs, or eventually bringing his advice onto podcasts and social media. He continued sharing that approach with runners for decades, right up until his death in February, at age 80, following complications from a stroke and brain bleeding.

Galloway is one of several figures NYRR will honor during this year’s marathon week. Lynn Blackstone, George Hirsch, and Percy Sutton will enter the NYRR Hall of Fame, while longtime running journalist Gordon Bakoulis will receive the George Hirsch Journalism Award. The honors come as the New York City Marathon celebrates 50 years since its move to the five-borough course in 1976.

#163. I Took Marijuana Edibles to Find Out If Weed Makes You Faster—Or If It Just Feels That Way

The ride felt easier and more immersive—find out if the data told a different story.

I still remember my first time in Colorado after weed was legalized. I walked into a dispensary and my mind was blown by the very chill and knowledgeable manager at the shop walking me through all the strains available. He pointed out the anticipated vibes around each one and which were the best options for activities like rides and trail runs.

Marijuana use in outdoor sports is not new, but efforts to study its effect on performance have been gaining steam. Everyone from the University of Colorado Boulder to the Gatorade Sports Science Institute is putting resources into how this substance impacts endurance sports.

More states have legalized recreational marijuana and many cyclists I’ve talked to have asked whether there are performance benefits or risks. While there are several helpful studies on the effects of marijuana on endurance athletes, none focus on cycling.

With few specific answers available, I wanted to put together my own test. Since I live in New Jersey, a state where recreational weed is legal, I bought a pack of edibles from a local dispensary and gathered all of the sensors I have available. Then I put together a simple study. In the safety of my own home, I would jump on Zwift, following the same route before and after taking edibles. The location was important. While research on marijuana’s impact on cycling performance is rare, multiple studies have shown that THC can impair coordination and slow reaction times, two factors that can increase the risk of cycling, especially outside the relatively controlled environment of my home trainer setup.

To keep outside variables in check, I rode the trainer through Zwift’s Loopin Lava route. I chose this route because I wanted something less than 60 minutes (including warmup and cooldown) that had sustained climbing sections as well as some flat and rolling sections to get a bit of variety. In all, it has about 690 feet of climbing over 11.5 miles.

I aimed to average about 185 watts (roughly zone two) on both tests—keeping my power output the same on both rides, I hoped, would reveal something about weed’s effects on my workout.

My home lab felt like it was made for this moment. As a health and fitness editor at Bicycling, and longtime fitness industry professional, I’ve been growing my collection of sensors for years—I was using a Garmin heart-rate sensor, a power meter built into the Wahoo trainer, a CORE temperature sensor, a Nix sweat sensor, and I used a pulse oximeter to check my oxygen saturation levels in 10-minute intervals. These sensors gave me insight into things I was curious about for the test—I even used my Coros Pace 4 as a backup. Does heart rate change? How does sweat rate and sweat content change after some gummies? Does internal body temperature or oxygen saturation rise or fall after a little weed? I was about to find out.

I did my baseline ride first, then took about a 90-minute break to let my internal temperature reset and let my body reset. Once I finished my first ride I took 40 milligrams of marijuana edibles and gave them some time to kick in (yes, that’s a relatively large dose; I wanted to make sure I experienced the full effects of the edibles on my riding in this not-too-scientific test).

I pulled all the data through Strava, the CORE app, the Nix app, and then pooled it into two columns of an Excel spreadsheet. This was the easiest way to get all the data into one place for analysis.

I opted for edibles after reading several peer-reviewed articles that found that smoking in general can cause changes in heart rate. Edibles would remove that variable, as well as make it easy to consume a target dose. With edibles the math was simple—4 gummies contained 40 milligrams. I had some idea what I was getting into. A 2023 study in the journal Sports Medicine, looked at the effects of marijuana on runners jogging on a treadmill.

One of its findings was that weed could help athletes get a jump on tapping into the runner’s high. “It is possible that exogenous cannabinoids like THC or CBD might activate the endocannabinoid system in a way that mimics the runner’s high,” said Laurel Gibson, PhD, a researcher on the project. It was time for me to find out.

I wasn't "in Barstow on the edge of the desert when the drugs began to kick in," as Hunter S. Thompson wrote in Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas—I was in my basement getting ready to get back on the trainer. I queued up a chill electronic playlist to tap into the beats with my pedal stroke. I did the same 15-minute warmup I did prior to the first ride while I got all my sensors dialed in. Toward the end of my warmup I noticed something—I was getting sucked into the ride. If you’ve ever been on a trainer ride, then you know that the monotony of riding indoors can make you want to hit the eject button as soon as possible. On my first ride I was watching the clock to see when I’d be done, but on this warmup I quickly felt myself getting more hooked on my cadence.

Once the test ride started, I felt like I was more immersed in the virtual world compared to the baseline ride—I was the avatar. As I spun up and down hills, I focused on my breathing and cadence. I felt locked in, in a way that couldn’t have been more different from the first ride. I just wanted to keep going.

Even though it felt harder to push the same watts on this ride, I didn’t want to stop once the route was done. I had to remind myself that I was doing this as an experiment and it was time to get off the bike—I could have kept pedaling around that virtual world for hours. Again—not surprising. The Sports Medicine study found that marijuana increases enjoyment, enhances recovery, and heightens motivation during workouts. In these ways, at least, it seems marijuana’s effects on cyclists are similar to the runners in the study.

It turns out weed is not a performance-enhancing drug for me. Comparing the two rides showed there was a noticeable difference in heart rate as well as body temperature—two traditional indicators of performance. During the roughly 32-minute effort, my average heart rate went up 28 beats per minute (bpm) while my max internal body temperature went up almost a full degree after taking the 40mg dose. That suggests the THC and CBD in the gummies had a negative effect on my performance. While I wasn’t too surprised by this, I was surprised by what I felt versus what the numbers showed.

For an expert opinion, I shared my results with Angela D. Bryan, PhD, adjunct professor, Division of Medical Oncology at the University of Colorado School of Medicine, editor in chief of Annals of Behavioral Medicine, and a researcher on the 2023 Sports Medicine study. She quickly zeroed in on my 40mg dose and the rise in heart rate. “That’s a huge dose, actually, and THC itself causes an acute increase in heart rate. So that’s why you saw that,” she said. Her note on heart rate is important because if THC raises heart rate, that in and of itself can impact performance.

I didn’t have a drop in my ability to sustain power, and I didn’t notice an inability to recover when I tried to put in a dig on the climb. The biggest performance takeaway I had is this: THC and CBD can raise heart rate while riding, which can impact performance. But oddly, in the moment I didn’t feel that I was working harder or that my heart was pounding faster. This is a different and potentially positive effect of marijuana.

Not everyone is training for high performance—a lot of us just want to ride more. During my edible test I didn’t dread getting on the trainer, and once I was on it, I didn’t want to get off. I might have had a higher heart rate, but I enjoyed the experience significantly more. I could see this fitting in on trainer rides in general and zone one, recovery, or zone two rides more specifically. Of course, more research needs to be done on the long-term effects of THC and CBD on athletes.

This was just one trial, at a relatively high dosage. Overall, I found the experience pleasant, and the impact on performance modest—and the idea of experiencing the “runner’s high” sooner is appealing—especially on trainer rides.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. #164. Does Magnesium Help You Lose Belly Fat?

We include products we think are useful for our readers. If you buy through links on this page, we may earn a small commission. Here’s our process

Magnesium is found in fatty fish, leafy greens, whole grains — and the supplement aisle.

The mighty mineral plays many essential roles in our bodies, but can it help tighten the belt buckle?

While magnesium can sneakily support weight loss in a few ways, that’s not its main gig.

“Magnesium alone is not a magic bullet for weight loss,” says Paunel Vukasinov, MD, a dual board-certified internist and obesity medicine specialist with Medical Offices of Manhattan.

“A comprehensive approach including diet, exercise, and other lifestyle changes are essential,” Vukasinov adds.

Here are a few ways magnesium may support weight loss, as explained by Vukasinov.

“Magnesium is not classified as an appetite suppressant,” Vukasinov says.

“However, by potentially stabilizing blood sugar and insulin levels, magnesium may reduce cravings and help prevent overeating. This effect can indirectly support weight loss.”

Vukasinov reminds us that no specific magnesium dosage is prescribed solely for fat loss.

With that in mind, the Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) for magnesium is:

Vukasinov says that sticking to the RDA ensures you meet your body’s needs without over-supplementing.

“Excessive intake does not enhance weight loss and may lead to adverse effects,” he adds.

According to Vukasinov, it’s best to get magnesium from food since a nutrient-dense diet, including whole foods, boosts your intake of other extra essentials like fiber, which improves overall health.

Here are some foods you can gobble up for the most magnesium:

If you know your diet isn’t cutting it, you can find magnesium supplements at major retailers, like Wal-Mart and Target, drug stores, or Amazon.

PSA: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) does not check the safety or effectiveness of dietary supplements, so it’s important to choose a reputable brand that undertakes third-party testing to prove the purity and quality of their products.

For some, magnesium supplements may cause a few unsavory side effects, including diarrhea, stomach upset, or cramping.

Remember that there are many forms of magnesium. Vukasinov points out that magnesium citrate or magnesium oxide can have a laxative effect (yikes).

Be sure you’re taking the best dose based on your RDA, and consider taking it with a meal to better avoid side effects.

Magnesium is not a miracle solution for weight loss, but getting enough of it can ensure that your body produces enough energy and gets enough sleep — both play a big hand in weight management.

Taking too much will have you gripping your belly with stomach pain or diarrhea, so stick to the daily recommended amounts.

#166. This Seated Yoga Pose Helps Build Full-Body Awareness

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about Marichyasana first appeared in the November-December 1987 issue of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

The symbols used in depicting the chakras are taken from Hindu mythology—conches, tridents, lotuses, cobras—and on the surface seem alien to the Western mind. But the meaning behind the symbols is universal and open for all to experience.

The sixth chakra of the kundalini system, called ajna chakra, is located between the eyebrows, and is traditionally regarded as the seat of the mind (manas). Ajna means “command,” because at this level of consciousness we train the conscious mind, through the practice of meditation, to intercede at the moment of reaction, and thus learn to overcome our greed, fear, desire, ambition, pride, anger—the various ways we “misuse” ourselves in the world.

This yogic idea of “command” closely resembles the principle of “inhibition” put forward in the early part of this century by F. M. Alexander. This young Australian actor introduced a method for developing body awareness—later known as the Alexander Technique—which is based on careful observation of the head and neck reflexes in such simple activities as sitting down, standing up, and walking.

During his stage career, Alexander had suffered from chronic hoarseness, which medical treatment could not cure. He finally concluded that he was using his voice incorrectly. Standing before a mirror, he noticed the tendency to throw his head back whenever he began a recitation—which put a definite strain on his voice, and also shortened his spine. When Alexander learned to inhibit the initial impulse to fling back his head, not only did he regain his voice, but his posture gradually improved, and the respiratory problems that had plagued him all his life vanished as well. Thus, in the Alexander Technique, inhibition of our habitual responses becomes the “means-whereby” we take conscious control of our lives.’

As Alexander himself observed, the movement of the head not only affects the curve of the cervical spine and the muscular tension of the neck, but also dictates a pattern of muscular response for the rest of the body. You can experience this for yourself by trying the following exercise.

First stand in Mountain Pose (Tadasana) with your feet a few inches apart and your hands on your hips. Then lift your chin to throw the head back, and move forward into Standing Forward Bend (Uttanasana). Feel how the back arches at the lumbar region, and how the weight of the body falls back onto the heels. For flexible students with hyperextended knees, this movement puts enormous strain on the back of the knees. When you come up from the forward bend position, first lift the head and arch the neck, and observe how strongly the muscles of the lower back must work to pull you up.

Now stand in Mountain Pose with your feet a few inches apart, and, firming your legs, allow the energy of the spine to lift through the crown of your head. As you move forward into Standing Forward Bend, keep the head in a neutral position by lengthening the cervical spine. By maintaining the head-neck relationship, you will find that the rest of the body responds differently as well—the lower back does not over-arch, and the weight stays forward on the feet, reducing the strain at the back of the knees. Many students have commented that kinesthetically this movement feels lighter and more effortless. Then, as you come up, do not lift the chin, but continue to lengthen through the crown of the head, and feel how the muscles of the lower abdomen now give strength and support to the movement, so that the front and back body work evenly.

In his scientific investigations of the head-neck reflexes in animals during the 1920s, Rudolph Magnus confirmed the principle that “in posture and movement the head leads and the body follows.” Magnus also conducted research on the so-called attitudinal reflexes. As Frank Pierce Jones reports, “The attitudinal reflexes with receptors in the labyrinths and in the joints of the neck […] are used by an animal to maintain a position that 1s assumed for some special purpose, like that of a cat… looking up at a piece of meat held high. The position taken by the head imposes on the rest of the body an attitude which is maintained as long as it is functional. According to Magnus, they are the most enduring and untiring of reflexes.”

Is it possible to contact these attitudinal reflexes in our practice of the asanas? Try the following two-part exercise, and determine for yourself. First come into Half Moon Pose (Ardha Chandrasana), balancing on the right leg and the right fingertips, with the left leg parallel to the floor, the left arm extended to the ceiling, and the torso facing directly forward.

Hold the position for half a minute, and, as you descend from the pose, concentrate mainly on keeping the left leg fully extended and the left kneecap lifted. Observe how the body and mind respond to these instructions.

Then repeat Half Moon Pose to the same side, but this time bring your awareness to the lengthening of the cervical spine, and maintain the head-neck relationship as you bend the right leg and bring the left leg back to the floor. Do you notice any difference in the quality of the movement?

In my experience, when I come down from Half Moon Pose by keeping the back leg straight, I feel awkward and clumsy, as though my leg were packed in a plaster cast. My chest tightens with anxiety, as though I were a pilot trying to land in a fog. I have no sense of where I am in space, no inner radar, and my back leg hits the floor with a thud. I am the victim of what Alexander calls “end-gaining”—I am thinking only of the goal.

On the other hand, when I keep my awareness on the length of the spine and the position of the head and neck, I glide out of the pose like a kite. My back leg remains straight, without mental coercion, and my back foot touches the floor with prehensile tact. But what I feel most is a sense of profound integration—that somehow, in awakening the attitudinal reflexes, I have aligned myself with my basic nature, so that all movement has become light and effortless. I am no longer concerned with the goal, only with the “means-whereby.”

Awareness of the head-neck relationship has given me new insight into a variety of poses, especially backbends and inverted poses, but most unexpectedly into Pose Dedicated to the Sage Marichi I, or Sage’s Pose I (Marichyasana I; Figure 1). Named after the mythological sage Marichi, the son of Brahma the Creator, this twist seated forward bend is one of the basic sitting poses, which begins as a twist and moves into a forward bend. For the purposes of this article, I have dealt separately with these two aspects of the pose. I would also caution those with lower back problems to practice the twisting variations only, and to omit the forward bending variations until they have guidance from a teacher.

The first variation of the Pose Dedicated to the Sage Marichi I twist is especially suitable for beginning students. Sit at the edge of a folded blanket with your legs extended and your spine erect, as for Staff Pose (Dandasana).

Draw the right thigh toward the chest, so that the right heel is in line with the right sitting bone, and the sole of the foot is in firm contact with the floor. The right hip may lift slightly off the blanket. Now bring your left hand onto the floor behind you, and lift the spine through the crown of the head as you turn the torso away from the bent knee. Place the back of the right arm against the inner right knee, keeping the right arm bent. Press the right knee against the arm, and the arm against the knee, as you continue to lift the spine and deepen the twist.

The head may turn either over the left shoulder or forward to look at the left foot (Figure 2). More flexible students may complete the Pose Dedicated to the Sage Marichi I twist by entwining the arms as follows. From the initial twisting position, turn the torso to face the extended leg, and lengthen the front of the spine forward, so that the right armpit slides down the right shinbone. Circle the right arm around the bent leg, placing the back of the hand at the right side of the waist. Then twist the rib cage away from the bent leg, and extend the left arm behind the back, taking hold of the left wrist with the right hand (Figure 3). Draw the forearms down toward the floor to help lift the sacrum and spine. If your hands do not quite meet, you can place a strap between them. Hold the position for about a minute, then repeat to the other side.

The following preparation for the Pose Dedicated to the Sage Marichi I seated forward bend works deeply in the hips. First sit at the edge of a folded blanket with your legs extended and your spine erect. Cross the left foot underneath the right leg, so that the left heel is directly in front of the right sitting bone, and the outer left leg rests on the floor. Draw the right foot back to the left ankle, so that the right shinbone is vertical. The metatarsals of the right foot should be in firm contact with the floor. Now lengthen the spine through the crown of the head, and bring the torso forward by lifting the sacrum and rotating the pelvis. Bring your right arm in front of the right leg, with the back armpit as close to the shinbone as possible. Hold the right leg snugly against your rib cage with the left hand, as you twine the right arm around the standing leg and place the back of the hand at the side of the waist. Extend the left arm in a wide circle around the back, and take hold of the right wrist with the left hand (Figure 4).

In this preparation, the right buttock lifts off the blanket and the weight of the body balances over the right foot, giving a deep stretch at the back of the right thigh and all around the outer hip. If the sole of the foot is not in complete contact with the floor, you may need to increase the height of the blanket, to help shift the body weight forward. When your weight is evenly balanced over the right foot, allow the torso to sink deeper into the pose with each exhalation, so that eventually the forehead rests on the floor. Hold this position for a minute or two, then repeat to the other side.

For the forward-bending variation of Pose Dedicated to the Sage Marichi I, sit at the edge of a folded blanket with your legs extended and your spine erect. Draw the right thigh to the chest, and place the right foot in line with the right sitting bone. Then bring your hands to the sides of the hips, pressing your fingertips into the floor to lift the sacrum and the lower back. Let the right knee drop out to the side several inches to create more space in the hip joint, as you rotate the pelvis forward and lengthen the front of the spine. Then take hold of the right shin with the left hand, and draw the right leg toward the chest. Extend the upper right arm out to the side, and place the right hand on the floor in line with the elbow. Press the upper arm against the shin to help you lengthen the spine even further (Figure 5).

When there is no gap between the inner right thigh and the rib cage, you are ready to complete the pose. Hold the right leg in position with the left hand, as you twist the right arm around the bent leg, placing the back of the hand against the outer waist. Then release the left hand from the right shin, and roll the left shoulder toward the ceiling to open the left side of the chest. Extend the left arm behind the back, taking hold of the left wrist with the right hand (Figure 1).

When the arms are entwined behind the back, it is time to look inward to adjust the balance of the pose. Notice first how the shoulder on the bent-leg side tends to hunch toward the ear in this position, causing the right side of the rib cage to overextend and the left side to contract (Figure 6). To correct this imbalance, draw the right sitting bone back toward the floor, and lengthen the left side of the rib cage forward. The shoulders should be level, and both sides of the rib cage should be evenly extended. The left thigh should remain firm, with the knee and foot pointing directly toward the ceiling (Figure 1).

The Pose Dedicated to the Sage Marichi I seated forward bend often gives a feeling of confinement or slavery—the arms are handcuffed around the bent leg, the shoulders are hunched in an attitude of despair, and the weight of the head hangs wearily down.

For me, freedom in this pose comes only when I bring my awareness to the movement of the head and neck. Therefore, instead of dropping the head forward, keep the crown of the head in line with the tailbone, and, as you draw the shoulders back, think of lengthening the front of the cervical spine. This inner movement calls into play the deeper muscles of the neck and allows the surface muscles to relax, so that the sides of the neck grow long and the front brain feels light and clear. Hold this position for one to two minutes, reaching the crown of the head further and further toward the foot of the extended. leg as you continue to lengthen the front spine. Then repeat to the other side.

In his excellent study of F. M. Alexander, Body Awareness in Action, Frank Pierce Jones comments on the special quality of awareness that characterizes the Alexander technique.

“To me it is an expansion of the field of consciousness […] in space and in time, so that you are taking in both yourself and your environment […] It is a unified field organized around the self as a center. At the beginning it has a very simple system of organization but it always takes in both the self (including the relation of the head to the trunk) and something of the environment […] [such as] the pressure of your feet against the floor.” This double mode of perception establishes a balance between internal needs and external demands, so that the individual is neither completely self-absorbed nor overly engrossed in the outer world.

When we practice yoga with this kind of awareness, we break down the arbitrary division between self and other and thus prepare ourselves for the experience of oneness or samadhi, which is the ultimate goal of yoga. In the kundalini system, samadhi is associated with the seventh and last chakra, located at the crown of the head. This chakra is called saharara, meaning “lotus with a thousand petals.”

“To live in the conscious mind is samadhi,” writes B. K. S. Iyengar.’ Elsewhere in the same work, he describes our spiritual evolution through yoga in this way: “The mind integrates the body and yet remains an observer, the body becomes mind and yet remains supremely alert as body.
