#183. Spring Allergies Can Cause Headaches. Here’s How to Deal

A stuffy nose and itchy, watery eyes are spring-allergy cornerstones—but they’re not the only symptoms that herald a pollen influx for some people. You might not immediately suspect a pulsing headache is due to allergies, but experts say it’s a common occurrence.

In fact, the same immune response that fills your nose with snot or leaves you sneezing up a storm can make your head throb. That’s especially true “if you have multiple seasonal allergies, for instance to grass and tree pollen; live near farms; or spend a lot of time outside during allergy season, being bombarded by pollen,” Beth Oller, MD, a family medicine physician in Stockton, Kansas, tells SELF. Keep reading to learn why allergies can spark headaches, plus how to tell if your head pain is allergy-related and find relief.

If you have spring allergies and breathe in pollen, “your immune system perceives it as a foreign invader,” Dr. Oller says, and releases a bunch of inflammatory chemicals like histamine. The resulting inflammation triggers swelling in your nasal cavities, which are connected to your sinuses, Rekha Raveendran, MD, allergist and immunologist at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center, tells SELF. The sinuses extend behind the cheekbones, eyes, and bridge of the nose, and up into the forehead—so when they get puffy, you can wind up with a sensation of facial pressure and also headache, she explains.

At the same time, experiencing the effects of spring allergies may spark migraine attacks in those with migraine. The surge of inflammation and congestion can irritate a nearby nerve that plays a role in migraine, and allergy-driven fatigue and insomnia can be migraine triggers in and of themselves. Research suggests that among people with migraine, those who also have allergies tend to have worse, more frequent attacks than those who don’t.

An allergy headache typically feels like a dull throbbing in your temples, cheeks, or forehead, and makes your face feel heavy. It comes along with congestion, Dr. Oller says, and lying down or tilting your head can increase the pressure. (FYI: This is the same kind of pain as you’d get with a sinus headache, which is caused by a viral or bacterial infection in your sinuses—both lead to mucus buildup and swelling within the sinuses.)

By contrast, migraine attacks (whether or not they’re precipitated by allergies) trigger intense pain on one side of the head. They often come along with nausea, and sensitivity to light and sound, which you would not typically find with allergy headaches, Dr. Raveendran says. Meanwhile, tension headaches tend to feel more like a band squeezing around the head, and cluster headaches spark a surge of pain in or around one eye.

If you get walloped with allergy headaches each year, Dr. Oller suggests starting on an oral antihistamine medication right about now. Pollen counts are rising, and antihistamines take a week or two of daily use to kick in, she explains. The non-drowsy options work best for daytime—think: cetirizine (Zyrtec), levocetirizine (Xyzal), loratadine (Claritin), or fexofenadine (Allegra). You can use the sleepiness-inducing diphenhydramine (Benadryl) at night, but just know that you shouldn’t make a habit of relying on it as a sleep aid.

Both doctors suggest pairing oral allergy meds with a nasal corticosteroid spray like fluticasone (Flonase) or triamcinolone (Nasocort). “They hit those mucus membranes and help decrease inflammation in that region,” Dr. Oller says. It’s best to take both drugs daily throughout allergy season, she adds, not just when you think you need them. (If your headaches are barely alleviated, or the pollen counts in your area are sky-high, you may also be able to safely increase your dose of these allergy meds to boost their efficacy.)

The less pollen that enters your airspace, the fewer symptoms you’ll experience. But you don’t have to stay cooped up to cut your exposure. Keeping your windows closed, using a high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filter in your HVAC system (or a portable air purifier that has one), and vacuuming often can make a difference, according to Dr. Oller.

Whenever you do spend ample time outside, Dr. Oller says to rinse off once you get home. This way, you’re not inhaling pollen any longer than you have to. While you’re at it, “shower your sinuses too,” Dr. Oller adds, with a nasal saline spray or Neti Pot. This helps clear some mucus to release pressure and offer temporary relief, Dr. Raveendran says.

If the congestion is making it feel like your face is chock-full of mucus, you might be tempted to reach for an OTC oral decongestant. But take note: While pseudoephedrine (Sudafed) can be helpful, it’s not recommended to use it more than a few days in a row, and isn’t a good choice if you have high blood pressure, Dr. Raveendran says. It’s a stimulant that can make some people feel jittery, or cause a fast heart rate or insomnia.

Nasal decongestants, which include phenylephrine- or oxymetazoline-based sprays (like Afrin and Vicks Sinex), can open up your nose fast but should only be used for three days at a time max, Dr. Raveendran adds. “There’s a risk of rebound congestion that leads to overall worsening of symptoms and addiction to the nasal decongestants,” she says.

Sometimes you just need in-the-moment relief for the head pain. In that case, you can pop an OTC pain reliever like ibuprofen (Advil), naproxen (Aleve), or acetaminophen (Tylenol), Dr. Oller says. The former two may be better at resolving allergy headaches because they combat inflammation. But it’s not advised to take these non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for more than 10 days straight (unless your doctor tells you otherwise) because of potential effects on your stomach and kidneys. Tylenol, by contrast, is generally safer to take long-term, though shouldn’t be combined with alcohol due to the risk for liver damage.

If you find that your allergy headaches have you reaching for pain relievers more than a few days in a row, check in with your primary care doctor or allergist. They may recommend a more intensive treatment, like prescription steroids, or suggest seeing an ear, nose, and throat doctor or neurologist, in case something else might be behind your head pain.

Building muscle on a vegetarian diet isn’t rocket science, but it requires some know-how. Here are some tips to keep you on track.

Let’s face it: protein is the MVP for muscle building and is even more critical when you’re vegetarian. Aim for around 1.6 – 2.2 g/kg/day. In other words, aim for 0.73 to 1 gram per pound of body weight per day. For example, if you weigh 150 pounds, this would mean you should consume about 110 to 150 grams of protein each day.

If that seems like a lot, don’t fret — there’s a smorgasbord of plant-based proteins to fuel your workouts and keep those muscles fed.

And hey, don’t forget about dairy and eggs if you’re a lacto-ovo vegetarian. These can be total game-changers in your diet.

Double-check that you get enough calories throughout the day to support muscle growth. Keep an eye on your macros — protein, carbs, and fats — because getting the balance right is crucial to maximizing your results.

For optimal muscle growth, it’s not just the total amount of protein you consume daily that matters but also how you distribute it throughout the day. To best support muscle growth and repair, aim to consume protein at each meal and snack, roughly every 3–4 hours. Sometimes, food alone might not cut it. That’s where supplements come in. There’s strong evidence that creatine supplementation helps with muscle building, and it offers even more benefits for vegan athletes compared to those who eat meat.

Consider adding a high-quality plant-based protein powder to your routine, especially after workouts when your body needs protein the most.

Also, don’t forget about B12 and iron, which can be tricky to get enough of in a vegetarian diet. A good multivitamin can help fill in the gaps.

#186. Laura Philipp Talks About Her “Full Set” of Medals and Second-Place Finish in Kona

Laura Philipp proved she’s one of the most dangerous bike-runners in the sport of triathlon by overcoming a seven-minute gap to the main group of swimmers and still finishing on the podium with a second-place finish in a time of 8:39:34.

Philipp struggled in the large swell of the bay, saying that she felt seasick during the swim – she would emerge almost exactly an hour later from the water in 23rd place. Philipp rode mostly solo through the field, splitting 4:43 on the bike (for the third-fastest split of the day) to come into T2 in ninth place, and then ran a 2:50:43 marathon (fastest of the day).

For Philipp this is a capstone for an extensive long-course career that began way back in 2014 with a pair of 70.3 podiums. Since then, Philipp has won 21 middle-distance events, a 70.3 World Championship podium (2016), eight Ironman/Challenge wins, two Ironman World Championship third-place finishes, and an Ironman World Championship win (2024). By Philipp’s own count her second-place finish in 2026 completes her “podium set” of Ironman World Championship finishes.

It’s no surprise that Philipp had the fastest run of the day, as she also owns the fastest Ironman World Championship run split with her 2:44:59 from Nice in 2024, but what surprised Philipp – especially on a day that saw so many other women struggle on the run – was that she felt so good.

Philipp spoke to Triathlete shortly after her second-place finish to unpack the day. Watch the full interview above.

With more than 40% of adults in the U.S. suffering from obesity, medical experts often tout different diets to aid with weight loss. But when it comes to cutting liver fat, keto is king according to a new report.

The study recently published in the Cell Press journal, found that low carbohydrate diets triggered the largest rise in glucagon, which is the hormone responsible for burning the fat stored inside the liver. Keto also offered the largest decline in blood insulin levels. “The most surprising finding was that participants in the ketogenic diet group didn’t experience an increase in blood fat or cholesterol levels,” said Max Petersen, the study’s first author at Washington University School of Medicine. “Despite consuming the most fat.”

42 obese adults with prediabetes and fatty liver disease were randomly assigned to one of three diets:

To make sure that participants followed their particular plan for 12 weeks, the scientists provided the appropriate foods and had regular meetings to make sure that the diet was being adhered to.

The ketogenic diet reduced liver fat by an average of 67%, outperforming the Mediterranean and low-fat groups, who had both lost around 45% liver fat. But the success of the ketogenic diet is even more notable when you consider that all three groups lost around the same amount of weight.

“We know weight loss can improve metabolic health in people who are obese,” said the study’s corresponding author, Samuel Klein. “Our data suggest that if you have high liver fat content and prediabetes, reducing carbohydrate intake can have important therapeutic effects on metabolism beyond just weight loss alone.”

Drilling into the details, the ketogenic diet derived 4% of its calories from carbohydrates, and while all three groups saw a reduction on body weight of around 10%, the low carb group almost doubled their results when it came to no longer meeting the criteria for prediabetes.

Scientists now hope that this information can inform those who wish to avoid Ozempic style medications or wish to eat a diet that works in tandem with their prescription, to make better choices regarding the foods that they eat. “GLP-1-based medications have revolutionized the therapy of obesity. We now have a very effective pharmacotherapy for achieving significant weight loss,” said Max Peterson. “But in addition, our study shows that the specific composition of the diet can give you added benefits.”

#189. The 6 Best Advanced GPS Running Watches for Top-Tier Training and Tracking

These high-tech timepieces can help you hit your splits.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

I review a ton of running watches, cycling through all of the various features and idiosyncrasies to find which watch would suit which runner best, which watches deserve a place on our lists, and which don’t measure up. Sometimes, there are watches that are really cool, and do a lot of work, but they offer more than what the average runner needs to log their daily miles and monitor their fitness. But for backwoods adventure runners, ultrarunners, or runners who put a lot of demand on their machines, advanced GPS running watches like the ones on this list offer a bit more of everything—from cellular and satellite connectivity to off-road trail mapping to sturdier cases, more multisport functionality, and all around just more.

As an ultrarunner, I am frequently testing watches for 50, 75, or even 100 miles at a stretch. Often these miles are spent deep in the woods in Upstate New York on trails that are poorly marked and pretty treacherous. Sometimes, there simply isn’t cell service to be had. On top of that, I routinely test them during Hyrox, kayaking, paddle boarding, weight training, hiking, and even skiing—when there’s actually snow on the ground. My daily runs tend toward miles spent in New York City, which you wouldn’t think is an issue, but the tall buildings can thwart GPS pretty hard.

Looking for more running tech? Read our reviews of the best wireless headphones for running, headlamps for runners, and basic running watches.

The Fenix 9 is not flawless, but dang, it is as close to it as I’ve ever tested.I’ve put over 300 miles on the Pro Solar, so I’ll get my little nitpicks out of the way first. Annoyingly, there’s a lag of about half a second to a second when you start a workout, and again when you switch between laps that the 8 did not have. It’s not the most annoying thing in the world, but alas. Also, the app is still the Garmin Connect app. (I will beat this drum until they fix it.)

Now? My happy place, the good stuff. The solar ring on the Pro Solar model puts this watch so far ahead of every other run watch on the market that it can’t even see the others from the rearview. The 51mm is rated for up to 57 days in smartwatch mode with solar, and the 47mm gets up to 34. In the 51mm’s max battery GPS mode, that stretches to 186 hours, or up to 1,000 with solar. I took this out in the backwoodsiest of backwoods Adirondack trails, where I forced it to rely wholly on satellite, and I ran it for 12 solid hours, and it barely ticked the battery.

And that multi-band GPS with SatIQ? It’s the best in class, and it locks you down in a hurry. The inReach satellite connectivity lets me run those backwoods and feel safe about doing so. (Though, I still bring a SatCom.)

It’s built like a beast without feeling like one. This is the first Fenix with a titanium case, plus a sapphire lens and a 10 ATM water rating, so rain, sweat, and my early morning postrun ocean swims don’t screw it up.

It’s chockablock with performance and training metrics, and with Epic, their new multiday activity tracker, it’s better than ever. It’s light on the wrist, and it’s easy to use even with sweaty or sea salty fingers.

My favorite little bonus is the flashlight. It’s dimmable and comes in white, red, or green, so it’s great for visibility on early morning runs and also for finding crap at the bottom of my purse.

The base Fenix 9 is a solid watch too, but the Pro Solar is the one I’d get. It’s simply a very fine watch.

You might not be familiar with this brand, but when I tell you, they are punching so far above their weight class with this watch that you would think a 10-year-old just knocked out Floyd Mayweather, I’m not kidding.

The Amazfit Balance Ultra costs $599.99. For that you get a Grade 5 titanium case, a sapphire lens, and a 10 ATM rating that also covers freediving and recreational scuba. It weighs 57 grams without the strap, which is a lot of watch for so little weight. It’s a bit on the thicker side, but not so high profile it’s going to get caught on doors.

Battery is where things start to get unbelievable. The 780 mAh cell battery is rated for up to 30 days of typical use and 10 with the always-on display. In accurate GPS mode you get 50 hours, and power-saving GPS stretches to about 90 in our testing. Unless you’re running through the weekend, you’ll hit your limit before the watch does.

For tracking, it uses dual-band GPS across six satellite systems that ends up acting just like a typical multiband GPS on par with a Coros or a Suunto. That is clutch when you run between tall buildings or under tree cover and your watch would otherwise decide you swam across the Hudson. The 1.5-inch AMOLED screen is bright enough that it can be read in direct sun for the most part.

I will say that the dang buttons on the side are far too easy to depress, leading to accidentally starting activities, but overall, it’s incredible.

The Garmin Enduro 3 is built for runners who crave distance and dependability. Everything about it feels engineered for endurance—the rugged design, precise tracking, and especially the solar-powered battery that seems to last forever. You don’t even think about charging most days; it just handles your training, races, and long trail days without missing a beat. The safety and satellite coverage give you extra peace of mind when you’re out alone, far from cell service or the nearest trailhead.

Two features stand out on every serious run. The Pack Weight tool adjusts your effort estimates based on how heavy your gear is, which makes your performance data feel more real—especially on long mountain efforts. And the Next Fork guide keeps you on track, showing how far it is to the next junction so that you don’t have to stop and fumble through maps. Add Garmin’s multi-band GPS into the mix, and route logs are spot-on, no matter how deep into the woods you go.

For ultrarunners or anyone training big, the Enduro 3 is reliability wrapped around your wrist—with battery life that feels almost unfair.

I’ve been using the Suunto Vertical 2 off and on for a while now, and I’ve come to see it as a true multisport powerhouse rather than an everyday watch. It’s the one I pull out when training or adventures get serious—long runs, big mountain weekends, or backcountry routes where accuracy and endurance matter more than aesthetics. What sets it apart immediately are its maps—they’re crisp, easy to read, and fully offline, which makes navigation seamless even in the most remote terrain.

Battery life is another standout feature. The Vertical 2 easily lasts up to 60 days in smartwatch mode and delivers exceptional runtime with dual-band GNSS tracking, something that still amazes me every time I scroll through my recorded routes after multi-hour training blocks. The titanium and sapphire glass construction give it a premium, expedition-ready feel, and the watch itself feels built to handle harsh conditions without flinching.

It’s definitely not what I’d wear every day—it’s large, rugged, and purpose-built—but that’s exactly the point. For athletes who bounce between cycling, running, skiing, hiking, and more, the Vertical 2 is a multisport dream, offering a level of mapping, tracking, and battery endurance suited for endless exploration.

The Garmin Forerunner 970 has been my daily watch for months, and it feels like the perfect blend of lifestyle usability and serious athletic performance. It’s light, comfortable, and sleek enough to wear all day—but underneath that understated design is a fully loaded training tool built for racing, coaching, and multidiscipline endurance work. Whether I’m tracking an interval session, planning an ultra-block, or guiding athletes through structured workouts, the 970 handles it all seamlessly.

GPS precision is exceptional thanks to its multi-band GNSS system, locking on quickly and maintaining accuracy even through tree cover and narrow streets. The built-in coaching and training readiness tools have become part of my daily routine—providing recovery insights, suggested sessions, and race forecasts that actually feel tailored. For multisport training, it transitions modes smoothly, syncing effortlessly with sensors and Garmin Connect data.

As someone who loves to spend their hard-earned money on running in a pack of fellow weirdos at races, the pace predictor and race features are a big draw for the Garmin Forerunner 970. I sync my races from Garmin Connect, and the watch spits out predicted times for 5K up to marathons based on my VO2 max, training load, and recent runs, updating as I log more miles. What seals it for me are the race markers overlaid on the course profile, showing projected splits and elevation-adjusted pacing so I can visualize where to surge or conserve energy without second-guessing midrace. It's like having a personal coach whispering realistic goal times right before the gun goes off, turning pricey pack running into a heart-thumping hunt for a PR.

Battery life remains solid, though not as extreme as Garmin’s solar or expedition-focused models, lasting up to 20 days in smartwatch mode. Add in smart notifications, music storage, contactless payments, and wrist-based navigation, and it becomes a rare hybrid—a true performance watch that fits effortlessly into everyday life.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is a vast improvement over the Ultra 3, which is a polite way of saying the Ultra 3 had room to grow.

GPS now locks on fast, Apple says there’s no change here, but other members of my team and I noticed a difference. It might be in the software updates, but it’s better. I'm no longer starting runs before the watch has made up its mind. Once it has locked on, though, it commits to a story that isn’t quite true. Distance runs consistently one to one and a half percent long. During a marathon, that’s a few tenths of a mile I didn't earn.

Battery, thankfully, is finally impressing me. It’s leaps and bounds better, and it charges absurdly fast. I top it up while the coffee brews and I take my shower, and by the time I’m done, it’s fully loaded and ready to go.

Heart rate is the big jump. Against a Holter monitor, it stayed within two to three bpm on steady efforts. Run hard and it drifts to five to seven. I do wish it sampled my heart rate every second of every day instead of every five, but overall I don’t think the difference is huge, and when you combine that with the beauty of their apps, it’s hardly a thing.

What’s missing for me is lactate threshold. I can live without many advanced run metrics, but I like knowing my threshold for training runs.

In their new and improved health app, the ECG and hypertension alerts are useful, the cycle insights are spot on, and the morning report doesn’t make me feel graded. Transit pay, apps, and phone integration are unmatched. Satellite calling is extremely easy compared to any other watch I’ve tried. It’s a freaking great watch, overall.

When you step into the world of high-end GPS running watches, the sheer number of options can feel overwhelming—until you see the immense power packed into these bad boys. The essentials are non-negotiable: rock-solid multi-band GPS precision, exceptional battery life (no one wants to lose tracking on a 50K run), accurate heart rate and recovery metrics, and seamless integration with your training plans. Every watch on this list delivers on those core requirements.

Where they start to spread their wings is everything layered on top. The bells and whistles are kinda wild. Things like dual-frequency GPS for navigating deep woods (or mountaintops), topo and trail maps that actually make sense when you’re lost, and multisport modes that keep up whether you’re running, swimming, skiing, triathlon training, or rolling through a Hyrox circuit. Barometric altitude readings, pulse ox sensors, and training readiness scores just round out the “how cooked am I?” data we’ve all come to both love and loathe in equal measure.

Some watches, though, don’t just tell you about your fitness—they could save your butt in a sticky situation. The Garmin Fenix 8 Pro works with Garmin’s inReach satellite system, letting you text or send an SOS nowhere near cell service. The Apple Watch Ultra takes a slightly different route with built-in satellite SOS and cellular, so if you’re off-grid and something goes sideways, you’re not shouting into the void. These are the kinds of features that make the difference between just tracking a run and actually trusting your gear if things go sideways.

Let’s be honest—most runners don’t need a watch this powerful. But if you’re out there chasing hours instead of miles, exploring trail networks that don’t even show up on Google Maps, or toggling between swim intervals, mountain climbs, and winter ski sessions, these make a world of difference. Basically, if you’re a runner like me with electricity in your veins and the ADHD that drives you toward multisport or off-the-beaten-trail running, these watches are for you.

One of the quietest but most important reasons these watches shine is safety. With incident detection, live tracking, fall alerts, and SOS tools that actually connect you to help, they turn your wrist into a mini rescue hub. The Garmins can ping your emergency contacts automatically or connect through inReach. The Apple Watch Ultra fires off emergency signals via satellite if you end up out of range. And even the Suunto Vertical and Coros Vertix 2S earn their stripes here with detailed offline maps and batteries that cruise through multi-day efforts.

Basically, these aren’t just training tools—they’re peace of mind on your wrist. When you’re 10 miles deep in a trail system and the forest gets quiet, it’s nice knowing your watch is smarter about directions and safety than your phone or maybe even you.

Cat Bowen, senior editor of commerce; reviews, is a seasoned runner with more than 20 years of distance running experience, including dozens of marathons, half marathons, and even a few ultra marathons. For over a decade, she has tested parenting, fitness, home, and running gear and written in-depth guides to help readers with their next purchase. Passionate about women’s health and neurodivergent inclusion, she advocates for closing research gaps and helping others—especially AudHD people—find joy in running and fitness.

#191. Can Swapping Out Your Plasma Slow the Aging Process?

Discovering the fountain of youth is an age-old pursuit (pun not intended). One of the latest clock-reversing experiments causing a buzz is a technique called therapeutic plasma exchange, a procedure that filters and replaces the liquid portion of your blood. A 2025 study in Aging Cell suggests the technique could lower biological age by two and a half years.

But before you start googling “plasma clinics near me,” it’s important to look past the headlines to what the study’s saying, and what it means—and doesn’t mean—about new plasma as an anti-aging elixir.

Plasma is more than just the liquid that surrounds the red and white blood cells in your bloodstream. Although it’s mostly water, it’s also rich in proteins, metabolites, hormones, and inflammatory signals—molecules that reflect and influence what’s happening across your organ systems, Andrea Maier, MD, PhD, geriatrician and board member of the Academy for Health and Lifespan Research, tells SELF.

“It’s a transport system like DHL, a vehicle to bring things from your brain to your muscles, from kidney to lungs, and so on. So it’s fluid with lots of information,” she says.

This makes it a smart focal point for longevity studies because it can capture a wide-angle view of your body’s internal state, also sometimes called your “biological age.” By measuring changes in the levels of thousands of circulating proteins in your plasma, you can get some sense of how well you’re functioning.

What that means is you may be 40, but your biology acts more like that of a 30-year-old—or a 50-year-old. It’s not a fixed or precise measurement, but it’s helpful health information, Keenan Walker, PhD, senior investigator at the National Institute on Aging, tells SELF.

“There’s no one biological age, but people try to estimate it,” he says. “And what studies have found is that people whose biological age is older than their chronological age are at greater risk for chronic conditions, diseases, and mortality.”

About 15 years ago, researchers started exploring the connection between plasma and the aging process. This led to experiments using a process called parabiosis, a surgical technique that links together the circulatory systems of two different organisms. In studies, researchers would stitch together the systems of old mice and young mice, with the hypothesis that if you circulated younger plasma in an older organism, the older organism’s body would reap the benefits.

And the studies did show that. Older mice who received the plasma of younger mice had more resilience to tissue and organ stress. This led to the development of using plasma exchange as a way to treat certain autoimmune diseases, neurological disorders, and blood cancers.

“So everything really came out of that question: Is there something in our circulation we could get rid of or infuse into it to be able to live longer?” says Dr. Maier. But there’s not a definitive answer to that question—yet.

In the Aging Cell study, researchers enrolled 42 people and exchanged their plasma with purified albumin (a blood protein) and saline. Some participants also got a type of immune therapy called IVIG added in. Researchers measured changes in their bodies with advanced lab tests that track aging at the molecular level.

At first glance, the results look significant: Some people in the study reduced their biological age by roughly 2.5 years. But Dr. Maier points out that this data comes from the middle of the study, not the end.

“If you are digging a little bit deeper, this ‘2.5 years younger’ is comparing people at midterm to the baseline, not at the end of the study and the baseline. At the end, the effect was nearly gone,” she says.

Part of the reason for this, says Dr. Maier, is you overwhelm your body when you take all its plasma out and reintroduce different plasma. The influx of young cells can produce a shift in your biological age, but then your body starts experiencing stress as it adapts to this major change, and your biomarkers swing back to what they were before. In other words, you may get some rejuvenation in the short-term, but it’s temporary.

Another noteworthy detail about the study was the health of the participants, says Dr. Walker. “Those who were less healthy saw a stronger intervention effect,” he says. “So I think it'll be important to find out for whom this works.”

As a concept, both Drs. Maier and Walker see some promise in blood-based interventions for improving overall health but hope to see a more personalized approach rather than a generalized non-specific plasma filtering process.

“I would call this a phase 1 study,” says Dr. Maier. “We’ve basically learned that we can safely do it, and now we have to see it in much bigger studies and look at the long-term effect. It’s not a crazy idea. It’s absolutely grounded in lots of evidence, but not for everybody. It needs to be more precise. The future is great in our field, and this is the first tiny step, but we should absolutely not implement it now in clinical practice because it is so rough on the body. I love innovation, and I love this study, but I think the future will give something else.”

#192. Bumps Inside Nose: Common Causes and Top Treatments

There are many possible causes for bumps inside your nose — some as harmless as a pimple, others that might need more attention. It’s easy to imagine the worst, but the truth is usually less alarming.

If you’ve got a painful, annoying, or strange bump in your nose, keep reading to learn what it might be, whether it’s worth worrying about, and how to deal with it.

So, what’s behind these bothersome nose bumps? Here are some common culprits:

This is inflammation of the nasal vestibule, the area just inside your nostrils, often caused by bacterial infections. It can lead to painful, red bumps sensitive to the touch. Common triggers include frequent nose-picking, blowing too hard, or even plucking nose hairs.

Like on your face, the pores inside your nose can become clogged with oil, dirt, and bacteria, leading to pimples. These can be painful and may swell, especially in such a sensitive area.

Non-cancerous growths can develop in the nasal passages or sinus lining due to chronic inflammation, allergies, or infections. While they’re usually painless, larger polyps can cause blockages, leading to breathing difficulties, a reduced sense of smell, or recurrent sinus infections.

When you pluck or trim nose hairs, the hair can sometimes grow back into the skin instead of out, causing an ingrown hair. If this becomes infected, it can result in a painful bump inside the nose.

A bump can also form inside the nose due to trauma, such as a blow to the nose, or even from something as simple as aggressive nose-picking. The trauma can cause the tissue to swell or become bruised. In some cases, a hard bump may form as the tissue heals.

Fluid-filled sacs that can form in your nose, usually harmless but sometimes uncomfortable.

A hard bump inside the nose might be due to problems with the cartilage, such as a deviated septum or cartilage overgrowth.

Small, benign bumps that may appear on or in the nose are often mistaken for pimples but are fibrous tissue growths.

Additionally, if you’re dealing with nasal polyps, a healthcare professional might prescribe steroid sprays to shrink them and reduce inflammation, making breathing easier.

On the other hand, if a bacterial infection is the culprit, as in cases of nasal vestibulitis, your doc may recommend a topical antibiotic like mupirocin. This ointment is applied directly inside the nose to target the infection, reduce redness, and promote healing.

While most nose bumps aren’t a big deal, some need more attention. Here’s when to make that appointment:

Even the slightest bump inside your nose can be a major annoyance. Causes vary from harmless pimples to things that require more attention, like polyps.

Self-care measures can usually ease discomfort and speed healing, but if it’s super painful or worrying discharge, it’s time to sniff out professional help.

#193. How to Build Wider Lats with These Comprehensive V-Taper Workout Routines

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Most lifters want lats for one reason:  the V-taper. Well-developed lats give your upper body that powerful look from the front, side, and back, and yes, they make T-shirts fit better.

Red Bull isn’t the only thing that gives you wings.

Besides looking awesome, the lats keep your shoulders stable, support better upper-body posture, and connect your arms to your torso, improving form during heavy lifts. Strong lats improve pulling mechanics, create a stronger pressing setup, and help your upper back stay in a better position during squats and deadlifts.

Here I’m going all things lats, including:

By the end, you’ll know how to train your lats for a stronger back, better pulls, healthier shoulders, and an upper body that fills out your T-shirt.

The lats, short for latissimus dorsi, are the body’s widest muscles and cover much of the back. They’re broad, flat, and fan-shaped, which is why well-developed lats help create that V-Taper look.

Because of their size, the lats attach to the

Because they attach to the upper arm and spine, they influence both shoulder movement and posture.

Shoulder adduction: When you pull your arm down toward your side.

Shoulder extension: When you pull your arm behind your body.

Shoulder internal rotation: When the inside of your shoulder joint brings your forearm and hand closer to you.

They also help with scapular depression, which pulls the shoulders down away from your ears and is an important part of good pulling form. Train those actions well, and you’ll build a wider back, stronger pulls, and better control from your shoulders through your hips.

We all know that lats are the engine behind rows, pull-ups, and chin-ups, but some don’t realize the vital role they play beyond them.

During the deadlift, strong, engaged lats help keep the bar close to your body as you pull. When the bar drifts away, the lift gets harder, and your lower back gets unhappy.

Your lats matter during the bench press, too. When engaged, they help create a stable base to press from, improve your pressing path, and transfer force from your leg drive to your upper body.

That is why strong lats aren’t just a “back day” thing: they set the table for better pressing form.

Pulling your lats down and back creates upper-body tightness for barbell back squat. Doing so helps stabilize the bar and keeps you in a stronger, more upright position instead of folding forward into a good morning.

The lats also matter for shoulder health and posture because they influence shoulder position and upper-body alignment. When the lats are balanced in length, they let the shoulder blades rest flat, and the shoulders open back naturally. This supports better posture.

And yes, they matter outside the gym, too. Pulling open heavy doors, climbing, carrying objects close to your body, and lifting things from the floor all involve the lats. Bigger lats create the look, but stronger lats help you pull, brace, carry, and move well.

Because the lats are large and their muscle fibers run in different directions, train them through several pulling paths. You need vertical pulling, horizontal pulling, straight-arm work, loaded stretches, and good form to keep the tension where it belongs.

Start Vertical: Pull-ups and chin-ups remain the gold standard, while lat pulldowns let you use multiple grips and body positions to target the lats from different angles to increase volume for size and strength.

Rows That Train The Lats: The Underhand dumbbell row is a great example. Use an underhand grip and pull the dumbbell back in an arc, keeping your elbow close to your torso, starting below your shoulder and ending near the outside of your hip. This shifts the focus from the upper back to the lats.

Straight-Arm Work: Straight-arm pulldowns and their variations are as close as you’ll get to a lat isolation exercise. They’re useful because they reduce bicep involvement, making them great for lifters who struggle to feel their lats.

Unilateral Variations: Bilateral variations let you use more load but often hide muscle imbalances between sides. Strengthening these imbalances improves performance and strength on bilateral lifts and enhances lat development between sides.

You know the exercises, but that’s only part of it. For maximum growth and strength, keep these four things in mind.

Feel the Stretch: All muscles, including the lats, respond well to the loaded stretch because you’ll work through a full range of motion and the muscle stays under tension longer. Performing chin-ups and pull-ups from a dead hang will have your lats saying thank you.

Don’t Go Crazy:  Good form, full range of motion, and shoulder mobility all matter. Train the lats hard, but keep the reps clean. Big lats are great, but big lats that move well are better.

Full Range of Motion: Own both ends of the rep. Reach into the stretch under control, then finish by pulling the elbows down, back, or toward the hips, depending on the exercise. Cutting the ROM short changes your gains.

Progressive Overload: Add load, reps, sets, range of motion, or better control over time. But don’t sacrifice lat tension, shoulder position, or form to move more weight.

Here are general recommendations that work for most lifters most of the time.

Use sets of three to six reps on heavier pulls. Good options include weighted pull-ups, heavy chin-ups, and lat pulldowns. Rest 2 to 3 minutes between sets, and keep the reps clean.

Use sets of eight to 15 reps on pulldowns, rows, dumbbell rows to the hip, seated machine rows, or cable rows. This is your bread-and-butter hypertrophy work. Use a full range of motion, control the stretch, and finish each rep by pulling the elbows toward the ribs or hips, depending on the exercise.

Use sets of 12 to 20 reps on straight-arm pulldowns, kneeling straight-arm pulldowns, cable pullovers, and band straight-arm pulldowns. These are great for lifters who struggle to feel their lats because these exercises isolate them.

Straight-arm pulldown variations are useful before deadlifting because engaging the lats helps maintain a neutral spine and keep the bar close. One or two sets of 10 to 15 reps work well as a primer.

Most lifters can train the lats directly two to three times per week.

Think of 12 to 16 direct lat sets per week as your weekly target. How you divide those sets depends on your goal.

If strength is the priority, spend more sets in the 3 to 6 rep range with weighted pull-ups, heavy pulldowns, chin-ups, and rows. If size is the goal, focus more work in the 8 to 15 rep range with pulldowns, rows, single-arm work, and machine or cable variations. If you struggle to feel your lats, include 12 to 20 rep sets of straight-arm pulldowns, pullovers, or band work.

Here’s an example of how to organize your weekly volume. 12 weekly sets might include four heavier sets, six muscle-building sets, and two higher-rep straight-arm sets. That gives you a fantastic combination of strength, size, and lat connection.

Using too much weight you cannot control might stroke the ego, but it does nothing for your gains. Here are a few more mistakes to watch out for to get the most out of your lat training.

Your hands hold the bar, but your elbows should lead the movement. When lifters focus only on pulling with their hands, chin-ups, pulldowns, and rows often turn into biceps-heavy exercises with a side order of forearm fatigue.

Fix: Drive your elbows down during pulldowns, pull your elbows toward your hips during rows, and tuck your shoulder blades into your back pocket for chin-ups.

Many lifters cut the top of pulldowns, pull-ups, and straight-arm exercises short. That leaves a lot of potential lat tension on the table, because the lats love a loaded stretch.

Fix: Reach overhead or forward under control, keep the ribs down, and feel the stretch without dumping on the shoulder joint. The goal is to control a stretch, not just hang through the connective tissue.

When the ribs flare, the lower back often arches, turning a lat exercise into a lower-back exercise. This can happen during pulldowns, pullovers, and straight-arm work when someone tries to create range they don’t own.

Fix: Keep the ribs stacked over the pelvis by breathing out and bracing the core on top of that. This gives the lats a better chance to lengthen and shorten without the lower back taking over.

If your shoulders shrug toward your ears during rows or pulldowns, your upper traps dominate. Doing so takes the focus off the lats and can lead to upper trap and neck pain.

Fix: Tell yourself to keep your shoulders away from your ears and your chest up. You do this by keeping your neck long.

Lat training has its share of gym myths because everyone wants a wider back. Some advice sounds good until you realize it ignores range of motion, elbow path, body position, and the fact that your biceps will love to steal the show if you let them.

Wide-grip pulldowns and pull-ups are great, but they aren’t magic — and they don’t build wide lats. A wide grip doesn’t automatically increase lat tension. In fact, it often shortens your range of motion, limits the load, and shifts stress to the shoulders and upper back for many lifters. Shoulder-width, medium, and neutral grips offer a longer ROM, and you can lift more weight.

Pull-ups and chin-ups are gold-standard lat builders — but the lats need more. The problem is that pull-ups lock you into a single line of pull. Because the lats are large and wide, with muscle fibers running in different directions, dumbbell and machine variations let you adjust your body position and grips to change the line of pull and target muscle fibers that chin-ups miss.

Rows hammer the upper back, but they can also hit the lats with the right setup, grip, and elbow path. Rowing high with flared elbows shifts more attention to the traps, rear delts, and upper back. Rowing back toward the hip with your elbow close gives the lats more work.

They assist with deadlifts, squats, bench press setup, posture, and shoulder control. So yes, train them for width. But don’t forget they also help you lift better when no one is admiring your V-taper.

The lats don’t need a separate “back day or bust” approach. You can train them hard during an upper-body session or weave them into a full-body workout.

WORKOUT 1: UPPER-BODY LAT-FOCUSED WORKOUT

Goal: Build lat size and strength while still training the chest, shoulders, upper back, and arms.

1A. Chin-up, Pull-Up, or Lat Pulldown: 4 sets of 6 to 12 reps

1B. Dumbbell Bench Press: 3 sets of 6 to 12 reps

2A. Underhand Dumbbell Row: 3 sets of 12 to 15 reps per side

2B. Dumbbell Overhead Press: 3 sets of 6 to 12 reps

3A. Chest-Supported Row: 3 sets of 10 to 15 reps

3B. Biceps Curl Variation: 3 sets of 10 to 15 reps

Goal: Train the lats as part of a full-body workout.

1A. Band-Resisted RDL: 3 sets of 6 to 8 reps

1B. Dumbbell Bench Press: 3 sets of 6 to 12 reps

2A. Half-Kneeling Single-Arm Lat Pulldowns: 3 sets of 12 to 15 reps per side

2B. Goblet Split Squat: 3 sets of 6 to 12 reps per side.

3A. Unilateral Cable Row: 2-3 sets of 15 reps per side

3B. Back Extension: 2-3sets of 12 to 15 reps

3C. Dumbbell Pullover: 2-3 sets of 10 to 15 reps

The winning formula is this: train the lats with vertical pulls, rows, straight-arm work, single-arm variations, and exercises that challenge the stretch position. Keep the ribs down, control the shoulders, pull toward the hips to engage more lats, and stop letting your biceps, traps, and lower back take over.

Remember to lock the lats in during your squat, bench, and deadlift because they are the difference between a sloppy rep and a clean one. Use enough volume to grow and enough weight to build muscle and strength, but never shortchange the range of motion.

If you do it right, you’ll need to buy more shirts.

#194. This U.K. Runner Had No Support Crew in Chicago. Then a Facebook Post Changed His Entire Marathon.

A Facebook plea from his uncle turned into signs, confetti, and people looking out for him across 26.2 miles.

As a marathon runner, I know how much crowd support can carry you through 26.2 miles. I tape my name to my shirt before races because sometimes one stranger screaming it at exactly the right moment is enough to keep your legs moving. But I’ve run New York twice, with friends and family scattered around the course, and even then, I’ve never had anything close to what Englishman Ethan Woodhead experienced in Chicago.

Ethan traveled from Guernsey to Chicago alone for Sunday’s marathon, which apparently didn’t sit quite right with his uncle, Phil Woodhead. Two days before the race, Phil dropped a request into a Chicago Marathon Facebook group to see whether the city might help make the course feel a little less lonely.

“My nephew has travelled across from Guernsey to run the marathon this year. He travelled solo and has no support in Chicago,” he wrote. “I want to be a good uncle and see if we can surprise him with an occasional cheer along the route!”

He included Ethan’s name, bib number (2024), and his goal of running around 2:30, then asked anyone who didn’t already have somebody to support to give him a shout.

That “occasional cheer” request reached considerably more than a few spectators. The post pulled in more than 6,600 likes, 582 comments, and 181 shares, with strangers staking out spots along the course to catch the U.K. runner. “I’ll be at mile 23, I even have an extra confetti popper for him,” one person wrote. Another promised to track him and look out for him around miles 12 to 14.

Ethan, meanwhile, was unaware his uncle was trying to crowdsource a cheering section for him. On Instagram after the race, he said the first hints started arriving about 10 hours after Phil’s post went up, when random messages landed in his DMs from people saying they were tracking him, making signs, and planning to cheer.

The messages weren’t just talk, either. "I had so much support on the course," Ethan told NBC Chicago. "I can’t even put it into words. It pulled me along the whole way.”

He joked on Instagram that fellow runners may have assumed he was some big-shot influencer, but his own description—“just a lad from Guernsey” who makes “stupid videos”—was a little less glamorous and a lot closer to reality.

Ethan came extremely close to the goal his uncle had broadcast to thousands of strangers, finishing in 2:31:31. He placed 245th overall, 228th among men, and 96th in the 25–29 division.

Phil didn’t need to be in Chicago to find out whether his idea worked, and he seemed almost as surprised by what his post set in motion as his nephew was by the people who showed up for him.

“He called me right after the marathon and said he had cheers on every street, on every mile,” Phil told NBC Chicago. “It didn’t cost anyone anything, it was just pure love, just pure wanting to do something nice for someone else. And that’s what I take from this. How wonderful is that?”

Sean Abrams was the Senior Editor, Growth and Engagement at Men’s Health. He’s a former hip hop dancer who likes long walks on the beach and large glasses of tequila. You can find his previous work at Maxim, Elite Daily, and AskMen.

#196. Obstructive Sleep Apnea Impacts Women Differently.

There are at least a dozen reasons why women may wake up with a headache, jitter with anxiety, or struggle to keep their eyes open at work, no matter how well they think they slept: menstruation, menopause, motherhood—the list truly goes on. But these symptoms, as vague as they are, could actually stem from a health condition that’s historically been deemed a “male disease”: obstructive sleep apnea, or OSA.

If you immediately pictured an older man snoozing on a couch and snoring like a lawn mower, you’re not alone. It wasn’t until the ’90s that researchers first recognized that OSA, which causes you to repeatedly stop breathing while asleep, often presents differently in women than it does in men. For starters women with the condition may not even snore.

There’s still much to discover about the biology underlying these distinctions, but research suggests that hormonal fluctuations throughout life, differences in upper airway anatomy, and even social stigmas about how women should sleep are likely at play.

“The disease itself was defined in men,” explains Jennifer Martin, PhD, a behavioral sleep medicine specialist and professor at Florida International University’s Herbert Wertheim College of Medicine in Miami. “The way men and women breathe when they’re asleep is not the same, and our definition of the disease doesn’t account for that.”

Although obstructive sleep apnea appears to be less common and typically milder in women (at least before menopause), studies suggest that the consequences of the disease, if left untreated, can be similar, if not worse, for us, making it vital to learn the signs and seek help. Here’s what we know about obstructive sleep apnea and its impact on women. Plus, experts explain how to advocate for the best care if you think you may have the condition.

Sleep apnea is one of several conditions that fall under the sleep-disordered breathing umbrella. The most common type is OSA, which happens when your upper airway repeatedly collapses during sleep, making it harder for air to reach your lungs, says Anita Valanju Shelgikar, MD, a sleep medicine physician with University of Michigan Health and president of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine.

The textbook symptoms of this condition—which, for the record, were determined based on studies mostly involving men—include loud snoring and dramatic gasps for air as a person tries to continue breathing while asleep. But this often isn’t the case for women, Dr. Shelgikar tells SELF. Instead, women with OSA are more likely to have nightmares, wake up multiple times a night, have trouble staying asleep, and deal with insomnia, which then causes symptoms like daytime fatigue, morning headaches, and mood swings. Women also have more hypopneas (shallow breaths with less oxygen flow), whereas men tend toward apneas (complete pauses in breathing).

Some experts speculate that it’s possible snoring isn’t commonly reported among women with this disorder because they’re embarrassed to talk about it, given society expects them to sleep like Disney princesses. But a growing body of research suggests that biology may better explain this and other sex-related differences in symptoms. For example, compared with men, women have smaller, more stable airways that are less likely to collapse (and in turn vibrate, making you snore) during sleep. Women also tend to have less fat around their necks, and before menopause they seemingly benefit from the protective effects of estrogen and progesterone, which interact with the respiratory system in a way that aids breathing.

All things considered, it makes sense why more men than women in the US have this condition, making up about 59% and 41% of obstructive sleep apnea patients, respectively. However, once women go through menopause, which causes their estrogen and progesterone levels to drop, the rate of OSA and the severity of symptoms in this group increases dramatically, Dr. Martin says. Studies have found that anywhere from 47% to 67% of postmenopausal women have obstructive sleep apnea, which is about the same as men in this age range (50 and older). The number of women who actually get diagnosed with the condition is a different story, though—more on that shortly.

Regardless of age, however, women still deal with more sleep apnea–related symptoms than men, Dr. Martin adds, even if they have a less severe form of the condition. This is likely because women have more “subtle breathing disturbances” during sleep that hurt the overall quality of their rest compared with men, Dr. Martin says.

Because women often don’t experience “classic” OSA symptoms, they end up being misdiagnosed or dismissed. “When [men] walk into a physician’s office and say they’re sleepy and they snore, they get a diagnostic test right away,” Dr. Martin says. “When a woman walks in and says, ‘I don’t sleep well, and I’m very fatigued during the day,’ they don’t often get referred” for screening. In fact, research suggests that men are nine times more likely to be referred for diagnostic testing than women.

Women with OSA commonly have their symptoms misattributed to conditions like depression, anxiety, insomnia, and menopause or even medication side effects, says Dr. Shelgikar, who is also a neurology professor at the University of Michigan Medical School. Not to mention women can have these other conditions as well, which might make their sleep apnea not only harder to detect but also worsen it. Take the double whammy that is insomnia and OSA: Having both of these disorders at the same time is more common among women than men, Dr. Martin says, and in some cases they may be given a sleep aid (such as diphenhydramine or a benzodiazepine) that can further relax their throat muscles, exacerbating their sleep apnea and leaving them even more oxygen-deprived.

And it doesn’t help that, as we talked about earlier, the diagnostic criteria for OSA are largely based on how the condition presents in men. “When we diagnose sleep apnea, we require one of two things to happen: A breathing interruption has to be associated either with a drop in oxygen levels or a brief awakening from sleep,” Dr. Martin says. “Women don’t have those very deep drops in oxygen levels that men do. So that means that the way we define the disease itself kind of biases us towards diagnosing it more in men than women.” What’s more, Medicare, which the vast majority of Americans ages 65 and older rely on for health insurance, only recognizes a sleep apnea diagnosis if a person has those steep drops in oxygen, Dr. Martin says. Those typical mid-slumber wake-ups don’t count on their own. So even “the criteria that Medicare forces people to use to define sleep apnea is very male-centric,” she adds.

Home sleep apnea tests, which are becoming increasingly common as a cheaper alternative to the gold standard in-lab exams, are also more prone to miss the condition in women. Because women tend to have fewer and milder events than men, these at-home tests may not be able to diagnose sleep apnea as accurately in this population, Dr. Martin says. They can be even more inaccurate in women with insomnia. These individuals “may not get enough sleep to get an accurate diagnosis,” she says, “so if they wear [the monitor] for six hours, but they’re only sleeping for four of them, it may look like they have less sleep apnea than they really do.”

That’s all to say that sleep apnea is likely much more common among women than the available data suggests, experts tell SELF. And that reality reveals a sobering point: A lot of women with this condition probably aren’t receiving the care they need, a delay that can, for some people, snowball into an avalanche of additional yet preventable health issues.

If left untreated, sleep apnea can have downstream effects on your health, particularly your heart, says Atul Malhotra, MD, research chief of pulmonary, critical care, and sleep medicine at UC San Diego Health. Every time you stop breathing, your body responds to the lack of oxygen by releasing the stress hormone adrenaline to jolt you awake so you take a breath. This happens really quickly; you are typically up for just a few seconds and probably won’t even remember it the next morning.

Over time this constant stress strains your cardiovascular system, Dr. Malhotra says, which may increase your risk for high blood pressure, heart attack, stroke, irregular heartbeat, and heart failure. Although the evidence is mixed, some research suggests that it’s more common for women with severe sleep apnea to experience cardiovascular complications than it is for men. Studies also show that women tend to have more health conditions upon diagnosis than men do, including thyroid disease, asthma, and depression. This raises the classic “chicken or the egg” question, but either way treating OSA can only help.

Because obstructive sleep apnea leads to low-quality shut-eye, it is also associated with memory and cognition issues and poor daytime alertness, which can boost the likelihood of car and workplace accidents (for certain high-risk jobs like those in the transportation and construction industries), Dr. Shelgikar says. Perhaps less discussed is how untreated sleep apnea affects our ability to care for ourselves and maintain relationships. “We don’t do a good job thinking about sleep apnea as a potential cause of mental health symptoms,” Dr. Martin says. In fact, research shows that managing OSA could actually help some people dealing with anxiety and depression improve their symptoms.

As researchers continue searching for answers, Dr. Martin points to a silver lining: There’s good evidence to suggest that women “benefit at least as much as men, if not more” from sleep apnea treatment, which is why it’s important to know what to look out for.

Although you’re quite literally working against decades of medical bias, it’s still possible to receive a sleep apnea diagnosis if you’re equipped with the right intel.

#197. Text Neck Exercises: Simple Moves to Ease Digital Strain

Whether you’re caught up in doomscrolling or just checking your work emails, chances are you’re spending a lot of time on your phone. But all that screen time can lead to a pesky condition called “text neck.” Hunching over your device can leave you with some severe aches and pains.

So, hold your phone up to eye level and check out these easy tips to get rid of text neck fast!

Also known as “tech neck,” text neck is a term coined by a chiropractor to describe the neck pain you might feel after spending too much time looking down at your phone.

Most of us check our phones with our heads tilted forward and down. When you do this for too long, the muscles in your neck get strained. The muscles in the back are overstretched, while the ones in the front are compressed.

If you have text neck, here’s what you might be dealing with:

But don’t get bent out of shape about overusing your favorite device. There’s no solid proof that your phone habits are to blame for your neck woes. Several studies found no connection between using your device and having neck or shoulder pain.

You could get a sore neck from overusing your muscles for many other reasons, like genetic factors, weight issues, or bad posture. “Text neck” might be a term concocted by a chiropractor to get your business. But, hey, we’re not judging.

To help ease text neck pain, try these simple exercises.

Aside from these cubicle-friendly exercises, here are some ideas to help keep text neck from being a regular pain in the y’know:

“Text neck” is the popular term for the head and neck pain caused by hunching over your device for too long. But don’t throw away your beloved device just yet. More research is needed to link “text neck” to your tech time.

In the meantime, sit up straight and do gentle exercises like neck rolls, chin tucks, and shoulder rolls. To prevent text neck from hitting you up on the reg, take regular breaks from your phone and seek out habits that help lengthen and strengthen your body. Your neck will thank you!

#198. Is a $600 Cycling Shoe Nearly 70 Percent Better Than a $350 One?

I compared Sidi’s Shot 3 and Genius X Wyve to see what the extra $250 gets you.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Is a $600 cycling shoe nearly 70 percent better than a $350 cycling shoe?

That’s the question I kept asking myself this summer as I rode in Sidi’s $600 Shot 3 ($550 at some retailers) and $350 Genius X Wyve.

And to be clear, I don’t consider a $350 cycling shoe inexpensive. These are both high-end shoes from one of the most storied brands in cycling. This isn’t a comparison between a bargain shoe and a race-day dream shoe. It’s about what spending more gets you, and whether you’ll notice the difference once you’re clipped in and riding.

I started with one of the clearest differences between the shoes: their soles. Sidi rates the Shot 3’s “R1FC carbon sole with Nexus Bridge” at 12 for stiffness. The Genius X Wyve’s “R3CC carbon-composite” sole gets a 6.

That’s a big difference on paper. Stiff carbon soles are a calling card of expensive cycling shoes, with an implied promise: Stiffer is better, and better is worth more money.

Research co-authored by Tripp Hurt, a biomechanics researcher at the University of Colorado Boulder, suggests the answer is more complicated than shoe marketing makes it sound. In one study, trained cyclists sprinted in shoes with soles of different stiffness. The researchers found that performance began to fall below a certain level of stiffness, but the differences between the stiffest and more flexible soles were small. Hurt has argued that, for most riders, chasing stiffness may matter less than finding a comfortable shoe that fits well.

Could I feel a difference on the bike? Yes. The Shot felt stiffer, but it didn’t feel twice as stiff as the Genius. Maybe, maybe, 10 percent stiffer at most. More importantly, I noticed no difference in performance or perceived effort that I could attribute to sole stiffness.

A bigger difference was weight. On my scale, the size 41.5 pair of Shots weighed 516 grams; the Genius pair weighed 627 grams. That’s a 111-gram difference, or 55.5 grams per shoe. To me, the lighter shoes feel easier to kick around. And when each foot is going around 80 to 100 times a minute, carrying less weight on each foot seems like it should add up.

But is that enough to spend about 70 percent more on the Shot? I’ve always preferred a light shoe, but even I struggle to articulate a compelling benefit beyond “It feels better.” For some riders, that may be reason enough.

If you’re obsessive about climbing and watts per kilogram, the Shot’s 111-gram weight advantage does reduce your system weight. All else equal, that could make you marginally faster on a climb where gravity is the main resistance. For an 80-kilogram rider-and-bike system, 111 grams is about a 0.14 percent weight reduction.

Both shoes use Sidi’s Millennium fit, which the company describes as having a “slightly wider forefoot” to accommodate a broader range of foot shapes. I used to love Sidi’s classic slipper fit, but my feet have changed as I’ve gotten older, and now I need more room. On my feet, the Millennium fit is notably roomier than Sidi’s classic shape and closer to how Specialized’s and Shimano’s shoes fit. But the Millennium fit is not a “wide fit” cycling shoe in the traditional sense.

I find it excellent: My toes can spread without hot spots, while the shoes remain secure and supportive.

But on Sidi’s recreational-to-performance fit scale, the Shot scores a 10 while the Genius scores a 6. I found that confounding. If both shoes use the Millennium fit, what explains the different ratings? I reached out to Sidi to help decode, but the company didn’t respond by publication.

On my feet, the Shot’s upper felt firmer and more supportive. The Genius was plusher, with a little more give. The shoes had about the same room, and both held my heel equally well. I’d describe the difference I felt like this: The Shot felt like a bear hug; the Genius, a swaddle.

I initially preferred how locked in the Shot felt. But as I did more and longer rides, the Genius proved more comfortable.

Both shoes use Sidi’s “NUUN 001C” aluminum dials, but arrange them differently. The Shot has both dials on the tongue, where they tighten laces that pull the shoe together. The Genius puts its dials on the side: The upper dial tightens an adjustable-length forefoot strap, while the lower uses the lacing to pull the closure together.

The Shot’s cleaner arrangement should be more aerodynamic and may help explain why it’s lighter. But I preferred the Genius’s closure. I like my upper closures as tight as possible, just a little bit shy of painful, and its adjustable forefoot strap gave me more ability to fine-tune the fit; and, at a similar tightness, the Genius felt more comfortable than the Shot. That let me cinch it tighter and get a more secure fit without sacrificing comfort.

The Genius is physically bulkier, so it was more likely to brush the crankarm as I pedaled. That never happened with the Shot. To prevent it, I needed to set the Genius cleats for a slightly wider stance; with the Shot, I could use a narrower Q-factor. Crankarm rub is a sensation I find very annoying. For me, the wider stance wasn’t a problem. I’m not particularly sensitive to Q-factor, but I know some riders are, so I wanted to share the difference.

One thing about both shoes I want to highlight: Sidi offers replacement parts for many current and older models, including dials, buckles, straps, and heel pads. Sidi shoes have a reputation for lasting, and access to replacement parts can help extend their life. When you’re spending $350 or $600 on a pair, that matters.

Frankly, both the Shot and the Genius are excellent shoes. But I ultimately preferred the less expensive Genius. It was simply more comfortable, and that comfort paid dividends in my riding. The Shot’s stiffness and weight advantages were noticeable, but they didn’t pay off in a way I valued.

Is the Shot a nearly 70 percent better shoe than the Genius X Wyve? For me, no. If you want the lightest, stiffest shoe and value those differences, the Shot may be worth the extra $250. But if comfort matters more, the Genius is the better shoe—and it costs less.

A gear editor for his entire career, Matt’s journey to becoming a leading cycling tech journalist started in 1995, and he’s been at it ever since; likely riding more cycling equipment than anyone on the planet along the way. Previous to his time with Bicycling, Matt worked in bike shops as a service manager, mechanic, and sales person. Based in Durango, Colorado, he enjoys riding and testing any and all kinds of bikes, so you’re just as likely to see him on a road bike dressed in Lycra at a Tuesday night worlds ride as you are to find him dressed in a full face helmet and pads riding a bike park on an enduro bike. He doesn’t race often, but he’s game for anything; having entered road races, criteriums, trials competitions, dual slalom, downhill races, enduros, stage races, short track, time trials, and gran fondos. Next up on his to-do list: a multi day bikepacking trip, and an e-bike race.

#199. I’m Picky About Running Shorts—This Newer Brand Nailed the Fit, Fabric, and Style

Miler’s Work Shorts balance run-ready function with a look that works after miles, too.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

I firmly believe running shorts matter more than running shoes—I’ll take a blister, bruised toenail, or hot spot over a nether regions rash any day—and the Bandit Vento Shorts have been my Platonic Ideal: pocket configuration, fit, liner. It all works for me. They were only a seasonal offering for a while, and I’d stock up on every drop (though they’re now a core piece available year-round). I can’t recommend them enough, but I’ve recently been reaching for a different pair.

Miler Running is one of my favorite newer running brands because it balances design and functionality equally. The brand uses imported fabrics and makes all its gear in New York’s garment district, something I’ll gladly pay a bit more for when shopping for running and civilian clothes. I got a pair of its Work 2-in-1 Running Shorts at the beginning of the year, and they’re easily my most-worn pair of 2026.

Miler’s Work Shorts pare back the pockets from Bandit’s Ventos, but I’m preferring the clean silhouette lately. It has two liner pockets for my phone or gels, plus a small key pocket on the waistband. Nothing bounces whether I’m on a long easy run or sprinting up a hill and letting my running form go out the window. The liner offers light compression that keeps me snug yet comfortable, and I haven’t had any chafing.

What impresses me most is the fabric—it’s extremely lightweight. I don’t pay much attention to the fabric weight of running apparel because I’m no Olympian. Shaving precious milliseconds off my mile times isn’t a concern. But man, these Miler shorts have me reconsidering that stance. It feels like I’m wearing next to nothing, next-level freedom of movement. Satisfy

As far as looks go, they easily pivot from workout to casual wear thanks to tonal branding and a subdued color. I’m all for loud colors and patterns—I ran my first marathon in leopard-lined shorts—but I like that Miler’s Work Shorts don’t scream “running”. They’ll seamlessly go from run-club run to run-club coffee afterward.

I won’t get on my soapbox here, but I will say I like spending money on brands that do more than just make and sell stuff. Miler hosted a Dirt City Series run club over the summer that promoted using and maintaining dirt roads and trails in New York City. In contrast, it recently began its Grid City Series, a guided run which explores the design and architecture around town. Not many run clubs open your eyes to an 18-mile dirt trail starting in Brooklyn, or the history of a SoHo facade; a zag amongst endless run club zigs.

I still wear my Bandit Ventos, and they’re a great pair to rotate, but Miler’s Work Shorts are my personal favorite of 2026. Their approach to fabric and design matches some of my favorite clothing brands, and the construction is comfortable and durable. “Look good, feel good” is an adage I wholeheartedly believe in. Miler adds “run good” to it.
