#201. I Counted Gear at the 2026 Ironman World Championship. This is What I Saw.

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

TJ Tollakson counts power meters at the 2026 Ironman World Championship bike check in. (Photo: Brad Kaminski/Triathlete)

How we reported: Editors from Triathlete, alongside other media outlets and tri industry reps have sent counters to Kailua-Kona, Hawaii, to count bikes and bike components at the Ironman World Championship for decades. This year, former pro and tri bike expert T.J. Tollakson assisted in counting power meters, while managing editor Abby Levene counted wheelsets.

I worked the first shift of the bike count at the 2026 Hawaii Ironman World Championship, and I’ve been part of the bike count at the world champs going back to 2006. You see a lot of trends come and go in that time, and some that stick. Sure, the winning bike brand is the headline grabber, but the most interesting stuff lies way beneath the surface.

My job this year was counting power meters as racers walked from Palani to the Kona pier, where the transition area and bike racks live for the Ironman World Championships. Fifteen years ago, the gold standard, an SRM crank-based power meter, cost about $3,400 and was an elite luxury item. Today, power meters are abundant and affordable, and the vast majority of the 2,000-plus bikes we counted on the pier had one. In fact, many brands sell power meters as a part of a moderately affordable complete bike — something nearly unthinkable less than a decade ago. This means the power meters blend gracefully into the overall bike’s design, making the count much harder than ever. There are also more brands than ever, and left-side-only meters make it tricky to spot them from the drive side (difficult, but not impossible for someone who has spent most of their life racing and working on tri bikes).

After hours of wiping the sweat from my brow, swatting buzzing fruit flies, and dodging “Banyan tree fruit droppings” (probably poop, but oh well), I’ve been able to sit down and truly dive deep into the depth of data. Here’s what I’ve learned.

Canyon won the Ironman World Championship bike count for the second time in Kona history (the Nice events notwithstanding). For most of the time I’ve been counting, Cervélo owned the Kona pier with a quarter of all bikes in the Ironman World Championship transition area. Canyon had four bikes in 2010. This year it had 509. What exactly does that mean? And how did the German brand get there?

Canyon is the story of this count: 509 bikes, 22.5% of everything that came through transition, and 122 more than Cervélo. That’s not a fluke year either; they were at the top of the 2024 Kona list with the men (483) and were right there with the women in 2025. (As a somewhat interesting side note, Canyon had a bigger in-person brand team in Kona than we’ve seen in years, so they’re paying attention.)

How Canyon got here matters, but there’s more to it than “they make great bikes.” Canyon sells direct-to-consumer (DTC), so there’s no brick-and-mortar shop margin built into the price, and they’ve been aggressive with discounts on top of that.

They also spend (very) big where world-championship-caliber triathletes can see it (the triathletes who roll their bikes out onto the Kona pier in October): pro sponsorships, age-group activations, and a presence in Kona race week that is hard to miss. That combination gobbled up market share. It is also expensive, and it hasn’t necessarily been profitable.

Follow the money and it lines up with the chart above:

Canyon already had good forward momentum before the big money showed up — and it’s likely that was what made it an attractive investment. With TSG as a minority investor, it went from 18 bikes in 2013 to 179 in 2019 (8.1% of the pier), but the first big jump was in 2017 (39 to 102).

Then GBL and LeBron came in in 2020, and it went to 15.5% in 2022 and 21% in 2024 after the start of the COVID pandemic. That’s the steepest part of the line, and it starts right after the checks cleared.

Now let’s look at the other side of the ledger:

GBL wrote its Canyon stake down 43% in one year, from €460M to €261M ($514.9M to $292M USD). According to GBL’s own numbers that takes the whole company from roughly €925M to around €525M ($1B to $587.6M USD), and it slipped again in 2025, even after GBL bought more of it.

Revenue fell 6-7% in 2025, EBITDA was down 34%, and in January 2026 Canyon announced up to 320 job cuts. The stated target is €1B (roughly $1.1B USD) in revenue by 2028.

So here’s my read. The market share on the pier is real; I counted it. But it was bought with private equity money (and a little bit of LeBron’s) at a loss. That works as long as the owners keep believing. The question for the next few counts is whether Canyon can hold 20%+ of Kona when the discounting has to stop and the books have to balance.

It’s also very important to note that Canyon makes more than just triathlon bikes — they have a popular road line, a gravel line, and a mountain bike line — and it’s unclear how much of their total sales come from triathlon. Canyon even sells e-bikes and commuter bikes. Cervelo, on the other hand, mostly sells tri, road, and some gravel (plus one e-bike model). Similarly, Canyon sponsors athletes from each of their racing-related categories, and specifically stakes in road cycling teams like CANYON//SRAM, Alpecin-Premier Tech, and Movistar.

DT Swiss was the number-one wheel brand on the pier: We counted 421 DT wheelsets (23.2%), with Zipp second at 327, and HED third at 149.

DT got there largely because of Canyon. Canyon specs race-day DT wheels on a lot of its tri bikes, so every Canyon that rolls onto the pier is very likely a DT wheelset too. That’s the power of OEM. Zipp sells to the athlete who chooses Zipp (whether aftermarket or on a few stock-ish completes). DT sells to Canyon, and Canyon sells 509 bikes.

And here’s the kicker. Canyon lost €38M ($42.5M USD) in 2024. DT Swiss is privately held, so we don’t see their books, but I’d bet they made money on every one of those wheels. Canyon took the risk and the losses to grow market share; DT Swiss got paid.

If you’re asking who really won the Kona bike count, I think it’s DT Swiss.

Eighteen years ago, hands up high and angled toward the sky was a radical position. People laughed at it. Now it’s the default for both the pros and for the age-groupers. Walk down the rack and you’ll see extensions tilted up, pads stacked, elbows narrow, bike after bike.

What’s changed recently is how people get there: Profile Design was still the number-one aerobar on the pier (497, 23.3%). Canyon’s integrated cockpit was second (284, 13.3%), then Bontrager (169) — both directly due to the fact that they come OEM on the first and third most popular brands on the pier. FastTT (125) was fourth with its custom 3D-printed extensions built to your arms, and that’s the direction everything is heading. Custom 3D-printed, carbon-integrated cockpits with hydration built right into the front end. The position stuck, but also the hardware got a lot more personal.

Bottles everywhere, and storage everywhere: behind the saddle, between the arms, inside the frame. The bike that just has two cages on the downtube is basically gone.

The biggest jump this year was integrated rear hydration, storage built into the frame or seatpost by the bike company itself. It was 5.9% of rear setups in 2025 and 19.7% this year (307). EZ Gains was the number-one rear setup at 353 (22.7%), then Profile Design (280) and X-Lab (266).

Up front, “Other” was the biggest category at 558, which indicates mostly custom, 3D-printed, and integrated systems that don’t fit any one brand. (2025 was a women’s-only race, so it’s not a perfect comparison, but the trend is obvious standing on the pier.)

The brands have figured out that the bottle can be part of the aero package, instead of a penalty on top of it. Hang the fuel where it’s out of the wind, fill the gap between your arms, and you’re actually faster. The average bike splits keep getting faster, and this is a big part of why.

We did see one age-group athlete attempt to check in a bike with a disc wheel cover, but he was forced to remove the cover before racking his bike. Kona still bans disc wheels because of the wind. Fine.

But look at what the fastest folks rode: Marten Van Riel (BEL), Frederic Funk (DEU), and Lisa Perterer (AUT) all had the HED Jet 180 out back; men’s winner Vincent Luis (FRA) rode an Evolve Charger Trispoke, and Norwegians Gustav Iden and Kristian Blummenfelt rode a Cadex prototype. The Jet 180 is a disc with a few holes in it. The Evolve and Cadex rears are the same deep-carbon idea but with a fat carbon tri-spoke.

These wheels exist because of the Kona rule, and they’re essentially discs made for Kona. It’s actually a wonder that these deep-dish configurations — or the arguably more aggressive double tri-spoke setup that athletes like Nick Thompson (AUS), Cam Wurf (AUS), Solveig Løvseth (NOR), and Regan Hollioake (AUS) all rode — aren’t completely ubiquitous in the pro bike racks, but of course everyone has varying degrees of handling skills in the gusty Big Island crosswinds.

If the wheel companies have already engineered their way around the ban, what is the ban doing? Athletes are buying a Kona-only wheel to ride the one race on the calendar that won’t let them use the wheel they already own? It’s time to allow discs — if nothing else than for the pros.

There were still plenty of rim brake bikes on the pier, but the number is dwindling fast. Zipp, ENVE, and DT Swiss don’t even make rim brake aero wheels anymore. If you see a rim brake bike in Kona now, it’s either at least five years old or the athlete is going for a retro vibe. I don’t expect to be counting many of them in a few more years.

This was my station at the 2026 count, so I’ll spend a few minutes here.

We saw 1,486 power meters for all bikes counted; that’s about 66% of the field. Last year it was 900 power meters on 1,529 bikes, about 59%. Remember: 15 years ago an SRM power meter was a $3,400 luxury item.

Quarq was number-one by a mile with 532 (35.8% of all power meters). Then Assioma (353), Garmin (201), Shimano (111), and 4iiii (102). Back in 2010 we counted 51 Quarqs. In 2011 it was 119 and in 2012 it was 191. Now it’s 532.

Here’s the number that jumped out at me. There were 776 SRAM cranksets on the pier, and 532 Quarqs. Not every Quarq is on a SRAM crank, but nearly all the modern ones are. That means SRAM is selling roughly 68.6% of its cranksets with a power meter built in. When SRAM bought Quarq in 2011, that’s precisely what they were buying.

Shimano is the opposite story: 1,004 Shimano cranksets, and only 111 Shimano power meters. That’s 11.1%. Shimano has struggled to make a power meter that is affordable and that people trust, so Shimano riders go to Assioma and Garmin pedals or a left-side crank arm meter instead. (Which also makes counting harder!) For example, we had 489 Assioma pedals but 353 Assioma power meters, so we have a data discrepancy. Left-side meters and power pedals are a lot easier to miss than a big Quarq spider.

In 2009 SRAM had 16.4% of the pier, Campagnolo still had 6.1%, and Shimano had literally everything else. SRAM climbed to about a quarter by 2013, then slid back when Shimano’s Di2 took over the tri world (Shimano peaked at 83.8% in 2016), but SRAM has been climbing ever since.

This year it was 913 SRAM groupsets to Shimano’s 1,511. Campagnolo had two. Two!

The reason is simple. SRAM has new wireless 12- and 13-speed options built for tri bikes. Shimano still doesn’t have a 12-speed tri groupset. If you want a 12-speed Dura-Ace on a tri bike, you are running 11-speed bar-end shifters with wires, adapters, and firmware updates to make it work. It works, but it’s a workaround. SRAM is the one making it easy right now, and if Shimano doesn’t answer soon, I think SRAM passes 40% next year.

#202. After Losing My Son, I Didn't Want to Be ‘Strong’

During my pregnancy with my son Milan, I remember sitting with a pain that didn’t feel normal. It was sharp, persistent, and unsettling in a way I couldn’t ignore. As a former labor and delivery nurse, I understood the risks in a way many patients do not. I knew what to watch for. I knew my history. I knew when something felt wrong. Yet when I raised concerns, they were not met with the urgency they deserved.

At the time of my pregnancy with Milan, I had already experienced a high-risk pregnancy and an emergency C-section during a previous pregnancy. I knew that the vertical incision on my uterus could put a future pregnancy at risk. I spoke up. I asked questions. I paid attention to my body. Still, when I experienced a uterine rupture, I was navigating a system that did not respond with the level of care and urgency that the moment required.

If someone with years of labor and delivery experience can recognize the signs, advocate for herself, and still be failed, what happens to the women with less information, fewer resources, or less confidence that they will be heard?

Conversations during Black Maternal Health Week often center around one urgent truth: Black women are still far more likely to die from pregnancy-related causes in this country than white women. This is not an assumption. It is a proven fact, and it should stop all of us in our tracks. It also does not only impact one socioeconomic group. It affects everyone, including some of the most visible and resourced women in the world.

As the founder of Mielle, my mission is to empower women, especially Black women, to express their authentic selves. At its core, that mission is about care, agency, and visibility, which is why conversations like this matter. It’s about showing up for every part of Black women’s experience. We need to talk more candidly about what happens to Black women who survive the trauma of miscarriage or stillbirth, and the prolonged mental health challenges that can follow, including postpartum depression.

Black women are expected to remain “strong” while navigating medical emergencies. We’re dismissed, told to wait, to calm down, and to trust a system that has not always earned that trust. We survive experiences that change our families and us forever. And then, too often, we are expected to do something just as impossible: keep going as if survival is the end of the story. It is not.

That is why Black Maternal Health Week cannot be about mortality alone. It must also be about what it means to live after trauma, preventable harm, and loss that reshapes your life.

The data make clear that this crisis is ongoing. Black women are about three times more likely to die from pregnancy-related causes than white women, and more than 80% of those deaths are considered preventable. Black infants also die at more than twice the rate of white infants. These are not random gaps. They reflect a healthcare system and a culture that too often normalizes Black women’s pain instead of responding to it.

Research shows that one in five women, or about 20%, report mistreatment during maternity care, but for Black women, that figure climbs to nearly 30%, reflecting more frequent experiences of bias, disrespect, and lack of autonomy in clinical settings. Nearly half of women say they have held back from asking questions or sharing concerns. In one of the most vulnerable moments of a person’s life, too many are already calculating whether speaking up will make things worse.

In my own life, grief did not arrive quietly. It entered my marriage, my motherhood, my body, my faith, and eventually my work. In my book, The Glory In Your Story, I write about how grief does not follow a timeline. It becomes part of who you are, and healing begins not by outrunning it, but by acknowledging it.

That matters because so many Black women are praised for being strong when what we actually need is space to be human. After losing Milan, I returned to work. I kept moving. I built Mielle. From the outside, it can look like a story of resilience. And in many ways, it is. But we have to be honest about the lessons we take from stories like mine.

The lesson should not be that Black women are uniquely equipped to carry devastating grief and still perform at a high level. It should not be that our resilience makes systemic failures acceptable. And it should not be that we have to turn survival into something productive just to make our pain legible.

Too often, we celebrate the comeback without sitting long enough with the conditions that made it necessary.

Faith carried me. Purpose helped me rebuild. But none of that changes the reality that more listening, better care, stronger hospital systems, and greater urgency might have changed my story. If we are serious about maternal health, we have to be just as serious about saying that clearly.

Black Maternal Health Week gives us an opportunity to think more broadly about what justice looks like. It looks like hospitals are equipped for emergencies. It looks like providers who listen to Black women the first time, without requiring patients to fight to be believed. It looks like support for families after loss–not just during a crisis. And it looks like making space for grief without expecting Black women to turn it into inspiration before we are ready.

It’s time that we honor not only the women we have lost, but also the women still here carrying what the system could not or would not hold for them. Survival is not the finish line. Being heard, protected, and cared for should be.

#203. Michal ‘Krizo’ Krizanek Dominates 2026 EVLS Prague Pro to Qualify for 2027 Mr. Olympia

Michal “Krizo” Krizanek has qualified for the 2027 Mr. Olympia final after the Slovakian slayed on stage at the 2026 EVLS Prague Pro. Here are all the results from an epic show in Europe.

Krizo, who also won the Prague Pro back in 2022, will now have a chance to better his career high, sixth place ‘O’ showing at next year’s event after a stunning display saw him take the $30,000 check and stamp his ticket to Las Vegas on Oct. 11.

On Sunday night, Krizo’s combination of size and conditioning made him the overall pick of the judges. “1st place,” wrote the big man in a celebratory comment via his official Instagram account. “Nomination for Olympia 2027 in the pocket.”

Krizo has also confirmed that he will step on stage again at the Slovakia Pro, scheduled for Oct. 25, 2026. “We are very much looking forward to further progress,” he added. Of course, the Prague Pro also played host to several other exciting divisions, including Mike Sommefeld winning in Classic, and Shuan Clarida topping 212. Here are the full results.

#204. Starvation Mode: How Caloric Restriction Affects Your Body

Cutting back on calories but not losing weight? You might wonder if you’ve gotten stuck in the twilight zone of so-called “starvation mode.”

Everyone from your personal trainer to your grandma may have warned you about this metabolic frenemy that keeps your body holding onto weight. But is starvation mode really a thing — or just an urban legend?

The concept of starvation mode is that when you restrict calories, your body has a “hold it right there” response. To prevent you from losing weight rapidly, your metabolism slows, conserving energy by reducing the calories it burns.

Research shows starvation mode — formally called adaptive thermogenesis or metabolic adaptation — is a legit phenomenon. It’s well documented that sometimes, the more weight you lose (and the more rapidly you do so), the more your body resists the process.

Evolutionarily speaking, this may be a holdover from when humans faced food scarcity and needed a mechanism for self-preservation. But in today’s world, starvation mode can be a frustrating roadblock to weight loss.

What does this metabolic hiccup look like? These symptoms may indicate that starvation mode is becoming a problem for your health:

Starvation mode isn’t the same thing as actual starving. In today’s modern food environment, true starvation is rare. If you’re eating regularly, you won’t experience life-threatening starvation.

However, your body might exhibit some of the same early signs as real starvation. These include the symptoms listed above.

Most commonly, though, starvation mode involves stalled weight loss. You may have hit the wall of adaptive thermogenesis when restricting calories and increasing physical activity without losing weight.

Getting into starvation mode can take just a few days, especially if those days involve severe calorie restriction.

So what counts as severe calorie restriction? Many experts advise not going below 1,200 calories per day for women and 1,500 calories per day for men unless supervised by a doctor. Anything below these numbers could land you in starvation mode faster.

Fortunately, getting your body out of starvation mode isn’t complicated.

First, there’s the obvious solution: Eat a few more calories. But we don’t mean just any calories. By adding a few more nutrient-dense foods (especially those with fiber and protein), you may find weight loss becomes easier, not harder. Both of these nutrients have links to weight loss — so they might help you get out of starvation mode without gaining weight.

If you’re feeling extremely depleted, you might take a temporary break from a weight loss diet to replenish your nutrient stores.

Choosing the proper exercise could also bump you out of starvation mode. Resistance exercises like weightlifting, yoga, push-ups, squats, and others build muscle, which increases your metabolic rate.

According to a 2014 study, people who participated in a 9-month resistance exercise program increased their resting metabolic rate — aka how many calories they burned at rest — by an average of 5%.

Weight loss is a balancing act. It’s normal to experience physical and emotional ups and downs.

That said, it’s time to see a doctor if you’re noticing symptoms like extreme fatigue or lethargy, constipation that lasts more than a few days, sensitivity to cold, or unusual mood changes. Your healthcare team can help you hit the sweet spot of weight loss without lingering in starvation mode.

Despite its name, being in starvation mode doesn’t mean you’ll starve. Instead, it’s a state in which your body has adapted to your weight loss efforts, giving you pushback on how many calories it burns. With strategies like tweaking your calorie intake and adding strength training, you can get out of this mode and back on the path to sustained weight loss.

#206. How Much Alcohol Can Runners Drink Without Derailing Training?

An alcohol researcher and a sports dietitian explain how runners can approach drinking to minimize its negative effects.

Recent research tells us that runners and alcohol don’t make ideal training partners. And yet, they sure do meet up a lot: Run clubs start and end at breweries, marathons offer wine tastings, and competitors break records annually at the Beer Mile World Classic.

For that reason, some runners may resist cutting alcohol from their training entirely—especially if a postrun beer provides an opportunity to spend some extra time with their running buddies. So the question becomes: “As a runner, what amount of alcohol can I consume before it starts to meaningfully affect my fitness and performance?”

The answer isn’t completely clear, Ron Maughan, PhD, honorary professor at the University of St. Andrews in Scotland, whose research includes the effects of alcohol on athletic performance and recovery, tells Runner’s World.

“An awful lot comes down to individual variability,” he says. “A small amount of alcohol that would have little effect on one person can have very profound effects on somebody else.”

Combine this with the fact that scientific evidence is limited—studies involving the effects of alcohol on sports performance can be more challenging to conduct for ethical and liability reasons—and there’s still a lot we don’t know, Maughan explains.

But we can still make some conclusions with a level of certainty. Alcohol has strong effects on the liver, can interfere with sleep, influences how we access our energy stores, and can impair our muscles’ ability to adapt and recover—all of which will derail training.

So is it possible to balance alcohol and a regular running routine without experiencing poor performance outcomes? Here’s what experts say.

Research indicates that consuming just one drink—the equivalent of five ounces of wine, 1.5 ounces of liquor, or a 12-ounce beer—within an hour of bedtime can negatively affect sleep quality. Specifically, researchers noted a decrease in rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, which helps support cognitive functions like memory, emotional regulation, and the ability to focus.

This might surprise some runners who rely on alcohol to help them fall asleep faster. “While sleep latency—how long it took you to get to sleep—may be better, your sleep architecture is very much disrupted,” says Pam Nisevich Bede, RD, CSSD, a registered dietitian and certified specialist in sports dietetics. “When we look at different sleep models in research, we see that sleep duration and quality significantly decrease.” This matters a lot for runners, because sleep is our number-one recovery tool.

Bede says alcohol’s impact on sleep is one of her first concerns for any athlete trying to recover efficiently from daily training sessions.

Beyond that, one drink can also affect your hydration status, because alcohol is a diuretic. “It’s been estimated that 1 gram of alcohol will cause you to produce about 10 milliliters of urine over and above what you would normally produce. So that can have negative consequences,” says Maughan, particularly if it leaves you dehydrated before a workout or race, as even mild dehydration can impair endurance performance.

He explains, however, that more dilute alcohol solutions, such as a pint of 5 percent alcohol by volume (ABV) beer, do not have the same dehydrating effects as, say, a shot of 40 percent ABV whiskey. “But neither are going to contribute to your overall hydration intake,” adds Bede. For this reason, she recommends drinking additional fluids and electrolytes alongside any alcohol you choose to consume to help offset the dehydrating effects.

In addition to hydration, alcohol affects the body’s metabolic response to food, which can disrupt our ability to meet nutritional needs during training. “If we consume alcohol and carbohydrates in a meal, the alcohol is metabolized first, so there is a delay in how available our nutrients would be from the meal,” Bede explains. Because the body can’t store alcohol—and recognizes it as a potentially toxic substance—the liver prioritizes breaking it down before other nutrients. This not only delays the recovery process, but also affects how our bodies regulate glucose.

“When I look at a glucose graph, I can see that someone is on this glucose roller coaster all night long because they had drinks at the evening meal. You’re trying to rest, repair, and recover. But behind the scenes, your body’s working really hard to metabolize the meal because it was delayed,” she explains. The result? You wake up feeling tired, under-recovered, and ill-equipped to take on a day of training.

Alcohol has strong effects on the liver, because that’s where alcohol is metabolized. And when the liver is busy clearing alcohol from your system, it’s not able to release the glucose from storage that your muscles use for fuel.

“The liver is not a great multitasker,” explains Bede. “So when glycogen storage is impacted, so is our insulin sensitivity and glucose metabolism—it’s a cascade of things that happen.” In practical terms, that can leave you with less readily available fuel for your next workout, making it feel harder to hit your usual paces.

In the long term, that cascade can eventually include liver and gut damage in cases of high-dose consumption, Maughan adds. It also increases the risk of inadequate nutrition. “You get calories from alcohol, but you don’t get any other nutrients, vitamins, or minerals,” he says. So, if a runner tries to balance their energy needs by eating less to make room for alcohol, they’ll miss out on the nutrition that allows them to recover and perform at their best.

Repeated alcohol exposure over the long term can also affect an individual’s ability to build and maintain muscle, Bede says.

According to a systematic review published in the Journal of Functional Morphology and Kinesiology, consuming alcohol after resistance exercise is associated with reduced muscle protein synthesis, the process through which our bodies build and repair muscle tissue. The review also found that drinking after exercise increased levels of the stress hormone cortisol while reducing testosterone and the amino acids your body uses for muscle protein synthesis. Together, those changes make it harder for your body to recover and get stronger after a workout. As a result, researchers believe this may compromise long-term muscular development and adaptations.

If you have an important workout, long run, or race coming up, Bede recommends cutting out all alcohol in the days leading up to it. “In practice, I would eliminate alcohol at least two days before, ideally three. Because alcohol impairs not only sleep and recovery, but hydration status, as well,” says Bede.

If you’re really looking to unveil your best performance, she suggests runners consider completely abstaining from alcohol during heavy training blocks.

If you do choose to drink alcohol in your training, think through your timing, says Bede. If possible, try to consume alcohol earlier in the day so your body has enough time to metabolize it before you go to sleep. That way, the effect on your sleep quality may not be as severe, and your recovery won’t be as hampered, she explains.

Another tip? Be proactive in making sure that you are on top of all the other recovery variables within your control. “If you’re absolutely going to drink, make sure everything else is buttoned up,” says Bede. “Can you make sure you’re eating regular meals with adequate carbohydrates and protein? Can you make sure you’re staying hydrated? Can you really prioritize sleep in the days prior? This can help minimize the metabolic effects.”

Nonalcoholic options can also be a great swap that allows you to engage socially. While some of those are high in sugar, Bede says this doesn’t concern her in the case of runners who need to replace glycogen after a hard training session. “If the nonalcoholic option is not your jam, just remember the importance of moderation,” she says. Direct your attention toward what your habits around alcohol look like most of the time—not just once in a while.

For many runners, it can be easier to abstain entirely from alcohol than to try to limit themselves to a small amount, Maughan says. But for those who do want to consume it alongside their training, he believes it is possible to do so without significant negative impacts on performance.

If pressed for an exact amount a runner can drink, here’s the one-size-fits-all answer he shares: “Not so much that it causes you problems, drains your finances, makes you unpleasant company, or interferes with your training the next day,” he says.

Morgan is a gear editor who has been with Runner’s World since 2017. She started as an intern ghostwriting The Warmup, a bygone version of the daily RW newsletter. Now, she tests and reviews anything you might find on runners’ feet-from crew socks and compression boots to carbon-plated super shoes.

A lifelong runner and shoe geek, Morgan has been chasing the perfect pair of kicks since she joined her grade school cross-country team. Since then, she ran as a Division I walk-on for the cross-country and track & field teams at the University of Delaware, where she studied English and Biology. She has one full marathon under her belt, and has raced more halfs and 5Ks than she can count.

#207. Need a Bike Rack for Fall Road Trips? 5 Prime Day Hitch, Trunk, and Roof Rack Picks Starting at Only $75

Save up to 34% on hitch, trunk, roof, and suction-cup bike racks during Prime Big Deal Days.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Now is a great time for a road trip to see fall foliage or hit your favorite mountain bike trails. Unfortunately, many of the best riding spots aren’t located within easy riding distance from your home. That means loading your bike onto your car, truck, or SUV and driving to a ride spot or trailhead, and a bike rack is the cleanest and most secure way to do it.

Racks are easier to use than removing wheels; they also free up space in your car and keep your interior clean from bike grease and dirt. Bike racks can be pricey, but I found some great options on sale for Amazon’s Prime Big Deals Days.

Bike racks come in three main styles: hitch racks, hanging rear racks, and roof racks. Most vehicles have compatibility with at least one type, but some cars and situations make fitting a rack challenging.

Hitch racks can’t be installed on some vehicles, especially models with a center exhaust. Many times, owners don’t want to add a hitch to a leased vehicle. (Plus, leaving a hitch rack installed can get you a parking fine in some cities…as I’ve personally discovered.)

Hanging racks are an economical solution. But they aren’t as secure as hitch and roof-mount systems. And increasingly, hanging racks are incompatible with newer cars and SUVs.

Roof racks can pose other difficulties. Some drivers don’t like the look of roof racks, especially when not in use. Roof racks can decrease your vehicle’s gas mileage and cause wind noise at highway speeds.

I’ve recommended the Saris Bones trunk rack for years. Its reliable design and easy installation have made it a go-to for riders. The updated Bones EX makes a good rack even better, and it’s still easy to install, load, and remove. Saris redesigned the frame, adding a curve that accommodates a wider range of vehicles, including hatchbacks and cars with spoilers.

Thanks to a ratcheting strap system that holds everything securely in place, the Bones EX is lightweight and rattles less than most other trunk racks. However, its bike weight capacity isn’t high (70 pounds total), and some full-suspension bikes won’t fit because the rear suspension gets in the way. Even with those downsides, it’s an outstanding rack for casual riders and expert cyclists alike, whether you make regular treks or only need it a few times a year. In addition to the standard two-bike rack we recommend, Saris offers a three-bike version.

The Swagman XTC2 is one of the most affordable 2-bike racks we recommend. This no-frills rack is a solid choice for budget-conscious riders. It fits both 1¼-inch and 2-inch receiver tubes, and it accommodates wheel sizes from 20 to 29 inches. However, with a total weight capacity of 70 pounds (35 pounds per bike), it’s not suitable for e-bikes.

As expected for this price, the rack has some trade-offs. The wheel hoops are adjustable, but not as smoothly or precisely as on more premium racks. The rack doesn’t tilt away from the vehicle when loaded, limiting access to tailgates or liftgates. Plus, you must remove the center support bar to load a bike on the inside tray.

Yet, the XTC2 is lightweight, durable, and very reasonably priced. If you’re willing to trade a bit of convenience for significant savings, the Swagman XTC2 is a reliable and practical option.

With its stellar carrying ability and shockingly low price for a heavy-duty hitch rack, the Saris Freedom carried every bike we threw at it. It supports up to two 60-pound bikes, so it’s strong enough for almost any bike (though some e-bikes will require removing the battery).

Its “drop-in” design makes loading easy by eliminating the need to adjust the holding arms—drop the bike into place, tighten the fixture straps, and you’re ready to go. The straps and ratchets require a bit of effort to cinch down, but our bikes always stay in place with little to no wobbling or rattling. We also love that the rack tilts, so you don’t lose access to the trunk on a trip.

The Freedom hitch rack isn’t without limitations, though. Because of its somewhat narrow trays, it cannot support bikes with fat tires, for example. That aside, it’s a hitch rack at an outstanding price that performs as well as many far more expensive options. Saris also makes a four-bike version for families and riding groups.

Roof racks were the preferred transport method for decades, and if you watch bike races, every race team and neutral support vehicle still uses the design. So, while roof racks have fallen out of fashion, they’re still a viable option for many riders.

If your car or SUV already has a roof rack, Swagman’s Upright single bike rack is a good, cheap solution. The five-pound aluminum rack attaches to your vehicle’s square, round, or oval crossbars that are up to three inches wide. It holds bikes with a lockable clamp arm that fits downtubes between one and two inches and secures the tires with tie straps.

This rack only holds bikes up to 35 pounds. It’s also incompatible with bikes with wheelbases longer than 49 inches or frames with an oddly shaped or very large downtube. So, check your bike’s measurements before ordering.

The Smart Suction attaches to your vehicle using high-strength suction cups. This makes it easy to install and remove, so it’s ideal for cyclists who park in cities and want to avoid rack theft. This rack might also be for you if you’re trying to maximize gas mileage when bikes aren’t on your vehicle or if you own a sports car and want a clean aesthetic.

Allen’s Smart Suction applies a creative technical solution to the anxiety you’re probably feeling right now, simply thinking about trusting your precious bicycle to suction cups. It features Bluetooth connectivity to signal your phone, Apple CarPlay, or Android Auto if suction drops or if the rack needs attention.

The Smart Suction Go: Compact can be quickly removed for storage when not in use. With its compact footprint and 12.6-pound weight, it takes up very little trunk space. I also know riders who throw one in their bike bag when they travel by air, so they have a rack for their rental car.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#208. Yoga and Overweight: Health Benefits and Tips for Getting Started

Part of the beauty of yoga is its accessibility for everyone. Yoga practitioners come in all shapes and sizes and are hella modifiable. If you have overweight, there’s 100% a place for you in the world of downward dogs, crescent lunges, and resting pigeons.

Check out these benefits of yoga for overweight.

For wellness, you’d be hard-pressed to find a more holistic practice than yoga. Your physical and mental health can get a boost from busting out your mat.

The limb-stretching, muscle-engaging, bodyweight-bearing nature of yoga has many physical benefits.

For starters, yoga may enhance your metabolism. An older study found that people who practiced had greater metabolic efficiency and lower weight than non-yogis.

It’s clear, too, that yoga’s combo of cardio and strength torches calories. A 160-pound person can burn around 180 calories per hour, popping in and out of poses. A 2021 study revealed that both Hatha and vinyasa yoga led to weight loss, with an average of 3.4 kilograms (7.5 pounds) lost over a 6-month.

Extra strength and flexibility are two other well-known upsides of the practice. Research shows that even sedentary folks can build these elements of fitness by taking up yoga. One study showed that, after 8 weeks of practicing at least twice a week (180 minutes), people with no prior yoga experience had greater muscle strength, endurance, flexibility, and cardio-respiratory fitness.

On the surface, yoga might look like mere stretching — but the practice goes far beyond the physical. Yoga engages the mind in all sorts of ways that may have benefits for overweight.

By training your brain toward calm and focus, yoga sessions encourage mindfulness. A mindful outlook can have far-reaching effects in multiple areas of life, like promoting mindful eating and greater body awareness.

As a form of self-care, yoga can also promote a healthier body image. In a 2018 study, young adults who made it a habit reported higher satisfaction levels with their bodies. Better self-esteem and motivation have also been linked to the practice.

Then, too, yoga’s stress-relieving effects might follow you off the mat and into the dining room. Some research has found that people who do yoga binge eat less often.

Wanna get started with yoga but aren’t sure how? We got you.

It all starts with setting realistic goals and expectations. If you’ve never practiced before, you won’t be pretzel-ing yourself into challenging poses like scorpion or crow overnight — and that’s OK. Consider setting smaller, step-wise goals, such as attending a 30-minute class twice a week or mastering a few basic poses. Little by little, you’ll work your way up to a more advanced practice.

It’s also wise to select a class (or video) for beginners. Check your gym or yoga studio’s schedule for introductory sessions, and don’t be afraid to let an instructor know before class that you may need some modifications. Most are happy to provide adaptations to make the class a better experience for beginners.

Meanwhile, if you’re pursuing a yoga practice for weight loss, remember to pair it with other healthy lifestyle practices for best results. Though stretching and holding poses burn calories, yoga might not take you to your weight loss goal alone. A balanced diet, cardio exercise, and sufficient sleep are other keys to achieving a healthy weight.

Yoga stereotypes of scantily clad gym babes in impossible contortions might make you feel somewhat intimidated about in-person classes. If you’re concerned that a gym session will make you self-conscious, start with an at-home practice. (YouTube is a treasure trove of classes and instructors explicitly geared for people with overweight.) All by yourself in your living room, there’s no one to impress.

Or, if you’re up for in-person yoga, let your instructor know your needs again. Modifications are always possible.

No matter where you practice, credit yourself for showing up for your health. And, at the beginning of your session, don’t forget to set an intention you find motivating or encouraging, such as “I am caring for my body” or “I am worthy of love and respect.”

Overweight doesn’t have to be a barrier to taking up yoga. Start small, knowing that you’ll get more comfortable with each session. With all the physical and mental health benefits a yoga practice provides — and all the modifications that make it more accessible — it’s worth a try, regardless of weight.

Last medically reviewed on August 31, 2024

#210. Exercise Is Doing More Than Building Muscle: It May Also Be Rewiring Your DNA

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

We’ve been saying exercise is good for your immune system for so long that the sentence barely means anything anymore. It’s right up there with vegetables are good for you and smoking is bad. Okay. Thanks. Anything else?

Then somebody finally starts looking under the hood.

A study published September 18 in Science Advances used some fairly sophisticated molecular tools to compare regular exercisers with sedentary people and found differences not merely in cholesterol, blood sugar or some other number your doctor circles in red. The differences went all the way down into metabolism, immune-cell gene activity and the accessibility of the genetic machinery those cells use to do their jobs. That’s considerably more interesting than telling us people who exercise tend to be healthier.

The researchers pulled data from the Chinese Immune Multi-omics Atlas, an enormous project that has profiled more than 10 million circulating immune cells from 428 adults. For this particular exercise analysis, they compared 40 regular exercisers with 46 sedentary subjects. The active group reported training at least three times a week and accumulating at least 150 minutes of moderate exercise or 75 minutes of vigorous exercise.

And this is where things get interesting.

The exercisers showed metabolic patterns associated with greater fatty-acid oxidation and antioxidant activity. Their immune cells also looked different. Researchers found changes involving cytotoxic T cells and natural killer cells, two components of the immune system involved in identifying and destroying infected or abnormal cells. They also found differences in chromatin accessibility, basically how available certain sections of genetic instructions are for the cell to use, along with changes in signaling associated with antigen presentation and inflammation.

In plain English, the bodies of people who exercised regularly appeared to be operating with a differently tuned metabolic and immune system.

Before somebody starts selling Immune Chromatin Activator Xtreme in a black bottle with lightning bolts on it, however, there’s a rather important catch: This study does not prove exercise caused those differences.

It’s cross-sectional. Researchers essentially took a molecular snapshot of people who exercise and people who don’t. Maybe exercise produced the differences. Very plausible. But perhaps people who exercise regularly also eat differently, sleep differently, have different body compositions or differ in some other way the study couldn’t completely untangle. The researchers also didn’t have the kind of detailed exercise information we’d need to start claiming that deadlifts improve natural killer cells more than rowing or that four workouts beat three.

And please don’t turn “exercise affects the immune system” into “exercise makes you immune to disease.” That’s not what the study says either. Immune biology is ridiculously complicated. More activity from an immune cell isn’t automatically better, and an immune system turned up to 11 isn’t necessarily desirable. Ask anyone with an autoimmune disease.

What makes this study important is something else. For years we’ve measured exercise by what we can see. Bodyweight. Waist circumference. Blood pressure. VO2 max. Muscle. Strength.

Those are obviously important, particularly to the M&F crowd, because nobody has ever stood in front of a mirror admiring his chromatin accessibility.

But underneath the stuff we can see, exercise is apparently associated with a massive amount of biological housekeeping.

That’s a useful thought the next time you have one of those workouts where nothing spectacular happens. No PR. No great pump. The scale hasn’t moved. You look exactly the same walking out of the gym  as you did walking in.

You may still have accomplished quite a bit.

The more science learns about exercise, the less it looks like something we do merely to improve the body.

It’s beginning to look like something we’re supposed to do.

#211. Which Running Gear Is—and Isn’t—Worth Your Money

Not every piece of gear is worth it—here’s how to tell.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Running, at its core, is a relatively low-gear sport, but people love to bemoan that it’s increasingly expensive. I agree—paying $120 for a long-sleeve T-shirt or shelling out hundreds for compression boots seems bonkers to me.

I’ve been running for 12 years now, and for most of that time, I’ve been a broke student or frugal post-grad. I enjoy the competitive element of running, so I typically invest only in pieces that affect my performance. While shopping, I commonly ask myself: Will this make me a better runner, or would it just be nice to have?

Here’s my hard-earned wisdom—from head to toe—about where to splurge and where to save a few bucks.

I rarely buy hats. And if I do, I buy them for cheap. Caps are a utility to me, and as long as they keep my face shaded and head ventilated, I don’t care too much about appearances. Plus, I sweat regardless, so the fancy ones that claim to be extra breathable seem pointless to me. Each time I go to a major marathon for work, I feel like I come home with at least one new cap. They’re a common freebie at brand events and expo booths.

This is another place where I save dough. I don’t obsess over fancy features like UV protection or worry if the material is ultra-breathable. I just wear sunscreen and go shirtless on a hot day.

I still have tech tees that my mom bought me in high school at the outlet mall, and some of my favorite tops have been clearance-rack finds at Marshalls. And you know those “free” shirts you get for signing up for a race? I wear them! Even if they’re ugly. Finally, I’m not afraid to wear cotton—it gets a bad rap, but there’s something poetic about sweat stains proving that you put in some effort.

For split shorts, I buy them cheap. For half tights, I splurge.

All I’m looking for in split shorts is a loose fit, a comfortable liner, and a little pocket for my house key. I like my short shorts short, so you’ll rarely see me wearing anything longer than a 5-inch inseam. My old Baleaf 3-inch and Nike Challenger 2-inch split shorts have served me well over the years.

Since half tights mean more material on my skin, investing in higher-quality fabrics is worth it. Plus, premium versions tend to have more-secure pockets. I used to hate running with my phone because I didn’t like carrying it, but I got a pair of Janji 8-inch trail half tights that have plenty of pockets and lock my phone into place. They’re worth the $98 to me.

This might be my hottest take yet, but I like cotton socks. There, I said it! Some of my favorite cheap socks come in a six-pack from Dick’s Sporting Goods. My feet sweat a lot, and I’ve found that socks that are mostly made of cotton help mop up the perspiration better than pricier, “sweat-wicking” polyester (ironic, I know). I will say, I do have some running-specific socks that I enjoy. I usually wear Near Earth crew socks during races (which are a steep $24 per pair). They look sleeker than my white cotton Nike crews, and they match my race-day outfit better since they’re logo-less.

I believe that trainers are the single most important investment in a running wardrobe. However, shoes are freakin’ expensive nowadays, and if you run a lot, the money adds up. While I don’t recommend buying used shoes, I often scour the internet for last year’s models. Shoe tech has gotten so good in recent years that the difference between the 2025 ver­sion of a popular trainer and the 2026 pair isn’t much, and yet saves you a decent amount of money. I’ve scored pairs of old models of the New Balance 1080 for under $100.

Most marathoning super shoes are north of $200, and while I certainly notice a performance improvement—they’re a nonnegotiable at the elite level now—I’m sparing with how often I lace them up. I do a lot of my workouts in trainers or in old racing shoes that are nearing the end of their lifespan so I can save my good pair for key workouts and races. Lately, my Adidas Adios Pro 5s ($275) have been my weapon of choice. On race weekends, I try to avoid wearing them on shakeout runs, walking around the city, or even on my warmup jog before my race, if I can help it. Many carbon-plated shoes start to degrade around 200 miles, so every mile counts.

Good news: High-quality sunglasses can be pretty affordable! Sunglasses are easy to forget in a hotel room or sit on in your car (I would know), so I’ve never splurged on a fancy pair. Goodr has been leading the charge, with polarized options starting at only $25. I have three pairs.

In high school, I bought a bare-bones Garmin Forerunner 10 for around $100, which I wore until the strap broke and I got frustrated with the glacially slow GPS signal. In college, I upgraded to the Forerunner 35 ($150). It served me well, but again, it was slow and lacked some basic features, like a lap button.

Now I have a Forerunner 955—close to the top-of-the-line at $500—that one of our gear editors passed along to me after he got a new watch. I like it better than my first two, but I’m not sure I would shell out my own money for one. I really only need the basics, not the fancy features like ground contact time or suggested workouts. One day, I dream of running with only a simple digital stopwatch, but I can’t will myself to leave the world of GPS yet.

Pennsylvania’s Lehigh Valley, where I live, can get cold, but I’ve found that cheap gloves do the trick. I’ve had a $30 pair of Nike basics from a sporting goods store that have done the job for close to a decade. Sometimes, if it’s abnormally cold, I’ll layer two pairs of thin gloves, thus eliminating the need for an expensive ultra-insulated pair.

Soft layers, like pullovers, hoodies, and long sleeves, don’t need to be fancy. I cherish my college sweatshirts. But shell layers—rain jackets, windbreakers, insulated jackets—are worth the investment. The difference between being wet and shivering versus dry and comfortable is enough to make me pay a little extra. My Lululemon Fast and Free jacket ($148) is lightweight and totally worth it.

Theo Kahler is the senior news editor at Runner’s World. He’s a former all-conference collegiate runner at Winthrop University, and he received his master’s degree in liberal arts studies from Wake Forest University, where he was a member of one of the top distance-running teams in the NCAA. Kahler has reported on the ground at major events such as the Paris Olympics, U.S. Olympic Trials, New York City Marathon, and Boston Marathon. He’s run 14:20 in the 5K, 1:05:37 in the half marathon, and finished 40th at the 2025 New York City Marathon. He enjoys spotting tracks from the sky on airplanes. (Look for colorful ovals around football fields.)

#212. The Easy Bike Maintenance Job That Can Make Every Ride Feel Better—Clean and Lube Your Chain

Use dish soap, an old T-shirt, and the right lube to keep your drivetrain running efficiently.

Prior to my time working in a shop, I was on a ride and I hadn’t been keeping up on my chain maintenance. During this gravel group ride, I was riding near one of my buddies, but my chain was squeaking so much I was embarrassed to even be riding in the group. I may not have known much at that time, but I knew enough that this was outside what is acceptable for a group ride.

Lubing your chain does more than just prevent you from looking like “that rider” in the group. When you lube (or wax) your chain properly it offers better shifting, improves wear issues on components, and is simply less distracting on the ride.

Whether you’ve ever been that rider where your chain is squeaking so loud that nobody wants to ride near you or you don’t want to end up in that situation, this story is especially for you. Here we’ll go through how to clean the chain (and the rest of the drivetrain), tips for lubing your chain, and when dry versus wet lube is the right call.

While you can purchase stiff, long-bristled brushes and degreasers designed specifically for the task, you can also use household items you probably already own, including dish soap, an old T-shirt, and a toothbrush or scrub brush.

Although lubing your chain is a distinct task, you should never clean your drivetrain without following up with some fresh lube. (More on that below.)

How to lube your chain depends on whether you’re using wet lube, or dry lube, or wax, a choice that depends on a number of factors. “It depends on where you’re riding, what kind of riding you’re doing, and how often you see yourself doing maintenance,” says Purdy.

For the typical novice, wet lube is best if you frequently ride in wet conditions or just want to get to and from work. It also lasts longer than dry lube, so it can be a good choice if you’re touring or doing high-volume training.

If you’re gravel riding or mountain biking in a dry climate, on the other hand, wet lube attracts and holds onto dust and sand, which creates more chain wear; in that case you’re better off with dry lube, says Purdy.

Remember, chain lubes will have precise application instructions that are essential to follow. Most high-quality lubes have a setting time, meaning you should give the lube time to sit and penetrate the chain's inner workings before wiping away the excess.

#213. A New Study Reveals 3 Migraine Triggers That Might Be Making Your Headaches Worse—See Them Here

Temperatures are starting to rise, with some parts of the US facing a record-setting early heat wave this week. But while you’re probably focused on staying cool, there’s one more thing that should be on your radar: a higher-than-usual risk of migraine headaches.

That’s the major takeaway from new research published in the journal Neurology: The study uncovered three lesser-known factors that can trigger migraine—and these triggers can crop up even more in the late spring and summer.

If you’re one of the 12% of Americans who deals with these headaches, this is information to keep in your back pocket. Here’s what the study found, plus how doctors who treat patients with migraine recommend protecting yourself.

For the study, researchers followed 7,032 people living in Israel for about a decade who suffered from migraines. During the study period, researchers looked at participants’ daily exposure to air pollution, along with tracking weather conditions. They also looked at how often and when people visited the hospital or their primary care doctor with a migraine. That data was compared to the levels of pollution and weather conditions on that particular day, along with seven days before that.

During the study period, 2,215 people (or 32%) had at least one visit to the hospital or a clinic with a migraine. The researchers also found that 47% of participants in the study bought triptan medications at one point or another—fast-acting prescription medications that are designed to stop a migraine—with most using at least two tablets a month.

Ultimately, the researchers discovered a link between three weather-related factors and migraine: air pollution, temperature (including UV exposure), and humidity. First, they found a correlation between higher levels of air pollution and the most number of visits to a hospital or clinic for a migraine. They also found that the day with the least visits to the hospital or clinic also had lower-than-average pollution levels. People with short-term exposure to high levels of nitrogen dioxide (a common pollutant from traffic exhaust) were 41% more likely to go to the hospital or clinic for migraine than people who weren’t exposed to high levels of the gas.

The study also showed that people who were exposed to high levels of UV rays from the sun on a given day were 23% more likely to visit a healthcare provider for migraine symptoms than those who weren’t. High temperatures and low humidity appear to be linked to more migraine headaches, likely because they amplify the effect of nitrogen dioxide, the researchers said.

With climate change intensifying how often we deal with heat waves and pollution, it’s important to consider these risk factors when it comes to migraine, the researchers wrote.

It’s important to note that the study didn’t prove that air pollution, heat, and lower humidity levels cause migraines—it just found a link between them. But doctors say there’s likely something here.

Air pollution can spark neuroinflammation (the immune system’s inflammatory response in the brain and spinal cord), which is a risk factor for migraine, Sana Ghafoor, MD, neurologist at Tufts Medical Center, tells SELF. This may cause a release of pain chemicals like calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) and substance P that can lead to a migraine, Dr. Ghafoor says.

Air pollution may be particularly problematic for people with allergies who also struggle with migraines, Clifford Segil, DO, a neurologist at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, California, tells SELF. The body may see air pollution as an allergen and mount an immune response, which can spark a migraine in people who are sensitive to this trigger, he explains.

Then, there’s the fact that heat can impact blood vessels and nerves. “When people heat up, nerves and blood vessels in tight locations can become irritated, as the diameter of a blood vessel or nerves increases with heat,” Dr. Segil says. That, too, can trigger a migraine. You’re also more susceptible to getting dehydrated when it’s hot out, Dr. Ghafoor says: “If you're overheated and dehydrated, those can also trigger migraines.”

Dr. Segil points out that high humidity common in the spring and summer (and not just that related to air pollution) can trigger migraines too. High humidity causes you to sweat and lose water, which can decrease the amount of blood in your blood vessels (if you don’t replace it), Dr. Segil says. “This decreases the diameter of blood vessels and can cause headaches, just like an increased blood vessel diameter,” he says.

Dr. Ghafoor says she often sees more patients have migraine headaches when high humidity strikes. “Even with small [atmospheric] pressure changes, it can activate nerve endings and sinuses, which can lead to the release of pain chemicals,” she says.

These are some of the most common migraine triggers, according to the US National Library of Medicine:

These foods and ingredients can also trigger migraines, per the US National Library of Medicine:

Migraine triggers are personal, making it important to do what you can to figure out yours and then try to avoid them as best as possible. (Dr. Ghafoor recommends keeping a headache diary to try to narrow things down.) But factors like air pollution, heat, and humidity can be tough to avoid.

If levels of air pollution are high in your area, Dr. Segil recommends wearing a face mask like an N95 when you need to be outdoors. Keeping your windows shut and running an air purifier can also help tamp down on pollution indoors. If you’d like, you can track pollution levels throughout the day and try to stay inside during peak times, Dr. Ghafoor says.

When heat and humidity strikes, Dr. Ghafoor recommends doing what you can to stay well hydrated. “Make sure that it’s not just water, but electrolytes too,” she says. “All of that is a very important part of lifestyle management for patients who have migraine.”

Ultimately, doing your best to try to figure out your triggers (and avoid them) can go a long way toward helping to keep you more comfortable on a regular basis. “Knowing and identifying migraine triggers is very important,” Dr. Ghafoor says. “It’s empowering the patient to understand their disease.”

#214. How to Calculate Your Rising and Moon Sign: A Beginner’s Guide

The sun sign is the *it girlie* of the “big three” elements in astrology.

But do you know about your moon sign and rising sign?

We chatted with an astrologer to understand what they are and how to calculate them.

According to Olga Verkhotina — astrologer and personal coach — the big three in astrology are your three most significant chart elements:

“While a natal chart contains so many more intricate details beyond just three elements, the big three is a way to determine the main highlights that make up your personality and overall temperament,” Verkhotina says.

Verkhotina explains that a rising sign is the zodiac sign that falls at the beginning of your First House — basically, the beginning of your natal chart.

“The First House in astrology is associated with a person’s identity, individual activity, even their appearance, and the sign that houses that theme gives its characteristics,” she says.

“Knowing your rising sign describes the way others may perceive you, the way your behavior comes across, as well as how you approach new situations in life.”

You’ll need: date, time and place of birth.

“Knowing the accurate time is important here because even 10 minutes can make a difference in the sign,” Verkhotina explains.

“Once you have the data, you can trust astrology software to calculate it for you. There are a lot of natal chart calculators online, so you can just search ‘rising sign calculator,'” Verkhotina says.

Pro tip: Verkhotina suggests reading horoscopes from your rising sign instead of your sun sign, saying it will likely give more personalized insights on which areas of your life might be impacted by current cosmic events.

“A moon sign describes the position of the moon on the zodiac wheel at the moment of your birth,” Verkhotina says.

She explains that the moon in astrology symbolizes:

“The moon sign helps you better understand how these themes demonstrate themselves in your life,” Verkhotina says.

Unlike the rising sign, you don’t have to have the precise time of birth to know your moon sign, although Verkhotina says it’s still recommended.

You can also use an online calculator to find your moon sign or refer to the ephemeris — a table showing the daily positions of planets.

Verkhotina describes the sun sign as the most important planet in your chart.

“It’s the center of your vitality, your ego, consciousness, and individuality at its core. That’s why it’s the most commonly known element in astrology,” she says.

It represents the zodiac sign the sun was in at the time of your birth, which Verkhotina says gives your individuality certain qualities associated with its specific sign.

“It’s important to understand that although the sun is a huge element in astrology, it doesn’t cover the nuances of one’s character,” Verkhotina explains.

Instead, she says it just represents overall traits.

Verkhotina adds that the specifics of your character are covered in the rest of your astrological chart. “This is why sometimes no two leos are the same,” she says.

This one is easy peasy — you don’t have to have your time or place of birth.

“The sun cycle is very similar every year, so you can look it up by the date, month and year of your birth. Each sign corresponds to a calendar date that year,” Verkhotina says.

Here’s each astro sign, in a nutshell, according to Verkhotina.

Your sun sign is important, but your moon and rising signs add extra details.

Your rising sign reflects your identity and how others see you, while your moon sign reveals your emotions and behavior.

To find these signs, you can use online birth chart calculators. Just make sure you have your birth date and time handy for accurate results.

Last medically reviewed on August 2, 2024

#215. Build an Ironman Pro-Approved Gear Closet With This Kona-Tested Gear

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Cooling Glacier Gloves were seen on podium finisher Matthew Marquadt during the 2026 Ironman World Championship in Kona. (Photo: Brad Kaminski/Triathlete)

As the pinnacle of triathlon (and with ruthless conditions that year after year best the top Ironman athletes), the Ironman World Championship in Kona has long been the proving ground for triathlon gear. New swimskins, more aerodynamic front forks, cooling technology, longer-tail helmets, compression technology – whatever wild gear pros can utilize to gain an advantage, they’ll try it in the lava fields.

Many of those products are prototypes or custom-made for that athlete by their sponsors. But some of them are commercially available, and we tracked down the pieces worn by the sport’s top pros at the 2026 Ironman World Championship so that you can add them to your own gear closet.

Wear the brand-new swimskin that Brit Lucy Charles-Barclay (first out of the water for the women before dropping out on the run) and South African Jamie Riddle (Riddle withdrew on the bike) wore on race day. This iteration of the Viper offers increased performance in the water because of its hydrodynamic materials, and now comes in a lighter color that keeps athletes visible in the water and cooler in direct sun.

If you want to break the mold and not get a Roka swimskin (there were a lot of pros in some version of Roka’s swimskins), you could go with another brand known for their no-holds-barred approach to swimskins and wetsuits. Both Kristian Blummenfelt and eventual runner-up Gustav Iden wore the DeBoer Tsunami 4.0, a sleeveless suit that boasts 3mm of buoyancy through the hips and core.

Race like 2023 Ironman world champion Sam Laidlow (FRA) in this radically designed helmet. In collaboration with Laidlow, Ekoi developed the helmet specifically for triathlon, not limiting itself to UCI rules. It boasts a lower ear flap and funnels air over your head and back and around your shoulders. This edition has a specific visor and “turbulator tape” to improve aerodynamics. The helmet was also worn by Patrick Lange (GER), Rudy von Berg (USA), and Julie Derron (SUI) on race day.

Co-developed with iron-distance world record holder Sam Laidlow (FRA) and seen on pros including Marjolaine Pierré (FRA), these single-use tape strips have been wind tunnel-tested and shown to save up to 8 watts. They are legal for the swim, and each strip features three rows of “aero dots” to reduce drag.

Three of the top bike split riders utilized these ultra-deep rear wheels from Hed: Belgian Marten Van Riel, German Frederic Funk, and Austrian Lisa Perterer. Hand-built in Minnesota, the wheel includes Hed’s carbon fairing and alloy rim construction, and it’s available in both rim brake and disc brake configurations.

Ride like the Olympic and world champion Kristian Blummenfelt with this pair of four-spoke carbon rims. They’re superlight, stiff, and have been developed through extensive wind-tunnel testing and data.

Always using the latest cutting-edge tech, Laidlow used these 299-gram cranks from Chinese brand Overfast that were released earlier this year. They’re not cheap, but they are a detail that can give you an edge on the bike.

Third-place finisher Matthew Marquadt (USA) and Lucy Charles-Barclay (GBR) were both seen wearing these cooling gloves on the bike and the run to help keep their core temperature in check. They utilize a proprietary water-activated fabric that cools your skin, plus airflow on the bike enhances the cooling process.

While triathletes have been stuffing ice in their kits and hats at aid stations for years, this simple $20 hat keeps that ice in a separate compartment so it stays in your hat and continues to cool your scalp and neck. Magnus Ditlev (DEN), who led for a big chunk of the day in Kona, wore this ice hat on the marathon.

These Hokas were worn on the run by not only the women’s champion, Taylor Knibb (USA), but also three other top-10 finishers – fifth-place Imogen Simmonds (SUI), sixth-place finisher Lisa Perterer (AUT), and 10th-place finisher Grace Thek (AUS). While definitely not the lightest shoe seen coming down Ali’i Drive, the carbon-fiber super shoe offers a split carbon-fiber plate with stability winglets and a long, gradual forefoot rocker for a comfortable and sustainable ride.

The recently released On shoe was seen on the likes of third-place finisher Julie Derron (SUI), fourth-place Kat Matthews (GBR), runner-up Gustav Iden (NOR), fifth-place Pierre Le Corre (FRA), and eighth-place Kristian Blummenfelt (NOR). It utilizes PEBA-based foam, separated into segments, compresses and rebounds freely for a smooth, responsive ride.

German Jonas Schomburg wore these top-of-the-line carbon-plated Asics on the way to his seventh-place finish in Kona. They feature Asics’ proprietary lightweight foam and a forward-propelling and minimal carbon plate to maintain the energy return into the late stages of a race.

#217. We Ran in the Saucony Endorphin Speed 6. It’s Snappier Than Ever, but Watch for Hot Spots

Our testers found a responsive, propulsive trainer with one noteworthy issue.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

We put in the mileage running in the Endorphin Speed 6 after Saucony announced its release exactly a month ago. It’s a companion shoe to Saucony’s marathon racers, the Endorphin Pro 5 and Endorphin Elite 3. The Speed 6 is a top choice as a go-to trainer for logging all those long runs before race day.

An improved beaded midsole foam and more tilted positioning of the rocker make this Endorphin Speed the snappiest one yet. It’s also an excellent alternative for runners who want a less aggressive plated racing shoe; the newly designed nylon plate is more compliant than rigid carbon fiber.

A minor caveat was that some of our testers experienced hot spots on their long runs due to the upper material. We let you know if it’s worth the risk.

With the Endorphin Speed 6, Saucony introduces Pwrrun PBX, a beaded PEBA foam that’s lighter and softer than Pwrrun PB, the foam used in previous iterations of the Speed. I felt the difference on my first run; the shoe’s cushioning doesn’t feel as dense and firm underfoot. It also feels more responsive. I stepped on the gas during a looped long run in an industrial complex with hills. Despite some lethargy on my part (take it from me: get those Z’s), the shoes helped me sail through the hard stretches that came later in my run.

Saucony also added 2 mm of height to increase the angle of the rocker. The nylon piece sandwiched in the shoe has ribbing and slots so it isn’t as stiff as carbon fiber. The combination of more angled rocker and more flexible nylon plate results in a snappier, more propulsive ride than you’d find in previous iterations of the shoe.

For Senior Health and Fitness Editor Kristen Wagner, who had never run in a plated shoe, the Endorphin Speed 6’s more malleable nylon plate allayed her worries of too volatile a ride.

“I really liked these shoes!” she said. “I was a little nervous to receive a speed shoe for testing, but was reassured when Jeff [Dengate] told me about the nylon plate (as opposed to a carbon plate, which would have been a first for me) and that he had worn the shoe on a few easy runs and did not die.”

Wagner tested the shoes on tempo runs, easy runs, and run/walk intervals. “I too can confirm I survived all of these, but I definitely enjoyed the shoe most at my faster paces. I felt like I was really able to take off in them and maintain a speed I was comfortable at.”

The Endorphin Speed is one of Runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate’s favorite shoes for its solid, speedy performance and value (the shoe is $180, which is much cheaper than the $240 Pro 5 and $290 Elite 3). He compared the Endorphin Speed 6 to earlier versions of the shoe and found he gravitated toward choosing to run faster workouts while testing it.

“Saucony added 2mm and switched foams, so it’s has good impact attenuation, but I found the shoe rides fairly harsh and snappy,” he said. “It’s a shoe I’m only reaching for on workout days.”

One of the improvements I liked Endorphin Speeds ago was the widened fit. The Speed 4 was more accommodating with a broader midfoot and roomy toebox. Fast forward to the Endorphin Speed 6, and I’m happy to say Saucony hasn’t gone the other way, narrowing the shoe’s foot shape. Our testers noted this too.

“I appreciated the upper tweaks,” said Dengate. “The forefoot feels a little roomier. I often have an issue where my pinkie toes go numb on long runs because of the Saucony toebox shape. But that hasn’t happened with this version. I’m still nudging against the mesh there, but the pressure isn’t bad and the shoe feels comfortable.”

However, unlike Dengate, the mesh affected my workouts. On a 12-miler, my toes felt tender by mile 4, and by mile 8 I was ready to sprint out of my shoes. Upon removing the Speeds post-workout, I found six of my toes (three on each foot) were racked with blisters. It was a conundrum for me—the toebox was roomy, but why were my feet pocked with fluid-filled bumps?

Wagner also experienced friction in the toebox while testing the shoes.

“During my first several wears, at varying paces and surfaces, I experienced hot spots around the toebox and on the sole of my right foot,” she said. “I tried adjusting the laces, which didn't seem to help. It wasn't until I swapped out my thicker socks with thin ones that this subsided.”

Perhaps I should follow Wagner’s advice (and peruse our Best Running Socks guide). The reason for my blistered toes: The Speed 6’s upper feels harsh. It’s comparable to the fruit netting supermarkets store mandarin oranges or avocados in.

Despite my ill-fated long run in the trainer, I’ve still been running in the Endorphin Speed 6 because I genuinely enjoy the shoe’s feel. All of the updates in the Speed 6—the beaded foam, the more flexible plate, the more angled rocker—make it a solid pick in my rotation for tempo runs and easy 4-milers.

But maybe I’m an outlier. Wagner found thin socks alleviated her discomfort. Dengate didn’t experience hot spots on his runs. And our third tester, Editor Ashley Tysiac, noted she didn’t get any blisters even though the shoe fit small.

I recommend using the Endorphin Speed 6 for its namesake: speedwork. And if you have a race coming up and don’t want to shell out over $250, it’s fine to go with nylon-plated shoes. They’re almost as good as carbon.
