#239. Kona 2026 DNF Files: What Happened to the Pros Who Didn’t Make it to the Finish Line

Jamie Riddle was one of the athletes who did not finish (DNF) at the 2026 Ironman World Championship. (Photo: Brad Kaminski/Triathlete)

Eleven men and 11 women pulled out of the 2026 Ironman World Championships in Kona on a particularly brutal day, with athletes citing significant waves and chop in the swim, unrelenting winds on the bike, and stifling humidity on the run.

With both men and women racing, it felt like a year of chaos and carnage, with twice as many athletes pulling out on course as we’ve seen in recent years.

For the men, that meant 21% of the field, very similar to 2024, when 12 men withdrew. However, it was a larger percentage of the women’s field at 23% – up from 19% the year before and 6% in 2023.

These numbers also don’t take into account those who were riding that fine line and only narrowly made it to the finish, graciously spared by Madame Pele in what little mercy she showed on Saturday.

One theory behind the number of DNFs is that athletes are now pushing the race harder from start to finish; with such strong, deep fields, there’s little room to ease off the pedal for even a second.

At the end of the day, Kona has always been such an unforgiving place. It might leave a couple dozen athletes satisfied, but it leaves a wake of others wanting more, ready to return or potentially ready to retire. Vincent Luis (FRA) managed to go out on top, but not everyone gets that fairytale ending. Today, we’re looking at the athletes who couldn’t make it across the line and the stories behind their days.

The 2024 Ironman World Champion was off to the perfect start in his final Kona race, swimming among the front pack and quickly transitioning onto the bike in an ideal position.

However, soon after heading out onto the Queen K, he began struggling with cramps that continued all the way up to Hawi.

He pulled over at one point next to his coach, and even though many of us assumed he would withdraw then, he continued all the way to the turnaround at Hawi. He later explained that he could not imagine running a marathon on those legs and that it “simply wasn’t possible.”

In a true champion’s spirit, however, he was back out on course – this time volunteering at an aid station, handing out supplies to the age-groupers battling the same extreme conditions.

The 2023 Ironman World Champion has made no secret of the fact that, even though he won the world title in Nice, winning in Kona has always been his biggest dream. Unfortunately, that dream quickly turned into a nightmare out on the bike course.

Speaking on the broadcast shortly after pulling out on the run, he shared that he had been suffering from a condition he described as Iliac Artery Fibrosis. Although he had managed to race through it before, he said it was restricting blood flow to his left leg starting on the bike, before his whole leg went numb once he started the run.

He then shared that he should probably head home to France for an operation as soon as possible so he can come back ready for next year.

“Less than 30 min away from achieving my biggest dream yesterday,” Ditlev shared on Instagram.

After a rough couple of years, it looked like Magnus Ditlev was not only back, but about to be crowned world champion. Kona’s 2024 runner-up was back to his best until roughly the final 10K of the run, when “suddenly the lights went out.”

He had pushed hard to make his way forward from the swim chase group and produced the fastest bike split of the day to enter T2 with a commanding lead. Remarkably, he held that lead for the majority of the run over the likes of Vincent Luis and Kristian Blummenfelt (NOR). Unfortunately, it just wasn’t quite enough to carry the tall Dane across the finish line, but it seems to have fueled the fire even more.

“Leading this race for so long into the marathon is the craziest experience I’ve ever had and definitely leaves me hungry for next year!”

After grabbing a last-minute Kona slot at Ironman Kalmar, Salvisberg said everything was going “perfectly” at the halfway point on the bike before, out of nowhere, he could only pedal with one leg.

“I felt like a pain in my hip and sit bone unlike anything I’ve ever experienced. I couldn’t turn my left leg over anymore, so I had to clip out and keep riding with just my right.

“I hoped it would ease up after a while, but it never did. I was determined to reach the finish line pedaling with one leg, but then a flat tire ended my day.”

The “Bison,” Rudy von Berg, was ready to leave it all out there on an island he has been coming to since he was a little kid. This time, however, it wouldn’t be the dream day he enjoyed with his third-place finish in 2024.

After a disappointing swim and a bike ride where he said his legs never showed up, he developed intense lower-stomach pain after 25km of running that “wasn’t anything like GI distress.” He attempted to make it to the finish by walking another hour and a half, but the pain worsened to the point where he couldn’t continue and had to take a car back to the finish.

This young Dutch athlete suffered a fate that many seemed to have in common – vomiting. For him, it started just 60K into the bike, eventually leaving his body unable to continue. Perhaps the worst part of the whole ordeal for Olij is that he has no idea why it happened, saying, “I used exactly the same nutrition strategy I’ve been using for the past three years.”

After finishing 11th at the Ironman World Championship in Nice, this strong cyclist was in the mix for a top-20 result before a sprained ankle 25K into the run abruptly ended his chances, leaving him unable to continue.

After a disappointing few years, Daniel Bækkegård would have hoped this race could reverse some of his fortunes, especially after a promising race at Ironman Kalmar earned him his slot.

Sadly, as he did in Nice in 2025, Bækkegård withdrew on the bike after a significantly slower swim immediately raised red flags. At this time, he hasn’t provided any further update.

In 2024, Trevor Foley was having a dream race and was in the perfect position late on the bike before a crash just before T2 ended his hopes of an incredible debut. This time around, it was sickness that began the night before that caused him to end his day. He was one of several athletes who fell ill leading into the event, including Chelsea Sodaro (USA), who wasn’t even able to start.

“Today was one of the most difficult sporting moments in my career thus far,” shared the South African hopeful. “The island did humble me,” he added, explaining that he had been dealing with a sciatic nerve injury that flared up in the early stages of the bike.

Shortly afterward, to add insult to injury, Riddle was assessed a penalty. Our photographer Brad Kaminski was in the right place to capture the moment Riddle decided to pull over and call it a day.

Citing concerns about the long-term damage of running a marathon after already suffering in the heat, the young Olympian decided to call it quits and wait for next year.

Heading into his sixth Ironman World Championship, Høgenhaug didn’t have high hopes, sharing that he hadn’t been where he wanted to be in training.

At this time, we don’t know whether that preparation played a part in his withdrawal, but an unusually slow swim alongside, Bækkegård hinted that something was off from the gun.

Returning to the Big Island for the second time, Canada’s Tamara Jewett would have hoped some of that experience would pay off. However, as we highlighted before the race, sometimes experience means little on race day.

She shared that, at this point, she doesn’t “have all the answers to what went wrong yesterday,” further explaining that she needs time to heal before getting back to racing:

“Some threads to follow and some very big signals that my body, mind, heart and soul need a big rest and some real replenishing before I’m back out there. So that starts now.”

With three podiums in 2026 to her name and an 11th-place finish on her Kona debut, this Danish bike-runner was tipped by Solveig Løvseth (NOR) as one to watch at the pre-race press conference. Sadly, after making it through the tough swim in almost 65 minutes, her race ended before she could show what she was truly capable of on the run. Perhaps the worst part was that she came into the race sitting fifth in the Ironman Pro Series standings but fell 10 places to 15th.

Having secured her Kona qualification at Ironman Hamburg, India Lee was heading in the right direction, picking up a podium at 70.3 Zell am See in the lead-up after setting her sights on Kona all year. Sadly, after making it through a tough swim and bike, she was unable to continue the marathon in the energy lab. Here’s how she described her struggles on social media: “From the start of the race I was in agony – my quads cramped early on in the swim, then legs were cramping from 10k into the bike. Desperate to stop all day, I kept hoping I could turn it around. A tortuous day wondering what it’s all for.”

Something seemed off from the start for the young French woman, who finished fifth at the Ironman 70.3 World Championship just over a month ago. After an unusually slow swim, Pierré made up some ground on the bike, but not as much as she typically does, recording the 21st-fastest bike split. She still attempted the marathon, but unlike last year, she wasn’t able to finish.

After first coming to the island as an age-grouper in 2022, Great Britain’s Rebecca Anderbury was hoping for a better result after being unable to cross the line as a pro the year before. However, once again, the conditions got the better of her. She shared that she was in such bad shape a couple of miles into the run that volunteers were telling her to stop.

After skipping the Ironman 70.3 World Championship to focus fully on Kona, the 2023 champion was doing everything she could to rewrite the heartbreaking ending to her 2025 race in the Energy Lab. However, in a cruel turn of events, after starting the run in second place and looking strong, she stopped running mere yards from where it had happened the year before. The broadcast showed her throwing up.

Thankfully, her husband and coach, Reece Barclay, was close by to help her, as he was last year. At this time, we don’t have an update from Charles-Barclay about exactly what happened. The broadcast mentioned possible seasickness from the swim, but that explanation remains unconfirmed.

One of the brightest young stars in Ironman racing was another athlete struck by illness during race week. Impressively, she started the race and was among the first chase group on the bike, but had nothing to give. Like many in her position, she had worked to peak for this race all year and was left frustrated at being unable to show her form.

Like many on this list, she remains as motivated as ever, sharing that, “You may well see me lining up for another IM before the end of the season.”

Yet another athlete struck by sickness, Danielle Lewis woke up the day before the race with a sore throat that progressed into her chest. By race morning, she felt feverish enough to question whether she should start. Still, she gave it a go and made it through the swim before withdrawing on the bike, with a headache and coughing leaving her little choice. She later shared that she had tested positive for influenza A, as Chelsea Sodaro (USA) had before the race.

Like Lange, Oliveira didn’t get a fairytale ending to her final race on the Big Island. Unlike Lange, however, this was the final race of her career, leaving her without another chance to rewrite the ending. She was among the front chase group behind Lucy Charles-Barclay (GBR) out of the water but withdrew before the run.

Hofmann started the race with a severe migraine that was causing an aura and “severe vision problems.” Somehow, she managed to continue despite her symptoms worsening on the bike and causing vomiting. She made it through the entire bike leg and even started the run. By then, however, her symptoms were so severe that she rolled her ankle more than once while trying to stumble forward.

After a long, tough swim, the Ironman Chattanooga bronze medalist hit the dreaded wall with 40-50K remaining on the bike. Still, she continued onto the run “with optimism,” but ultimately decided to pull out rather than risk making a lingering foot issue worse by trying to finish.

#240. Nopales Benefits: Why You Might Add Cactus to Your Diet

Looking at a cactus with its threatening spikes and tough skin, you might not immediately think, “Yep, that’s a thing I could eat.” But guess what? Some forms of cacti are edible, tasty, and quite good for you!

Check out why it might be a good idea to pal around with nopales, the pads of the prickly pear cactus.

The nopal cactus, also known as the prickly pear or the opuntia, is a shrub-like, flowering cactus native to parts of Mexico, Arizona, the Mediterranean, Australia, and other desert regions. It might be recognized by its multitude of connected pads with flowering blooms. (A pad in bloom looks a little like a flat, green paw.)

Nopales flowers are filled with a viscous, seeded substance often used in jams, jellies, pies, cakes, and other sweets. But the stems, leaves, and entire pad (with spines removed, obvs) are also edible. Traditional Mexican preparations include boiling, grilling, and sautéing.

Science is still examining the possible benefits of nopales, so some touted wellness perks are fairly tentative. Here’s a look at what we know about these desert fruits.

Almost any time you see bright colors in edible fruits, it’s a sign they contain antioxidants. This is def true for Nopales!

Older studies have found that the fruit inside their flowers is rich in antioxidants like ascorbic acid, phenolics, and a mixture of betacyanin and betaxanthin. These compounds help fight inflammation by kicking harmful free radicals out of your cells.

Since they combat inflammation, the antioxidants in prickly pear could improve joint mobility. In a 2020 study, people who drank 3 ounces of prickly pear juice daily for 8 weeks had better range of motion and greater ease with daily activities than a control group who drank a placebo.

Research suggests nopales may help steady blood sugar. A 2014 study found that people with type 2 diabetes who ate nopales with a high-carb breakfast had significantly lower blood sugar and insulin levels compared to those who didn’t. However, this study only included 14 participants.

In 2019, a larger systematic review assessed the fruit’s potential for blood sugar regulation. While it found insufficient evidence to support using nopales to reduce the risk of type 2 diabetes, the authors noted it might significantly reduce blood glucose levels.

Showing your liver some love might involve adding nopales (or a glass of nopal juice) to your diet. According to research from 2023, this has to do with prickly pear’s effects on triglycerides. By helping reduce triglyceride accumulation, nopales could relieve stress on the liver.

Whether you’ve overdone it on booze or are down with a stomach bug, it’s important to rehydrate with a drink that contains electrolytes. Consider prickly pear juice as your back-on-the-wagon beverage. It’s got potassium, magnesium, and calcium to help rebalance your electrolyte levels.

If you can track down fresh nopales where you live, cooking it yourself is a fun (if somewhat complicated) way to take advantage of its benefits. If not, look for prickly pear products, such as juices, being sure to check for added sugars.

You can also take a supplement. Nopales supplements typically contain 500-650 milligrams (mg) per day.

While a prickly pear smoothie or nopales salad can be a healthy addition to your diet, consuming this cactus fruit may have some less-than-desirable side effects, like:

If you’re new to nopales, take it slow at first to see how your body responds.

Don’t let the “prickly” in prickly pear keep you away from this desert gem. When prepared correctly, nopales are unique, nutritious food. Check ’em out when your fruit basket needs something a little different.

#243. Wahoo Elemnt Bike Computers Are Up to $152 Off for Prime Big Deal Days—Here’s Which Model We’d Buy

Wahoo’s Bolt, Roam, and Ace are discounted—here’s which one fits your riding best.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Amazon’s Prime Big Deals Days have arrived, and our editors have been combing through the on-sale items to find the best discounts on must-have cycling gear. GPS-equipped cycling computers are one of the first things we check on Prime Days because they’re often a chance to save cash on top-performing, editor-favorite head units.

This Prime Big Deal Days, Wahoo’s three Elemnt cycling computer models are on sale for $119 to $152 off. Wahoo packs these head units with features: Each offers turn-by-turn navigation, color displays, Strava compatibility, and a Summit function that shows a detailed profile of upcoming climbs.

Several Bicycling editors and test team staff use Wahoo Elemnt computers on their personal bikes. Wahoo computers are also popular in the pro peloton and used by top pros, including Tour de France champion Tadej Pogačar, World Champion Brandon McNulty, Olympic gold medalist Kristen Faulkner, and multi-discipline threat Mathieu van der Poel.

Out of Wahoo’s three Elemnt cycling computers, the Roam V3 is the best choice for most cyclists. It features a 2.8-inch touchscreen display, making it easier to read and operate than the Bolt’s 2.3-inch button-only interface. However, the Roam isn’t as physically imposing as the Ace.

Other upgrades Wahoo packs into the Roam V3 over the Bolt include spoken-word navigation, up to 25 hours (claimed) of battery life, and 64 GB storage for routes and maps. Plus, the Roam has another feature we love: A digital bike bell. It’s perfect for around town or on shared-use paths and rail trails.

Like the sound of the Roam but want something smaller and lighter? Then the Elemnt Bolt V3 is for you. With its half-inch smaller screen, slightly smaller battery, and less storage, the Roam weighs 25 grams less than the mid-sized Wahoo option. This makes it a great choice for gram-counting road riders, mountain bikers who don’t want a big computer on their bars, or cyclists who want their ride data displayed without all of the extras and fluff.

The Elemnt Ace is the biggest, baddest cycling computer you can buy, dwarfing the Bolt V3 and even bigger than other “large” head units like the Garmin Edge 105 and Hammerhead Karoo. At first, the Ace’s 3.8-inch touchscreen display and 4.9 x 2.8 x 0.8-inch overall size look out of place on many road and gravel bikes.

However, after a few days of use, you get used to it—you might even find it hard returning to a smaller computer. The large screen makes it easier to read maps and navigate, see speed or power data, and manage multiple metrics simultaneously. Other bonuses of the Ace’s large size include longer battery life (up to 30 hours, claimed) and an integrated wind sensor.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#244. This Overlooked Workout Helps You Build Endurance Without Making Every Run Harder

Coaches explain how to use a medium-long run to build a stronger aerobic base.

Most marathon training plans prioritize two or three quality sessions each week: some combination of an interval workout, a tempo effort, and a weekend long run. But between ordinary easy efforts and the aforementioned weekend long run, there’s a valuable space for aerobic development most runners don’t take advantage of to improve performance.

This is where the medium-long run comes into play.

Coaches explain how this overlooked training tool can help you build more aerobic endurance, add mileage without making every day harder, and arrive at your goal race stronger and more resilient.

Run coach and author Matt Fitzgerald, cofounder of 80/20 Endurance, defines a medium-long run as a run longer than your standard easy run, but shorter than your long run. For example, if you typically run five or six miles on easy days and top out at 14 or 15 miles for your long run, a medium-long run might be eight to 11 miles. However, if your longest run is only 10 miles, your medium-long run should be shorter.

In other words, the medium-long run occupies a middle ground. It does not have a universal mileage prescription. The important part is its role in the week: It gives runners another opportunity for aerobic work between their standard easy runs and their longest session, says ultramarathon runner and USA Triathlon-certified coach Nick Farr.

When you first introduce these runs into your training, Fitzgerald recommends keeping them easy. A medium-long run describes the session’s duration and purpose, rather than a pace target. It can include race-specific work later in a training block (more on this later), but it begins as a way to spend a little more time building aerobic fitness.

Fitzgerald’s central argument in favor of the medium-long run is that runners can gain more from building weekly mileage than from fixating on the distance of one long run.

For marathoners and ultrarunners, “your average running mileage for the week as a whole is more predictive of how you'll do in a race than the distance of your longest run,” he says.

This does not mean the long run is unimportant. But when it is dramatically longer than every other session in the week, it can take on an outsized recovery cost.

Consider a runner who logs four five-mile efforts during the week and then runs 15 to 20 miles on Sunday. That long run is far more stressful than anything else in their plan, Fitzgerald says, and the runner may need much of the next week to bounce back.

A medium-long run can distribute some of that endurance work more evenly. Instead of tacking an extra mile onto every run—a move that makes every day a little harder—you lengthen only the medium session and protect the volume of the lighter days before and after, Farr explains. This helps runners increase their weekly training volume while preserving a weekly frequency they can consistently handle.

Fitzgerald suggests the groups who benefit the most from this workout structure are marathoners and ultrarunners who want to establish a stronger aerobic foundation.

But Farr sees benefits for runners who might be less likely to think this type of session is for them: He views the workout as especially useful for masters runners, newer runners, and runners with packed schedules. For masters runners, a midweek medium-long run can allow for better recovery and reduce injury risk that comes from making the weekend long run as high-mileage as possible. For newer runners, extending one existing session by a mile can add volume before they are ready to add a fifth or sixth running day to their schedule. And busy runners only have to make extra time for more miles on one day, rather than all week.

One important caveat: Although it’s not as demanding as a long run, a medium-long run generally replaces one harder workout, Fitzgerald says. It is not an invitation to add a fourth tough session to a week that already includes intervals, tempo work, and a long run.

First, determine the distance of your medium-long run.

For someone running six miles on easy days with a 14-mile long run, Fitzgerald suggests beginning with an eight- to 8.5-mile medium-long run. Then, use the first one as a guide: How did you feel after your run? Was it manageable? Did you recover well? Did it leave you with enough energy for the rest of your training week?

If you answer yes to these questions, you can work on building from there, Fitzgerald says.

As previously mentioned, Fitzgerald’s rule of thumb is no more than three quality sessions per week. If your training schedule currently includes a Tuesday interval workout, Friday tempo, and Sunday long run, a medium-long run would replace either the Tuesday or Friday quality session—keeping the easy days intact. The key is allowing enough recovery between the week’s most demanding sessions, Fitzgerald continues.

As far as when to add a medium-long run during your training block, Fitzgerald suggests incorporating it after you’ve built up a base and you’re transitioning into race-specific training. For most runners, that’s about 12 to 16 weeks before race day. Waiting until the final few weeks before a marathon to add in this workout does not leave enough time to build the session safely or reap much benefit from it, he explains.

Start with an extended easy run, then increase the distance in small increments. For example, moving from nine to 9.5 to 10 miles provides a fresh training stimulus without turning the session into another long run after only a few weeks.

Eventually, the run reaches a practical ceiling. If making it longer would put it too close to your weekly long-run distance, Fitzgerald recommends adding controlled intensity instead: a fast finish, short surges, or some marathon-specific work within the run.

Why it works: “This two-for-one session combines the benefits of a high-intensity interval workout with the endurance benefits of a longer run,” Fitzgerald explains. “Because the surges are pretty quick, I would most likely schedule it earlier in a half-marathon or marathon training block or closer to race day in a 5K or 10K training block, scaling the overall duration and interval number to the fitness level of the individual athlete.”

*Critical velocity is a pace you could sustain for 30 minutes in a race environment, somewhere between 5K to 10K pace for most runners.

Why it works: “This is a challenging workout that is best done within a few weeks of tapering for a longer race when you're already pretty fit,” Fitzgerald says. “It develops the ability to run fast on tired legs, which is key to performance at the half-marathon distance and up.”

By adding quality to these longer midweek sessions, “you’re getting in a little extra intensity because you’ve only got so many opportunities to do it,” Fitzgerald says, “but you’re not simply making the medium-long run too hard.”

Use two simple guardrails to protect your effort: First, the run should remain substantially shorter than your longest long run. Second, it should leave you moderately fatigued, but not seriously depleted. In other words, it’s fine to feel tired after a long run, but an easy medium-long run should not wreck the next several days of training.

The most useful feedback may be how the rest of your running feels that week. Fitzgerald believes runners should feel good most of the time, even at peak training. If your usual ratio of good runs to “meh” runs begins tilting toward “meh,” that is a sign you should probably dial back your training, he says.

But when executed well, the medium-long run bridges the gap between easy runs and the long run to build a more complete aerobic week, and helps you reach the starting line healthy enough to race at your fullest potential.

Surgery and other cosmetic methods for turkey neck can offer impressive results.

Are you not into cosmetic procedures or surgery? Neck-toning exercises and facial yoga movements may offer some improvement. However, loose skin is generally not tightened naturally.

Loose neck skin is normal (and honestly v common).

Still, these simple moves may result in toned neck muscles. Just be careful so you don’t wind up with an actual pain in the neck. If you can, it’s best to chat with a healthcare professional first.

#247. A $500 Adidas ‘Hyper Shoe’ Is Dominating the World Marathon Majors This Year—and It’s Not Even Close

Since its release in April, the Pro Evo 3 has been worn by seven of the last eight World Marathon Major winners.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

If you’ve hung around the finish line of a World Marathon Major this year, you might have seen a similar scene play out.

The winner crosses the finish line, celebrates, then, moments after running at a pace incomprehensible to most of us, poses with a pair of shoes and hoists them into the air.

Lately, it’s been the same pair of shoes.

Since Adidas unveiled the Adizero Adios Pro Evo 3 days before the London Marathon in April, the shoe has been on the feet of seven of the past eight winners of World Marathon Majors. The $500 super shoe weighs under 100 grams—about the same as a stick of butter—and Adidas claims it has “11 percent greater forefoot energy return” than its predecessor, the Pro Evo 2.

The Pro Evo 3 is part of a growing category of shoes referred to as “hyper shoes” by the shoe nerd community. These are ultralight, advanced marathon shoes that are designed specifically for elite athletes, not the rest of us mortals. The bouncy, lightweight foam can feel unstable to the average runner; they’re designed for speed over comfort and durability. Hyper shoes are also often considerably more expensive than the brands’ more accessible super shoes, like the Adios Pro 5. (The Pro Evo 3 is rarely available to purchase, but Adidas is restocking it on October 29.)

While other brands have ventured into hyper shoes, including Nike with the Apex and Asics with the Metaspeed Ray, Adidas has dominated the front of marathon races lately.

Sabastian Sawe wore the Pro Evo 3 when he set the world record, 1:59:30, at the London Marathon, and Tigst Assefa wore it when she ran the women’s-only world record of 2:15:41 the same day. At the Berlin Marathon in September—an Adidas-sponsored race—the Pro Evo 3 was worn by the entire men’s and women’s podiums. Since the Pro Evo 3 debuted, it has appeared on the podium in 15 of 24 available spots at World Marathon Majors.

Here’s a look at the shoe choice for the winners of the World Marathon Majors so far this year. (The final major on the 2026 calendar, the NYC Marathon, is set for November 1.)

Men’s winner: Tadesse TakeleShoe: Adidas Adizero Adios Pro Evo 1

Women’s winner: Brigid KosgeiShoe: Nike Vaporfly 4

Men’s winner: John KorirShoe: Asics Metaspeed Sky prototype

Women’s winner: Sharon LokediShoe: Under Armour Velociti Elite 3

Men’s winner: Sabastian SaweShoe: Adidas Adizero Adios Pro Evo 3

Women’s winner: Tigst AssefaShoe: Adidas Adizero Adios Pro Evo 3

Men’s winner: Addisu GobenaShoe: Nike Alphafly 4 prototype

Women’s winner: Peres JepchirchirShoe: Adidas Adizero Adios Pro Evo 3

Men’s winner: Guye AdolaShoe: Adidas Adizero Adios Pro Evo 3

Women’s winner: Tigst AssefaShoe: Adidas Adizero Adios Pro Evo 3 (development version)

Men’s winner: Amos KiprutoShoe: Adidas Adizero Adios Pro Evo 3

Women’s winner: Hawi FeysaShoe: Adidas Adizero Adios Pro Evo 3

When super shoes first started appearing in major races in the late 2010s, Nike dominated. The Vaporfly, and later the Alphafly, were synonymous with elite marathons and brands rushed to produce their own.

But this time, in the hyper shoe era, Adidas has emerged as the industry leader—and other brands are racing to keep up. Asics debuted the Metaspeed Ray last year, a lighter alternative to its Edge and Sky, and Nike announced the Apex ahead of last week’s Chicago Marathon, which the brand claims has up to 40 percent more energy return than the Alphafly 3.

The New York City Marathon on November 1 is the final chance for other brands to break up Adidas on the podium this year. Adidas will be led by former winners Benson Kipruto and Sheila Chepkirui. But athletes like Hellen Obiri (On) and Deresa Geleta (Nike) could spoil the party. It’s also worth noting that Nike and Adidas have historically had the deepest pockets to sponsor the world’s best runners, so there’s a bit of a pay-to-play element.

Either way, Adidas has had plenty to celebrate during the 2026 season. The super shoe wars are heating up, and the Pro Evo 3 has the biggest target on its back.

Theo Kahler is the senior news editor at Runner’s World. He’s a former all-conference collegiate runner at Winthrop University, and he received his master’s degree in liberal arts studies from Wake Forest University, where he was a member of one of the top distance-running teams in the NCAA. Kahler has reported on the ground at major events such as the Paris Olympics, U.S. Olympic Trials, New York City Marathon, and Boston Marathon. He’s run 14:20 in the 5K, 1:05:37 in the half marathon, and finished 40th at the 2025 New York City Marathon. He enjoys spotting tracks from the sky on airplanes. #248. Zone 2 Training Transforms Your Fitness and Health—Experts Explain How to Execute It

We explain why the majority of your rides should hit this effort and how to make the most of the miles.

Even if you’re not completely familiar with your power or heart rate training zones, you’ve probably heard that you should spend a majority of your time in the saddle riding at an effort that allows you to chat with your cycling buddies. This intensity, known as zone 2 training, provides a bunch of payoffs in terms of fitness and performance.

Also referred to as the aerobic zone, conversational pace, or all-day pace—though those titles can be slightly misleading—this effort can get confusing to master.

To help you conquer it, we explain exactly what zone 2 training means, why it matters, how it can help your performance, and how to do it for maximum gains.

🚴🏽 Ready to take on your fastest ride yet? Our How to Ride Faster program will help you make it happen!

Considered the leading global expert on all things zone 2, Iñigo San Millán, Ph.D., has spent three decades studying the effects of training in this aerobic zone. The former cyclist has worked with clinical populations dealing with diabetes, and he’s working with the upper echelon of the cycling world.

When he spoke to Bicycling a while back, he was in the middle of a rainstorm in France after chasing Tadej Pogačar up a Tour de France climb. “Let’s be clear,” he joked. “A normal person would be in zone 5 trying to keep up with Pogačar in his zone 2.”

That’s the just beginning of the nuances around this aerobic zone that’s gotten so much press coverage in recent years. (This fact bemuses San Millán, as someone who spent decades toiling away in labs and in the field on this work before it went viral.)

Before we get into the how to do zone 2 training, let’s briefly dig into the science side, which explains why it’s so important.

San Millán’s original interest in zone 2 came when he realized that optimal cellular mitochondrial function (the powerhouse of our cells) is key for both health and performance.

While you can’t see your mitochondria making moves when you exercise, you can feel how well your muscles clear lactate that’s produced by more intense exercise. “When you don’t clear lactate correctly, it builds up in the blood, and that’s a sign that your mitochondria are not keeping up very well,” says San Millán.

He started to notice that training more in the aerobic-based zone 2—the zone where the body produces lactate but is able to clear it equally quickly—allowed athletes to better clear the lactate from their muscles when they did increase their intensity and lactate production. Essentially, training at this lower intensity allowed them to train harder at higher intensities.

The same effect applies to pro athletes and recreational cyclists: Training that aerobic zone where the body is burning fat rather than glycogen improves both performance and health outcomes, thanks to how it improves mitochondrial function.

What makes zone 2 training particularly interesting is that it’s one of the few training stimuli that’s as good for health and longevity as it is for performance. San Millán’s research has found that many clinical populations—those with certain cancers, type 2 diabetes, and other metabolic diseases—have significant mitochondrial dysfunction.

While exercise alone isn’t a cure-all, San Millán found that adding in a protocol of zone 2-based exercise led to significant health improvements for those populations. Meanwhile, it also makes top pros like Pogačar get up hills faster.

Because it’s become so popular, there are many misconceptions around zone 2 training.

For starters, there’s the question of “what is zone 2?” Most people will say it’s all-day pace, conversational pace, or refer to it as LSD (long slow distance). But often, the pace you’re riding at in zone 2 is a bit harder than you may think. “You should be able to hold a conversation,” says San Millán. “But it shouldn’t be easy to do so. If it’s easy to chat, that’s more zone 1 recovery versus zone 2.”

It’s also not that slow. Again, see Pogačar’s “all-day pace,” which is likely faster than most of us could do on our best threshold testing day.

On the flip side, popular health and wellness blogs who’ve honed in on zone 2 will talk about walking as a great way to get in some zone 2 exercise. That may work for someone who doesn’t regularly exercise, but if you are training regularly, you’ll need to make that walk pretty brisk in order to move from zone 1 training into zone 2.

In other words: Zone 2 is different for everyone. The most important thing is to pay attention to your own effort to make sure you’re hitting the right intensity.

Also, if you got interested in zone 2 for health reasons, you may think that it’s all that you ever need to do. However, San Millán is quick to point out that while it’s the building block for cyclists, you do still need to do intervals and harder efforts if you want to make gains in your cycling. After all, if you never go hard, why did you bother improving that mitochondrial function that allows you to push the intensity in the first place?

While zone 2 trains you to be efficient at burning fat, once you get above that zone, you start burning glucose for fuel—and that’s something you need to train your body for, rather than hoping that on race day, you’ll magically be really good at going hard after training solely in zone 2.

The ultimate test for finding your zone 2 pace is a lactate test, because zone 2 is where your body is clearing the lactate you produce during exercise, not letting it accumulate.

While in an ideal universe, San Millán would send you to a lab for lactate testing in order to find your zone 2 pace, you can also base it off of your functional threshold power or heart rate. (Use this chart to help determine your pace.)

However, San Millán believes that FTP tests aren’t a perfect power-setting option when it comes to zone 2. Use that as a starting point, but make sure the power or heart rate matches up with the correct feeling: Your zone 2 pace should be sustainable for a few hours, and you should be able to hold a conversation, though it shouldn’t feel easy to do so.

Kristen Legan, gravel cycling coach and winner of the 350-mile Unbound XL in 2023, knows a thing or two about spending a lot of time in zone 2. When you’re training for races like the XL, most of your time is spent in the aerobic zone, though as with racers like Pogačar, she does need to spend some time going really freaking fast.

She says that even if you aren’t riding for six hours, it should feel like you could if you wanted to. “Zone 2 is the pace that you can sustain for a really long time—as long as you’re eating and drinking!” says Legan. (Often, the reason zone 2 starts to feel harder as the ride gets longer is fuel-based, not leg- or lung-based.)

However, while this sounds like the ride should be easy, don’t confuse conversational with “easy pace.” “Zone 1 is a recovery or easy ride,” says Legan. “In these rides, you’re in easy gears, you’re really relaxed, and the goal is just getting your body moving. It’s not about pressure on the pedals. Zone 2 is a bit harder than that.”

“You can pay attention to your heart rate monitor or power meter to make sure you’re staying in the zone if you aren’t comfortable with relying on your perceived exertion,” says Legan. “But I think just trying to keep that conversational pace—testing out talking while you’re riding if you need to check in—is the best way to ensure you stay in the zone.”

To be quite honest, zone 2 can take some practice to perfect, considering it runs the fine line right between going too easy and going too hard. Don’t get discouraged if you struggle with it at first!

“It takes practice to do zone 2,” says Legan. “But the more you do it, it will become easier and easier to just fall into it rather than staying in the easier zone 1 or ratcheting up to zone 3 or higher.”

“As athletes, I think a lot of us hate that feeling of needing to shift down, because we just want to be pushing all the time, and we want to feel like we’re getting work done,” says Legan. “It takes mental practice to just be okay with not trying to speed up a hill.”

Don’t forget, outside influences can affect your zone 2 pace, too—it’s not a steady marker, says San Millán. In heat or at altitude, for example, you may see a 10 percent decrease in the power you’re able to hold while staying within your zone 2 heart rate, because the environment is also taxing the body.

“Ideally, someone would be training three to four days a week in zone 2,” says San Millán. “But these sessions don’t need to be as long as you might think. People always assume zone 2 rides need to be three or more hours to ‘count,’ but even 90 minutes in zone 2 will show good results.”

If you are hoping to do longer races, obviously adding more volume on some rides will be beneficial, but that 90 minutes can improve your mitochondrial function.

For most cyclists, Legan says that the breakdown of hours spent in zone 2 should be about 80 percent of time there, with 20 percent spent in intervals and recovery from said intervals. “Whether you’re a crit racer, road racer, or a gravel racer, that breakdown works—you just do different intervals in the other 20 percent of your time. But the biggest physiological boost comes from that time in zone 2,” she says.

When you’re on a zone 2 ride outside, don’t panic if you go slightly above or below your zone as you go up a hill (or descend down one). Get comfortable shifting into an easy gear and spinning away on hills to keep your effort as close to zone 2 as possible, but San Millán says that even if 80 percent of your ride is in zone 2, that’s a good ride!

Like most things, training in zone 2 takes time before you see major benefits. “You’ll start getting some adaptations after a couple of months if you’re training in zone 2 consistently,” San Millán says. But the real improvements come after a year of keeping your zone 2 training consistent, while still adding in intervals and high-intensity work occasionally.

“I compare training in zone 2 to planting a vineyard,” he adds. “In the first season of planting, you’re not going to have any harvest even if you do all the right preparation. You’ll see some vines, you’ll see that it’s coming, but you won’t have grapes yet. But the second year... that’s when you have that first harvest.”

#250. Thai Massage Therapy: Benefits and What to Expect

Feeling stressed? Whether you unwind with yoga or a relaxing massage, Thai massage combines the best of both worlds, benefiting your mind and body. Here’s everything you need to know!

Thai massage is a special kind of bodywork that blends relaxation with flexibility. Think of it as a gentle, full-body, more active experience. It’s all about boosting your flexibility and energizing your body. Just a heads-up: napping during a Thai massage might be a challenge!

Drawing from Ayurvedic and traditional Chinese medicine, this ancient technique mixes assisted yoga stretches, acupressure, and soothing rocking for 60 to 90 minutes. Unlike Western-style massages at a local spa, Thai massage takes place on a mat on the floor. A certified therapist will work to stretch your muscles and apply pressure along your body’s energy lines, known as sen, to release stress with a graceful, rhythmic touch.

You can schedule a Thai massage at many spas, massage clinics, and even some yoga studios, but make sure you find someone with the proper training and certification to give you an authentic experience.

When you arrive for a Thai massage, you might be given some comfy clothes, like a T-shirt and drawstring pants. You’ll remove your shoes, silence your phone, place your jewelry in a small dish, and settle onto a floor mat. Before the session, let the therapist know if you have any injuries.

If this is your first session, it can be intense, so focus on breathing and relaxing. You’ll likely start on your back, with the therapist beginning on your feet and legs. Since the therapist uses their body weight to guide you, it might initially feel a bit weird. Some discomfort is normal as your body stretches, but don’t hesitate to let your therapist know if anything feels uncomfortable.As the session progresses, you’ll likely switch positions, including flipping onto your belly or trying various other postures. Go with the flow as your therapist guides you through stretches and yoga-like moves designed to open up your joints, move your energy, and release tension. Keep breathing and communicate with your therapist throughout the process.

As the session wraps up, you’ll enjoy some gentle rocking motions to ease you out of the massage. You might feel sore afterward, especially if it’s your first Thai massage, so hydrate and rest. You’ll likely feel incredibly relaxed, more flexible, and energized.

Pro tip: Clear your mind and be open to guidance. While the stretches may feel awkward initially, allow yourself to let go. This can help you fully experience the massage’s benefits.

Your Thai massage experience won’t resemble a Western-style deep tissue massage. You won’t be naked under a sheet on a raised massage table, and the massage therapist won’t be using long, deep strokes to work your muscles.The other significant difference is that, like some forms of yoga, Thai massage has a spiritual element based on Buddhism. As they use the weight of their bodies to work on your body, your therapist is also trained to send you kind, loving, healing vibes. The ultimate goal is to help you feel better by allowing your energy to flow throughout your body.

The ancient practice of Thai massage combines assisted yoga stretches, acupressure, and rhythmic rocking to unknot your body and get your inner energy flowing. Unlike Western massage techniques, you’ll be fully clothed on a floor mat, with the massage therapist using their entire body to release your tension.

Permit yourself to let go, and expect an active, sometimes intense, full-body experience that leaves you relaxed and energized.

Last medically reviewed on July 31, 2024

#251. Everyone Wants This Unapproved Weight Loss Drug—And Some Have Found a Way to Get It

For all the hype surrounding GLP-1 weight loss medications like Wegovy and Zepbound, these drugs don’t work for everyone. Nearly 17% of people on these medications are considered “non-responders,” leaving them looking for a different solution. But there’s a buzzy new medication waiting in the wings. While it’s not yet approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), people are already seeking it out.

It’s called retatrutide, and it’s a triple-agonist medication, which means it acts on three different receptors in the body. By comparison, Wegovy (semaglutide) acts on one receptor, while Zepbound (tirzepatide) works on two.

Retatrutide is already being hailed as a game changer in an area of health that’s already welcomed plenty of impressive medications in the past few years. In fact, clinical trial results show that it’s so effective for weight loss that some people have dropped out of the trials because they felt that they lost too much weight.

But retatrutide is still being tested in clinical trials. Eli Lilly, which makes reatrutide and Zepbound, hasn’t even submitted the trial results yet to the FDA for approval. So this is still an experimental medication—and versions of it are being sold online for cheap.

Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, California, tells SELF that retatrutide is “not really available” for use just yet, short of signing up for a clinical trial. There is no set timeline for when it will hit the market, given that clinical trial results have not yet been submitted to the FDA.

If you’ve struggled with losing weight on a GLP-1 medication or just want to pay significantly less for what appears to be the next big thing in weight loss drugs, it’s understandable to be tempted to add this to your cart. Here’s why doctors recommend resisting the urge.

Retatrutide is similar to GLP-1 medications in a few ways. Namely, it’s used for weight loss and is given once a week through an injection. Like Wegovy, Ozempic, and Zepbound, retatrutide works by reducing appetite and slowing digestion.

But retatrutide has more going on than that. This medication acts on three hormone receptors in the body—glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), gastric inhibitory polypeptide (GIP), and glucagon (GCG). “This is the first one in the pipeline to work on three different receptors,” says Dr. Ali. “The theory is that the more receptors it affects, the more effective the drug will be.”

The medication is currently in phase-three clinical trials, and it’s had some impressive results that suggest it could be the most effective drug for weight loss yet. The latest clinical trial results show that participants lost an average of 28.7% of their body weight on the highest dose of retatrutide over 68 weeks. By comparison, tirzepatide users lost an average of 15% to 22.5% over 72 weeks during clinical trials, and semaglutide users lost 10% to 15% of their body weight over 68 weeks during clinical trials.

It takes a little detective work, but there are some pharmacies that are selling the drug online.

In fact, this has become such an issue that the FDA issued a press release in early February, stressing that it’s illegal to sell retatrutide (and fellow experimental weight loss medication cagrilintide) right now. That includes picking up the medication from a compounding pharmacy.

“Retatrutide and cagrilintide cannot be used in compounding under federal law,” the release states. “Additionally, these are not components of FDA-approved drugs and have not been found safe and effective for any condition.”

The FDA also noted that its officials have issued warning letters to companies that are distributing these medications.

This is hardly shocking, but doctors really want you to take a pass on using retatrutide before it’s FDA-approved.

“People should wait to take medications until they are approved by the FDA to maximize safety,” Richard Siegel, MD, codirector of the Diabetes and Lipid Center at Tufts Medical Center and endocrinologist at Tufts Medicine Weight & Wellness Center–Stoneham, tells SELF. “All scientific data in animals initially and then humans are carefully reviewed by the FDA for any signals that a medication may be harmful.”

That includes side effects you might experience now or in the future, Dr. Ali points out. Compounding pharmacies have become a gray area. They’re able to legally produce and sell their own versions of popular medications when the FDA-approved versions are in shortage. But technically this is no longer legal once the medications are out of shortage.

But compounded drugs aren’t carefully regulated and may not even have the same ingredients or concentration as the medication they’re designed to mimic, Dr. Siegel says. “While these medications may be safe, there is less oversight in their production,” he says.

Dr. Ali warns against going directly through a compounding pharmacy, noting that it’s safer to work with your health care provider if you plan to go this route. “The worst-case scenario is that you’re getting something unsafe or ineffective,” he says.

But, with all medications, Dr. Ali says it’s best to use the FDA-approved version whenever possible. “It’s going to work in a predictable way, and the side effect profile will be well-studied,” he says.

Dr. Siegel points out that there are a lot of options to lose weight right now. And, if you haven’t had success on one, he recommends talking to your healthcare provider about trying a different medication or strategy. If you haven’t had luck while working with a primary care physician, Dr. Ali suggests seeing an obesity medicine specialist who will be more knowledgeable about treatment options.

“Medications for weight management are a powerful tool that should be used together with a comprehensive lifestyle plan focusing on self-monitoring, optimal nutrition, and an exercise prescription, including both aerobic and resistance components,” Dr. Siegel says. Meaning, people who have the best results do more than take medication—they also focus on nutrition and exercise.

If you’re interested in taking a weight loss medication or your existing treatment isn’t working, talk to a healthcare provider who specializes in this area. “These medications are designed for people with significant weight to lose,” Dr. Ali says. “Most likely, they will need to be taken long-term.” That makes getting a well-vetted medication from a reputable source even more important, he points out.

#253. The 9 Best Running Headlamps of 2026, Tested by Runners

We tested running headlamps on dark roads, technical trails, and long-distance runs to find the best options for brightness, comfort, and battery life.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Running before sunrise has always been my favorite kind of solitude—the crisp air, your world reduced to breath and motion, and that small, bright circle of light guiding the path. Trouble is, not all headlamps are equal companions for those moments. Some bounce, some dim when you need them most, and some feel like you strapped a miner’s rig to your forehead.

After years of chasing light through winter training runs, I can say this: the right headlamp isn’t just another piece of gear—it’s a safety essential and a quiet confidence booster. Whether you’re managing early morning tempo runs or logging your weekly long run through dusk, I’ve tested the brightest, lightest, and most comfortable contenders out there to help you find your perfect match.

This guide pulls from years of real-world testing—trails, road miles, battery panic in 20-degree wind chills—and distills it into clear advice you can use before you buy.

I’ve been covering endurance gear and running tech for over a decade—testing hydration vests in the Rockies, shoes in the Catskills, and headlamps in New York’s five boroughs. For this guide, I focused on hands-on daylight-to-dark testing across road and trail environments. Also, some of these headlamps were chosen by our other resident ultramarathoner, Pat Heine-Holmberg, who is frequently seen running in the pitch dark throughout the mountains of Europe.

This lamp grabbed the best overall because of the combination of comfort, durability, brightness, and battery type. The 800 Pro hit the sweet spot on long runs. Its balanced front and rear design meant zero bounce, even during faster intervals. The sweat-wicking strap kept things comfy in muggy conditions. The beam-spread was both wide and focused, letting me scan the road ahead and side trails with ease.

Fast USB-C charging was perfect for dark winter mornings where I forgot to recharge overnight—30 minutes got me through another 90-minute run. It’s bulkier than some, and the rear battery can press against hats, but the battery life was reliable and lasted through multiple workouts. The price is steep, yet you’re getting serious quality and durability for regular runners. The only reason mine died is because of heat damage from a melting battery near the lamp that happened ONLY because I used an aftermarket battery. I am repurchasing this one for sure.

If you don’t need 800-plus lumens or ultramarathon battery life, the Black Diamond Spot 400-R gives you nearly everything most runners need at a much lower price.

Black Diamond’s Spot 400-R is a favorite of Heine-Holmberg. It’s light enough that it never feels distracting, and the tap-sensitive controls let you adjust brightness mid-stride without having to fumble for buttons. The quality is solid—it will survive several drops and still work perfectly, though the plastic build doesn’t have the same premium feel as pricier models. Brightness is decent for daily roads and park runs, but you may find it a little lacking for really dark trail sections. With reliable charging and a simple, straightforward design, it’s perfect for beginners or anyone who values ease over bells and whistles.

The Petzl Swift RL is the headlamp to buy if your runs regularly transition between city streets, wooded trails, and changing terrain. On twisting trails, the headlamp switches modes automatically, and the lightweight one-handed fit is a major plus for on-the-fly adjustments. You can take it out in heavy drizzle, and its water resistance will hold up; it will never slip off or feel even remotely uncomfortable. I will say this one does get a bit warmer than others, and that battery doesn’t last as long as some due to the high lumens, but I still run with it often. (I also like it for cleaning under beds and other furniture. So bright!)

The adaptive tech makes it a standout for anyone moving between road and trail. If you crave versatility and a sturdy, intelligent beam, this is one of the best.

The Petzl Swift LT is the definition of ultra-minimalist, barely tipping the scale at just 1.2 ounces (35 grams). This headlamp fits into a jacket pocket or running belt with room to spare, making it my go-to for city runs, fastpacking, or as a backup light on longer trail outings. The single-button interface is intuitive, with three white light settings easily toggled: low (5 lm, 50 hours), standard (100 lm, 3 hours), and max (380 lm, 2 hours), as well as a red light for night vision and a red strobe for emergencies. The rubber cord strap is stable but can dig in if overtightened; it really shines for shorter runs and activities where weight and packability trump long runtime. The burn time on max is modest, but for shorter daily runs or to keep stashed in your vest, it’s an incredibly reliable, genuinely featherweight option.

The Fenix HM65R-T V2.0 is a spotlight for serious night runs. Its power and beam distance are unmatched—you could light a whole forest trail. The wide strap stays put even without a cross strap. The new sport fit, silicone-based headband held tight during speedwork and didn’t pinch, but the weight was noticeable after the first hour. Its magnesium build is tough and shrugs off hard rain or accidental drops. Customizable beams let you switch for technical rocks versus open road, though learning the button system took time and patience on first use. For ultra races or backcountry adventures, few headlamps offer more certainty, provided you don’t mind the bulk.

Black Diamond’s Deploy 325 is a featherlight, low-profile running headlamp that virtually disappears on your forehead but still delivers up to 325 lumens for pre-dawn or after-dark miles. A slim housing, foam padding, and flexible wing band keep it stable and bounce-free, even on technical trails, while the compact shape fits easily under a hat or into a vest pocket. USB-C recharging and an IPX4 water-resistance rating make it a grab-and-go option for runners who want reliable light without bulk, though its shorter runtime and lack of extra features suit training runs more than all-night adventures.Black Diamond Deploy 325 Review

The Black Diamond Sprinter 500 is a runner-focused headlamp built for serious pre-dawn and after-dark miles, with a bright 500-lumen beam and a rear red strobe for visibility in traffic. Its ultra-thin, balanced design spreads weight between front lamp and rear battery, while a perforated elastic band and optional top strap keep it stable over long runs. Dual-Fuel tech lets you use the included BD 1800 rechargeable battery or swap in AAA cells, and on-board USB charging plus PowerTap brightness control make it easy to top up and quickly boost light when you hit unlit roads or trails.Black Diamond Sprinter 500 Review

I’ve been running with the BioLite Dash 450 for early mornings and post-work miles, and it’s become one of my faves for easy pace miles. At 450 lumens, it’s bright enough to clearly light dark roads and wooded paths, with a focused beam that reaches far ahead without feeling harsh, though, my dog isn’t a huge fan when he accidentally stares into the gleam. The slim, moisture-wicking band sits comfortably and doesn’t bounce, even during some light tempo efforts, and that’s largely due to the overall adjustability of it. It has multiple points of adjustment, making sure that it sits well and correctly on your noggin.

I like the rear red light for added safety and visibility in traffic, a crucial feature for road running. The easy USB-C recharge is convenient, eliminating the need for specialized cables.

Battery life holds up reliably for most of my longer runs, and the different light modes let me quickly adjust based on terrain and traffic. It’s lightweight, practical, and truly runner-smart.

I love that I can get 15 seconds of 1,500 lumens if I need it in the bear-ridden trails of upstate New York, but also that I can keep it at a lower lumen rate, and run for hours and hours without worrying about killing it. I stay alive by avoiding bears, and it stays alive by avoiding battery drain.The adjustable output makes it easy to match the light to the moment: bright on fast descents, dialed back on smooth, runnable stretches. Most of my night is spent with the light on low, and so I’m not worried about zapping the power or losing my light—a gift when I'm deep into a race. That battery and power does come at a price, though. This is the heaviest headlamp on the list. But when you’re 110 miles into 175, or if you’re on a wild trail, this is incredible.

The cross strap is another big pro for this lamp. With a band over the top and around my head, it stays planted. On hard technical scrambles, when I’m hauling myself over rock and my head is constantly moving, the beam stays exactly where I aimed it instead of bouncing or sliding down my forehead.

🔌Choose a built-in rechargeable battery if...

You mostly run before or after work, have easy access to charging, and want the lightest, simplest setup.

🔋Choose replaceable rechargeable batteries if...

You regularly run trails after dark, race ultramarathons, or need the ability to swap in a fresh battery during long efforts.

You want a dependable backup system or travel somewhere charging isn’t guaranteed.

You need maximum flexibility for overnight races, multi-day runs, or remote trail running.

A running headlamp should feel snug, but not tight; it shouldn’t bounce, and it should distribute the weight as evenly as possible so you don’t feel your head drooping midrun. Here’s what to look for:

These are the easiest because they don’t stick out, and they’re very light. They’re great for road and everyday training, and people who get headaches from lamps easily. They’re not the most stable, so they can bounce on tricky scrambles.

A cross strap helps keep your headlamp from bouncing, and it is better balanced. This is the best for big scrambles and gnarly night work.

The balance is amazing on this because you have weight in the front and the back, but it’s a pain for hats, ponytails, hoods, and any other headgear.

Most headlamps fit okay over a hat or winter headband, don’t fiddle with the strap until you get it set over the headband or cap.

How long should a headlamp last for a 100-mile race?

You need to plan for the hours of darkness—not your total race time. For the majority of 100-mile races, you'll spend about six to 14 hours running at night, depending on the time of year, your pace, and the race itself. Grab a lamp with power enough to get you through that and pack an extra battery or lamp in your drop kit.

Should ultrarunners carry a second headlamp?

Yes. Absolutely. 100 percent yes. Even if your lamp says it will go the distance, it might get messed up, crap might happen. Pack an extra (or two).

Are rechargeable headlamps good for ultramarathons?

They can be, but only with advanced prep. Rechargeable headlamps are convenient for training and shorter trail races, but you’re going to need to pack extra battery packs in your drop kits or charge at an aid station, which could mess up your time.

Can you change a headlamp battery during a race?

Not really. Very few work when plugged into power, so bring extra battery packs.

#254. The Fastest Shoes at the 2026 Ironman World Championship

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Taylor Knibb wore Hoka Rocket X3 and Vincent Luis wore Nike Apex on their way to winning the 2026 Ironman World Championship. (Photo: Abby Levene/Triathlete and Sean M. Haffey/Getty Images)

How We Reported This: Triathlete’s Abby Levene was on the ground in Kona reporting on the 2026 Ironman World Championship, documenting the shoes on the feet of the top 10 men and women. Together with Outside’s Senior Gear Editor Jonathon Beverly, they tapped into their knowledge from testing 20-plus pairs of super shoes currently on the market to provide analysis of the athletes’ choices.

The 2026 Ironman World Championship proved, once again, that this event may just be the toughest endurance feat on Earth. A choppy swim and a windy bike gave way to a hot and especially humid run with blow-ups and meltdowns not even Hollywood would dare to script. Watching the top contenders run down Ali’i in the early stages of the marathon, one thing that struck our team on the ground in Kona was just how unique the running shoe demands are in these conditions.

Even the fastest Ironman atheltes in the world are very tired by the time they slip on their super shoes. That fatigue showed when looking down at their feet, as we were doing while taking note of what shoes athletes were wearing out on the course. (I.e., we saw a lot of pronating in tippier models.) Throw in the hills and being constantly wet as athletes doused themselves in water, and it’s no surprise to us that many of the top finishers traded weight and responsiveness for a bit more stability and comfort.

The most popular shoe? The On Cloudboom Strike 2, worn by six out of the 20 men and women in the top 10. And not only is it a proven performer on the feet of the elite, but it also shines as a race-day shoe for the rest of us. But it wasn’t on the feet of either winner or any of the top finishers who don’t have a shoe sponsor. Read on for our full analysis of the shoes worn by the top 10 men and women.

Like her patient run strategy, Taylor Knibb’s shoe choice was designed to let her run strong every kilometer, all the way to the finish. The Hoka Rocket X3 is not nearly the lightest super shoe racer, at 7.4 ounces, nor does it have the newest, bounciest foam. But the two layers of tried-and-true, soft and responsive PEBA, the split carbon-fiber plate with stability winglets, and the long, gradual forefoot rocker all support a comfortable, efficient, stable, and sustainable stride — exactly what you want to take you through the end of an Ironman.

So it’s not surprising that it was the choice shoe with the other Hoka athletes in the top 10 (all of whom came from the women’s race), plus unsponsored Lisa Perterer. Several of our testers said the Rocket X3 was gentle enough to use for training, and it is a smart choice for non-elites tackling the long miles of the marathon.

Running shoe: New Balance FuelCell SC Elite v5

Runner-up Laura Philipp — who ran a 2:50:43 for the fastest women’s run split of the day — also made a safe choice for footwear, selecting the discontinued SC Elite v5 over the newer v6. The v5 is an ounce heavier than the v6, and retains a PEBA-based midsole rather than the livelier TPEE-EVA found in the v6. But the v5 has a smooth, grounded ride that emphasizes comfort, with a gentle compression, rebound, and rocker. Like the Hoka Rocket X3, many use the SC Elite v5 as a training shoe, and it isn’t a surprise that it treated Philipp well in the late stages of the marathon. Bonus: closeout prices are a steal if you grab a pair now before they are gone.

We weren’t surprised to see On’s recently released Cloudboom Strike 2 on the podium (Spoiler alert: we’re naming it the best marathon racing shoe in our fall road-running shoe guide). After a rough start with some overly firm models, On has caught and surpassed the field with their latest super shoe.

Instead of On’s signature hollowed-out clouds, the midsole now has two grooves in the forefoot that split the foam into separate segments under the heel, ball, and toe. This lets the soft, PEBA-based foam — that we loved in the original strike — compress and rebound more freely, for a smooth, responsive feel. A wide forefoot and plate keep the stance stable and push-off powerful. It’s light and explosive enough for elite speed, but forgiving and supportive enough to take care of tired legs and those with imperfect strides.

World Champion Vincent Luis wore a shoe that the rest of us can’t get until January 2027: the Nike Apex. But Nike has revealed enough that we can predict how it will ride: fast and über-bouncy. Two innovations stand out: stacked Air Zoom units in the forefoot, and zero-drop geometry, meaning the forefoot also has 40 millimeters under it, eight more than the Alphafly 3. As its name suggests, we anticipate the Apex will cater to the front of the pack, delivering explosive push-offs for those with strong, powerful strides who stay up on their toes.

Unsurprisingly, the rest of the On athletes also opted for the smooth and stable Cloudboom Strike 2. That includes Gustav Iden, who ran a 2:36:58 marathon for the fastest men’s run split of the day. That was almost good enough to run down Luis — Iden came within 39 seconds at one point. But he ran out of gas at the 38K mark, he told us at the finish line.

The top-performing athlete of the day who doesn’t have a shoe sponsor, Matthew Marquardt, chose his familiar, proven Adios Pro 4 instead of the new Pro 5, just released September 22. (That decision, he said beforehand, was because he didn’t have enough time to run in the Pro 5 before the race.)

The Pro 4 was widely praised by testers of all speeds and strides for its soft-but-not-squishy, responsive ride from the TPEE midsole, and smooth roll over Adidas’s signature, independent energy rods that served in lieu of a full plate. In terms of softness, bounce, and rocker, the Pro 4 struck a nice, middle-of-the-road balance among super shoes, making it pretty perfect both when flying on fresh legs and when doing the survival shuffle. The new Pro 5 has significant changes in the foam and plate, so if you like the 4, stock up now.

Running shoe: Adidas Adizero Adios Pro Evo 3

The Pro Evo 3 speaks for itself in both design and performance. At 3.5 ounces — the lightest supershoe ever made — with an innovative, U-shaped carbon-fiber rim surrounding the midsole instead of a full embedded plate, the shoe has already broken the marathon world record, scorching a 1:59:30 at London 2026.

We have yet to test the Evo 3, but reports indicate the uncompressed supercritical TPEE midsole is softer than ever, and the perimeter rim lets your foot sink into that softness deeper than ever, then launches you forward — if you have the stability and stride that’s able to keep it driving in the right direction.

The Evo 3 most likely won’t feel supportive enough for any runner whose form starts to wobble at all when fatigued, but it has proven unsurpassed at optimizing the powerful stride of champion runners.

When I first started marathoning, the conventional shoe wisdom was that on race day it was wiser to stick with a lightweight training shoe that you had put long miles on than to opt for a thin, light racing flat. “Stick with old friends,” was the marathon gear mantra.

Super shoes have altered that calculus somewhat by being both ultralight and cushioned, but still the majority of the top finishers in Kona followed the old advice and stuck with trusted models (or new versions with minor updates). They raced in shoes that prioritized smooth, dependable support over having the lightest weight and the most explosive trampoline rebound. And it worked: the old friends didn’t hold them back or let them down.

The one caveat to that theme was the four athletes racing in Asics, two of whom are unsponsored. That included New Zealand’s Hannah Berry, who of all the super shoes on the market opted for the exceptionally light and responsive but also essentially tractionless and pretty tippy Asics Metaspeed Ray, a shoe our testing team found best for shorter distances.

A second observation from the diverse list of top shoes reflects something I’ve noticed as a wear-tester: with each new generation of super shoes, they’ve become increasingly similar in softness, rebound, and effectiveness. The length and steepness of the rocker, the sole width, the fit, and subtle nuances in the foam’s response affect how well a shoe will complement your stride, but when you find one that flows in harmony with your preferred movement path, you can be confident that it has the right stuff to enhance your efficiency, whether it’s a Hoka, On, Adidas, Asics, New Balance, Nike, Brooks, Puma, Saucony, or Topo.

#257. Skin in the Game: Is Adapalene or Salicylic Acid Better for Acne?

If you have acne, you probably know more about skincare than most people. You might even impress friends with terms like “adapalene” and “salicylic acid.”

But do you know what each treatment does for your skin and if one is better for acne? Let’s find out!

Salicylic acid is a keratolytic agent commonly found in over-the-counter creams, face washes, masks, and gels. While it’s often used for acne, it can also help with dandruff, psoriasis, seborrheic dermatitis, calluses, and warts.

Adapalene, often known by its brand name Differin, is a topical retinoid. It comes in various forms, such as gels, cleansers, and creams. And just like salicylic acid, it’s available over-the-counter without a prescription.

On a chemical level, adapalene and salicylic acid work in different ways to clear acne.

Salicylic acid breaks down a protein called keratin in the outer layer of the skin. Studies show this helps remove the buildup of dead skin cells. It also reduces inflammation in the skin, calming the redness that often comes with breakouts.

Adapalene, on the other hand, is a retinoid. And what, you may ask, is a retinoid? It’s a derivative of vitamin A that attaches to receptors in the skin. Doing so prompts cell turnover to speed up, helping skin regenerate more quickly and lowering the likelihood of clogged pores.

So… what do these differences mean for acne? Both adapalene and salicylic acid can treat skin prone to breakouts (though it’s not recommended to use them together since this can over-irritate your skin).

Which one is more potent may depend on your acne type. Research shows that adapalene was among the best treatments for comedonal acne (aka whiteheads and blackheads), whereas salicylic acid was less effective and more affordable.

Long story short: Your dermatologist can help determine which is the smarter choice for your type of acne.

Studies haven’t directly compared adapalene and salicylic acid for blackheads, but both can help. Blackheads form from plugged hair follicles, and salicylic acid’s exfoliating action can clear clogged pores. Adapalene increases cell turnover, which can also help remove blackheads.

Adapalene is a retinoid. Retinoids are well-established anti-aging agents because they stimulate new cell growth and promote collagen production. Some studies have also shown anti-aging benefits from salicylic acid.

While salicylic acid, due to its exfoliating properties, can help reduce wrinkles, adapalene is generally more effective for addressing aging-related concerns like wrinkles.

Adapalene is an over-the-counter acne treatment — so prescription-strength options may work better. According to the American Academy of Dermatology, some of the most potent acne treatments include antibiotics and isotretinoin.

Adapalene isn’t a magic wand for acne. It may be an ideal choice for some people, but depending on your skin type and sensitivity level, salicylic acid, other OTC products, or even a prescription treatment might be your best bet.

Research shows that adapalene can be just as strong for zapping zits as benzoyl peroxide (another potentially powerful weapon in the battle against acne). A 2024 study, for example, found that 0.1% topical adapalene was as safe and effective as a 4% benzoyl peroxide solution in people of color.

Though adapalene may be an effective acne treatment, it’s not the pinnacle of retinoid strength. Of the four “generations” of retinoids, adapalene is considered third-generation. Fourth-generation retinoids are typically stronger and have higher specificity to retinoic acid receptors in the skin. For this reason, they’re available only by prescription.

Feel free to experiment with adapalene and salicylic acid to see which works best for you — after all, it’s your face! You might find one more effective for your skin. For expert advice, be sure to consult your dermatologist.

Last medically reviewed on July 31, 2024

Having the right cold-weather running gear isn’t a total cure for the winter blues, but it sure makes it easier to exit your vehicle at the trailhead. With the right attitude and some fun and functional new accessories that’ll keep you toasty without overheating, you too can continue your year-round training and enjoy the benefits of breathing fresh air, no matter how frigid or dark.
