The Rail XC comes in several colors and options, so be sure to choose the Fototec if you’re looking for light-adjusting lenses.

Other sunglasses to consider: The Goodr Bolt G provides full eye coverage and has an adjustable nosepiece. It has polarized lenses with UV44 protection. And it’s only $45.

Take our advice: The first thing you should reach for is a pair of thin gloves to wear with shorts and a T-shirt, since fingers often get chilly first. As winds pick up and the temperature dips even lower, swap the tee for a long-sleeve shirt, then progress to pants and a jacket when conditions worsen.

Smart runners know to dress in layers. A thin jacket can be tied around your waist easily if you find yourself too warm. Beneath that, look for a synthetic or light merino base layer that will wick sweat away from your skin, or wear a half-zip top that you can use like a window—open it to dump heat quickly so you don’t get too clammy. Running vests are also good options for versatile layering.

You can apply the same concept to your hands. As the temperature gets too low for lightweight gloves, slip a mitten over top to boost your warmth and comfort. Modern materials even allow you to operate your smartphone or watch without taking your hands out of the mittens.

What about your head? If it’s cold, you’ll be cold. Unless you’re bald, you might find a hat to be too warm on any days when it’s not cold enough to snow. In that case, consider putting on a headband or Buff, which you can use to shield your dome from the cold wind relentlessly pounding your forehead.

Why should I wear winter running shoes in the winter?

Winterized shoes are definitely a great option to consider in the cold months for grip on slippery surfaces and a layer of added protection so your feet don’t go numb midrun, which could result in injury.

Some waterproof / weather-resistant running shoes have a different lug pattern and rubber outsole composite for increased traction on snow and ice. The waterproof upper also prevents saturation from running through snow, which keeps your feet from freezing.

What are signs I should look out for weather-wise when it comes to deciding what to wear?

This excellent guide about Running in Cold Weather presents a good rule of thumb before you head out for a workout when it’s below freezing so you don’t overheat:

Add 10 to 20 degrees to the temperature to determine how you should dress outside. For example, if it’s 30 degrees, dress for 40- to 50-degree weather

Short runs: dress for 10 to 15 degrees warmer

Long runs: dress for 20 degrees warmer since you’ll be out longer and have more risk of overheating

But, before you add to the outside temp, also consider Real Feel and windchill. You may need to layer more if it’s colder than the initial outside temperature.

#259. As a Bike Shop Manager, I’ve Seen Pre-Ride Bike Checks Go Wrong—Here’s 7 Ways to Get It Right

A shop-tested checklist for tires, brakes, drivetrain, bearings, and the timing that prevents last-minute panic.

I’ve spent a lot of time working in bike shops—one of the biggest mistakes I’ve seen people make before a big ride or event is to do a pre-ride bike check the day before their ride. When they’re going through the bike maybe they over-torque and break a bolt or maybe they realize one of their wheels is out of true and needs some attention. Either way one day is not enough time for a lot of shops to get something done—especially during peak season.

As I prepped my bike for UnPaved Pennsylvania, I thought about the checklist and timing I use to prepare for a big ride. Instead of running through the bike the day before a ride as a pre-ride check, run through it about a week to a week and a half out from your ride. This gives enough time to do a pre-bike check, test ride, then even gives a week to get some small service done at a local shop.

This checklist is how I work through my bike to make sure I’m ready to pedal to the finish. There are still things to do the day before your ride, but those things consist of making sure electronics are charged, bottles are filled, and nutrition is together (and I always check tire pressure right before rolling out). Coming from someone who has fielded a lot of shop calls on a Friday from people that have a race Saturday and need something done—go through the bike several days before you roll out.

Follow this step-by-step checklist for you to have confidence rolling into your next big ride this fall.

Place your bike in a repair stand. If the bike is just a little dusty, just give it a good wipe down with a rag. If it is truly dirty, remove both wheels and wash it thoroughly. Keep your eyes out for any cracks or frame issues while cleaning the bike. I know this is worst case scenario, but I’ve seen it happen before.

If the drivetrain is grimy, spray the bike chain and derailleurs with degreaser and let sit for a few minutes. Fill the bucket with warm, soapy water. Wet a sponge, hold it on the chain, and turn the crank to draw the chain through the sponge until the links are clean. Clean the crankset and derailleurs as well. Then clean the frame and parts (including the wheels) with a fresh sponge. Rinse by dripping water from above. (Don’t spray high-pressure water directly at the bike because this can force water into the bearings.) Dry the bike and all parts with clean rags.

If you spot a piece of debris lodged in your tire, try carefully picking it out. Inspect your bike tires for cracks, cuts, blisters, and baldness. Replace tires as needed.

Also, check tire seating. There are lines on the base of the sidewalls that should sit just above the rim all the way around. If they dip below the rim edge or rise above it, the tire is not seated properly. If you find any of these problems, deflate the tire and reinflate it, making sure that it seats correctly. Reinstall the wheels on the bike, making sure that they are centered in the frame and the quick-releases are properly tightened.

If you run tubeless, this is a good time to check sealant as well. Before a big ride (especially off-road) I tend to top off sealant because I’d rather have a little more than too little. The best way to check sealant is to remove the tire, check sealant, and reinstall the tire. Admittedly, I don’t always go this route. My quick check is to remove the wheel and shake it to check if I can feel the sealant sloshing around in the tire—you will likely be able to hear it in there as well. If you can’t hear anything, it’s worth taking off the tire to inspect and see if there’s a lot of dried sealant. If there is this can impact how well the sealant does what it’s supposed to: seal.

You want to check and snug chainring bolts from time to time. Though major components should not come loose during normal use, it is still wise to check them periodically. Without forcing, tighten crank bolts, pedals, chainring bolts, stem binder, handlebar binder, seat binder, seat bolt, brake and derailleur attaching nuts/bolts, and bottle cage screws. (Everything is turned clockwise to tighten except the left pedal, which is turned counterclockwise.)

Also, make sure all your repair gear is in proper working order, including a pump or CO2 inflator. This is a good time to check if your extra AXS battery is charged and check if your electronic pump is charged, if using those pieces of gear. Another key is to make sure your extra tube (bring an extra tube on a long ride) is in good working order.

Keeping your chain and other bike parts properly lubricated is critical to a properly functioning—not to mention quiet—bike. If they are not internally routed, lube your bike’s shifter cables where they pass under the bottom bracket. Lube the chain, then shift through the gears repeatedly to test derailleur adjustments.

Because the rear derailleur’s cable is longer and gets more use, it’s more likely to go out of adjustment. Each click of the rear shift lever should cause the bike chain to immediately jump to the next cog. If not, the cable has probably stretched slightly, or you may have mistakenly adjusted it too tight. If the chain hesitates to go to a larger cog, the cable is slightly loose. If the chain is slow in moving to a smaller cog, the cable is too tight. Fix slow shifts to larger cogs by turning the adjustment barrel on the rear of the derailleur counterclockwise in half-turn increments. For slow shifts to smaller cogs, do the opposite.

For electronic shifting systems, do the same test, running through both front and rear shifting to make sure everything is operating properly. If you do discover any problems, consult the appropriate troubleshooting manual for your components to help diagnose and remedy the problem. Adjusting electronic systems is typically much easier than traditional mechanical shifting drivetrains. In fact, as long as your battery is adequately charged, it’s unlikely you’ll have to do much adjusting at all. Just make sure you’re fully charged before the big ride. Without a charged battery, your electronic system will not work, and there are few things worse than being stuck in one gear all day.

If things are out of alignment and you can’t figure out why, it could be the derailleur hanger. This is one more reason to get this checklist done at least a week out from your big ride. If your hanger is out of alignment sometimes it can be bent back, but other times it needs to be replaced. If you have a universal derailleur hanger (UDH), then it is pretty accessible at most shops. Otherwise the part may have to be ordered. A derailleur hanger is one part I always like to have an extra one or two of at home that are specific to the bikes I have.

Disc brakes are being found on more and more modern bikes, especially hydraulic disc brakes. If your hydraulic disc brakes feel soft or your brake levers come all the way to the bars, then it’s likely time to call the local shop for a brake bleed. With that being said, there are still things you can check on these brakes at home. While the wheels are in the bike, spin the wheel to eye up the rotor—it can help to have a flashlight here. While the wheel is spinning, check if you hear the rotor hitting the brake pad. If it’s hitting, you will hear a noticeable noise, and you can confirm by shining the flashlight between the rotors and pads. If it’s rubbing, the rotor may need to be realigned, or the calipers may need to get reset. Once you check the rotor, then drop the wheel out to check the pads with the flashlight; there should be at least 1.5 mm of meat on the pads.

For rim brake pads, a small turn of your brake’s barrel adjuster will move your pads in or out. Inspect all four of your bike’s brake pads. If the grooves are worn away, it’s time to replace the pads. Make sure that they strike the rim squarely. If not, use an Allen wrench to loosen the nut that secures the pad and reposition it. Squeeze the brake levers to feel the action. The pads should strike the rim well before the levers approach the handlebar. If not, tighten the brake by turning the barrels on the brake calipers. If it’s one piece, turn it counterclockwise until the pads are 1/8- to 1/4-inch away from the rim.

When I’m checking out my brake pads, I will also typically eye up my wheel as it comes through the frame to see if the wheel is out of true. Using the frame as a bit of a guide, it’s easier to see if the wheel has any wobble. If it needs to be realigned and truing a wheel is outside your scope, then see if your local shop has the time to true a wheel before your big ride. This is one more reason why it’s important to run through your bike at least a week before your big ride.

Make sure there is no play in your headset by properly tightening the stem cap: Stand in front of the bike, holding the fork in one hand and the down tube in the other. Push and pull on the fork to check for any movement in the headset. Rotate the fork slowly from side to side to feel for roughness. If it’s loose or tight, loosen the stem bolts, then remove play or tightness by adjusting the Allen screw atop the stem, and finish by securing the stem bolts.

Now check the bottom bracket bearings: Stand beside the frame, hold the crank arms, and push and pull, feeling for play. Most bottom brackets are sealed and reliable. If yours is loose, have a shop remove the crank arms and adjust it.

Once you’ve run through all these steps, take your bike for a short test ride. Shift and brake repeatedly, making adjustments as necessary. Very consciously listen for any rattles or other unwanted noises while you ride. I even like to wear my exact kit I’ll be wearing on the upcoming ride to make sure everything is tested together. Now you’re ready for your big ride—confident that as long as your body cooperates, there is nothing to prevent you from successfully getting to the finish line.

Keep in mind shops can sometimes squeeze in a wheel true, pad swap, or chain replacement throughout the course of a few days, but that doesn’t mean they can also do a full tune-up on the bike while it’s there. I used to let customers know that we would do our best to squeeze the smaller services in before an event, but come back afterward for a full tune-up. This also ensures your bike gets the love it needs after your big ride.

#260. Why Are People Taking CoQ10 Supplements for Longevity, and Do They Work?

Coenzyme Q10, or CoQ10, was once a niche supplement, known best in wellness circles for its possible benefits for heart health and fertility. But now the antioxidant’s star is rising for a new reason: its purported longevity-boosting powers.

The appeal of CoQ10 has grown as researchers have explored its effects on various conditions, with small studies revealing, for example, it may help boost insulin sensitivity, cut the frequency of migraine attacks, and alleviate muscle aches from statins used for high cholesterol. But as of late, there’s excitement around its broader anti-aging potential because of how it supports our mitochondria, which you may remember from high school biology as the “powerhouse of the cell.”

That role has punched CoQ10’s ticket into the longevity club, alongside other supplements thought to lend a hand to mitochondria (like urolithin A and nicotinamide mononucleotide, or NMN). There’s even a synthetic derivative of CoQ10 designed specifically for better absorption by mitochondria, which is called mitoquinone (or MitoQ), that’s gaining hype among celeb trainers and athletes for boosting energy, recovery, and “cellular health.”

But is CoQ10 all it’s cracked up to be when it comes to longevity? Read on to learn more before grabbing a bottle of this supplement.

Our cells naturally produce CoQ10, a molecule that acts like a conveyor belt for charged particles inside our mitochondria, enabling them to “efficiently create adenosine triphosphate, or ATP,” the “currency for cellular energy,” Anthony Molina, PhD, a professor of medicine at UC San Diego who studies aging biomarkers, tells SELF. That’s a big deal, as all cells rely on that energy to complete their daily functions. As we age, both the number and energy-producing powers of mitochondria drop off—a process involved in the development of many age-related diseases, Dr. Molina points out. Meanwhile, CoQ10 levels also decline with age, leading to the idea that we should take it in supplement form for better mitochondrial (and, in turn, overall) health.

Beyond its role in energy production, CoQ10 is also an antioxidant that is “very powerful in capturing free radicals,” or volatile molecules that can harm cells, Daria Mochly-Rosen, PhD, a professor of chemical and systems biology at Stanford University and coauthor of The Life Machines: How Taking Care of Your Mitochondria Can Transform Your Health, tells SELF. By stabilizing those molecules, CoQ10 may help to keep that damage (a.k.a. oxidative stress) from piling up and also contributing to aging and the development of chronic disease.

Separately, CoQ10 has potential benefits as it relates to cardiovascular health: It’s anti-inflammatory and may also improve the function of blood vessels, helping regulate blood pressure, JoAnn E. Manson, MD, DrPH, chief of the division of preventive medicine at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and professor of Medicine at Harvard Medical School, tells SELF. These upsides could lower risk for heart disease, the number-one killer in the US.

Despite the promising mechanisms above, “the evidence base just isn’t yet there,” Dr. Manson says. The studies we do have on CoQ10 and longevity are in mice and rats—and while a few suggest a lifespan-extending effect, or a way to reverse some cognitive decline once it starts, others show no anti-aging upsides in healthy animals. Besides, “we find again and again that humans are not just large, non-hairy mice,” Dr. Mochly-Rosen points out, “so we can’t assume the results transfer.”

Studies in people have been focused on CoQ10 as an intervention for specific diseases, particularly cardiovascular ones. All the experts say the strongest evidence for longevity is in those with heart failure, who have low CoQ10 levels—taking the supplement alongside standard treatment has been shown to reduce the need for hospitalization and risk of early death, possibly because of its mitochondrial perks.

But logistically, it’s a lot trickier to prove that CoQ10 prolongs life in healthy people versus in those with a medical condition or known CoQ10 deficiency. In the absence of these studies, it might be tempting to take a logical leap: If we know CoQ10 supports mitochondrial function, and levels of both dip with age and disease, supplementing with CoQ10 seems like it should help you live longer. But the problem is, we don’t know exactly what drives the mitochondrial issues that occur with age, Dr. Molina says. “So maybe you’re not taking a shot in the dark because we know that mitochondria has something to do with healthy aging, but using CoQ10 as the tool is like taking a shot in a dimly lit room,” he says. “It’s not clear whether you’re hitting the right target.”

As with any supplement, it’s best to ask your doctor before adding CoQ10 to your routine. While there’s a good deal of data to suggest it’s safe and well-tolerated, there are some people who shouldn’t take it, generally because of interactions with prescription drugs, Dr. Molina points out. The main concern is with blood thinners (a.k.a. anticoagulants) like warfarin (which are often prescribed after a blood clot)—CoQ10 could make these drugs less effective, Dr. Manson says. It’s also extra important to check in with your doctor first if you take insulin or are receiving treatment for cancer. Though CoQ10 doesn’t usually cause side effects, you could also wind up with some mild GI upset or insomnia, Dr. Manson adds.

There’s also the quality-control problem that comes with any supplement. These are not subjected to the same FDA regulations as medications are, meaning you can’t know for sure that you’re getting what the bottle promises. Studies of certain CoQ10 supplements have found that they contained less of the antioxidant than the amount listed on the label, Dr. Mochly-Rosen notes. Your best defense against winding up with a sugar pill is to find a product that’s been third-party verified, she says—look for the “NSF certified” or “USP verified” stamp.

#262. Nip Slip? The Ultimate Guide to Inverted Nipples

Inverted nipples face inward rather than outward. Though usually harmless, it’s best to check with a healthcare professional to get shy nips the all-clear.

Nipples come in all shapes, including inverted ones. If yours are more like innies than outies, you’re not alone! Inverted nipples, also known as retracted or invaginated, are common and usually harmless.

Nipples can range from popping out when stimulated to constantly staying retracted. While usually harmless, knowing the causes and potential treatments is wise, especially if there’s discomfort. Keep reading to learn more!

Inverted nipples mean your chest cherries retract inward instead of protruding outward. They can be a genetic gift or something that happens over time.

Often, they’re just doing their own thing, but understanding the different grades can help you know if action is warranted.

Nipple inversion comes in three grades, according to the level of drama. Let’s break it down so you know what’s going on with those inward-facing nips.

Grade 1 inverted nipples are like the shy party guests who need a little encouragement to join the fun. They can pop out with stimulation, like a chilly breeze or a gentle touch.

These are the least inverted and usually don’t cause any trouble.

Grade 2 inverted nipples are a bit more stubborn. They can be coaxed out with some effort, but they’re quick to retreat. They might need a bit more attention, mainly if they cause discomfort or issues with breastfeeding.

Grade 3 inverted nipples are the ultimate homebodies. They’re fully retracted and rarely, if ever, make an appearance. These are the most inverted and might need surgical intervention if they’re causing any issues.

So, why do some nipples decide to turn inward instead of standing out proudly? There are a few reasons this might happen:

Sometimes, you’re born with inverted nipples. Doctors call this congenital inversion.

If your parents or siblings have inverted nipples, there’s a higher chance you might too. It’s like inheriting your mom’s eye color or your dad’s knack for bad jokes — genetics is a big player.

For some new parents, the process of chestfeeding can lead to changes in breast tissue that cause nipple inversion. Your boobs are trying to adjust to their new role, and sometimes, things get a little flipped around!

While this can be temporary, it may also stick around long term.

There are a few other culprits that can cause nipples to go inward. These include:

Remember, if your nipples decide to play hide-and-seek and it’s out of the blue, a quick chat with a healthcare professional is always wise to make sure everything’s A-OK. And if there’s pain, nipple discharge, itchy nipples, or bleeding nipples, do so sooner rather than later.

Several options are available for treating nipple inversion:

Gentle manipulation and massage with your fingers can temporarily draw out the nipple.

While this method can help with mild cases (Grade 1), it often provides short-lasting results and needs to be repeated regularly.

Useful for chestfeeding peeps! Nipple shields are soft, silicone covers that fit over the nipple and help coax the nipples outward, making nursing easier.

They provide gentle and continuous pressure that encourages the nipple to protrude.

These devices create a vacuum around the nipple, gently drawing it out gradually. They can be worn for several hours a day over weeks or months to achieve the desired result.

For more severe cases (Grade 2 and 3), a minor surgical procedure can permanently correct nipple inversion.

It involves making small incisions at the nipple’s base to release the tight tissue pulling inward. It’s usually done under local anesthesia and has a quick recovery time.

If they aren’t causing problems, there’s no medical reason to fix them. It’s a personal choice based on comfort and aesthetics.

Grade 1 and sometimes Grade 2 nipples can pop out with stimulation. Grade 3 nipples typically don’t. They’re super shy!

Yes, inverted nipples can be inherited. If family members have them, you might have them, too.

Inverted nipples are a common and typically harmless condition. They could run in the family, show up after breastfeeding, or result from an injury or infection.

Often, they need no treatment. But if they cause issues or occur suddenly, it’s wise to check with a healthcare professional.

#264. Apple Watch Ultra 4 Review: Is It the Best Watch for Most Runners? Maybe.

Apple finally built an Ultra that fixes the things that bugged me about its predecessor. It’s still not a Garmin, and that’s okay.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

I’ve worn a lot of watches on a lot of long runs. In fact, I’ve tested nearly every running watch from every major brand from Garmin to Samsung to Coros to Suunto. When a new flagship arrives, I’m not looking for what the brand tells me or what it reads like on a spec sheet. I want to see how the dang thing works on my wrist, and what it tells me about my body on a random Monday morning run.

After weeks with the Apple Watch Ultra 4, here’s my short answer: this is a vast improvement over the Ultra 3. It isn’t flawless, and I’ll get specific about where it falls short. But for a huge number of runners, it’s the best watch you can buy.

Generational upgrades are often a polish job. This one isn’t. There are four main improvements that impressed me, and each one changed how I used and viewed the watch day to day:

🔋 Battery life and charging speed. Battery life used to suck, and charging was meh at best. That’s no longer the case.

🫀 The heart rate sensor. They’ve completely redesigned it from soup to nuts and it’s loads better.

⚠️ ECG and hypertension alerts. The health suite feels more mature and more useful when combined with the improved health app.

📍 GPS acquisition. The Ultra 3 made you wait, and sometimes the signal never found you. The 4 gets the connection.

I’ll take these upgrades in turn, starting with the one that affects you the most as a runner.

If you’ve ever stood on a cold sidewalk waving your wrist at the sky, you know the particular misery of a watch that can’t find satellites. The Ultra 3 was fine on this front, but “fine” included enough hesitation that I’d often start my run before it had locked on. Apple tells me that there’s been no change, but whether it’s the system or the updates, it has improved.

The Ultra 4 connects fast. I press start, glance down, and it’s ready. Over weeks of runs in open parks, tree-lined streets, and between tall buildings, I didn’t feel delayed or annoyed with the pace of the connections. I want a watch that’s ready when I am, and now this is that watch.

Now the first caveat. Once the Ultra 4 locks on, it’s consistent, but it’s consistently off. Across my testing, the watch measured the distance 1 to 1.5 percent long. During a marathon, that’s a few tenths of a mile of ghost distance. On a casual 5K, or a simple run and go, you won’t notice or care. (And hey, more distance on Strava, am I right?) On a tempo run where you’re chasing a specific pace, or when you’re testing your distance mettle, you might.

The heart rate sensor is where this watch made the biggest leap over the Ultra 3, and also where I have the most nuanced thoughts. I tested it against an external EKG/Holter monitor, which is a much stricter standard than a typical chest strap comparison. (I do not have this specifically for testing. I have this because my heart—though strong AF—sometimes likes to do a little jig or tempo work of its own when I shift my meds.)

👍 During steady workouts, walking, and easy jogging, the Ultra 4 was excellent. It stayed within two to three beats per minute of the Holter. That’s remarkable for a wrist-based optical sensor, and simply put, throughout the day, I’m trusting it.

👎 When I ran harder, the gap widened. The difference between the watch and the Holter grew to between five and seven beats per minute. It’s not catastrophic in terms of variability, and it’s a clear improvement on what I saw from the Ultra 3. But it’s noticeable, and if you train by heart rate zones, it can nudge you into the wrong zone at the margins. But honestly, if you’re doing HR training, you should grab a chest strap. Compared with the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro, which even during hard runs was only off between three and six beats per minute, it was a bit disappointing.

Part of the story is sampling rate. Throughout the day, the Apple Watch records your heart rate roughly every five seconds. The Garmin records it every single second.

Over time, that gap matters. When you’re tracking heart rate variability and recovery trends across weeks and months, a denser stream of data gives you a cleaner picture. Five-second sampling means more smoothing, and smoothing can hide the small spikes and dips that tell you how you’re truly recovering or truly struggling.

Battery anxiety has defined the Apple Watch for years, and the Ultra line was supposed to solve it. The Ultra 3 improved things—a little. The Ultra 4 actually has good battery life, undersold even by Apple’s spec sheet, and just as important, it charges extremely fast. They say you can get two full days in GPS mode. In testing, I ran this thing like I was running for a few days for every minute I wasn’t asleep. In that level of heavy use, I can get three days out of this.

The ECG on the Ultra 4 is noticeably improved over the Ultra 3, and the hypertension alert is seriously nifty. I don’t want to overstate this. These are screening tools, not diagnoses, and they’re not a replacement for a doctor. But for a runner who’s logging the over-90-mile weeks that I do, an early nudge that something’s off in your cardiovascular system is worth a lot. The mechanisms haven’t changed, but the health app and integrated systems is easier and everything makes more sense.

As someone who unfortunately menstruates, I’ve found the cycle insights on this watch are freaking spot on. Whether you’re trying to conceive, trying not to, or trying to figure out how perimenopause is affecting your body, the data and the way it’s presented give a lot of clarity and help, especially when you’re training for a marathon, and the red tent looms.

Now for the part where I give the Garmin its due. The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is not a dedicated running watch, and it doesn’t pretend to be.

I’m missing lactate threshold and some other running metrics available on Garmin, and to get deeper insights, you have to go into the fitness app to find those, which feels strange when you can get to everything else in the Health app.

Also, offline mapping isn’t straightforward or easy. Apple Watches are truly designed to be used either with your phone, or connected to cellular. It does have satellite connectivity for emergencies when you’re out of range, though, and it’s simpler to use than the Garmin satellite comms.

There’s one metric I think a lot of runners would genuinely miss, and that’s lactate threshold. Garmin has it. Apple still does not.

Lactate threshold is the pace or heart rate at which your body starts accumulating fatigue faster than it can clear it. Knowing your own lactate threshold is incredibly useful when you're training for distance. It tells you how hard you can push in a tempo run, helps you set meaningful zones, and shows how your fitness is changing over a training block.

Here’s where the Ultra 4 runs away from the competition: The smartwatch experience is the foundation.

Transit pay is seamless. I tap my wrist at a turnstile and walk right through, with no phone, no card fumbling, no button pushing. The same goes for my digital ID card for work.

The app ecosystem is unmatched. You simply will not find a better app system on any running watch. Apple knows what it’s doing here. Every workout app I use connected perfectly and worked the way I expected.

The phone integration is a delight. I can open my phone, write and send text messages, make calls, and change my music, all from my wrist. When I’m running, I don’t need to dig for my phone or break my stride to skip a track.

It’s heavy. Compared with a dedicated running watch, the Ultra 4 feels like a brick. For short runs it’s fine. On long runs, I lowkey wanted to throw it off my wrist until I got used to it. For ultra-distance running, I noped out and took it off.

The shape. This one’s personal, and your thoughts may vary. I’d love to see Apple offer a different form factor. The Ultra’s rugged, squared-off look works for some wrists and not for others, and a slimmer, more rounded option would suit a lot of runners better.

If I were starting out as a runner, I’d choose this watch without hesitation. The same goes for a runner who leans into an integrated, connected life and wants simplicity and straightforward use. The setup is easy, the interface makes sense, and the health features are impressive and easy to use. You don’t need a manual or a run coach to get a lot out of it.

Who should look elsewhere? Ultrarunners, and anyone who trains seriously by heart rate zones at high intensity or relies on advanced running dynamics, will still find the Garmin a better fit. The Fenix 9 Pro’s tighter heart rate accuracy at speed, one-second sampling, and lactate threshold are real advantages for that crowd. Not to mention that extra distance you’re getting in the Garmin which you don’t get from AWU4. (And again, the weight of the watch.)

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is a vast improvement over the Ultra 3, and not just in one area. Better battery life with very fast charging, a stronger heart rate sensor, improved ECG and hypertension alerts, and faster GPS all come together into a watch that simply makes it a better watch overall.

It isn’t perfect. Distance runs consistently 1 to 1.5 percent long. Heart rate accuracy drifts to five to seven beats per minute off during hard running, and the five-second sampling can limit how useful your HRV and recovery data is over time. It’s heavier than I’d like and short on the deeper running metrics, with lactate threshold the one I’d really push Apple to add.

#265. What Is ‘Fiber Training’—And Why Should You Be Doing It?

With the fibermaxxing fad encouraging people to prioritize this chronically neglected nutrient, one issue keeps coming up: the side effects. As important as hitting your daily fiber goal is, your body doesn’t always make doing so easy. Fiber is difficult for your digestive system to break down and has to be handed off to bacteria in the colon instead (which is kind of its point), so piling on too much too fast can result in a barrage of painful, awkward, or inconvenient digestive symptoms—bloating, gas, stomach cramps, the whole nine yards.

To be clear, GI distress isn’t a sign to abandon your pursuit of a higher-fiber diet. “Even with fiber becoming a growing trend, people still greatly underestimate its importance and, also, just how many ways it benefits the human body,” Desiree Nielsen, RD, a recipe developer with a focus on plant-based nutrition, tells SELF. You’re probably familiar with fiber’s ability to keep you full, stave off constipation, and support gut health, but it wears plenty of other hats too, like lowering “bad” LDL cholesterol and stabilizing your blood sugar (not to mention reducing your risk for a slew of diseases in the long run). In fact, overlooking fiber is one of the top nutrition mistakes people make, according to experts.

But if you feel apprehensive at the thought of fighting constant stomach discomfort in the process of working to correct a fiber deficiency, we don’t blame you. In fact, it’s a complaint that Lisa Ganjhu, DO, a gastroenterologist at NYU Langone Health, hears all the time at work: “I have a lot of patients that will say ‘I ate more fiber, and now I’m really bloated and crampy,’” she says. Thankfully, there’s a way to curtail those disagreeable side effects so you can (comfortably) continue your fiber journey: a strategy Nielsen calls fiber training. Here’s what that involves, and how to start developing those “muscles.”

Fiber training is exactly what it sounds like: training your body to handle fiber better. It’s all about “slow, consistent increases in fiber to help you build your tolerance…while minimizing the potential symptoms,” Nielsen says.

You can think of fiber training kind of like preparing for a race. “In much the same way that you wouldn’t go out and run a marathon tomorrow if you haven’t run a mile before,” you need to work your way up to a high-fiber diet, Nielsen says. Similarly, Dr. Ganjhu compares it to a weightlifting regimen. Rather than lifting 50-pound weights right off the bat, “you kind of have to adjust slowly,” she says. “You start off with 10. When that becomes easy, you go to 20, then you go to 30”—and so on.

Fiber training is especially critical if you’re constipated at the outset, as many people are, according to Nielsen. Even though fiber can help prevent and alleviate constipation, too much at once can actually make an existing issue worse by overwhelming your gut. “When you add a ton of fiber to an already backed-up system, it’s kind of like a bottleneck on the highway,” Nielsen says: If you try to shoehorn four lanes into one, you’re going to end up with a jam on your hands.

Now that you know fiber training entails steadily increasing your fiber intake, you’re probably wondering what that looks like on a more practical level. Before we share specifics, some context for how much fiber you actually need might be helpful. Per the federal Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020-2025, women should aim for 28 grams of fiber daily from ages 19 to 30, 25 grams of fiber daily from ages 31 to 50, and 22 grams of fiber daily starting at age 51, though some experts recommend even more—a helpful set of parameters if you’re not sure where to start.

While the ideal amount of fiber to add to your diet while fiber training can vary from person to person depending on health needs (like a constipation issue), most people are “looking at [adding] probably three to five grams at a time,” Nielsen says.

With that in mind, you’ll want to choose a food that has a fiber content in that ballpark—say, an apple (around four grams of fiber), a half-cup of chickpeas (around five grams of fiber), a tablespoon of chia seeds (around five grams of fiber), or two tablespoons of ground flax (around four grams of fiber)—and eat a serving every single day until you feel like your body has adjusted (read: you’re not experiencing any additional bloating, gas, or other GI side effects). This process typically takes around five to seven days, according to Nielsen, but everyone’s digestive system is different, so don’t worry if you need more (or less!) time. “It really is about listening to your body and individualizing the rate at which you increase,” Nielsen says. “You have to follow your symptoms and go slow,” Dr. Ganjhu agrees.

Then, you can tack on another dose—like a second apple, a full cup of chickpeas, two tablespoons of chia seeds, or four tablespoons of ground flax. Continue increasing your fiber intake in these increments (and at this pace) until you’ve hit your daily fiber goal. If you’re a 35-year-old woman starting from scratch, reaching 25 grams of fiber—the recommended daily amount for that age—would take around five five-gram doses, six four-gram doses, or eight three-gram doses, for example.

People who are constipated may want to specifically fiber train with foods that are low in FODMAPs—fermentable carbohydrates particularly hard on sensitive stomachs—according to Nielsen. Like we said above, increasing your fiber intake when you’re backed up can, well, backfire, so low-FODMAP foods are more likely to be a safe bet than their high-FODMAP counterparts. Kiwis, which contain four grams of fiber in a two-fruit serving, are an especially strong option if you fall into this category (and they’ve even been specifically studied as a dietary constipation treatment), Nielsen says. Similarly, she adds, a gentle fiber supplement like Metamucil, which is made from psyllium husk, also “provides a lot of the benefits, but tends to be less irritating to a troubled system.”

Another tip: If you’re constipated, make sure to drink plenty of water as well (though the oft-referenced eight-glasses-a-day requirement is something of a myth!). Because fiber needs water to work its stool-softening magic, insufficient fluids could leave your bowel movements hard and dry, exacerbating the problem.

Whatever new fiber sources you choose, taking this slow-and-steady approach should help ease the transition to a higher intake. “If you’re someone who doesn’t eat a lot of fiber and all of a sudden you start eating 30 grams of it, the colon is just not going to know how to manage that efficiently,” Dr. Ganjhu says. But by leveling up little by little? You can heighten that “colonic fitness”—and sidestep the worst of the awkward stage.

#266. Editor-Tested Cycling Gear Is On Sale for Amazon’s Prime Big Deals Days

Upgrade your fall rides with early deals on cycling apparel, accessories, helmets, tires, radar, and more for Prime Big Deal Days.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Autumn is our favorite riding season. It means crisp mornings, pleasant afternoons, and seeing lots of great foliage. Whether you’re riding on pavement, gravel roads, singletrack trails, or your local bike paths, your bike and gear probably need some upgrades after a full summer of riding.

For Amazon’s Prime Big Deals Days on October 6 and 7, top cycling brands are offering great deals on clothing and accessories, including best-tested items from Bicycling’s gear team. In addition to the big Prime Day deals, REI, bike brands, and other retailers are offering deep discounts on cycling equipment, components, apparel, and accessories you need for your autumn rides.

Prime Day sales are a great chance to stock up on frequently used consumables—such as tubes, tire sealant, chain lube, and nutrition products—and for grabbing the gear you need for fall rides. They’re also a great way to save money on usually pricey fall riding apparel: If you’ve been holding out on buying a new vest, arm warmers, jerseys, a jacket, or even shoes, some brands are offering deep discounts on cycling clothing and accessories.

Below are sales and deals hubs for several top online cycling gear and bike retailers, plus links to sales from leading clothing brands and bike companies. These are some of the best deals on editor-tested gear we’ve spotted so far. Bookmark this page and return for updates as even more deals come online.

➜ AMAZON ➜ REI ➜ BACKCOUNTRY ➜ COMPETITIVE CYCLIST ➜ CAPO ➜ ORNOT ➜ WAHOO ➜ SPECIALIZED ➜ CANNONDALE ➜ LECTRIC E-BIKE ➜ VELOTRIC E-BIKE

Electric mini-inflators burst onto the scene a couple of years ago and have quickly become a rider favorite for pumping up your tires at home, at the trailhead, or on rides. Of the inflators we’ve used, Cycplus’ AS2 Ultra is our top-tested pick and a favorite of Bicycling editors. It’s compact, lightweight, and has an accurate gauge. In our testing of 11 electric pumps, it inflated a road tire to 65 psi in under 43 seconds, and filled four tires before running out of power.

Stainless bottles have become popular among cyclists over the past several seasons. They keep water chilled on hot rides and don’t give your water a funny plastic taste. CamelBak’s Stainless Podium is loved by many gravel and off-road riders, particularly with its open/closed twist-lock cap. The Podium Stainless also came out on top in our heat testing last summer.

Elite road and gravel helmets offer low weight, excellent ventilation, and great looks. However, those benefits usually come at a high cost. Giro’s Agilis Mips helmet is a great option if you want a pro-level look and performance without the associated price

Weighing 299 grams (size medium), my Agilis is only 15 grams heavier than Giro’s premium Aries Spherical model—and the Agilis costs significantly less. The Agilis is very well-ventilated, comparable to the priciest lids on all but the hottest of rides.

This helmet features Mips technology to protect your brain from rotational forces in a crash, and Giro’s Hardbody co-molded shell to better protect it from small bumps and dings when not on your head. Plus, the Agilis is equipped with the Roc-Loc dial system to ensure a proper fit.

Arm warmers are among the most versatile pieces of cycling clothing you can own. This magical piece of kit turns your short-sleeve jersey into a long-sleeve in seconds—and you can change back to short sleeves again mid-ride if the temps rise.

I’ve owned many pairs of arm warmers over the last three decades, and I rarely ride without them on my arms or in my jersey pocket during the autumn months. Assos makes some of the best clothes out there, and the Evo arm warmers are a steal for the price. They’re easy to pull on or off while riding, and they don’t sag.

The best, quickest way to improve your bike’s comfort, speed, and control is to swap out old or stock tires. Vittoria’s Corsa Pro road tires are among the fastest and most compliant tires you can find. They’re available in widths from 24mm to 32mm and feature a cotton, tubeless-compatible casing that sets up easily.

Cycling radar has improved my road riding experience more in the last year than any other product. These devices detect and track vehicles approaching from behind and give you a little warning to react. However, our extensive ride testing has shown that not all cycling radars perform as advertised. This is particularly true of low-cost units.

Garmin’s Varia RTL515 is our benchmark cycling radar. It consistently detects and tracks vehicles and rarely signals “ghost cars” (false-positive results) when no cars are actually present. This reliability helps us trust it more than other similarly priced radar systems.

Modern bike computers do much more than display speed and distance. These devices are a critical information hub for many cyclists. Cycling computers can record ride metrics, display real-time performance data, and help you navigate—but that’s only scratching the surface of their capabilities.

The Elemnt Bolt 3 is Wahoo’s tiny-but-mighty cycling-specific computer. Wahoo equips it with a 2.3-inch high-resolution screen, up to 20 hours of battery life, and integration with Strava, Komoot, and other popular cycling platforms.

Another great option is the Hammerhead Karoo. This head unit features a 3.2-inch color touchscreen Gorilla Glass display and up to 35 hours of run time. The Karoo stands out for its mapping and navigation. The navigation, combined with its pop-up hill climb feature and ability to sideload apps, it makes the Karoo my overall favorite.

Putting your bike in your car is a hassle; it takes up passenger or storage space, and you often need to remove one or both wheels to fit it inside. Roof racks are an option, but they require lifting your bike overhead, which can be awkward on many SUVs. Additionally, roof racks decrease gas mileage and can pose clearance issues with garages, overpasses, and tree limbs. Trunk racks are another solution, but they don’t fit every vehicle and usually cannot accommodate heavy bikes.

This makes hitch racks the best solution for safely transporting your bike. Our favorite Cheap Hitch Rack is the Swagman XTC2. This rack holds two bikes (up to 35 pounds each) with wheel sizes from 20 to 29 inches, and it fits both 1¼-inch and 2-inch receiver tubes. The XTC2 is lightweight, durable, and very reasonably priced. If you’re willing to trade a bit of convenience for significant savings, the Swagman XTC2 is a reliable and practical option.

Bib shorts are great for long road and gravel rides. They don’t sag, and the bib straps keep them from floating around underneath you. Cargo bibs take it up a notch; the Endura Alltrack adds pockets on the thighs and lower back. They’re handy for carrying snacks, your phone, or extra layers.

Scottish brand Endura makes some excellent cycling clothing—like these Alltrack bib shorts—that combine performance and durability at a reasonable price.

POC makes comfortable, well-ventilated helmets for road, gravel, and mountain biking. The Kortal is a trail-style helmet, featuring an adjustable visor, room to stow your glasses or goggles, and plenty of airflow for hot summer trail rides. The straps are also comfortable, something that often bugs me on other lids.

Fresh bar tape is the quickest and most cost-effective way to improve the look, feel, and comfort of any road or gravel bike. I’ve used Fizik tape on several bikes that have come in for testing, and have also bought it for my personal bikes. It has enough cushion, reliable grip, and is easy to wrap. You can’t ask for much more from bar tape.

While many riders are adding electric mini-inflators to their tool kits, a quality floor pump remains an essential part of every cyclist’s arsenal. They never run out of batteries, pump as many tires as your arms can handle, and are easy to use.

Riders and mechanics have trusted Topeak’s JoeBlow pumps for decades—because they work. Although many JoeBlow models are low-cost and utilitarian, the JoeBlow Ace DX is a Cadillac-level floor pump. It features alloy construction with a metal chuck and can inflate tires up to 260 psi, with three different inflation modes: high-volume, standard, or high-pressure.

TPU tubes are a great way to save weight, and they’re also faster than traditional butyl inner tubes. In his story, “The Best Bang for Your Buck Upgrade Is Not What You Think,” Test Editor Dan Chabanov explains why a simple swap can save you watts:

The more complex and impactful way Latex and TPU tubes improve performance is by lowering the bike's rolling resistance, which comes from internal friction or energy loss due to hysteresis. Latex and TPU tubes are made from thinner and more flexible material than butyl tubes, which allows them to better deform to road imperfections and give up less energy. This means that with constant effort from the rider, a bike with better tubes will roll faster than one with standard butyl inner tubes.

#267. L-Tyrosine Supplements: Benefits for Your Brain and Body

L-tyrosine is an amino acid (AKA protein building block) that supports your body, from your muscles to your noggin.

It’s a non-essential amino acid, which means your body can make it on its own, so you don’t have to get it from food

That being said, consuming foods high in L-tyrosine or taking supplements could have extra cognitive and physical benefits – here’s what to know.

L-tyrosine is an amino acid that the body produces naturally. Though your bod can prob create enough of the stuff on its own, some research suggests that supplementing with it can boost your mood and help regulate your stress response.

L-tyrosine helps make many vital chemical messengers, such as:

Supplementing with L-tyrosine is believed by some to boost levels of dopamine, adrenalin, and norepinephrine in particular.

Foods naturally high in tyrosine include:

L-tyrosine may improve your memory and mental alertness. Since L-tyrosine increases dopamine availability in your body, experts think it may boost your cognitive performance. In addition to reward centers, dopamine is linked to working memory processes and plays a key role in the brain’s aging process.

In a 2019 review of several studies, researchers found that a higher intake of L-tyrosine was linked to improved cognition. It also improved executive functions like brain flexibility, convergent thinking, and reasoning.

However, researchers noted that L-tyrosine is most effective when dopamine and norepinephrine levels are reduced (which basically means when you feel stressed AF).

Some L-tyrosine supplement companies claim that their products are both mood boosters and antidepressants, but the results are mixed.

L-tyrosine increases dopamine, the feel-good hormone that’s linked to reward processing and also addiction. In general, it’s been shown to be a vital regulator of mood, behavior, and brainpower – so it makes sense that getting enough of it could benefit your mood, too.

However, the research on supplementation of tyrosine for depression is super dated, so it’s challenging to draw any definitive conclusions RN. (Plus, depression is also a super complex condition that involves more than just dopamine depletion.)

And though there are some people dubbing L-tyrosine “natural Adderall” for its purported beneficial effect on ADHD, so far, there’s no research to support these claims yet, either. (Though it *is* true that there seems to be a link between ADHD and altered dopamine levels.)

Phenylketonuria is a rare genetic disorder in which the body can’t properly process another essential amino acid, phenylalanine.

Since those with the disorder may also be deficient in L-tyrosine, some experts think that supplementing with it could help relieve some symptoms like seizures or skin rashes.

However, according to a 2021 review of several studies, there is not enough evidence to say for sure.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) considers taking L-tyrosine supplements generally safe.

That being said, it’s not recommended to mix with the following medications:

It’s not advisable to take it if you’re pregnant or breastfeeding.

Research suggests that L-tyrosine supplementation likely benefits your brainpower under stress. It also may benefit conditions like depression, but more research is needed to know for sure.

Like any supplement, it is a good idea to contact your healthcare provider before adding it to your medicine cabinet, especially if you have preexisting health conditions or take medications.

#269. The Fastest Pro Bikes at the 2026 Ironman World Championship in Kona

Gregory Barnaby rode a Pinarello Bolide TR9 and Taylor Knibb rode a Trek Speed Concept SLR 9 on their ways to the fastest bike splits of the 2026 Ironman World Championship. (Photo: Brad Kaminski/Triathlete)

For the first time since 2019, the men and women shared the Queen K on the same day. With the draft zone finally stretched to 20 meters in Kona, riders who could hold big watts were rewarded. The roads were wet early before the heat and humidity cranked up, and the women’s times ran slower than last year (American Taylor Knibb’s 4:40:06 was roughly nine minutes off her 2025 ride).

Like always, we only count athletes who made it to the finish line. That means you won’t see Magnus Ditlev (DNK), who led into T2 after a 4:06:47 split before his DNF, or Great Britain’s Lucy Charles-Barclay (4:45:12), whose day ended on the run. Penalties also baked some extra time into a few splits: Gustav Iden (NOR), Matthew Marquardt (USA), Julie Derron (CHE), and Regan Hollioake (AUS) each served three minutes in the box.

The biggest gear story was up front. All 10 of the fastest men raced 1x drivetrains. SRAM Red, Shimano Dura-Ace, and even a Vision setup. The women went the other way: Eight of the top 10 stuck with a front derailleur, including the winner, and only Laura Philipp (DEU) and Hollioake went 1x.

Wheels followed the usual Kona theme: deep rear, slightly shallower front, but trispokes were everywhere. Princeton, Evolve, Black Inc, and Parcours all had one under a top 10 rider, and three riders (Belgian Marten Van Riel, German Frederic Funk, and Austrian Lisa Perterer) rolled the massive HED Jet 180 out back.

And a shout-out to Marquardt: his 4:11:27 included a three-minute stop in the Waikoloa penalty tent, and he still rode within five seconds of the day’s fastest split.

Barnaby debuted a brand-new Pinarello Bolide TR9 on the eve of the race and promptly went out and posted the fastest bike split among finishers on it. He rode a 1x Shimano Dura-Ace Di2 drivetrain with a custom aero chainring, DT Swiss ARC 1100 80 wheels front and rear on Vittoria Corsa Pro tires, and MOST aerobars. One bottle between the arms, one behind the saddle, and a Rudy Project TT helmet rounded it out. Nothing beats that new bike feeling, unless of course, it is new and you’re riding it to the fastest bike split in Kona!

Marquardt’s Speed Concept was the most meaningful bike in the race: custom dark red paint covered in dozens of small white initials, each one for a friend, family member, or fan affected by cancer. (Marquardt is also in medical school and raced in a kit featuring The James, Ohio State’s cancer center, prominently.) He ran a SRAM Red 1x drivetrain with an aero chainring, Princeton CarbonWorks trispokes rear, Mach 7580 front, a molded one-piece armrest cockpit, and a MET TT helmet. Oh, and he built a behind-the-saddle bottle mount out of LEGOs (it stayed home on race day). Even with a three-minute stop at Waikoloa, he came off the bike in third and held on for the podium.

Thompson rode the Factor ONE SP. We saw this bike at Nice for the 70.3 Worlds and it is basically Factor’s ONE road platform with a purpose-built TT front end. Thompson used a SRAM Red 1x drivetrain. Factor’s in-house wheel brand handled the rest: a Black Inc Three trispoke up front and a Hyper 62 in the back.

The second Bolide TR9 in the top four belonged to Wurf, who swam 41st and rode himself all the way up to 13th on the road by T2. His bike matched Barnaby’s paint but not his parts: Princeton CarbonWorks trispokes front and rear, Continental Grand Prix 5000 TT tires, a 1x Shimano Dura-Ace drivetrain with a carbon aero chainring, MOST aerobars, and TriRig mounts between the arms and behind the saddle.

Long had the biggest bike move of the day, going from 42nd out of the water to 12th by T2 on the latest Trek Speed Concept SLR 9. He paired a 1x SRAM drivetrain with ENVE wheels (SES 100 Pro front and rear) on Continental Grand Prix 5000 TT tires. You couldn’t miss it, either: bright yellow paint with pink TREK lettering (“Powerbar bike,” as one commenter put it), “YO YO YO” on the seatstay, a SRAM crank, and Evolve extensions up front.

Breivold retired in December, came back in March, and made his first Kona count. His white V-PRi ran Vision Metron 81 SL Disc wheels (81mm deep), Vision aerobars, and a 1x Vision drivetrain, with a Pirelli tire up front and a Continental out back. TriRig mounts held bottles between the arms and behind the saddle.

Blummenfelt’s Giant Trinity ran a Digirit 1x drivetrain, CADEX Aero 4-Spoke wheels (50mm front, deep prototype rear), and CADEX aerobars, with TriRig mounts between the arms and behind the saddle.

The new world champ rode near the front all day and rolled into T2 in sixth alongside Blummenfelt. His S-Works Shiv TT (in the same wave paint as Paula Findlay’s) ran a SRAM Red 1x drivetrain with a big aero chainring and wheels: a carbon-spoked Helikon C107sl up front (107mm deep!) and a Charger Trispoke in the back.

Van Riel raced with an image of fellow Wuustwezel native Marc Herremans on his helmet. His Speed Concept SLR 9 ran a SRAM Red 1x drivetrain and HED wheels in custom pink-and-blue graphics. It ran a Vanquish V84 front and a Jet 180 rear.

Funk’s Cube wore custom purple-and-blue paint with “What the Funk” on the seat tube (we love it). He ran SRAM Red 1x on an SRM power meter crankset, a HED Vanquish V62 front with a Jet 180 rear, and TriRig bottle mounts.

Knibb skipped the TT helmet for a vented road lid. She passed Lucy Charles-Barclay around mile 33 and traded the lead with her all the way out to Hawi before finally pulling away (2:32 up with 20K to go). Her white and grey Speed Concept SLR 9 ran a SRAM Red 2x drivetrain, Drag2Zero extensions, Continental Grand Prix 5000 tires, and Bontrager Aeolus RSL wheels (a 62 up front and a 75 out back).

The defending champ was more than six minutes down at 138K and still closed all the way to third at T2. She stuck with the formula that won her the title last year: a Felt IA 2.0 with a SRAM Red 2x drivetrain and Princeton CarbonWorks Mach 7580 trispokes front and rear (now in the third-gen TSV3 version, which Princeton says is built around 28–30mm tires). Drag2Zero extensions and TriRig mounts finished it off.

Philipp came out of the water 30th, more than eight minutes down, and rode herself right back into it. The big change on her pearl-white Speedmax CFR: she ditched last year’s 2x Dura-Ace Di2 for SRAM Red XPLR 13-speed AXS 1x (10–46 cassette, UDH hanger), driven by an SRM Origin Aero crankset with a Carbon-Ti aero chainring and a gold chain. Wheels were Swiss Side Hadron 850s on 28mm Schwalbe Pro One Aero tires, with a Canyon cockpit and integrated bottle, an Ergon 3D-printed saddle, and an Abus TT helmet. Look closely, and you’ll find a bunny in sunglasses and “Kick Ass” on the frame!

On her Kona debut, fan favorite Findlay rode into T2 in seventh, just 5:24 behind Knibb. Her S-Works Shiv wore the same black and white wave paint as Luis’ bike. Paula chose SRAM Red AXS 2x and Zipp NSW wheels (a 454 up front and an 858 out back). A Speeco cockpit and an X-Lab Torpedo between the arms completed her matching look.

Perterer changed just about everything from last year. She went from a Lapierre Aerostorm to a Ventum Tempus, from Shimano to SRAM Red 2x, and from DT Swiss to HED (a Vanquish V62 front and Jet 180 rear) in custom leopard print to match her kit. The bike has AeroGain armrests up front.

Simmonds led the chase behind Knibb and Charles-Barclay early on. Her white Speedmax CFR ran a 2x Shimano Dura-Ace Di2 drivetrain on an SRM crankset, DT Swiss ARC 1100 80 wheels front and rear, and Continental Grand Prix 5000 TT tires. She chose Canyon’s integrated cockpit and bottles between the arms and behind the saddle.

Berry kept her maroon Cervélo P5 and 2x Shimano Dura-Ace Di2, but swapped last year’s HED wheels for Shimano’s new Dura-Ace C60 front and a C90 rear, which had a few people online asking questions. Cervélo extensions, TriRig mounts between the arms and behind the saddle, and a MET TT helmet rounded out her rig.

Hollioake’s split includes a three-minute drafting penalty that pushed her from 4:19 down to 7:59. She also changed bikes, going from last year’s Trek Speed Concept to a Cervélo P5 with SRAM Red 1x and Parcours 3S GT trispokes front and rear. She stuck with her Sync aerobars.

Derron was third on the road at 17 miles before a three-minute penalty sent her back to eighth at T2. Despite the deficit, she still ran onto the podium in her Kona debut. Her white Speedmax CFR ran 2x Shimano Dura-Ace Di2 with an aero outer ring and a CeramicSpeed oversized pulley cage. She chose DT Swiss ARC 1100 wheels (deeper in the back), a Continental Aero front tire, and a GP5000 TT rear. Her cockpit included Canyon’s integrated bars. She used a Selle Italia saddle in a very forward position.

Wilms raced a black S-Works Shiv with an Evolve Charger rear wheel, Zipp 858 NSW front, and Continental Grand Prix 5000 TT tires. Her 2x Dura-Ace Di2 setup used an Ultegra(!) front derailleur with Carbon-Ti chainrings and a 4iiii power meter, plus FastTT extensions.

#270. How to Fuel When You’re Injured—and Support a Stronger Recovery

Sports dietitians explain why cutting calories when you’re hurt can backfire, and what your body actually needs to heal.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Sports nutrition feels complicated enough when you’re healthy. When you’re injured and taking time off from running to recover, knowing what and when to eat can become even more confusing.

In reality, the building blocks of a nourishing runner’s diet don’t change that much during injury, Laura Reece, MS, RD, director of nutrition at Women’s Health, Sports & Performance Medical in Brighton, Massachusetts, tells Runner’s World. Food provides the raw materials and energy your body needs to repair damage and rebuild stronger, whether you’re recovering from a set of hard mile repeats or a torn Achilles tendon.

But some nuances can prove beneficial during the recovery process. “Nutrition has healing properties,” including improving bone health and reducing inflammation, says Rebecca McConville, RD, CSSD, author of the book Finding Your Sweet Spot. Here, three sports dietitians explain how to fuel your comeback.

Don’t let an injury derail your training. Dive into the Runner’s World Guide to Common Running Injuries to learn how to spot, treat, recover from, and prevent injuries, and visit the Runner’s World Guide to Nutrition and Fueling to develop a healthy fueling routine that supports your training plan.

“The biggest mistake that a lot of runners make is they all of a sudden feel like they’re not running, they’re not using as much energy, so they end up pulling their calories or carbohydrates way down,” Reece says. “But cutting out foods or food groups can slow your recovery, because your body needs calories to heal.”

The process of repairing and rebuilding tissue is energy-intensive. Surgery can raise your metabolic rate—the amount of energy you burn at rest—by about 20 percent, an effect that can last weeks after you leave the operating room, says Emily Barnhart, R.D., a board certified sports dietitian with the U.S. Olympic and Paralympic Committee.

If you’re on crutches, walking is more taxing than it is without them. Physical therapy and cross-training, too, require fuel. What’s more, many runners are underfueled in the first place (more on that in a minute) and restricting further when you’re hurt could prolong your recovery and damage your health.

“I’ve talked to hundreds of injured athletes at this point,” Barnhart says. “I’ve only ever had to tell two, ‘Hey, I think you might be eating too much.’ The majority of them, it’s like, ‘We need to increase things.’” That means eating regularly throughout the day, including all three macronutrients (protein, carbohydrates, and fats) at each meal.

Protein provides the building blocks for tissue repair; think of them like bricks, Barnhart says. Carbohydrates act as the construction workers, providing energy for the healing process and for physical therapy and other activities. Fats—especially omega-3s and other healthy fats found in foods like avocado and walnuts—reduce inflammation, support hormone health, and also act as an energy source when you’re resting or working at a lower heart rate, Reece says. Barnhart thinks of them as “the garbage trucks that keep our construction site nice and clean and functioning properly.”

The exact ratios and amounts might change as healing proceeds, Barnhart says. Early on—after surgery, or if you’re in a cast or walking boot—she recommends athletes bump up their protein intake, aiming for 1.8 to 2.2 grams per kilogram of bodyweight (about .8 to 1 gram per pound) daily. A good carb goal at this stage, meanwhile, is 3 to 5 grams of carbohydrates per kilogram of bodyweight per day (about 1.3 to 2.3 grams per pound, or one to two fist-sized servings per meal).

As you progress through physical therapy and return to running, your carb needs will likely increase. Depending on how hard you’re training, you may need 5 to 12 grams per kilogram of bodyweight per day (about 2.3 to 5.4 grams per pound), Barnhart says. Meanwhile, you can ease up slightly on the protein: experts recommend 1.2 to 2 grams of protein per kilogram of bodyweight (about .5 to .9 grams per pound) for healthy athletes.

Eating a wide variety of nutritious foods—including colorful fruits and veggies, whole grains, and complete proteins like chicken, eggs, and soy—is the best way to cover your bases when it comes to vitamins and minerals, Reece says.

Barnhart suggests aiming for three daily servings of dairy or other calcium-rich foods and five servings of anti-inflammatory foods (think cherries, berries, and fatty fish like salmon). Many anti-inflammatory foods are also higher in fiber. That’s helpful, because taking pain medications, or even just being out of your usual running routine, can lead to digestive issues, McConville says.

Some supplements might also add value during the healing process. Barnhart frequently recommends injured athletes take omega-3 fatty acids, since these anti-inflammatory fats promote heart, brain, and muscle health, and most Americans fall short in their diet. Look for a brand that contains at least 300 to 500 milligrams of EPA and DHA, Barnhart says.

Especially if you don’t eat much dairy, calcium supplements—to the tune of two 500-milligram doses per day—can support bone health. Barnhart notes that it’s also worth getting a blood test for vitamin D, and supplementing if your levels are low.

For tendon injuries, collagen may reduce pain and create more resilient tissue, she says; runners who want to try it can take at least 15 grams 30 to 60 minutes before physical therapy or other activities. And there’s some evidence that creatine enhances your ability to rebuild muscle as you’re returning to full activity.

But supplements are secondary to a nutritious diet and not a replacement. If you’re not eating enough overall, your body won’t be able to absorb or use any extra nutrients you take in, Reece points out.

Especially if you’re having surgery or your injury restricts your mobility, the logistics of putting meals together can prove challenging. “The more you can conserve your energy to go into healing, the better off, and you want to make sure you’re getting as many nourishing foods as possible,” McConville says.

She frequently works with athletes on a game plan to stock their kitchen with less stress. For example, you might have groceries delivered, prep baggies with ingredients for smoothies or crock-pot meals before a scheduled operation, or ask your friends to set up a meal train. Or, try something she calls Dr. DoorDash: sprucing up and extending delivery meals (say, ordering a pasta dish and stirring in more veggies, or piling protein on top of ready-made salads).

Sure, you’re not sweating through an hourlong run—but you still need plenty of fluids. Staying hydrated keeps blood flowing to and from healing tissues, carrying nutrients to the injured area and shuttling away waste products, McConville says. Fluids also keep muscles and other injured tissues supple. Consider which feels healthier and more resilient, a juicy steak or a stick of beef jerky, Barnhart says.

One rule of thumb is to drink an ounce of water or other liquid for every pound of bodyweight per day, with an extra 16 to 20 ounces per hour of activity (and yes, physical therapy counts), McConville says. You can also monitor the color of your urine stream—ideally, it’ll be light yellow, like lemonade—or check that you’re peeing about once every two hours. Also watch for warning signs of dehydration, such as headaches, achy muscles, and dry skin.

Once you’ve dialed in the details, it’s worth looking again at the bigger picture of whether you’re eating enough. Underfueling not only hampers healing, it could also be a factor in why you got hurt in the first place. Low energy availability—which occurs when you don’t eat enough to replace the calories you’ve burned—can turn into a condition called relative energy deficiency in sport, or REDs. Often, REDs manifests in injuries, especially to bones, McConville says.

While low energy availability and REDs can be linked to an eating disorder or disordered eating, many runners eat too little without realizing it. If you have a bone stress injury—and especially if you’ve had multiple, or one that’s in a high-risk area, such as the sacrum or the femoral neck—consider getting a workup from a physician and/or dietitian, including a bone density scan, blood tests, and an assessment of how you’re fueling, Reece recommends.

Besides REDs, another potential culprit is a nutrient absorption issue. For example, runners with undiagnosed celiac disease have trouble absorbing calcium, vitamin D, iron, and other nutrients when they eat gluten. This can weaken bones and increase your risk for stress fractures until it’s managed with treatments like a gluten-free diet, Reece says.

Regardless of how or why you got hurt, the recovery period is a great time to check in with a sports dietitian. Injuries are challenging, physically and mentally. Dietitians—along with therapists, as needed—can help with concerns about body image, weight gain, and disordered eating that sometimes arise when you’re hurt.

“Injury gives your critical voice a megaphone,” Barnhart says. “A lot of us get a lot of self-pride and self-worth from the activities that our bodies get to do. When that’s taken away from us, we can feel quite down.”

When you can’t run, shoring up your nutrition gives you a positive goal to focus on. Filling in any dietary gaps can ensure you heal properly and aren’t operating at a deficit when you return to running. And dietitians can help you set up healthy habits around fueling that pay off in feeling good and performing well when you get back to training. “As dietitians, we hear this all the time: ‘Nutrition is the one thing I haven’t tried,’” McConville says. “Really, it should be one of the very first things.”

Cindy is a freelance health and fitness writer, author, and podcaster who’s contributed regularly to Runner’s World since 2013. She’s the coauthor of both Breakthrough Women’s Running: Dream Big and Train Smart and Rebound: Train Your Mind to Bounce Back Stronger from Sports Injuries, a book about the psychology of sports injury from Bloomsbury Sport. Cindy specializes in covering injury prevention and recovery, everyday athletes accomplishing extraordinary things, and the active community in her beloved Chicago, where winter forges deep bonds between those brave enough to train through it.
