#271. Average Cycling Speed by Age Group: How Fast Should You Be?

Strava reveals cyclists’ true pace. Are you slower—or faster—than average?

Who doesn’t love a little friendly competition? While “fast” means something different to every cyclist, there’s data from Strava that points to the average speeds we’re riding on the road and on the dirt, divided by our different age groups.

If you haven’t yet familiarized yourself with the average cycling speed for your age group, it can be a fun challenge to get acquainted with this number to see how you stack up to your cycling peers. It could also tell you a lot about your own fitness and performance.

🚴🏽 Ready to take on your fastest ride yet? Our How to Ride Faster program will help you make it happen!

Considering competitive cyclists win their races by tearing through the miles faster than their rivals, speed is an area where you might want to gauge your own performance. Or at least, you may want to know how your standard pace compares with other people’s average cycling speeds.

To give you the info you need, we gathered stats on average bicycling speeds from Strava. Plus, we chatted with experts to find out how you can find your own fast.

Strava, the app that makes it easy to track your cycling (and other) activity to store, share, and celebrate your progress with friends, has an abundance of information from users across the country and around the world. They specifically pulled data on average cycling speeds and distances for users in the United States, breaking it down farther by leisure rides versus commutes, as well as pavement rides versus dirt rides, to help provide a little context for the data.

Keep in mind, this doesn’t provide information on the type of bike used or the terrain (for example, flat versus hills), which of course would further affect speeds.

In a nutshell, the average cycling speed for leisure rides performed on pavement (in miles per hour) is 14.1 mph, with an average distance of 19.2 miles. Leisure rides on dirt saw an average speed of 8.3 mph, with an average distance of 10.6 miles.

While it’s impossible to know for sure, it’s easy to guess that the leisure rides performed on dirt involve rougher trails and terrain than those performed on pavement, which likely contributes to the lower average cycling speeds and distances.

Commutes, on the other hand, tended to be shorter, with slightly slower speeds when performed on pavement, but slightly faster speeds on dirt, when compared to the leisure ride counterparts. Specifically, commutes on pavement saw an average cycling speed of 12.1 mph (slower than the leisure ride on pavement), with an average distance of 4.7 miles, and commutes on dirt saw an average cycling speed of 9.8 mph (faster than the leisure ride on dirt), with an average distance of 5.1 miles.

When you think of the pavement and dirt conditions that might be encountered during a commute, these discrepancies make sense. For example, a commute on pavement is likely to be impacted by traffic and stop lights or other commuters, which is likely to slow a person down. Likewise, the type of dirt track that might be used for a commute is more likely to be an urban bike trail that’s well-kept and reasonably flat, making it easier to go faster than on a longer trail ride done for leisure purposes, where the terrain and trail may be trickier.

Of course, these average cycling speed stats are heavily influenced by a wide variety of factors, including terrain, the type of bike being used, and the intent of the ride (like leisure versus training versus racing). Even the location—like a city commute where you’re subject to traffic, pedestrians, and stop lights will impact your speed more than a ride taking place on a bike trail or a quiet country road. And of course, the distance of the ride can’t be overlooked. Someone training for a short race or event is likely to speed through the miles more quickly than someone training for a longer event.

“There are a number of factors that contribute to cycling speed,” says Simone Provenzano, avid cyclist and an assistant professor and director of the master of science in exercise physiology program at the University of Mary Hardin-Baylor. “Time-trial or triathlon bikes are more aerodynamic than road bikes, which are more aerodynamic than gravel, cyclocross, or mountain bikes.”

“On a flat surface, with all other factors the same, time trial bikes will be faster than others,” Provenzano adds. “Plus, tires impact cycling speed—the more grip a tire has, the more it will slow you down. Therefore, smoother tires will be faster. Road surface, bearings, mechanical intricacies—they can all make a difference. Then there is general terrain and environmental factors. Is it windy? Are you going up hill? These will make you slower, while going downhill or riding with the wind will make you faster.”

It’s not just the bike and the environment that contribute. “Cycling speed depends on power and cadence. The more power and cadence I use, the faster I go. Therefore, cycling speed is highly dependent on an individual’s cardiovascular and muscular fitness,” Provenzano says.

Your fitness also depends on where and how you train. If someone regularly goes on long rides on flat terrain, they may have developed a good baseline fitness for those conditions, but if they switch things up and hit some hills with steep inclines? Their muscular fitness is unlikely to be prepared for the challenge, and the power just won’t be there. As a result, their typical speed will suffer.

All of these factors combined help explain why Provenzano says when it comes to coaching, “It’s simply impossible to prescribe a general cycling speed to anyone.”

While you might want to be conscientious of average cycling speeds for different circumstances, it’s important not to get too caught up in the comparison game. Instead, mentally file away the data as information, and spend more time finding the right speed for you, understanding that it’s likely to vary from ride to ride depending on the aforementioned circumstances.

That said, with training and time, you can work toward gradually increasing your own speeds (comparing your personal changes and improvements), as one of several indicators that can help prove all your time on the bike is paying off in improved fitness and health.

With a few average cycling speeds filed away in your brain for reference, what really matters is your own training and improvement over time. That means finding a workout intensity that’s going to help you meet your long-term goals, rather than focusing on a specific training speed. “Prescribing intensity by heart rate or power is a better way to help the general population. Heart rate monitors are cheap and available in many formats (like watches, chest straps, or forearm straps). Power meters, on the other hand, can be quite expensive,” Provenzano says.

She suggests using a CTS Field Test for heart rate or power to help you determine the appropriate cycling intensities you should shoot for during training. You could also opt for an FTP test, as it provides a similar range for training intensities.

Based on your test results, you can then use percentage ranges of power or heart rate (whichever you tracked during your test) to gauge the appropriate intensity levels to shoot for when performing a variety of different workout types, like endurance miles, tempo, or power intervals.

“Most time should be spent in the ‘endurance’ zone. All other intensities should only make up about 20 percent of cycling time in a variety of intervals. The harder the intensity, the less time is spent at that intensity,” Provenzano explains.

Cycling speed demons aren’t built in a day, so it’s important to put a reasonable plan in place to develop your cardiovascular and muscular endurance over time, which will eventually help improve your speed.

“Beginner cyclists should take it slow and give themselves time to adjust to the cycling environment. Start with shorter distances and gradually increase your range by about 10 percent per week. Monitor your progress as you go and take rest days when needed so you don’t become fatigued over time,” says Caroline Grainger, ISSA-certified personal trainer.

Provenzano also suggests making time for group rides on the weekend. Not only do these rides allow you to train in a more social environment, but group rides offer training opportunities you might not seek out on your own. “These rides are usually mixed with a lot of endurance miles, but also some power surges and uphill terrain,” she says.

Other than your longer, weekend group rides, Provenzano suggests making time for two to three interval rides during the week to help improve muscular fitness and power. After having completed your CTS or FTP test, you can use the suggested heart rate or power guidelines to help guide your intensity level. These shorter rides may last up to about an hour, making them easier to fit in during a busy week.

Provenzano offers the following sample ride to follow:

As you start following a structured cycling plan using power or heart rate to keep your intensity where you want it, you can also keep track of your average speeds and how they change over time.

This is especially helpful when using an app, like Strava, to track your courses, which allows you to compare apples to apples (rather than trying to compare a 10-mile course on flat pavement to a 10-mile course on hilly trails, for instance). That way, if you know you completed a particular course at a particular speed a month ago while training at a “tempo” intensity, and you complete the same course faster the next time you do it, you’ll know your efforts are paying off.

Laura Williams, M.S., ACSM EP-C holds a master's degree in exercise and sport science and is a certified exercise physiologist through the American College of Sports Medicine. She also holds sports nutritionist, youth fitness, sports conditioning, and behavioral change specialist certifications through the American Council on Exercise. She has been writing on health, fitness, and wellness for 12 years, with bylines appearing online and in print for Men's Health, Healthline, Verywell Fit, The Healthy, Giddy, Thrillist, Men's Journal, Reader's Digest, and Runner's World. After losing her first husband to cancer in 2018, she moved to Costa Rica to use surfing, beach running, and horseback riding as part of her healing process. There, she met her current husband, had her son, and now splits time between Texas and Costa Rica.

#272. Bye-Bye Bites: 14 Ways to Get Rid of Mosquito Bites Overnight

Wondering how to get rid of mosquito bites overnight? Discover simple home remedies for quick relief. From crushed ice to aloe vera, explore easy solutions to soothe itching and inflammation for a peaceful night’s sleep.

If you’re caught without bug bite cream or ointment, don’t worry — plenty of simple home remedies can provide quick relief. From soothing aloe vera to the calming effects of oatmeal, discover easy solutions to alleviate itching and inflammation so you can sleep peacefully.

Just as you’d ice an injury, icing a bug bite can help decrease inflammation and temporarily numb the pain.

If icy cold treatments aren’t your vibe, you can apply heat instead to soothe your bump.

Aloe vera gel does more than soothe sunburns! It can also help ease bug bites and help them heal.

Baking soda can remove the itch. To make a paste, mix 1 tablespoon of it with a splash of water (not too much). Apply it to your bite as you would zit cream. Keep it on for 10 minutes before rinsing it off.

Did you know basil (yes, like the kind in your pasta) has a rich history as a skin infection remedy? It contains antioxidants that may bring down bug bite inflammation.

To whip up your own basil rub, boil a couple cups of water with 1/2 ounce of dried basil leaves. Cool the mixture before applying it to a washcloth and gently massaging it onto the bite for sweet relief.

You already know apple cider vinegar (fermented liquid from apples) is a huge player in the natural remedy world.

Some people use it to clean due to its antimicrobial effects, and others mix it into food or drinks for its possible health benefits (like helping with blood sugar issues).

Its beauty with bites is that it can help ease burning or stinging while disinfecting your scratchy little bump.

Onion juice (while not delicious) has antifungal and antibacterial properties, which could possibly help ward off infection. Plus, it could make your bite sting less. Just dab a bit of raw onion juice onto your bites. The downside? We’re not sure how well it works … and it’s kinda stinky.

Thyme has been used to help with skin concerns for a long time. You can use it to help decrease irritation by chopping it up and applying the teeny leaves directly to your bite for 10 minutes. You can also boil thyme, soak a cloth in the cooled liquid, and wrap it around your bite.

Peppermint oil may work as an anti-itch agent. Mix it with carrier oil (like olive oil) before applying it to your skin, though!

Another natural anti-itcher and astringent, lemon balm, may be helpful. You can either apply a lemon balm cream or chop up the leaves and apply them right to the bite.

Witch hazel is a natural wonder with many uses for skin concerns such as acne and psoriasis. It can tackle inflammation and burning while helping your bug bite heal.

This herb may work, but the science is a little dicey. On its own, arnica is toxic, so any over-the-counter products you find have been carefully diluted for your safety.

The yummy tea that calms and soothes at bedtime has many other uses, including potentially calming an irritated bug bite. Steep the tea bag for 20 minutes before squeezing it out and applying it to your bite once it’s cooled.

Blend minced garlic with petroleum jelly or fragrance-free lotion. Place the mixture on your bite for 10 minutes before removing it and applying a cool cloth.

Icing the bite for 10 minutes and then placing a mixture of baking soda and water on it for 10 minutes is a strong choice.

Though not tested for this purpose, some people turn to Vicks to soothe mosquito bites. It’s possible that its antibacterial and anti-inflammatory properties could help heal and soothe mosquito bites. But FYI, this product isn’t considered the best defense against mosquito bites.

Some toothpastes are cooling, so that sensation may offer temporary relief. Some people use toothpaste on insect bites since many toothpastes contain astringents, which can help shrink tissues.

Using repellent to prevent bug bites is a good idea. PSA: DEET and lemon eucalyptus oil are safe ways to repel insects.

Mosquitoes are low-key little monsters that cause the most insect bites worldwide. Most bites aren’t serious, but mosquitoes can potentially carry diseases.

Ointments, creams, or simple home remedies can help stop the pesky itch after bites. But remember that some natural substances can cause allergic reactions. That said, it’s always a good idea to do a patch test first.

#273. Yes, Your Feet Age. Dermal Fillers Can Help

Barefoot walks on the beach. A day in their favorite high heels. A long training walk ahead of the Camano de Santiago. These are the goals—big and small—of women undergoing foot filler treatments.

Using an injectable filler—such as hyaluronic acid or body fat—to add padding to sore feet is not new, though it is gaining in popularity. As early as the 1960s, medical-grade silicone has been used to puff up padding deflated by age, years of wear and tear, and fashionable footwear, especially high heels. All of this puts intense pressure on the balls of the feet—otherwise known as the metatarsals.

Over time, the fatty cushion on the bottom of your feet dissipates. Fat pad atrophy affects 30% of people over the age of 60. Without that natural cushion, the bones in your feet come into closer contact with the ground, which causes a deep bruise-like pain in the heels or balls of the feet when walking barefoot or standing for long periods.

For some perspective, look at the doughy wonders that are baby feet and compare them to yours. As we age, wear and tear breaks down that plush tissue. And if you put your feet to heavy use, you’ll wear down that cushion quicker. Some of that internal cushioning can be restored—even if just temporarily—with the injection of dermal fillers.

“It’s getting very popular because people are already familiar with it for aesthetic [uses],” says Ben Pearl, DPM, a podiatrist at Arlington Foot and Ankle in Arlington, Virginia. Dr. Pearl specializes in sports medicine and treats endurance athletes looking to restore cushion lost in their feet from pounding the pavement.

Patients don’t have just one choice for injectables, though. Many of the same options available for cosmetic use have also shown promise for feet. There’s hyaluronic acid filler, which adds physical volume and cushioning, and calcium hydroxylapatite, such as Radiesse, which adds firm volume while also promoting new collagen growth. Sometimes human body fat is used as the injectable, known as adipose tissue, a practice that is quickly becoming the preferred method.

“[A fat injection] actually recruits your body to rebuild the fat pad in that area so it has a much longer duration,” says Anne Sharkey, DPM, of Soley Podiatry in Austin. Fat allografts from brands like Liposana and Leneva may last as long as two years, compared to hyaluronic acid fillers, which typically need a touch up in six to nine months.

This type of regenerative medicine is appealing to patients. It’s not a promise that the foot will return to its former glory, but that it will be “as close to normal as possible,” says Dr. Pearl.

Dr. Sharkey and Dr. Pearl have both seen positive results from their patients. Scientific studies corroborate the efficacy of the treatment as well. One small study looking at patients with metatarsal pain found five patients had no more pain six months post-hyaluronic acid injections, and those who still had pain could wear high heels twice as long as they could before the injections. Another study surveying patients who had been injected with body fat reported that their pain improved by more than 70 percent on average, 20 months post injection.

While there are a growing number of cosmetic clinics offering the procedure, Dr. Pearl cautions against allowing just any injector at it. That’s because injecting filler into feet is a more complex procedure than an aesthetic injection. For one, knowing where to inject requires an understanding of the foot’s pressure points. In his own practice, Dr. Pearl uses ultrasound to help determine where to replace the fat to offload the pain. Additionally, Dr. Pearl notes, the skin is much tougher on the feet than the face, making it a more complicated area to inject.

This is one reason why Dr. Sharkey set up her practice to include a nail salon—combining cosmetology and podiatry. Her patients are already familiar with dermal fillers. Within the attached nail salon you can get manicures, pedicures, ingrown nail treatment, toenail reconstruction, or dermal fillers for feet.

Try not to groan, but it depends. The cost of the procedure is influenced by how much filler is injected, and which brand is used. Other factors that affect cost include how your provider bills the procedure, and how much experience they have with dermal filler injections.

For cosmetic use, the American Society of Plastic Surgeons places the average cost of hyaluronic acid filler treatment at $715. They estimate nonhyaluronic acid fillers, including Radiesse, Sculptra, and Liposana to cost $901 on average per treatment. However, the feet will almost certainly require more filler than the face, so you can expect the cost to be higher.

But will insurance cover it? Unlikely. “Even though it isn't technically cosmetic, it may not be considered medically necessary, because these procedures are often considered elective and cosmetic branding has a box drawn around it,” says Mark Welter, chief strategy and growth officer at Welter Healthcare Partners, a healthcare business management firm.

If you’re transparent with your provider about any financial concerns you have, they can work with you to find a middle ground between pain relief and high costs. Dr. Sharkey, for example, will often offer her patients more affordable hyaluronic acid fillers as temporary pain relief until they’re ready to dive into a more expensive fat injection.

If injectables aren’t accessible to you, there are other ways to deal with foot pain. Here are some options, most of which require a low financial investment.

A podiatrist can help walk you through any of these options and come up with a plan to minimize your pain.

#274. Hickey Stages: Understanding and Managing Love Bites Effectively

Hickeys, or as scientists call them, subdermal hematomas, are love’s graffiti. If you’ve ever scrambled for scarves or turtlenecks, welcome to the kissing booth of knowledge! Join us as we navigate the lifecycle of hickeys, from their eye-catching start to their subtle fade, and learn how to speed up their departure.

A hickey, medically known as a subdermal contusion or hematoma, is simply a bruise that forms as a result of vigorous kissing or sucking on soft skin, typically around the neck. This intense suction causes the tiny blood vessels under the skin, a.k.a. capillaries, to burst and release blood into the surrounding tissues. The immediate result? An unmistakable red or purple mark that gradually shifts to a darker shade as it heals.

From a medical standpoint, hickeys are intriguing. They showcase the skin’s sensitivity and the body’s rapid response to minor vascular injury. Not so romantic when you think about it scientifically, right? But hey, it’s all part of the human experience of showing affection — or something like that.

When you get a hickey, your body starts a healing process that resembles how it deals with other bruises. Here’s a more detailed look at each stage of a hickey’s life cycle.

Immediately after the passionate moment, a hickey appears on the skin, screaming in shades of bright red or deep purple. This initial coloration is due to blood from the ruptured capillaries pooling beneath the skin’s surface in response to the suction. It’s your skin’s way of signaling that there’s been some minor internal damage in that area.

As the hickey begins to heal, it undergoes a whole wardrobe of color transformations, showcasing your body’s metabolic process at work.

Initially, the hickey darkens as the blood begins to oxidize. Then, after a few days, the body starts to break down and reabsorb the blood, so it turns lighter — going from blue to green to brown and, finally, mellow yellow. This rainbow journey reflects the breakdown of hemoglobin, the iron-containing substance in the blood, into biliverdin and bilirubin.

Finally, your hickey starts to ghost you. Over a week or two, depending on factors like your skin type, overall health, how severe the hickey was., and how your body rides the healing waves, the last traces of your hickey fade into nothing.

During this stage, the body’s immune system clears away the remaining by-products of the broken-down blood. White blood cells swoop in like a cleanup crew at a festival, gobbling up and digesting the debris in a process called phagocytosis, while increased blood flow to the area helps to flush out the remnants.

Need a hickey gone yesterday? Here’s how to help your hickey heal. Start with a cold pack — grab a spoon from the freezer or a chilled gel pack and gently press it against your hickey. This will help reduce any swelling and scatter the blood pooling under your skin, which can help minimize that bold bruise.

After using cold treatment for the first 48 hours, it’s time to turn up the heat. Switch to warm compresses to get the blood flowing smoothly again. A few minutes a few times a day invites more circulation to the hickey zone, helping you hustle through healing and clear out the blood remnants more swiftly.

You can also try a dab of comfrey ointment. Research shows it may reduce bruise size and coloration for some peeps.

Caught off guard? A little concealer or foundation over the hickey makes it less noticeable.

Not into makeup? Scarves and high-necked shirts are also great accessories for your camouflage arsenal.

Typically, a hickey will last anywhere from 5 days to 2 weeks, depending on its severity and your body’s healing capabilities.

Communication is key! Let your partner know your feelings about receiving a hickey — some might find it fun, while others may prefer to keep their necks clear.

While generally harmless, hickeys can sometimes lead to complications like skin infections or, very rarely, blood clots. It’s best to keep the affection gentle to avoid any issues.

Hickeys are nothing more than bruises in disguise. They start as bright red to purple love stamps and gradually fade over several days to a couple of weeks. Speed up the process with heat and cold packs or a splodge of comfrey cream.

Remember, the best approach to handling hickeys — like all aspects of relationships — is communication and care. So go forth, love responsibly, and keep a scarf handy, just in case!

#275. The 10 Best Men’s Running Pants to Usher in Cold Weather

These pants and tights keep you warm without overheating when it’s below freezing.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

There comes a point every year when bare-legged running is no longer feasible. For some, that’s a sign to head indoors and find the treadmill. For others, it’s time for a wardrobe adjustment: putting on some pants. The best running pants and tights make cold-weather running not just tolerable, but enjoyable. That means you can bypass the treadmill and get outside, even when frosty temperatures, icy winds, snow, and rain are in the forecast.

After nearly seven years living in Southern California, I’ve returned to a colder climate (northern Michigan) and have been getting reacquainted with wintertime running—and that means my tights and running pants have come back into regular rotation. I’ve been amazed at what a difference they make. With my trusty merino tights, for example, I can run comfortably even in single-digit temperatures. No matter which kind of bottoms you prefer, the picks in this guide will help you achieve that same state of wintertime running bliss.

I selected the pants and tights below based on my own experience with wintertime running, online reviews, and input from RW staff. My background: I’ve covered running shoes and apparel for almost a decade, writing for Runner’s World, InsideHook, Men’s Journal, and other outlets. Apart from my stint in California, I have run outdoors (in both pants and tights) through many snowy, cold winters in the Midwest and Northeast.

In addition to using my own gear knowledge and experience, I also incorporated feedback from RW Runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate and Running Reviews Editor Amanda Furrer and pants-and-tights testing notes from RW staffers. RW staff tested several picks in this guide, including the Best Overall and Best Value options, and two of the picks—Best for Wind Protection and Best Merino Tights—are based on my own firsthand testing.

A clear favorite among RW testers, Brooks’s Momentum Thermal Tights will take the sting out of cold weather and help you maintain your motivation to run on the frostiest of winter mornings. They’re made from a stretchy blend of polyester and spandex, and the fabric has a brushed interior for a fleece-like feel against your legs. Three pockets—a zippered rear waistband pocket and two elastic drop-in pockets on the thighs—keep a lockdown hold on your phone, keys, and gels, and the internal drawcord waistband ensures a slip-free fit.

Testers wore these tights in temperatures as low as 20 degrees Fahrenheit, and they felt “super toasty” even when the wind picked up. Testers also appreciated the wide, flat waistband, which felt comfortable on the run.

The latest version also has a new feature: zippers at the ankles. This was a critique from previous testers who felt the tights tricky to get on and off over large feet. The zippered ankles are a major game change, making the Brookers Momentum Thermal reign supreme.

New Balance’s RC Pocket Tights are an outstanding value. They fall on the lower end of the running tights pricing spectrum, but their premium fit and feature set make them an especially good buy.

In RW testing, the tights stood out for their exceptionally stretchy fabric and body-hugging fit: They feel great and stay in place while running (the drawstring offers extra insurance, but it’s really not necessary). Better yet, they have a surprisingly large amount of storage. A zippered pocket at the back can tote a phone, while two drop-in thigh pockets and dual drop-in rear pockets at the back provide plenty of real estate for gels or other small essentials.

One drawback: The fit at the ankles is a bit tight, so getting these tights around larger calves can require some finessing. Overall, though, they’re a reliable choice for temperatures down to around 30 degrees Fahrenheit.

Want more reflectivity? The New Balance Reflective RC Heat Tight 28" has hard-to-miss reflective strips and patterns on the legs to optimize visibility on your runs.

The Fast and Free Tight went through a massive design update to emphasize comfort along with functionality. The waistband flexes more to prevent uncomfortable constriction. “It’s comfortable and doesn’t dig in at all,” said Dengate, who tested the tights.

The new exterior drawcord demonstrates lululemon’s eye for detail; it provides a smooth band fit instead of a bunched cord tucked under.

The material, lululemon’s nylon/elastane Nulux, feels silky to the touch and provides warmth in mild to cold temperatures. The tights are also customizable. If you want less leg, bartacks on the seamless cuffs guide you on where to trim.

“The ankle opening is neat. There are three bartacks along the stitched and welded seams, leading me to believe that I could shorten these up if I really wanted to.” Dengate referenced Ciele’s FSTTight, which also has trimmable leg openings. “The main body material obviously won’t fray because it’s not reinforced in any manner at the ankle.

The Fast and Free has some reflective detail, which is ideal if your runs are in low light. It also has just the right amount of storage, including sizable side pockets and a back rear pocket to store your phone.

When you’re running in remote areas, getting too cold isn’t just uncomfortable—it can be dangerous. Bandit’s Superwarm pants will keep you protected from wintry conditions on the trail.

They’re made with a DWR-treated, woven stretch fabric at the front and back for good freedom of movement and weather protection (it’ll repel raindrops and block wind). That textile is paired with a knit synthetic fabric made from hollow yarns that insulate your legs while also venting moisture, so you stay dry and warm. Both fabrics are brushed for a soft texture, and the drawstring waistband helps you dial in a perfect fit.

The rear zippered pocket will house your phone, but you’ll likely need a belt or pack for other stuff—items will likely bounce a bit in the zippered side pockets. Even so, these pants deliver strong warmth and weather resistance, and their trim silhouette makes them less bulky than typical joggers.

Not available in your size (or favorite color)? We also recommend Bandit’s Stamina Tights, which have seven waterproof pockets and an anti-chafing waistband with an external drawstring.

Fans of the Trail Half Tight appreciated that their favorite short came with a long inseam. The Janji M’s Trail Tight provides 28 inches of coverage with nylon/spandex material that’s soft and not too heavy on the legs.

Tester and Editor Theo Kahler, who ran the New York City Marathon in 2:24:12 wearing the Janji Half Tight, appreciated all the storage the cold-weather version had to offer.

“These have as much storage as you could ask for,” he said. “There are two pockets on each side of your legs, plus a big pocket in the back and there's even a small pouch in the front for a key. The Janji tights are great for carrying loads of gels—I can fit eight comfortably—and the side pockets can accommodate a phone easily.”

According to Kahler, the tights were slightly more constrictive than the half tight version, so you may want to size up.

You know those early winter, late spring days when the weather is iffy and it’s cool but not quite cold? The On Performance Tights are the kind of bottoms to reach for when you don’t want to think twice about running out without extra coverage—or worry about overheating.

The Performance Tights are made of On’s quick-drying DryTec fabric, which is composed of polyamide and elastane. Dengate described the fit as not too compressive, and “cozy.” He ran with his phone, discovering the pockets had good stretch and the tights didn’t slip down despite the extra weight.

“On a lot of tights, I have to take the phone out of the case,” he said. “Then I worry I’ll drop it if I grab it for a midrun text or photo. No problem here.”

While the tights protected his legs from windburn and didn’t overheat in mild temps, Dengate recommends not wearing these in the snow.

“I won’t reach for these when temps hit freezing—it’s just too thin,” he said. “They really move with you well, though, and you don’t feel even the slightest tug when you stride out.”

Blustery winds can make even milder temperatures feel brutal, but these Wind Shield Pants (along with a windbreaker jacket) will be an effective shield. I wore them on a recent run along the shore of Lake Michigan, and the pants completely blocked the lake breeze and kept me cozy. I used one of the two zippered thigh pockets to keep my phone secure without jostling, and the wide drawstring waistband delivered a slip-free fit.

The Wind Shield Pants have a subtle fleece interior lining at the legs, and they stretch well, but their slim silhouette makes them difficult to wear over tights or shorts. Yet that’s less of a drawback than you might think: Their wind-blocking power makes these pants warmer than they appear, so you won’t need to layer up so much.

The Bislett is a proudly old-school design: Tracksmith based them on a pair of U.S.-made, stirrup-equipped running pants from the ’80s. The brand updated them with a modern performance fabric that’s truly excellent—it’s super durable, warm, and keeps your legs protected from wind and rain. The stirrups prevent the pants from riding up above your ankles and contribute to an overall snug fit.

They’re not quite tights, but they’re definitely more form-fitting than a typical pair of running pants. Dengate loved their warmth and weather protection, and the premium fabric makes the Bislett a worthy investment. “These are going to outlast any of your other tights,” he said.

Can’t decide between pants and tights? We also recommend the brand’s Session Pants. The Session Pants have a tailored fit that’s equally functional for workouts and comfy for lounging during downtime.

My Smartwool Intraknit tights were stuffed in my underwear drawer for years, but now that I live in Michigan, they’ve become an essential part of my running wardrobe. I absolutely love wearing them. The secret sauce here is the merino wool: The fibers have a crinkled shape that traps heat while also venting moisture, keeping me in a Goldilocks state of warm-but-not-sweaty while running.

These tights also have a soft, itch-free texture, and they stretch easily to accommodate movement. I usually layer them under a pair of lightweight pants or shorts, and they’ve kept me totally comfortable while running (and biking) in frigid single-digit temperatures.

While many runners avoid pants with looser fits, sometimes the extra room has advantages, and the Dash Pant shows why. McDonough appreciated the Dash’s roomy design and lightweight fabric, noting it “makes them perfect for layering” over a pair of tights for extra warmth in freezing weather. And when the temperatures rise a bit, you can wear the Dash pants on their own. They feature wind- and water-resistant front panels to protect you from the elements, and the right zippered pocket has an elastic sleeve to secure your phone. Bonus: These pants are comfy enough for post-run lounging, too.

First off, think about the wintertime conditions you’ll face. If you never run in the rain, for example, you won’t need pants or tights that are water- resistant. If temperatures dip well below freezing where you live, look for pants that insulate, as you’ll need the extra warmth. Here are the main components to keep in mind as you shop for running pants and tights.

The fabric is arguably the most important feature in any pair of pants or tights. Most are made from synthetic fabrics like polyester. This material wicks sweat and doesn’t absorb moisture, so it won’t soak like cotton and weigh you down. Tights and pants usually have some elastane (a.k.a. spandex or Lycra) blended in, which helps them stretch. This is essential for a snug fit and good freedom of movement.

Many pants and tights are designed with brushed or fleece interiors; this fluffy texture traps heat and makes them feel soft and warm. If you prefer natural fabrics, look for tights made with merino wool (it’s usually blended with synthetics for better durability). Merino wicks sweat and provides excellent temperature regulation, which makes it a great choice for wintertime running.

Pockets: It Depends On What You Can Run With—and Without

Most pants and tights have at least one or two pockets, and they can provide helpful storage when running. If you want to store heavier items like your phone, look for a zippered pocket located at the rear along the waistband or an elastic sleeve along the thigh—these are the best spots to keep your phone from jostling around as you run. For storing smaller items like gels, look for pants and tights with zippered side pockets or drop-in pockets along the waistband. Of course, pockets aren’t strictly necessary. You can also use a running belt or hydration pack for storage.

How Weatherproofing Protects You Wind, Rain, and Snow

If you run in the rain or battle icy breezes in the winter, look for pants or tights that’ll resist water and wind. Some models, like the Bandit Superwarm Run Pant, feature DWR finishes that cause raindrops to bead up and roll off, rather than soaking into the fabric, so you stay dry. Others, like the Patagonia Wind Shield Pants, have engineered fabric panels that resist airflow and block the wind, keeping you warmer.

What’s the difference between men’s and women’s tights?

Men’s and women’s tights are designed to fit the different contours of male and female bodies. Women’s tights typically have wider waistbands for a snug fit over the waist—female waists tend to be narrower relative to the hips than men’s waists.

Men’s tights are also cut differently, with more room in the crotch, a straighter fit through the thighs, and wider ankles than women’s versions. The exact differences will vary from one model to another, however.

That’s up to you! Wearing shorts or pants over your tights gives you an extra layer of protection from cold and wind, keeping you warmer, but they definitely add bulk to your running outfit. I prefer to wear pants or shorts over my tights, but plenty of guys wear tights alone, and that’s totally fine.

I start to consider pants or tights when temperatures dip below 40 degrees Fahrenheit, though your personal “time for pants” threshold may be lower or higher and change based on how far you’re running.

When cold weather hits in the fall, I’ll start with a windbreaker or insulated running jacket before bringing pants or tights into the mix—these top layers keep me comfortable even if my legs are more exposed.

Another factor to consider: If you get too hot, you can always remove a jacket, but you can’t take off your pants or tights (unless you have shorts underneath).

#276. I Tested Nearly a Dozen Electric Inflators. The Tiny Cycplus AS2 Is the One I’d Carry on Most Rides

Small enough for a jersey pocket, the AS2 Ultra can replace CO2 on most road and gravel rides.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Bicycle tire technology and our understanding of inflation pressure have changed significantly over the past two decades. However, until recently, the tools used to add that air have remained largely the same. Most cyclists traditionally relied on floor pumps, mini pumps, frame pumps, or carbon dioxide cartridges. Then, seemingly out of nowhere, compact electric inflators burst onto the scene.

Electric inflators aren’t entirely new to me. I first encountered them during my cyclocross racing days, when they were considerably less compact. At the time, they appealed to racers who needed to inflate numerous tires quickly and repeatedly to very precise pressures.

Those early models resembled cordless drills, with a short inflation hose where the drill bit would normally sit. They were useful around the pits but far too large to carry comfortably during a ride.

The category looks completely different today. Riders can now choose from numerous rechargeable, pocket-sized inflators equipped with digital pressure gauges. After testing nearly a dozen models from ten brands, the Cycplus AS2 Ultra emerged as the option most cyclists should consider.

The most immediately noticeable thing about the AS2 Ultra is its size. It measures just 2.5 by 1.75 by 1 inch and weighs 107 grams with the included silicone sleeve.

In laboratory testing, it inflated a 28mm road tire from completely flat to 65 psi in 42 seconds. Filling a 45mm gravel tire to 30 psi required 47 seconds, while bringing a 2.3-inch mountain bike tire to 20 psi took 45 seconds.

Those times aren’t necessarily quicker than using a CO2 cartridge, but they’re comparable to what an enthusiastic rider could achieve with a quality floor pump.

Against the other electric inflators in our test, the AS2 Ultra ranked third, fifth, and fourth in inflation speed for the respective tire sizes. Raw speed, however, isn’t its greatest strength. Its digital gauge was the most accurate we tested, reading just 1 psi off the verified pressure.

Battery performance was also impressive considering the unit’s compact dimensions. The AS2 Ultra completed four tire inflations before running out of power during the fifth.

Its main weakness was operating temperature; in testing, the unit reached approximately 91 degrees Fahrenheit. That’s about 10 degrees hotter than most competing inflators. Cycplus includes a silicone sleeve that helps address this issue by insulating your hands and protecting the device if dropped.

During normal use, such as topping up tires or making small pressure adjustments before a ride, the heat was never noticeable enough to concern me. The inflator got considerably warmer when filling a tire from flat, but it still didn’t feel unsafe.

Temperature deserves extra attention when using thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) tubes with plastic or other non-metal valve bodies. Heat transferred directly from an inflator can potentially deform or melt a plastic valve. The included extension hose reduces that risk, although it makes the overall setup less compact. Personally, I recommend avoiding tubes with non-metal valve stems whenever possible.

I’ll admit that I wasn’t initially excited about electric inflators. They seemed like clever gadgets designed to solve a problem that didn’t really exist. After spending a year using several inflators, however, I’m no longer eager to return to my old routine.

My opinion started changing while riding new bikes, wheels, and tires off-road: Finding the ideal pressure for an unfamiliar setup previously meant carrying both a mini pump and a separate digital gauge. Using a compact electric inflator helped quicken those experiments and much of the guesswork was eliminated.

Eventually, carrying multiple tools that performed overlapping duties stopped making sense. I simplified each bike’s repair kit to a spare tube, tire lever, and multitool, then carried the electric inflator in a jersey pocket.

Size remained my biggest reservation. Most of the inflators I tested were compact enough to carry in a travel toolbox, car trunk, or pre-ride setup. Even so, many still felt too bulky for a minimalist road-riding kit.

That’s where the AS2 Ultra distinguishes itself. It’s only slightly larger than an Apple AirPods Pro case and effectively disappears inside a jersey pocket. It also makes roadside flat repairs considerably less tedious.

I’ve used it to help with several flats during group rides. Other riders inevitably commented on the sound—the AS2 Ultra produces approximately 70 decibels and is undeniably noisy—but everyone was happy to avoid hand-pumping a tire or sacrificing a CO2 cartridge.

Battery life was my final major concern. Adding another rechargeable device to my cycling equipment wasn’t particularly appealing. More importantly, an electric inflator is useless if you discover a dead battery when you’re stranded with a flat.

In practice, the AS2 Ultra could go several weeks of handling routine pressure adjustments and pre-ride top-ups. I also didn’t observe meaningful battery loss while it was stored.

My routine became simple: Whenever I used it to inflate a completely flat tire, I recharged it afterward. That was no more difficult than remembering to replace a spent CO2 cartridge in a repair kit.

After a year with the AS2 Ultra, I see it as a replacement for CO2, not a manual mini pump. The AS2 Ultra is now my preferred option on any ride where I was previously comfortable carrying only cartridges

For remote backcountry routes or rough adventures where self-sufficiency is critical, I would still carry a manual pump. Electronics can fail, batteries can run out, and redundancy matters when help is far away.

The Cycplus AS2 Ultra isn’t the fastest electric inflator out there. Instead, it succeeds by offering an excellent combination of portability, gauge accuracy, battery capacity, and everyday usability.

It is genuinely small enough for a jersey pocket, and its pressure readings were more accurate than those of every other model in our test. The battery can also manage several inflations before requiring a recharge. Together, those qualities make it more practical than competing inflators that may work slightly faster but occupy considerably more space.

More importantly, the AS2 Ultra makes checking and adjusting tire pressure convenient enough that you’re likely to do it more often. Whether you’re dialing in a new gravel setup, topping up your tires before leaving home, or repairing a roadside flat, pressing a button is substantially easier than pumping by hand.

That convenience changes the experience more than I expected. Inflation becomes a quick, repeatable task rather than another pre-ride chore.

After a year of regular use, the AS2 Ultra has effectively displaced CO2 cartridges in my repair kit. It’s the easier and more practical choice for most road and gravel rides. A traditional pump remains sensible for remote trips where backup equipment is important; for everyday cycling, the AS2 Ultra is one of the few electric inflators that truly earns its place in a jersey pocket.

Test Editor Dan Chabanov got his start in cycling as a New York City bike messenger but quickly found his way into road and cyclocross racing, competing in professional cyclocross races from 2009 to 2019 and winning a Master’s National Championship title in 2018. Prior to joining Bicycling in 2021, Dan worked as part of the race organization for the Red Hook Crit, as a coach with EnduranceWERX, as well as a freelance writer and photographer.

#277. 5 Signs You’re in a One-Sided Friendship, According to Experts

Welcome to Asking for a Friend, a weekly series dedicated to solving the messy, awkward, and confusing parts of modern friendship. Because truth is, our platonic relationships are often the most complicated. Send us your friendship dilemmas here, and we might feature one in a future column.

Most friendships will never be truly 50/50, but at the very least they run on an unspoken agreement: both people show up, reach out, and add some fuel to the tank that keeps the engine going. If that balance consistently feels off—not just once or twice, but over the course of weeks or months—it’s hard not to wonder whether something deeper is going on.

You might notice in small but telling ways: Looking back at your messages, it dawns on you that you’re initiating every conversation. They call, if at all, only when they’re bored or when it’s convenient. And then there’s the sharper sting of noticing how effortlessly they find time for other people—just not for you (a surprisingly common frustration you can read more about here).

To be fair, life can get in the way—people get busy, schedules clash, and our friends can’t always be as available as we’d like—but that doesn’t make it any less frustrating or stop you from feeling resentful when you’re waiting days for a simple “How are you?” But how do you know if this is a temporary lapse or a more unhealthy one-sided friendship? Here are the biggest red flags therapists want you to watch out for.

Look through your texts and DMs: Are you always the first to send a message? When’s the last time they suggested hanging out? You can also experiment by not reaching out to see how long it takes for them to initiate contact. If weeks (or months) go by without a word, their silence may indicate who’s really holding this connection together.

“At a minimum, a good friend (even a busy one) will periodically check in out of curiosity and interest,” Tiana Leeds, LMFT, a therapist based in Santa Barbara, California, tells SELF. After all, someone who truly cares about you should want to know what’s going on in your life, which is why if they consistently don’t try to get in touch (or only expect you to do so), they may not be genuinely interested in your world.

Venting to your friends is natural—some would even argue it can strengthen your bond. That said, being there for each other is supposed to be a two-way street, Hope Kelaher, LCSW, author of Here to Make Friends: How to Make Friends as an Adult, tells SELF.

If someone unloads their laundry list of problems but doesn’t listen to yours, “they’re likely using you as their on-call therapist,” Kelaher says. This one-directional dynamic could look like a person who constantly complains about their boss but changes the subject whenever you open up about your work-related stress. Or they dominate dinner conversations with their dating disasters, yet they’re “busy,” uninterested, or MIA when you need relationship advice. Over time, investing all your time and energy into people who won’t give back can drain your energy, Leeds says, and leave you feeling neglected by a person who’s supposed to have your back.

Maybe they insist on eating at restaurants near their place, which means you have to travel across town every single time. They only reach out when “better” plans fall through (“Hey, my dinner got canceled. What are you doing tonight?”), making you feel more like an afterthought than a priority. More subtly, perhaps they’re only interested in brief 15-minute coffee chats that fit their schedule instead of a dedicated dinner or movie night.

“In a healthy relationship there should always be a give-and-take,” Kelaher says, meaning both people need to compromise. So it’s disheartening when, again and again, someone you’d do anything for won’t meet you halfway (sometimes literally).

Your friend might be a workaholic or chronically forgetful (which, don’t get us wrong, is still frustrating). But that alone doesn’t mean your bond is one-sided.

Instead, “consider the bigger picture and ask yourself, ‘Is their behavior a reflection of not caring about me, or just a difference in availability and communication style?’” Leeds says. As an example, someone who takes five business days to reply to anyone’s messages may not be singling you out. What’s more telling, though, is if that same person who’s “too swamped” to text you regularly posts Instagram stories of brunches, dinners, and post-work meetups with others in their social circle. Or if your usually punctual friend (who’s known for being reliable) is comfortable canceling plans only with you. These inconsistencies, Kelaher says, suggest that they’re perfectly capable of showing up—just not for you.

Let’s say you mentioned how important it would be to have support at your first 5K race. A friend who truly cares might surprise you at the finish line with flowers, or at the very least shoot over a heartfelt “Good luck!” or “Congrats!” In a one-sided friendship, however, this kind of consideration may be missing entirely. They might downplay your achievement (“Sorry I couldn’t make it, but it was such a short race!”) or forget your big day without a hint of apology.

True friends go the extra mile to celebrate your successes and be there during tough moments. That’s why if someone repeatedly forgets significant events like your birthday, or rarely shows empathy for your challenges (like a scary medical procedure, a high-stakes presentation), they may not be as invested as they should be.

Therapists recommended bringing up your concerns non-confrontationally.

Ideally, their response can give you a glimpse into whether they’re aware of this imbalance and, more importantly, if they’re willing to work on it. That said, you can’t force someone to be a good friend, so if they don’t care enough to show up for you, know that you deserve better. “After all, friendships take work, Leeds says. “But it’s not meant to be done by just one person.”

#278. Why the Ironman World Championship Remains Uncrackable

Lucy Charles-Barclay runs the 2026 Ironman World Championship marathon before withdrawing from the race. (Photo: Brad Kaminski/Triathlete)

Every triathlete racing the Ironman World Championship has a strategy, whether or not they admit it. Sometimes, their preparation is all about cracking the Kona code; others work on staying on Madame Pele’s good side. But whether the solution to performing well on the Big Island is pragmatism or spiritualism, you’d have thought that after almost 50 years we might have figured it out.

But one thing yesterday’s Ironman World Championship race proved was that – despite analyzing every last nanobyte of data on training, nutrition, race tactics, or psychology – we’re about as close to the right answer as those endurance pioneers were in 1978.

Like it or not, the reputation of this contest was borne of triathletes crawling to the finish line. And like it or not, in the shadow of Julie Moss, we still don’t seem to be able to move beyond that.

We try, of course. More electrolytes, more nutrition, more ice, more ways to cool ourselves. But even if any or all of these things work, they only allow elite performers to turn the dial up just a little bit more: “Oh, so that cooling headband works on the run? Great, I can push harder on the bike.”

But yesterday’s race wasn’t just chaotic throughout; it was bewildering. Even during the madcap events of the 2025 women’s smack-down, drag-out affair, we could at least hold firm to the modern-day conviction that once you get to the top of Palani Road, you’ll be safe from imploding. As Solveig Løvseth showed us yesterday: not anymore.

The Norwegian only needed to roll through town and it was job done, so she pushed too hard for too long. But did she? It looked as if she had raced as patiently as she had in 2025: mature beyond her years and experience. And for the first 8 hours 28 minutes, it again went perfectly.

And that exact timestamp might be important. Because unlike in 2025, when it marked her crossing the finish line, this time it marked a wobble, which turned to a stumble, which turned to a lengthy lie-down on the asphalt.

Because of the tougher conditions, yesterday’s race was going to take just those few crucial minutes longer, and it proved the difference between back-to-back wins and walking across the finish line half an hour later, with not just the Kona title but also the Ironman Pro Series cash ripped away.

But that’s just one hypothesis. We can all be armchair quarterbacks, but show me the example of the athlete who clearly got their strategy wrong, and I’ll show you an example of an athlete who also got their race strategy wrong, using the exact opposite strategy.

Some athletes planned their whole season around staying fresh for this race; others raced around the world with abandon. Who is right? We still don’t know.

For example, no one was more focused than Lucy Charles-Barclay, who pulled out of defending her Ironman 70.3 world title to pin all her hopes on regaining the Kona crown.

Last year, her race ended in the Natural Energy Lab, and we can be confident her team is as professional as it gets when it comes to pinpointing why and looking to solve it. This year, she pulled out in the Natural Energy Lab, just yards from the same spot.

In contrast, Taylor Knibb, who also had a meltdown last year, won to complete the rare Ironman 70.3 and Ironman World Championship double in the same year. So Knibb got it right, while Charles-Barclay got it wrong?

Maybe, but by Knibb’s own admission, it was also a struggle in the swim, her power was well below par towards the end of the bike leg, and her marathon, at just under three hours, wasn’t quick given her talents. Perhaps Knibb recognized the warning signs and dialed it back earlier, but it’s tough to be certain.

Both athletes have the same coach, Dan Lorang. At least one of his athletes made it to the finish line this year, but there is more analysis to be done, more data to be crunched.

Magnus Ditlev was another with a single-race focus, having only started twice this year and not raced since July. For much of the race, he looked like flying the flag for Denmark as the only Scandinavian country alongside Norway to have won the Ironman World Championship. Until five miles from the finish, when he barely looked capable of making it from one end of an aid station to the other.

The list goes on. Sam Laidlow dropped out early in the marathon, citing a lack of blood flow to his leg. Kristian Blummenfelt fell away just when he seemed primed to make his move. Patrick Lange is the finest marathon runner and arguably the finest course exponent we’ve seen in Hawaii; his results here far outweigh anything he has achieved elsewhere. His final race ended with cramps in the small town of Hawi, halfway through the bike leg.

As much as there are tales of woe which experience suggests could be avoided, so too are there are success stories which logic says shouldn’t happen.

Laura Philipp, who was in hospital earlier in the year with acute abdominal and back pain, had, against common wisdom, raced herself into form, finishing second and topping the Ironman Pro Series. Yet everyone thought she was supposed to be cooked before she turned up.

Julie Derron walked stretches of the marathon before rallying for third. Kat Matthews had a topsy-turvy race that started with a solid swim, saw her lose 15 minutes on the bike to Taylor Knibb, and then saw her run past more than a dozen athletes to finish fourth.

At least we can say experience counts in Kona. It’s often been beneficial to grab a top three before going on to win. Or can we? Before yesterday, Knibb and Vincent Luis, who had signaled this as his retirement race (and post-race told us that was still very much the plan), had won a grand total of zero Ironmans. So we can park that theory too.

The Ironman World Championship: the race that keeps on giving on the island that keeps on taking, with the unpredictability that keeps us coming back.

#279. Undercuts for Women: Benefits, Styles, and Types

Is it time to give your hairstyle and scalp a breath of fresh air? Say hello to the undercut hairstyle, a fashion-forward solution that can elevate your look and promote skin health.

By significantly reducing hair volume, undercuts allow for improved air circulation around the scalp. The result? Less trapped heat and moisture — factors that can contribute to fungal infections, scalp acne, dandruff, and dermatitis.

Whether you’re battling irritation or want to give your “do” a new lease on life, continue reading to learn how undercut hairstyles can be your ally in style and scalp health.

An undercut involves shaving or cutting hair very short on the sides or back of the head while leaving the hair on top longer.

Originally popular in men’s hairstyling, the undercut has crossed gender boundaries and gained popularity among peeps seeking a hairstyle that stands out.

It’s a style that offers a stark contrast and is often used to add an edge to an otherwise conventional look. So whether it’s a side undercut, undercut pixie, mullet undercut, or nape undercut, these hairstyles for women, men, and folks of all genders enhance individuality while offering practical benefits like reduced drying time and less hair maintenance.

Choosing an undercut means embracing a hairstyle with a “heady” mix of aesthetic and practical benefits. Here’s why an undercut might be the refreshing change you need.

Ready to turn heads? The standout feature of an undercut is undoubtedly its unique appearance. Hidden under the longer layers, it packs a punch of boldness you can flaunt or conceal — whatever fits your vibe. You can control the reveal, whether you’re showcasing that edgy undercut for a night out or keeping it classy for the office.

Got a mane that’s more lioness than laid-back? An undercut might be your new BFF. Strategically shaving or trimming the hair short on the sides or back dramatically dials down the volume. This means your thick, voluminous hair becomes way easier to manage and style, turning a heavy head of hair into something light and breezy.

And the best part? You get to keep all the styling potential without any of the hassle. It’s a practical solution that doesn’t sacrifice style for comfort.

Are you chasing the clock every morning? An undercut could slash your prep time. With less hair to fuss over, you can breeze through your washing, drying, and styling routine faster than you can say “snooze button.”

This trimmed-down approach is a time-saver and reduces the daily wear and tear from blow dryers and straighteners, keeping hair healthier in the long run.

Undercuts reduce your scalp’s weight and improve hair follicle airflow. This keeps the scalp cooler and reduces the buildup of sweat and oil that can lead to scalp irritation, dermatitis, and dandruff. As a result, undercuts could lead to more robust, healthier hair growth.

Ready to shake up your style with a cool undercut? Here’s a rundown of some options to add a dash of daring to your daily look:

Are you looking for a dramatic change without total commitment? Try the side-swept undercut.

This style features a sleek shave on one side of the head, just above the ear, while keeping the hair on top and the other side longer.

It’s perfect for folks who love to play with contrast — sweep the top hair over to the shaved side for an instant bold statement.

If subtlety is more your speed, this undercut is a wicked choice. It’s a shaved area tucked away at the back of the head or underneath the top layer of hair so that it can play a fantastic game of hide-and-seek.

Wear your hair down for a business-as-usual look, or tie it up to reveal a sneaky, stylish surprise. It’s an excellent choice for peeps wanting a touch of edge.

Are you feeling bold and artistic? Design Undercuts take personal expression to the next level. These chic undercuts are masterpieces, boasting intricate geometric patterns, sweet floral motifs, or any design that speaks to you.

Do you prefer a more understated yet stylish look? The tapered undercut starts very short near the ear and gracefully lengthens as it ascends the head, blending with your other locks.

It’s a softer version of the undercut that pairs beautifully with bob or lob cuts and offers a gentle nod to the undercut trend without going full-throttle.

The undercut hair offers both style and substance. It reduces styling time and promotes scalp health. By alleviating the weight and allowing the scalp to breathe, undercuts can help minimize issues like overheating and irritation, especially during warmer months.

Whether you’re drawn to the edgy designs or the subtle tapered style, an undercut could be a clever hack to simplify your morning routine. More time for coffee, less time with the comb!

Last medically reviewed on June 30, 2024

#280. How a Second Weekly Speed Workout Helped Me Break 1:30 in the Half Marathon

An extra quality session can boost half marathon fitness—if you’re ready for the added load.

In my 39th year, after a steady stream of successful races, it was time to level up my training. Fresh off the hardest marathon training block I’ve ever pulled off and a hard-fought, mixed-emotion PR in Boston, I wanted to use that momentum and strong foundation to go hard for a fall half marathon.

To do that, my training partner suggested we add a speed workout to my 12-week half marathon training cycle, bumping us up from one to two speed workouts, plus a long run with race-pace miles.

She was convinced the extra workout, which would focus on 10K and half marathon paces—essentially tempo efforts—would elevate me to the next tier of fitness. I was quietly eyeing my first sub-1:30 half marathon, hoping this would offer the tipping point.

At its core, a training plan should introduce different stimuli—frequency, volume, and intensity—to keep your body adapting and getting stronger (but not all at once). For this half marathon training block, we swapped out an easy run on Monday for another day of speedwork, which meant adding the intensity variable because I was already running a speed workout on Wednesday.

This was designed to offer a few benefits:

“Simply said, this [additional workout] helps to elevate your athletic ceiling,” says Hiruni Wijayaratne, a coach with My Olympic Coach, and a Sri Lankan record holder in the half marathon. “It replaces the easy run with something that’s higher quality.”

Instead of alternating between tempo paces and faster, 5K paces in my once-a-week speed session, having a day dedicated strictly to tempo got me very comfortable at 10K and goal half marathon pace. These paces can be tricky to nail down because they’re not easy to hold but they don’t have you redlining the effort, either.

These efforts “are the bread and butter of someone who’s distance training,” Wijayaratne tells me. “They bridge the gap between high-intensity speedwork and recovery. It’s really important to have that in-between because it builds your aerobic engine so you can sustain the effort for a long amount of time.”

The extra speed day also forced my body to run another quality workout two days later, on tired legs. In the first few weeks of the cycle, I was really feeling it. My right hamstring acted up; I became diligent at hamstring and glute-specific strength and stretch exercises (and lots of foam rolling).

Eventually, though, my body adjusted to the increased intensity, and with adequate sleep and nutrition, I was able to hit the workout, recover, and hit the next one.

“The hallmark of getting faster as an athlete is increasing performance and continuing to balance that stress and rest,” says Holly Benner, co-owner of Metta Performance, a run-coaching service and a certified leadership and performance coach. “You have to absorb that workout,” meaning you’re able to recover and then hit the next workout consistently.

“You can add a workout but you don’t then require two days off to make the next one happen,” she says.

There was no question about the physical benefits of adding another speed day to my training block. I was regularly running 6:50 pace, my goal race pace, and low 6:30s for a 10K pace, something I’d never done before. From a psychological standpoint, my second speed workout boosted my confidence as race day approached.

“A lot of people underappreciate the mental confidence you gain doing that work, closer together in the week, repeating it time after time,” Wijayaratne says. “There are days in training when you didn’t feel fresh, but you found the rhythm. You need that exact skill set to help navigate races when you’re not feeling perfect.”

For me, it wasn’t necessarily how I was feeling in a particular workout on a particular day, but the sum of its parts that not only gave me confidence, mentally, but made it possible to hold pace on race day. For example, my peak long run was 15 miles: 5 miles easy, 3 miles at half marathon pace, 2 miles easy, 2 miles at half marathon pace, 2 miles easy, 1 mile at half marathon pace—and placed at the end of a difficult week, workout wise. The long run was challenging but I nailed the paces and ended on my fastest mile.

The fact that I was able to do that given the cumulative fatigue, including that second speed workout, and load of 10 weeks of training told me that I absolutely could run my A goal of a sub-1:30 half marathon.

It had been five years since I set my sights on a half marathon PR when I picked the Philadelphia Distance Run this past September. The timing was right, and it’s a pretty fast course.

Over the years I have focused on adjusting training paces to match faster finishing times, with fewer changes to the types of workouts I’ve run. This additional speed workout was adding intensity to the cycle, yes, but because the prescribed paces were 10K and half marathon, the workout was really guiding me toward half marathon success, specifically. It wasn’t just about hitting a faster speed, but holding a difficult pace and getting more comfortable with it.

“Tempo efforts teach discipline,” Wijayaratne says. “As an athlete, you’re learning how to settle in [to a pace] and avoid yo-yoing. You’re committing to being uncomfortable, which is really important for racing and performing.”

These paces are also low-risk and high-reward, she says. “It’s a low fire that’s cooking for a long time so you get away with doing more of it, versus short, explosive, high-intensity speed work.”

In other words: You can get a lot out of each 30- to 40-minute session without totally destroying yourself.

Dedicating a weekly workout to this crucial pace on Mondays also opened up my Wednesday workout to focus on quicker speeds, like 5K pace, to recruit more powerful fast-twitch muscles and promote higher leg turnover.

When we run at faster paces, we create more neuromuscular connections between the nerves and muscles, Benner says. That means we get better at recruiting fast-twitch muscles to run more efficiently, more forcefully—like uphill or accelerating—and holding a faster pace toward the end of a race when we’re otherwise fatigued.

“If you’re running faster more than once a week,” Benner says, “You’re going to help cement that connection.”

Mixing up the paces will also make you a well-rounded runner, Wijayaratne says. “Training programs are recipes,” she explains. “You need a little spice, a little of that, not just one of everything. Great runners go beyond doing one pace. They teach their bodies to have different gears.”

The bottom line? This second speed workout allowed me to focus on goal race pace, embrace discomfort for a long period of time, strengthen my aerobic capacity and musculoskeletal system, and get better at recruiting crucial fast-twitch muscles, while balancing out my faster paces and longer runs.

There needs to be a readiness checklist before a runner decides to add a second speed workout to the training plan, Wijayaratne says. Although she didn’t coach me during this block, Wijayaratne has worked with me long enough to know that my consistency, fitness, and ability allowed for this step-up in training.

She points to three things runners should think about before adding another workout:

You should have a strong training base already, which consists of regular running, including one speed workout per week, being injury-free and running consistently for at least eight weeks (with at least four to six weeks in a focused training block), and having a low risk of dipping into energy deficiency (either via nutrition or sleep).

“Before you build a second floor of your house, your foundation needs to be strong,” Wijayaratne says.

You should be able to schedule quality days (workouts that require a warmup and cooldown, like a speed workout) with at least one buffer day in between.

Assess whether a second speed workout is working for you. This is the testing phase, Wijayaratne says.

After you’ve done a quality workout, the next day you may feel a little sore, but the day after that, if there isn’t any lingering stiffness, aches, or pains, “you can proceed safely.” If not? Scale back and try again.

This second workout shouldn’t come at the cost of injury or burnout, Wijayaratne adds.

For 12 weeks, I hammered two speed workouts and one long run. Those long runs had race-pace miles about every two weeks. My body knew what a 6:50 mile felt like. It was revving to go on race day. Mile after mile clicked by, all within a couple of seconds of each other, smooth, comfortable.

In the last 5K, I needed to accelerate slightly, to adjust for the inevitability of not running perfect tangents. (I ran 13.1 miles in 1:29:21, but crossed the finish line at 13.17 miles in 1:29:46, my official time.)

I finished in pure elation, yelling, “I did it!” to anyone who would listen.

I know the second speed workout helped me achieve my goal, but experts suggest using the second speed workout sparingly and thoughtfully. Wijayaratne says, generally, additional workouts should be added in the building and peak phases of training, which follow the base-building phase.

I added the workout because I wanted a breakthrough performance, but it can also be beneficial for runners who are finding themselves in a rut or a performance plateau as it spices up training, Wijayaratne says.

“That extra day is a lever, not a baseline,” Wijayaratne says. “A lever shouldn’t be down all the time. You should be using it strategically.”

Over an extended period of time, the extra intensity and load could contribute to the risk of injury, fatigue, and all-around burnout.

As race day approached, I told my training partners that I wouldn’t continue this second workout as a new norm. I was tired.

Heather is the former food and nutrition editor for Runner’s World, the author of The Runner’s World Vegetarian Cookbook, and a nine-time marathoner with a best of 3:23. She’s also proud of her 19:40 5K and 5:33 mile. Heather is an RRCA certified run coach.
