#281. Are Single Older Ladies Really Happy Without Marriage? Experts Weigh In

At some point in most women’s lives, a familiar line of thinking creeps in—whether on its own or planted by well-meaning parents: What if I don’t get married? What if I never find my person and end up alone?

For Joan, the panic hit in her 30s—strong enough to land her in a psychologist’s office. Back then, she says, “a woman who didn’t want a husband was assumed to have something wrong with her.” But her therapist—married with children, yet more open-minded than most—didn’t try to correct her with cheesy motivational mantras or fear tactics about a “ticking clock.” Instead, she asked a different question: What kind of husband would you want, if you had one?

Joan listed a few traits. Someone busy, she recalls saying. Someone deeply absorbed in his own life—his job, his hobbies, his community.

“So you'd want someone intellectually stimulating?” her therapist asked.

“No,” Joan replied. “I’d want someone who’s never home.”

It landed as a joke, though deep down, it wasn’t. What came from that session was an almost accidental realization that sounded radical at the time (it was around 1980): “Some people genuinely live their best lives independently,” Joan tells me. Now 79, single, and uninterested in changing her relationship status, she has spent decades proving her theory true.

For much of modern history, women like Joan were cast as anomalies, freaks, or worse: cautionary tales. There’s “the childless cat lady.” The “old maid.” The “lonely spinster.” Singlehood was framed as a transitional phase, a temporary stop on the way to finding the One. Not an end goal, and certainly not a fulfilling one.

But the stigma is softening—and the older, unmarried women of this generation are living proof that a life without a husband isn’t a fallback; it’s a deeply satisfying choice.

You can see it in the collective fatigue around modern dating (78% of users on apps including Tinder, Hinge, and Bumble reported feeling burnt out, per a recent Forbes Health survey). Young adults in their mid 20s to early 30s (the supposed “prime marriage years”) are having far less sex than previous generations, with sexual inactivity up roughly 50% for women over the past decade. The shift shows up in pop culture too—in particular, the growing appetite for plots that sideline romance in favor of friendship, independence, and chosen families (like in Barbie and Wicked).

But perhaps the clearest proof is in lived experiences. The several 70-somethings I spoke with for this story have been single for decades—and aren’t wishing they’d done it any differently. If anything, their lives carry a sense of ease and expansiveness. Many describe weekly, laughter-filled girls’ nights and happy hours; solo trips planned on a whim; financial freedom to buy property, adopt pets, start small businesses…literally do whatever they want, whenever they want. A few still date casually, dipping in and out of steamy flings only when it suits them. Others have opted out of romance entirely. “My favorite part?” one 73-year-old woman tells me bluntly. “Not having to bicker or put up with an incompetent man. That’s probably why I’m the least stressed I’ve ever been.”

Across their stories, there’s no regret or hint of “missing out.” Just single older ladies enjoying where they are—nothing like the caricatures of the bitter man-hater or the desperate, unlucky romantic we’re used to seeing.

As Joan is quick to point out, “not everyone starts off wanting a romantic relationship and then moves on to singlehood as Plan B.” It’s a perspective that’s become increasingly common, so much so that sociologist Bella DePaulo, PhD, built a framework (and wrote a book) about it: being Single at Heart. These are women (including herself) who don’t end up alone; they orient toward it as a genuine preference.

“I still smile when I think about the men I dated when I was a very young adult,” Dr. DePaulo, 72, tells me. “But I remember even more fondly how I felt when each of those relationships ended: finally free.”

The practical benefits of singledom—solitude, strong friendships, fewer relational stressors—aren’t exclusive to unmarried folks. “But in my opinion, couples are never free the way single people are,” Dr. DePaulo says. The difference, she claims, is psychological: the ability to structure a day, a life, or a passing thought without reflexively factoring in another person’s needs or reactions. “A romantic partner is also there in your mind almost all the time,” Dr. DePaulo points out—even if only on the periphery. “That might be comforting for some. But it can also feel a bit unwelcome, as if they’re always considering what their significant other may be wanting or feeling.” Remove that, and your attention and energy become fully your own.

Of course, the ability to choose this lifestyle is relatively recent. For centuries, marriage wasn’t just a matter of romance—women relied on it for financial stability, social acceptance, and a sanctioned path to family, Kris Marsh, PhD, sociologist and author of The Love Jones Cohort: Single and Living Alone in the Black Middle Class, tells SELF. But with greater access to education, careers, and economic independence (along with broader definitions of intimacy, family, and fulfillment), the pressure to couple up has eased. As of 2023, 42% of US adults were unpartnered, according to the Pew Research Center (up from 29% in 1990). And among the non-daters younger than 50, half aren’t interested in a relationship—though enjoying your single status doesn’t have to involve an anti-love attitude.

“Now, a lot of women are looking for something additive,” Dr. Marsh says. “I’ve heard over and over, ‘I’m already in a very good place on my own. So you can’t be a distraction. You can’t disrupt my peace.’” Though for most, that epiphany doesn’t happen overnight.

Alice Foster, who recently turned 80, is a classic example of someone who followed the cultural script handed to many in her generation: marry young, raise children, enjoy the stability. “It was fine, but I felt like it was never really about me,” Foster tells SELF. “It wasn’t my life.”

In 1988, her marriage ended in divorce—though what followed wasn’t the loss she had been taught to fear. It was space. Peace. Recalibration. She moved upstate. Went back to school. Built a new career in nursing. Slowly, she began constructing a life that finally felt like her own.

“I feel like I’m in my 50s. It’s been so fun,” she reflects. “I love being retired. I love traveling. I love having people visit me. I love not having to answer to anybody. I’ve been single for so long and loving this life so much that, honestly, I don’t want to get tied down.” And that, experts say, is often how it works.

Rather than being a fixed moral stance or a lifelong rejection of romance, singlehood tends to be a lived, flexible experience—an acceptance of being on your own that you don’t always realize you’re choosing until later. Maybe, like Foster, you leave an unsatisfying marriage. You pull back on exhaustive online dating. You decide this is the year you’ll focus on work, hobbies, or travel. Over time, you stop planning life around the possibility of a relationship…and start seeing that you already have the joy you thought only a husband could provide.

Still, a question tends to linger: Are these women actually happy?

Recent research suggests yes—in fact, satisfaction with singlehood tends to increase with age, starting for people in their 40s. Despite cultural progress, there’s still skepticism as to why anyone would willingly stay single. Whereas married people are taken at their word when they claim fulfillment (even though we know that’s not always true), those who deviate face public scrutiny. “They have to be extra strong, exceptionally confident to stand comfortably in their singleness and validate to the world that they are, in fact, thriving,” Dr. Marsh adds—an expectation that flattens single older ladies into either a hyper-independent success story or a pitiable failure, with little room for nuance.

But that pressure can have an unintended effect too. After decades of being asked by society to justify their lifestyle, many simply stop performing. All of the women I spoke with didn’t overexplain. They weren’t defensive. They didn’t seem especially interested in winning me over.

It takes a certain kind of confidence and clarity to stop shaping your life around what’s expected and historically rewarded, and instead follow what feels good, without apology. What you get then, as Dr. Marsh has observed in her research, is a quieter, rarer form of happiness—one that isn’t performed and doesn’t ask for external validation. Instead, it feels much more genuine. It endures.

#282. The Painful Truth About Saddle Sores: 3 Myths Cyclists Need to Stop Believing

Learn what causes saddle sores, how to prevent them, and when to find a medical professional

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Recently, I was testing a new bike with a saddle that I wasn’t excited about straight out of the box. Fortunately, I have ridden a lot of different saddles over the years with different shapes, sizes, and construction—unfortunately that meant I had a gut feeling this saddle was not going to be my friend.

I’m not new to saddle sores, but it has been a long time since I had to deal with one. On my second ride with this test bike, I started to feel one coming on, so I tried to keep the area clean and dry. Then I took the bike out for a longer test of about 50 miles and it became apparent about halfway through the ride that the saddle sore was here to stay.

Saddle sores are a part of cycling for many cyclists, but they don’t have to be. Saddle sores can be a sore subject to talk about, but it’s important to address anything that takes away from the experience of a ride. Here we’ll talk about the difference between saddle sores and saddle soreness, three common myths around saddle sores, and give you a few tips on what to do if one creeps in on a ride.

Before diving into the myths, it will be helpful to talk about the difference between saddle sores and saddle soreness. “Saddle soreness may be considered for any local irritation, discomfort, bruising or chafing of the skin. Friction or rubbing can lead to irritation and may be the first sign of a developing saddle sore,” says Steve Mathews. He’s the registered physical therapist who started Chamois Butt’r back in 1988 to help alleviate some of these pain points for cyclists.

“A saddle sore is a more localized skin irritation and may involve an inflamed hair follicle or, in some cases, an infected hair follicle, which is called a boil. When skin becomes irritated or damaged, from repeated friction or riding with an ingrown hair, bacteria that normally live on the skin can enter the damaged area and sometimes cause an infection,” Mathews continues.

I’ve been riding bikes consistently for over two decades and I have rarely gotten saddle sores. Some things like riding multiple days in a row in wet conditions, lower-quality chamois, or simply the wrong saddles have been the culprit much of the time for my experience. Part of getting through saddle soreness is riding more, but if you’re a cyclist experiencing saddle sores there is likely something else going on.

“Common factors that can lead to sores include improper bicycle fit, a poorly fitting or incompatible saddle, poorly fitting riding shorts or bibs, too much riding time without gradual adaptation, improper fitting or lower-quality shorts, and of course, friction. We like to help reduce friction by applying high quality chamois cream directly to your skin or cycling chamois, like Chamois Butt’r,” says Mathews.

While I was working in a bike shop I sold a lot of saddles, and I’ve spent a lot of my own time trying different saddles too. One of the biggest mistakes I would see people making was around saddle choice. If people were uncomfortable on the bike the typical move was to go for a super wide and ultra padded saddle—regardless of sit bone width, bike type, or rider position. Saddles are so subjective and what works for one person won’t necessarily work for another.

Mathews and I both agree that a wider saddle can increase heat, moisture, and friction. I’ve seen people go for saddles so wide that it caused friction in places they did not expect. “The goal is to find a saddle that helps reduce pressure on your touch points and minimize friction. Look for saddles that fit your anatomy and help reduce pressure on your sit bones. This allows you to distribute your weight more evenly across your sit bones,” says Mathews.

Any of the saddle sores that I’ve experienced I was able to treat them at home, but that’s not always the case for everyone. I know several people who have had saddle sores linger to the point of needing medical attention. If it lasts more than a few weeks, gets infected, or is extremely painful, it’s worth getting it checked out by a medical professional. “Once you have a sore, especially if the skin is broken, don’t assume more chamois cream will treat it,” says Mathews.

“The best approach is prevention. Try to determine what may have brought the saddle sore on and address the cause: friction, bike position, quality of your bib shorts, fatigue, overtraining, or an ingrown hair,” says Mathews.

The best ways I have found to reduce the likelihood of saddle sores are to not ride in wet chamois (as best as possible), using lower quality or older chamois, and use the right saddle. On long rides I use something like Chamois Butt’r (the Ultra is my favorite for long rides) to prevent too much friction.

Mathews added some tips like: apply an antibacterial ointment directly to the saddle sore, don’t stay in your riding shorts for much time after you ride, dry yourself thoroughly after riding, reach for cotton underwear for more air flow after a ride, and cleanse the entire area on and around the saddle sore with an antibacterial cleanser each time you bathe. For the last tip he noted, “I use a surgical scrub product that is available at most pharmacies.”

This is where things are subjective—I have friends who do multiday bike tours and don’t wear a chamois at all. These tips are a jumping off point to help you find what works for you. And remember if you start developing any additional symptoms from saddle sores, or it is overly painful and won’t go away, get it checked out by a medical professional.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

#283. Toot Toot! 6 Tips to Prevent Protein Farts

Protein farts are a common, albeit smelly, side effect of high-protein diets. They happen because of how proteins are digested. But(t) don’t worry! We have some tips to help you say goodbye to those pungent protein toots without giving up your gains.

Protein farts are episodes of flatulence that don’t smell too pleasant! They’re generally due to upping your protein intake from supplements like protein shakes.

And while these butt whistles may be embarrassing, you’ll be glad to know they’re generally harmless.

Farts consist of different gases. The most stinky odors usually come from your gut bacteria, producing sulfur-containing compounds as they break down food. The main culprit is hydrogen sulfide, which gives off a characteristic rotten egg smell, yum!

But why do your protein choices lead to thunder from down under?

Well, there’s not much evidence that a high-protein diet causes protein farts. However, there’s some anecdotal evidence that supplementary protein — like protein bars, protein shakes, and powder powders — increases flatulence, but it’s likely due to non-protein ingredients like lactose.

Supplements containing whey protein or casein are derived from milk and are high in lactose, which can increase flatulence. If your body can’t properly digest lactose, it ends up in your colon, where bacteria feast on it, producing — you guessed it — more gas and cheek flapping.

So, whey protein can throw a curveball for those who are lactose intolerant or sensitive. Surprisingly, it might also stir up digestive drama even for folks who typically handle dairy like champs, potentially due to additives like fart-inducing sweeteners or thickeners.

Some people may also have more significant issues digesting protein. Proteins are big, complex molecules — breaking them down is no small task for your gut. Plant-based protein supplements, like those based on soya beans, may also worsen flatulence.

FYI: Another reason why flatulence is common with protein powders and supplements is due to the addition of artificial sweeteners in the powders and bars, like sugar alcohols, sucralose, sorbitol, xylitol, and stevia.

If you’re looking to continue your protein regimen without becoming a walking, talking whoopee cushion, here are some strategic adjustments you can make:

Don’t just dive into the deep end with your protein intake — wade in slowly. Gradually increasing the amount of protein you consume allows your digestive system to adjust without getting overwhelmed. This step-by-step approach can help minimize the likelihood of excessive gas.

Keep the water flowing. Drinking plenty of water is crucial as it helps your digestive system handle higher protein levels more efficiently. Proper hydration aids in the breakdown and absorption of nutrients, which can help prevent gas buildup.

Sometimes, your body needs a little extra help. Enzyme supplements like Beano or Lactaid can be game-changers, especially if you consume proteins that your body struggles with. These supplements help break down proteins and lactose, making digestion smoother and less gassy.

Variety isn’t just the spice of life — it can also be the solution to your protein fart problems. If whey protein tends to upset your stomach, explore other options like plant-based or animal-based proteins that might be easier to digest. Diversifying your protein sources can also ensure you get a broad range of nutrients.

What you blend your protein powder with can make a big difference. If you’re whipping up a protein shake, be mindful of adding high-fiber fruits and vegetables, as these can also increase gas production. Try to find a balance that allows you to enjoy the benefits of protein and fiber without the extra flatulence.

Introducing probiotics into your diet can improve your gut health, which can help manage and reduce gas production. Whether through supplements or probiotic-rich foods like yogurt, kefir, or sauerkraut, boosting your gut flora can aid in better overall digestion and less discomfort from gas.

Protein farts are a rather windy side effect of a high-protein diet, but they don’t have to knock you off course. Try easing into your protein consumption, staying hydrated, diversifying your protein sources, and integrating enzyme supplements or probiotics to max those gains, minus the stink bombs!

Last medically reviewed on June 30, 2024

#284. Brandon McNulty’s New Rainbow Colnago Is Here—and It’s Surprisingly Close to the Bike You Can Buy

McNulty’s new Colnago gets rainbow bands, chrome logos, and a hidden Montreal tribute.

Only six days ago, Brandon McNulty attacked and rode clear of the lead group with a little over 30 kilometers to go in the UCI World Championships men’s road race. That winning move on the streets of Montreal clinched victory for the 28-year-old Arizonan, who brought home America’s first elite men’s road win in 33 years.

This morning, at a service course set up in a hotel parking lot in Bologna, Italy, Bicycling was on hand as Colnago presented the freshly minted World Champion with his new, custom-painted race bikes before tomorrow’s Giro dell’Emilia one-day race. McNulty’s size large Y1Rs bikes—three in total: a race bike and two spares—are finished in a glitter dark clearcoat over raw carbon with chrome Colnago logos. As is customary for the reigning UCI World Champion, the bike has the famous “arc en ciel” rainbow bands across its fork, seat tube, and seat stays. A nice detail is the date of McNulty’s race win (“27.09.2026”) and a Canadian maple leaf hidden on the frame’s headtube behind the bayonet fork.

In addition to the custom-painted Y1Rs, UAE Team Emirates XRG team sponsor Pissei were on hand to unveil the World Champion’s new rainbow stripes on a selection of speedsuits, jerseys, and bib shorts. McNulty also had fresh MET Manta aero helmets to match the white World Champ kits.

Before Colnago presented the custom bikes to the World Champion, I was granted exclusive access to the glittery machines. I checked out details on McNulty’s bikes and watched as team mechanics put finishing touches to ensure they were set up to his liking and had identical fit dimensions.

Frameset: Colnago Y1Rs, size LWheels: Enve SES 4.5 ProTires: Continental GP5000 TT, 700x28cDrivetrain: Shimano Dura-Ace Di2, R9170, 2x12-speedCrankset: Shimano Dura-Ace with power meter, 170mm armsChainrings: 54/40T (Carbon-Ti rings on race bike, Dura-Ace on spares)Cassette: Shimano Dura-Ace, 12-speed, 11-34TPedals: Shimano Dura-Ace, R9100Cockpit: Colnago one-piece, 145mm extension, 377/400mm widthSaddle: Fizik Antares R1Cages: Elite Lightweight Carbon

What stands out about Brandon McNulty’s new bike is how similar it is to a Y1Rs you can walk into bike shops and buy. While this Y1Rs has custom paint and artwork of a World Champion, McNulty’s bike doesn’t use the recently spotted prototype Shimano road parts, and even his pedals are R9100 models and not the newly unveiled R9300 models. The only noticeable special parts are the Bikone ceramic bearing bottom bracket and Carbon-Ti UDH-compatible hanger. The primary race bike also has Carbon-Ti chainrings.

McNulty’s component details were also not far off what many of us ride. Although he has larger chainrings than many of us typically use, his bike also has a wide-range 11-34T cassette. Similarly, he was not riding super short cranks; the Dura-Ace arms are marked 170mm. For tires, McNulty’s wheelsets for the Giro dell’Emilia have 28 mm-wide Continental GP5000 TTs.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#285. I Ran 2:25 at the Chicago Marathon—and Felt Like I Failed. Until I Remembered This.

When tough conditions made my goal pace difficult, I found a way to get to the finish line without spiraling.

I’ve had the Chicago Marathon circled on my calendar for well over a year. I love the city of Chicago, and it’s one of the fastest courses in the world, so my excitement built throughout 2026, especially after I had to pull out of my planned spring marathon due to an Achilles issue.

Going into marathon weekend, I knew the weather would be a factor. Forecasts called for temps in the low 60s at the start, with high humidity and sun exposure. But my prerace plan was firm. My coach wanted me to approach the race aggressively and “not leave anything on the table.”

After adjusting slightly for conditions, I had two main goals: finish in the top 50 overall and break the 2:20 barrier. The plan was to run a 5:15 to 5:20 pace and hang on as long as I could.

From the opening mile, I knew it was going to be a long day. My heart rate quickly climbed into the low 180s—far too high to sustain for two-plus hours—and, even after settling into my pace, I never felt smooth. The rest of the race was damage control. My 5:15 miles slowed to 5:20s, which slowed to 5:25s, which—by the final 10K—slowed to a 6:00 pace.

I finished the race in 2:25:07, good for 118th place and about a minute slower than my personal best of 2:24:12. Not a total disaster, by any means, but my yearlong dream of PRing had been deferred.

As I walked through the finishing chute, I was a mess of emotions. But one thing kept my head high. I took a swing and went for an ambitious goal and simply didn’t have it on the day. Instead of feeling sorry for myself, I took pride in knowing that I didn’t cower and held it together.

That’s the tough part about the marathon. Your training might go well, you successfully avoid getting sick during the taper, you carb-load like a madman—and it simply isn’t enough. There are only so many times you can run an all-out marathon each year, and it seems unfair when the weather (or your legs) don’t cooperate. But you signed up for it. It comes with the territory. It’s a hard pill to swallow, but it shouldn’t discourage you from signing up for the next one.

After taking some time to process the race, I’ve found plenty of positive takeaways, even though the result wasn’t what I envisioned.

It’s tempting, during a tough race, to spiral and convince yourself that an off day is an indictment of your training or dedication to the sport. But sometimes, you have to take one on the chin. And most of the time, the end result isn’t as bad as your mid-marathon brain will try to convince you.

Theo Kahler is the senior news editor at Runner’s World. He’s a former all-conference collegiate runner at Winthrop University, and he received his master’s degree in liberal arts studies from Wake Forest University, where he was a member of one of the top distance-running teams in the NCAA. Kahler has reported on the ground at major events such as the Paris Olympics, U.S. Olympic Trials, New York City Marathon, and Boston Marathon. He’s run 14:20 in the 5K, 1:05:37 in the half marathon, and finished 40th at the 2025 New York City Marathon. He enjoys spotting tracks from the sky on airplanes. (Look for colorful ovals around football fields.)

#286. 6 Supplements Doctors Actually Take

These days, it seems like everyone is taking a supplement—to look better, think better, sleep better, relax better, poop better, or work out better. And you’re not imagining things: Half of adults and one-third of children in the United States take supplements regularly, according to the Office of Dietary Supplements.

Supplements may be ubiquitous, but many experts have serious reservations about their rise. First, most physicians recommend obtaining nutrients directly from food rather than a pill or capsule. Second, supplements aren’t reviewed for safety and effectiveness by the FDA before they hit shelves. Because of all the concerns surrounding supplements, Jeffrey Linder, MD, MPH, a general internist and professor of medicine at the Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine, takes a dim view of the category overall: In fact, “a vast majority of supplements are probably worthless,” he tells SELF.

Still, there are exceptions to every rule—and supplements are no different. Many experts, as it turns out, do take some type of supplement, but they are choosy about which ones they select. Read on to learn more about six they actually use.

How it works: Vitamin D plays key roles in bone health and immune function. In fact, low vitamin D is associated with a wide swath of medical conditions, according to Dr. Linder—including cancer, autoimmune diseases, infectious diseases, and cardiovascular issues (and, famously, seasonal affective disorder, or SAD).

Why some docs like it: Vitamin D deficiency is widespread, especially among people who live at northern latitudes that don’t see as much sun during the winter, and people with darker skin. What’s more, few foods contain significant amounts of vitamin D, so it’s tough to source enough from your diet. Lawrence Green, MD, a dermatologist and clinical professor at the George Washington University School of Medicine and Health Sciences, tells SELF that these two factors make vitamin D a rare nutrient “we do need to take supplements for.” Nearly every single one of the eight doctors who spoke with SELF for this article said they take a vitamin D supplement, especially in the winter, though the frequency and dosage varied.

What to keep in mind: Most docs recommend vitamin D3 (also known as cholecalciferol) over vitamin D2 (also known as ergocalciferol), as studies have shown that D3 is more effective at raising vitamin D levels in your blood. Whichever option you decide on, try to take it with food—specifically, an item that contains fat. Because vitamin D is a fat-soluble nutrient, it “absorbs better that way,” Sara Velayati, MD, an obesity medicine specialist at Montefiore Einstein and an assistant professor at Albert Einstein College of Medicine in New York City, tells SELF. For this reason, Dr. Green makes a point of taking his supplements with breakfast or dinner. “The fattier and thicker the meal,” the better, he says.

What it does: Calcium is a mineral that helps build and maintain strong bones and teeth. Women in their 40s approaching menopausal age should make it a particular priority to ensure their intake is adequate, Rachel Pessah-Pollack, MD, an endocrinologist at NYU Langone Health and a clinical professor at the NYU Grossman School of Medicine, tells SELF, as the physical changes that come with perimenopause and menopause can heighten bone loss and downstream health conditions like osteoporosis.

Who takes it: Like the other supplements on this list, calcium is best sourced from your diet, Dr. Pessah-Pollack says. “But if you’re not able to (I try to get dairy products but often come up short), a supplement is needed.” She takes a combined calcium and vitamin D tablet daily, as vitamin D helps calcium absorb.

How to take it: “The type of calcium supplements you are taking matters,” Dr. Pessah-Pollack says. Calcium carbonate and calcium citrate are the two most common. “Calcium carbonate should be taken with food because it requires gastric acid to be absorbed,” Dr. Pessah-Pollack says. Calcium citrate is an alternative that can be taken with or without food.

How it works: Magnesium is a mineral that can enhance sleep and muscle recovery. Research has also shown that it’s effective at preventing migraines, Raquel Zemtsov, MD, MPH, a family medicine doctor and assistant professor at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine, tells SELF.

Why some docs like it: In addition to Dr. Zemtsov, who takes magnesium to stave off migraine symptoms, Dr. Velayati takes magnesium for the sleep benefits. Likewise, Sheeva Talebian, MD, a reproductive endocrinologist at CCRM Fertility of New York, and Kathleen Jordan, MD, an internal medicine physician and chief medical officer at Midi Health, also turn to it at bedtime to boost their shut-eye.

What to keep in mind: Some types of magnesium are better tolerated, says Dr. Velayati—something to note if you’re especially sensitive to side effects. Magnesium glycinate “avoids the gastrointestinal upset caused by magnesium oxides and magnesium citrates,” for example, Dr. Jordan says. Depending on your needs, however, magnesium glycinate might not be the best option: Magnesium oxide is the recommended magnesium type for migraines, so that’s the one Dr. Zemtsov keeps on hand, for example. Taking magnesium with food can also help prevent GI distress, according to Dr. Velayati.

How it works: Omega-3 fatty acids are polyunsaturated fats that are important for cardiovascular health. Common omega-3 supplements include fish oil and krill oil.

Why some docs like it: Dr. Jordan, Dr. Talebian, and Dr. Velayati all take omega-3s. “With their anti-inflammatory properties and association with improved brain health, this is a popular supplement among physicians, myself included,” Dr. Jordan, who takes krill oil, says. Similarly, Dr. Velayati dabbles in fish oil, but takes it selectively. “The right dose really depends on the goal, but I don’t think it’s necessary for everyone,” she says.

What to keep in mind: Fish oil supplements can have a characteristic fishy aftertaste, so it might take some trial and error to find one that works for you (read: doesn’t leave you gagging). What’s more, absorption and bioavailability can be a challenge, according to Dr. Jordan. Because omega-3s, like vitamin D, are fat-soluble, taking fish oil with a meal that contains fat can help skirt this problem. Some claim krill oil doesn’t cause the dreaded aftertaste as much as fish oil, and evidence suggests it’s also better absorbed by the body.

How it works: Iron, a mineral, acts as an essential ingredient in hemoglobin, a protein found in your red blood cells. Without enough iron, your blood won’t be able to carry out its core task of delivering oxygen to organs and tissues, resulting in anemia.

Why some docs like it: Iron deficiency is common in women due to the loss of blood during menstruation every month. “Occasionally, despite trying my hardest to seek out iron-rich foods, I still develop an iron deficiency,” Dr. Zemtsov says. When that happens, she takes ferrous gluconate (a particular type of iron supplement) every other day to treat or prevent anemia, since research shows iron supplements are better absorbed and cause fewer side effects that way. Dr. Jordan also takes iron supplements, citing the advantages for sleep, hair health, and overall energy.

What to keep in mind: Iron absorption is enhanced by vitamin C, so pairing your iron supplement with a food that contains vitamin C or even a vitamin C supplement—as Dr. Zemtsov does—can be helpful.

How it works: Fiber, a type of carb, boosts digestion in a variety of ways: It keeps you full, helps prevent constipation, and supports bowel health. Besides the GI stuff, it also serves other functions in your body, including stabilizing your blood sugar and lowering “bad” LDL cholesterol.

Why some docs like it: “Unless you are that rare woman who regularly gets in her 25 to 30 grams per day, extra fiber intake is beneficial for almost everyone, and addresses multiple issues for me personally, including prediabetes and a rising cholesterol level,” Dr. Jordan says. She takes a fiber supplement as needed, on days when she doesn’t manage to hit her goal.

What to keep in mind: If your body isn’t acclimated to a high fiber intake, suddenly bombarding it could cause some digestive distress (think gas and bloating), so start slow to ease the transition. You’ll also need to increase your water intake simultaneously, since fiber requires water to work.

“When someone is considering a supplement, I usually recommend having a specific reason for taking it”—like a confirmed nutritional deficiency, Dr. Velayati says. “Overall, I view supplements as a way to fill a gap, not a substitute for good nutrition, sleep, exercise, and evidence-based medical care.” The bottom line: Supplements are really meant for plugging holes in your diet.

#287. Vibration Plate Benefits, According to a Weightlifting Coach

Vibration plates are like mini surfboards that give you a good shimmy while you’re exercising. Though you won’t find a mountain of extensive research behind them, you may be impressed by their possible benefits.

We asked a weightlifting coach to explain and show us how to add good vibrations to our workout routine.

These machines, which look like platforms or scales, are designed to activate something called whole-body vibration (WBV). WBV makes the body work harder by forcing it to contract muscles automatically.

Fans of WBV like to perform classic exercises on top of these machines, including:

Research points to WBV’s ability to boost blood flow.

Weightlifting coach Jarrod Nobbe explains that vibration plates help move blood by stimulating muscle contractions through rapid vibrations.

“The rhythmic contraction and relaxation of muscles help pump blood more efficiently throughout the body,” he says.

As Nobbe adds, movement generally increases blood flow and core temperature, preparing the body for activity. This means vibration plates may be an excellent warm-up activity.

A 2021 study showed that WBV can be an alternative exercise for older adults, boosting the effects of strengthening exercise.

Nobbe says this is because WBV engages muscles in a way that mimics resistance training.

“The vibrations activate and force muscles to contract and relax multiple times per second, which can lead to gains in muscle strength and endurance over time, especially when combined with specific exercises,” he says.

Nobbe points to some anecdotal evidence suggesting that regular use of vibration plates may help boost energy levels, possibly thanks to increased blood circulation and enhanced muscle activation.

“Ultimately, I stand by the idea that movement is medicine,” Nobbe says. “Tons of research already proves that regular physical activity boosts mood, mental health, and promotes energy levels.”

Nobbe says WBV may reduce muscle soreness, stiffness, and inflammation by encouraging blood flow to the muscles. This, he explains, aids in faster recovery post-exercise or injury.

WBV has been shown to improve bone mineral density, which Nobbe points out may positively affect those at risk of osteoporosis.

“The mechanical vibrations stimulate bone cells, potentially leading to increased bone density and strength, delivering the same positive bone health benefits of resistance training,” he says.

“Unfortunately, vibration plates aren’t a one-stop shop for weight loss,” Nobbe says.

He explains that vibration plates alone are unlikely to significantly reduce belly fat without dietary changes and additional exercise.

“While vibration plates can contribute to overall calorie expenditure and muscle activation, targeted fat loss requires a comprehensive approach including diet, cardio exercise, and resistance training,” he says.

These tips will help you stand on your vibration plate with a slight bend at your knee or perform exercises on top of it.

More research is needed around WBV — AKA what happens when you use a vibration plate — but existing smaller research is promising.

Use your machine carefully, and remember to maintain a healthy lifestyle and workout routine.

Last medically reviewed on June 27, 2024

#288. Your Ultimate Guide to the 2026 Ironman World Championship in Kona

Triathletes scout the swim course ahead of the 2026 Ironman World Championship. (Photo: Brad Kaminski/Triathlete)

It’s almost time for the 2026 Ironman World Championship, with men and women coming together to share the course for the first time since 2019 in a renewed one-day format. The Big Island is buzzing, and so are we, because there’s nothing like the Super Bowl of triathlon!

The pro start list is set, and fans of triathlon are placing their bets: Can Kat Matthews break her runner-up streak (2025, 2024, and 2022)? Will Kristian Blummenfelt find redemption for his blunders in Kona 2024? Can Taylor Knibb pull off the elusive 70.3 Worlds/Kona double victory? We’re following all the storylines and offering deep expert insights into what might happen during the biggest triathlon race of the year.

Hear from long-time triathlon data expert Thorsten Radde, get the latest news from award-winning journalist Tim Heming, and read detailed profiles and inspiring stories from Sarah Wassner Flynn. The Triathlete team will be on site in Hawaii starting race week, so bookmark this page and return regularly for everything you need to know leading into the big showdown.

This is your expert swim-bike-run countdown to Kona.

Despite decades of data, advanced nutrition, and precision pacing, Kona proves time and again that science is no match for Madame Pele. Tim Heming reflects on how this year’s race demonstrated that the Kona code is still uncrackable – and that’s exactly why we keep coming back.

Beyond her inspiring victory on the Big Island, Taylor Knibb’s message reminded us why endurance sports create a bond unlike any other. Triathlete senior editor Susan Lacke reflects on why Knibb’s win hit us all right in the feels.

Every year, Kona inspires – and this year was no exception. Triathlete photographer Brad Kaminski captured moments you likely didn’t see on the race broadcast, letting you re-live the race through his lens.

Feeling wrecked today? You’re not alone. From muscle micro-tears and brain fog to gut distress, science explains why racing – or even watching – the Ironman World Championship in Hawaii leaves you utterly steamrolled for days.

Julie Derron overcame a 3-minute bike penalty and an early blow up on the run to finish third in her Ironman World Championship Debut. Hear what she had to say in her post-race interview with Triathlete.

Imogen Simmonds had a steady day on her way to placing fifth overall at the 2026 Ironman World Championship. Here’s what she had to say about her race in Kona, which she described as “so beyond my expectations.”

Despite serving a 2-minute penalty, Matthew Marquardt had the second-fastest bike split (just 5 seconds behind Gregory Barnaby) and ran a consistent marathon to take third place. Here’s what the American had to say after his best day in Kona to date.

Kristian Blummenfelt finished eighth at the 2026 Ironman World Championship despite spending much of the race in podium contention. He shares what happened halfway through the run – and how he’s feeling after the race.

After serving a 3-minute penalty on the bike, Gustav Iden overcame a nearly 9-minute deficit at the start of the run to take second place behind Vincent Luis. In this post-race interview, the Norwegian takes us through his day.

The Frenchman went to some dark places in training to win the 2026 Ironman World Championship in his debut – and final race as a pro triathlete. Here’s what he had to say after his Kona victory.

American Taylor Knibb became just the second American to win the Ironman World Championship in 30 years with a dramatic victory in Kona. And she has thoughts. We caught up with the delightfully quick-witted Taylor Knibb after she finished what she started last year.

The 2026 Ironman World Championship was eagerly anticipated as a return to one day of racing for men and women for the first time in seven years. But despite sharing the same course, the men’s and women’s pro races could not have been more different. At the link below, see our race-day live blog and race recaps of two thrilling races on the Big Island.

It’s the final task before 2,500 triathletes race the 2026 Ironman World Championship: putting the bikes down for the night on the Kona Pier. Staff photographer Brad Kaminski was at age-group bike check-in today, spotting the fastest, freshest, and funkiest rigs rolling through. See the full gallery at the link below.

As the Ironman World Championship returns to a single-day competition in Kona, it has ended a drought in cutting-edge gear and tech launches that had become a logistical burden with the split locations. Read more from editor-in-chief Chris Foster on the new gear trends he’s spotting on pro and age-group bikes this year.

2022 Ironman world champion Chelsea Sodaro has withdrawn from this weekend’s race, Triathlete confirmed today. The American’s absence means only three of the four past women’s champions on this weekend’s start list will race at Kona 2026: Solveig Løvseth (NOR), Laura Philipp (DEU), and Lucy Charles-Barclay (GBR).

Ever wanted to ride on a Cam Wurf-designed bike? The Aussie pro gave us a sneak peek at the Pinarello F TR triathlon bike, which will make its race debut on the Big Island this weekend. See all the details, plus learn how Wurf and his fellow pros helped dial in the design, which will be available for global purchase in January 2027.

From missing champions and awkward silences to bold race strategies and emotional farewells, there was plenty to unpack at the 2026 Ironman World Championship pro press conference. If you didn’t catch the livestream, we’ve pulled some of the most interesting quotes from top pros on the dais. Also, can we talk about Lucy Charles-Barclay’s socks?

On Thursdays, we wear undies and run down the street. The Kona Underpants Run is one of the most beloved pre-race experiences at the Ironman World Championship, and this year’s race was just as cheeky as ever. Read about how this weird race came to be, plus see staff photographer Brad Kaminski’s snaps from the run, at the link below.

“It’s been a long time since we had a truly exciting and innovative batch of new (and new-ish) products in Kona, but 2026 does not disappoint,” writes Editor-in-Chief Chris Foster of this year’s product launches at the Ironman World Championship. From double-decker hats to virtual swimming to superlightweight crank arms, read on for the most interesting new products spotted around the island.

Yes, Aliʻi Drive is where everything is happening this week, but if you want to find some breath amidst the bustle, Chris Foster has shared his top-secret favorite spots from the past decade of covering the Ironman World Championship. From quiet run routes to the best poke on the island (and no long lines to get it), get the insider info here.

The 2026 Ironman World Championship pro field is full of rivalries, dark horses, and world-class speed. But who has the best odds of winning? That’s exactly the question TriRating analyst Thorsten Radde answers for us in his analysis of this year’s Kona contenders. Get the full rundown on who to watch, key matchups, and what to expect at the 2026 Ironman World Championships at the link below.

The 2026 Ironman World Championship in Kona is returning to a single-day event, bringing high-stakes racing, increased athlete density, and a renewed focus on fairness. So how will Ironman keep the Kona bike leg a draft-free affair and mitigate the impact of the men’s race on the women’s as the two fields share the course? We sent contributor Tim Heming to find out – at the link below, read his interviews with Ironman’s head referee, Jimmy Riccitello, and RaceRanger CEO James Elvery.

A showdown awaits in the women’s race this weekend, and it’s going to be a good one. Can Lucy Charles-Barclay and Taylor Knibb hold off the heat and a stacked chase pack featuring defending champ Solveig Løvseth, run course record-holder Kat Matthews, and Nice winner Laura Philipp?

Read our full preview of the 2026 Ironman World Championship Women’s Race at the link below.

The 2026 Men’s Ironman World Championship in Kona is shaping up to be an absolute thriller! Without defending champion Casper Stornes, who takes the crown on the Big Island? From Sam Laidlow’s powerhouse bike pace to the epic late-run battle brewing between Kristian Blummenfelt, Gustav Iden, and Marten Van Riel, TriRating expert Thorsten Radde breaks down everything you need to know ahead of Saturday’s showdown.

Everyone’s favorite race-week tradition is now streaming. “Breakfast With Bob,” featuring Bob Babbitt and your favorite pro triathletes, is rolling out new episodes every day on the Big Island. If you want to see your favorite athletes in-person, head to Huggo’s on Ali’i Drive to watch the filming; for the rest of the triathlon world, head to the link below to stream Babbitt’s interviews with Taylor Knibb, Laura Philipp, Patrick Lange, and more.

At 82 years old, Bob Plant is the oldest athlete racing the 2026 Ironman World Championship in Kona. The American has survived bike crashes, broken bones, and shingles – and he isn’t just looking to finish. He’s racing to win. Read Sarah Wassner Flynn’s inspiring profile below.

Watch out for the box jellyfish, Kona athletes! A predicted bloom is heading toward coastal waters, impacting the Hoʻala Training Swim just one week before the 2026 Ironman World Championship.

At the link below, learn what the Hawaiʻi State Department of Health and local ER experts have to say about the risks, how to stay safe, and what this forecast means for race day.

Think Ironman’s tourism dollars are an automatic win for the Big Island? It’s more complicated than that, writes triathlete and Kailua-Kona resident Sara Stover. From closed roads, strained infrastructure, and lost wages to the disruption of daily life and sacred cultural spaces, local residents bear a bigger cost to host the Ironman World Championship.

Before you assume the island should just be grateful for the tourist dollars, take a moment to read the article at the link in bio and understand what life is really like for the people who call Kailua-Kona home year-round – and how we, as visitors, can show up with gratitude and respect.

The title of “Ironman World Champion” is one that can never be taken away – just ask four-time winner Chrissie Wellington or eight-time champ Paula Newby-Fraser. But as many of these legends will tell you, being first down Ali’i Drive on the Big Island wasn’t their only accomplishment in life. Contributor Tim Heming tracked down the women who have won Kona, stretching all the way back to 1979, to answer the question: Where are they now?

Ever wondered what happens after crossing the Kona finish line? We sent contributor Tim Heming to find out. From aviation and academia to coaching new legends, see where every male Ironman World Champion is today.

At 79, breast cancer survivor Linda Ashmore has conquered open-water records and world championships. As the oldest female competitor in Kona, she proves that extraordinary endurance is built on grit, joy, and relentless motion. Read Sarah Wassner Flynn’s inspiring profile of Ashmore at the link below.

Eighteen-year-old Francesca DelPresto was an avid softball player, but after seeing some triathlon content on social media, she decided to give it a try. Now, she’s lining up at the 2026 Ironman World Championship as the youngest woman racing in the field. Read how an algorithm inspired her journey from the diamond to the starting line at the link below.

For decades, qualifying for the Ironman World Championship in Kailua-Kona was the pinnacle of endurance sports. But as entry fees climb and travel expenses surge, many athletes are asking a tough question: Is Kona still worth it?

In this roundtable discussion, four triathletes explore the financial, physical, and emotional return on investment for age-groupers and pros alike targeting Aliʻi Drive.

Norway’s Casper Stornes will not defend his Ironman World Championship title this year after a bike crash on the Big Island, caused by high winds.

“Apparently there is a storm coming to the island, and I was unlucky – there was a hard blow on my front wheel, and it got twisted out, and I lost control of the bike and flew over my handlebars,” he said on a video posted to Instagram. “Luckily enough, I didn’t take out Gustav [Iden], who was on my wheel. How he got away from that one, it’s insane.”

Stornes said he fell on his shoulder, breaking his collarbone. He also sustained a vertebral fracture.

Stornes’ withdrawal is the first big name on the pro start list for this year’s Ironman World Championship. See the updated start list at the button below.

In 2026, the Ironman World Championship in Kona returns to a single-day format, reuniting couples on the iconic 140.6-mile course on the same start line for the first time since 2019. Discover how power pairs like the Fejfars and Borowiks are celebrating shared training, mutual support, and the ultimate finish line together on the Big Island.

Long before high-tech carbon supershoes and specialized sports fuel took over transition areas, Ironman looked very different – and so did its corporate sponsors. Ahead of the Ironman World Championship, Sarah Wassner Flynn takes a look at how Ironman brand partnerships have evolved from scrappy early days to a global marketing engine.

Only four triathletes in history have won both the Ironman 70.3 World Championship and Kona in the same year. Could Taylor Knibb be the fifth? After her dominating win at this year’s 70.3 Worlds in Nice, France, the American sure looks like she could pull it off. Triathlete contributor Tim Heming sat down with two athletes who have done exactly that – Craig “Crowie” Alexander and Leanda Cave – about the brutal reality of the double win and what it would take for Knibb to pull it off this year.

Twenty years after winning his last Ironman World Championship title – and 15 years after life-saving open-heart surgery abruptly ended his pro career – “The Norminator” is heading back to the Big Island! Normann Stadler is officially returning to Kona, but this time, the goal isn’t breaking bike split records or chasing the top of the podium. He’s lining up as an age-grouper for the pure love of the sport, gratitude, and a brand-new perspective. Sarah Wassner Flynn caught up with the legend ahead of this year’s race, where he hopes to write a new ending to his triathlon career.

Does “course experience” actually win Kona? The data says no. Thorsten Radde crunched the numbers on the pro field for the 2026 Ironman World Championship, and the math debunks some of triathlon’s biggest myths. Read the full breakdown to see what the stats actually tell us about who has a shot at the crown this year.

Four female world champions and five male world champions are on the start list for the 2026 Ironman World Championship. Review the full list, see which countries have the strongest representation, and check whether your favorite pro athlete qualified.

In April 2025, Ironman announced the Ironman World Championship would return to a one-day format with men and women competing on the Big Island. In 2022, the championship was two days in Kona – one day for men and one for women – but that put too much strain on the locals, requiring another solution.

The next three years involved split-gender championships rotating between Nice and Kona. Returning to a one-day format is what Ironman said surveys showed the triathlon community preferred.

#290. Before You Start Your Next Marathon Training Cycle, Ask Yourself These 3 Questions

Run coaches explain how to conduct a postrace debrief that leads to faster race times, smarter training, and more enjoyment.

Before you sign up for your next marathon, take a closer look at your last one. Whether you clocked a PR or fell short of your goal, jumping into another race without examining your previous training cycle makes you more likely to repeat the same mistakes. Instead, understand why you got the result you did, and it’ll lead to greater improvements over the long term.

“Some runners can get stuck in the trap of racing a marathon every four to six months and treating it like they’re just checking a box and moving on, without actually celebrating and processing it,” Elizabeth Corkum, a.k.a. Coach Corky, an RRCA-, UESCA-, and USATF-certified run coach, tells Runner’s World. “Giving more thoughtfulness to each race and training cycle is what leads to bigger breakthroughs and more enjoyment in the marathon.”

That’s why it’s important to take time for a little postrace reflection: It helps you learn about yourself as a runner so you can make smart training adjustments. Then you keep improving from one marathon cycle to the next, Corkum explains. Without a debrief, you risk making the same mistakes over and over again.

So how do you conduct this type of marathon recap, exactly? Coaches share the questions to consider so you gain insight into the pros and cons of your training and performance and make the right changes in your next buildup.

Runners tend to focus more on where they went wrong in training instead of what they did right—especially if they didn’t hit their time goal. But instead of digging into the negatives right away, you should analyze the triumphs, as they’re just as crucial to inspect, Greg McMillan, head run coach and founder of McMillan Running, tells Runner’s World. More specifically, consider whether you enjoyed training and how it fit into your lifestyle.

“The training can easily become a grind if it’s too hard to fit into your life, particularly if you’re going to do a lot of marathons,” McMillan explains. “In order to be sustainable, you need to make sure you enjoy it.”

Honestly ask yourself how compatible your last marathon training cycle was with your daily life. Look for the moments when your running, work, and family schedules all came together harmoniously.

For example, you might realize that morning workouts fit well around your kids’ sports practices on Tuesdays and Thursdays, or that an extra midweek rest day didn’t set you back—it actually helped you manage stress when work got busy. These observations allow you to make small adjustments so you can relish the journey of marathon training, not just the destination of race day.

“Consider your workouts, mileage, long runs—all those things are important. But go beyond that,” says McMillan. “Ask yourself: What did I enjoy? How did training fit into my work and family life? Where can I modify the training to better fit me as a whole person?”

Once you have those insights, you can begin making changes that help you develop holistically as a runner—not just a person who gets progressively better at following a training plan.

Now that you’ve identified the framework that makes your training sustainable and enjoyable, turn your attention to individual elements that need the most improvement. This means taking a look at the big picture of your entire marathon cycle, as well as zooming in on your race preparations and the day itself. Ask yourself, “What was my biggest limiting factor, and where did I struggle the most?”

Oftentimes, runners will realize that there was always one type of workout that felt especially hard or that they were never able to nail. Or, maybe they’ll notice that any time life got busy, they dropped the ball on strength work, mobility drills, or stretching, Corkum says.

Once you notice those weak points, you can ask yourself specifically what made those things difficult. For example, if you struggled with track workouts, was it because your fitness wasn’t there yet, or were other factors—like inadequate sleep or fueling—at play?

“It’s not always as simple as saying, ‘Well, I think I needed to push harder in my track workouts.’ Maybe not. Maybe you weren’t eating enough carbohydrates and you weren’t able to perform as well, in which case you’d want to focus on nutrition,” Corkum says. Find the driver behind your weakest points in training, and then brainstorm realistic fixes that you can commit to for the next marathon cycle.

After examining your training log, put race day through the same line of questioning. What got in the way of you running your best from the starting line through the finish? If it was something within your control—like you mentally fell apart in the later miles—you might need a “thinking plan” for how you’ll talk yourself through hard parts in your next race, says McMillan.

“Look back on periods of the marathon where you weren’t in an optimal mindset—maybe you were frustrated, dreading, or just having a pity party,” he says. “Chart out how you want to think for each 5K of the race so you can control more of the dialogue in your head.”

If you were mentally strong—maybe GI distress slowed you down instead—identify exactly how you can dial in your fueling and hydration strategies, he adds.

After you’ve unpacked what you didn’t get right, end your reflection by circling back to the positives. Ask yourself: What did I do really well in training? What workouts or routines made me feel most prepared for race day?

Start by considering the parts of your training that gave you the most confidence or built an aspect of your fitness that you found especially helpful, McMillan says. “It doesn’t have to be the workouts. It could be fueling, taking care of your body, or something outside of running entirely.”

Make a list of those confidence boosters, then determine exactly how you can prioritize them in your upcoming training cycle—even if that means taking a red pen to other parts of your 16-week plan. For example, if your workouts went better after you got eight hours of sleep, maybe you cut a few miles from a morning run here and there to make sure you get adequate shut-eye.

Finally, Corkum says when her athletes ask themselves this final question about their strengths, they come away from a race with a greater sense of accomplishment. “They’re really proud when they look back on the cards life dealt them in that training cycle—and maybe there’s still disappointment if their dream didn’t come to fruition,” she says. “But they’ll realize they should celebrate regardless, because it’s not just one day; it’s months of hard work to get there.”

When you reflect on that hard work, you come away from your race with more than just a finish time: You appreciate every successful workout more, better understand where you can improve, and toe your next starting line as a smarter, stronger marathoner.

Morgan is a gear editor who has been with Runner’s World since 2017. She started as an intern ghostwriting The Warmup, a bygone version of the daily RW newsletter. Now, she tests and reviews anything you might find on runners’ feet-from crew socks and compression boots to carbon-plated super shoes.

A lifelong runner and shoe geek, Morgan has been chasing the perfect pair of kicks since she joined her grade school cross-country team. Since then, she ran as a Division I walk-on for the cross-country and track & field teams at the University of Delaware, where she studied English and Biology. She has one full marathon under her belt, and has raced more halfs and 5Ks than she can count.

#291. What Is ‘Nonnamaxxing’? The Italian Grandma Lifestyle Might Be the Secret to Longevity

When I moved to Italy in 2024, one of the first things I noticed was the very particular way Italian nonne, or grandmas, live. They walk everywhere, frequently across the city, without any assistance. Many of them are dressed to the nines, but they also don’t try to hide their age.

I was then delighted—and unsurprised—when I came across a new wellness trend making the rounds on social media. “Nonnamaxxing” is the idea that anyone can maximize their life if they just embrace the habits of Italian grandmas. It happens to be sensible guidance.

There’s certainly a lot to learn from Italian grandmothers. Italy leads the European Union in life expectancy, and it’s a country where the number of centenarians is growing. A cluster of villages in Sardinia is one of the world’s five Blue Zones. Online guidance includes ditching social media, eating homemade everything, wearing cotton nightgowns, and welcoming unhurried lunches with friends. Some of these suggestions line up with how I’ve seen Italian grandmas live. But as a health and science journalist, I’ve noticed there’s more to it than what looks good on Instagram or TikTok. In fact, Licia Fertz, a 96-year-old Italian nonna based in Viterbo, Italy, tells SELF, quite the opposite is true.

“I put on my makeup and dress in cheerful colors, even if I’m not leaving the house, because presenting yourself well is an act of self-love,” Fertz says.

It seems that Italian nonne are the health gurus we all need. Read on to learn their secrets to a happier, healthier, and longer life.

I rarely see Italian nonne who don’t look their age. In fact, it’s one of the first things I noticed when I moved here. At the pools and beaches, it doesn’t matter how old they are; women, nonne included, frequently wear bikinis. Honestly, it’s refreshing and emphasizes a cultural mindset that aging is a natural part of life.

Fertz tells SELF that this mindset is key to her living a long and healthy life. “Never think of yourself as old,” says Fertz. “You are born young.”

It turns out that as you age, having a more positive attitude about getting older could help you live longer too. A recent study found an association between how women view aging and the actual pace at which they age.

Sonja Lyubomirsky, a distinguished professor of psychology at the University of California, Riverside, and author of How To Feel Loved, tells SELF that a mindset is like putting on a pair of glasses or a coat. “It certainly matters very much what our mindset is when we think about aging,” Lyubomirsky says. “Is it a gift? Is it about wisdom, maturity, and the richness of life, or is it about deterioration and loss?” Both can be true, she says. “But you can choose.”

At school pick-up for my daughter, I don’t only see other parents. I also see Italian nonne. That’s because Italian grandmas are very involved in their grandkids’ lives and take an active role in caregiving. In fact, for better or worse, the Italian economy is supported by the unpaid labor of Italian grandmothers—and this is well-known and discussed in local mom groups.

Research shows that caregiving later in life may lead to better aging and act as a buffer against cognitive decline. One recent study found that grandparents who provided childcare—ranging from caring for sick grandkids, helping with homework, or driving them to school—scored higher on memory and verbal fluency tests compared with those who didn’t help with childcare.

“I live with my grandson,” Fertz tells SELF. “I’m a great-grandmother, and every day spent with my great-granddaughter is a gift that never ceases to amaze me.”

Even if you’re not a grandparent, helping others can yield similar health benefits. According to research published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine, people who volunteered more than 100 hours a year—versus those who volunteered zero hours a year—had a reduced risk of mortality, more optimism, and purpose in their lives.

Italian cities and villages are highly walkable, meaning walking isn’t something people do for exercise; it’s just a way of life. Even if someone has a car, sometimes a destination is only reachable by foot because Italy’s infamously narrow streets. Gas is also more expensive in Italy. While this might be inconvenient for some, a walking-first lifestyle happens to be associated with longevity.

“Walking is the most fundamental form of human physical activity and many, many hundreds of studies confirm that walking helps people age slower and better,” Daniel Lieberman, a professor of Human Evolutionary Biology at Harvard University, tells SELF. “Walking helps you age well.”

Paola Mariotti, a pediatrician and nonna based in Florence, Italy, tells SELF that walking is very important to her, and was very important to her own grandparents, who didn’t have a car and walked everywhere. Today, as a more modern nonna, Mariotti focuses on walking at least 5,000 steps a day—which she tracks on her phone—but strives to get 10,000 steps or more, if possible, each day.

Much of America isn’t walkable, but a 2025 study published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine found that even 15 minutes of fast walking a day can reduce premature death.

At cafés in Italy, I’m always struck by how Italian nonne drink un caffè. Usually, she is just enjoying her coffee and watching people walk by, rather than scrolling on her phone or sending emails on her laptop. Some might call this the dolce far niente, which means the sweetness of doing nothing. While it’s true that these moments of pause and presence are more common in Italy, there’s something deeper to them. They reflect how, as a culture, Italians are content to live more mindfully. They appreciate quality over quantity and don’t feel the need to constantly multitask for the sake of being productive.

In fact, Jonathan Alpert, a psychotherapist in New York, tells SELF that he thinks nonnamaxxing has less to do with actual Italian grandmothers and more about Gen Z’s desire to escape hustle culture. “The appeal here is the fantasy of a life that feels grounded, warm, and unhurried,” Alpert says. “A lot of younger people are burned out by the pressure to constantly optimize themselves, be productive, and turn their lives into content.”

While in the moment, multitasking can feel like you’re being more efficient, researchers say that it actually does the opposite and can lead to increased stress levels.

The antidote to hustle culture is a mindful one. This can be as simple as just enjoying a coffee without much else, as it’s been found that people who stay in the present moment age better and with more resilience.

In Italy, there’s an emphasis on eating what’s in season. In fact, my local market provides customers with a chart that identifies exactly what fruits and vegetables are in season each month. This lifestyle isn’t exactly optional—produce that’s out-of-season is harder to come by. Antonino De Lorenzo, professor emeritus of human nutrition at the University of Rome Tor Vergata, tells SELF that the value isn’t in the variety of food, but in what’s gained when you choose seasonal produce, which is food that is less likely to have preservatives and industrial products.

“Freshness, variety, ripeness, and preparation methods can all exert a significant influence on a food’s nutritional profile,” De Lorenzo says. “A high-quality diet, maintained over time, promotes healthier aging, characterized by better preservation of physical, mental, and cognitive functions, as well as reduced exposure to major chronic diseases.”

Indeed, the Mediterranean diet, which focuses on olive oil, vegetables, fruits, whole grains and legumes—all popular in Italy—has been linked to longevity. As researchers tend to emphasize, the Mediterranean diet isn’t a fad diet. It’s a way of life.

Italian grandmas are stereotypically known for being connected to their communities and neighbors—maybe even a bit too much, in the sense that it can veer into nosiness. Viral videos on social media have joked that Italian nonne are Italy’s security systems.

“The most important thing for living a long and happy life? Don’t isolate yourself,” Fertz says. “Always stay in touch with people, travel, plan outings, and get out of the house.”

According to a study in The American Journal of Geriatric Psychiatry, having a sense of purpose can help preserve cognitive function as you age. A separate study found that people with a higher sense of purpose had a reduced risk for depression and loneliness. Whether that is being in-the-know in your community, or finding a hobby to keep you busy, the key is to feel connected and busy.

Because boredom, Fertz says, is “the one thing that truly makes you old.”

#292. What's Love Got to Do With It? The Relationship Cycle Explained

Relationships aren’t just about candlelit dinners and cozy sofa nights — they’re complex AF, filled with ups, downs, twists, and turns. From the first flush of love to the settled comfort of commitment, relationships have stages that evolve with time.

Each relationship phase serves a unique purpose, helping you learn more about each other, yourself, and the kind of relationship you want to build. Understanding the dynamics of these stages is crucial for any couple (or throuple!) aiming to develop a lasting bond.

Whether you’re in the throes of a new romance or navigating the challenges of a long-term commitment, continue reading to learn how to rock each phase like a pro.

From those “can’t eat, can’t sleep” early days to the “let’s build an empire” moments, each relationship stage is like a season of your fave drama binge. But, like any good drama, the plot thickens as time passes and things change. Here’s what to expect, month by month:

Welcome to the love bubble, where everything about your significant other seems nothing short of magical. The positives overshadow any negatives, creating a blissfully skewed balance sheet of love. It lasts from about 6 months to 2 years for most peeps, but many folks say they are still madly in love even after 20 years together!

Research shows that during this stage, the prefrontal cortex, which is crucial for critically judging others, shows decreased activity. In other words, you’re less likely to focus on your partner’s faults and more likely to overlook their flaws.

Lurve also activates specific areas in the brain that are driven by goals and rewards. These areas are rich in dopamine and oxytocin receptors, chemicals that make you feel good and bonded to others. They encourage you to pursue and maintain a relationship because it feels rewarding and fulfilling.

If the euphoric stage is the wild, pulse-racing party of love, the early attachment stage is the cozy after-party where things get real comfortable. In the thrilling initial phase, your brain is doped up on dopamine, but as this initial buzz begins to mellow, a more sophisticated part of the brain starts to step up — the ventral pallidum.

Now, after the first year or so, deeper bonds are formed, helped along by attachment hormones like vasopressin and oxytocin, also fondly known as “the love hormone.” These hormones help transform the electric excitement of new love into a warm, enduring attachment.

Hold tight because the crisis stage hits around 5 to 7 years, and it’s a true test of your relationship’s resilience. This phase often feels like a rollercoaster, where life’s challenges can either pull you apart or push you closer together. Many couples experience a drift during this time, and how you handle it — either by addressing the issues head-on or continuing to drift — can define your future together.

Significant life events, like becoming parents, often occur during this stage and can intensify the pressure. These events can either strengthen your bond through shared responsibilities and mutual love or strain it to the breaking point. Successfully navigating this stage means moving beyond mere survival to fostering a deeper, more meaningful connection.

If you’ve made it this far, congrats, you’re in the deep attachment stage! Post-crisis, you’re looking at 7 years and beyond where you settle into that deep, comfy love. No more daily fireworks — now it’s about a slow-burning ember that warms the house.

You know each other inside and out, warts and all. It’s about unconditional support, knowing looks across crowded rooms, and being each other’s rock. Welcome to the good life!

Every relationship is a blend of sweet and sour and everything in between. Understanding the stages, from the initial euphoria to the deep attachment stage, helps you embrace the journey, keep your bond strong, and prepare your heart for whatever comes next. So buckle up and enjoy the ride — it’ll be worth it!

Last medically reviewed on June 26, 2024
