#293. The 5 Best Running Gloves for Logging Cold-Weather Miles

Not feeling the tips of your fingers on a run is unacceptable—these gloves provide wind resistance and warmth.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

The first snowfall can be magical, but overcast skies and visible breath during a run can dampen the enthusiasm of any runner impatient for spring. To survive the everlasting cold, the trick is to layer properly so you don’t feel miserable during winter training. Stocking up on a winter running jacket, leggings, and pants is a no-brainer, but don’t forget to accessorize. I’m talking gloves here.

As a constantly cold person who has three sweatshirts piled onto the back of her office desk chair, I’ll never forget that one Santa 5-Miler when I left my gloves in my car. As I squeezed my hands into fists trying to retain warmth as I raced, I swore to never again run a winter race without full coverage over my five digits.

This winter has tested my cold-weather tolerance, dipping below zero degrees more than once. But it’s a perfect breeding ground for glove—and mitten—testing. Here are my top picks.

I’ve worked at RW for eight years and started running XC in high school. I learned to embrace the cold this year, testing most of the gloves included on this list. I judged them by insulation, dexterity, and fit. I also had a little help from male staffers, who tested the men’s version of gloves—and became aghast learning that the women’s wasn’t similar.

Contributor Nick Hilden also provides tips on what to look for when shopping for gloves and answers your frequently asked questions on when to wear them, and on sizing and fit.

The Smartwool Active Fleece Insulated Glove is included in our Best Winter Gear for Runners guide because it checks off all the boxes: double-knit insulation, reflective lining, windproof panels, and touchscreen-compatible fingertips. The stitching on the long cuffs ensures a secure, tailored fit around the wrists.

The Active Fleece kept my fingers warm for an hour during 32-degree and slightly below freezing runs. When the temperature dropped to 20, my fingers started to ache after a half hour in the cold.

My main critique is that they’re unisex sizing only. Even the smallest size, extra small, left some room above my fingertips, which made it difficult to grasp items I pocketed and zippers. The patch on the palm didn’t reach past my thumb and forefinger, which would have provided a soft area for nose wiping.

When you’re pitting gloves against mittens, it’s dexterity versus warmth. Gloves allow you to use your fingers but gloves keep them together, thereby minimizing heat loss.

Even though I felt like I was running with oven mitts on my hands (the sizing is small/medium, medium/large), the Convertible Zip Mittens were great for braving workouts that dipped into the teens—and tens. The extra room also allows for doubling up if you really want to head out when it’s minus 1 degree Fahrenheit or less.

The Velcro tabs allow you to tighten the fit around the wrists, and the interior lining feels as plush as the felt on my very authentic Robin Hood hat from Nottingham.

If you’re prone to losing a mate when things come in pairs, TrailHeads sees you: a buckle guarantees your left and right mitt won’t be separated. Afraid of losing both mitts? Attach them to a carabiner on your duffel using the loops on the cuffs. The reflective zipper is a nice touch if you need to use your fingers midrun.

My one issue with the mittens: the material on the thumbs leaves snot trails.

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com

My coworkers thought I was heading out on the slopes or wearing garden gloves, but the Ibex Kilometer isn’t just for skiers (or gardeners). After a stretch of testing during a brief stay in New York City, the Kilometer gets my runner seal of approval. I tested them while logging runs in Central Park and the Hudson River Greenway, hitting gusts of wind on rolling hills and by the water. Temperatures varied from 20 to 40 degrees; the Kilometer made my workouts more bearable.

The leather palms had excellent grip when I ran holding my phone, trying to find the best route back to my hotel. My fingers were shielded from the river’s wind chill and the ribbed cuffs kept my wrists toasty. But the biggest win for me was the soft, absorbent patch of fabric on each thumb. They were perfect for swiping my very runny nose when the wind speed was 15 mph.

If you run with your phone and whip it out a bunch of times midrun, these are your gloves; almost the entire palm is patterned with silicone grips. The fingertips are touchscreen-compatible and sizing is sex-specific, which translates to no bunched fingers or agitation trying to scroll.

These gloves aren’t for extreme weather, but they’re great when things start to get nippy or when you’re heading out for a short winter run. However, there’s one thing TrailHeads must rectify: It’s a travesty that only the men’s version has a nose wipe patch. Why did they skimp on this feature with the women’s edition?

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com

These aren’t the cotton gloves you wore in grade school. The Smartwool Liner offers so much more in terms of warmth and quality; it all starts with the woven material.

The fabric is merino wool, which regulates warmth, controls odors, and dries fast. The fingertips are touchscreen-compatible, and you’re not limited to a small patch on the thumb when you need to wipe your nose (the glove itself is real estate). The ribbed cuffs fit snug, even on small wrists. They’re great to wear when the temperature is mid-30s; maybe even lower if you don’t have near-Raynaud’s hands like mine.

Winter runners should look for a pair of lightweight gloves that are warm enough to keep your hands cozy, but breathable enough to let air circulate. Look for technical fabrics—polyester and other synthetic materials are often your best bet for finding that balance.

Some blends are better than others though. In case of bad weather, it also makes sense to keep an eye out for a weather-resistant material that can protect against rain and snow, as well as cold, cutting winds. Moisture-wicking materials, such as merino wool, can also help deal with sweat and mitigate the impact of cold rain.

I also like when a glove fabric contains a small amount of a stretchy material, such as Spandex or elastane, to ensure the gloves fit comfortably and snug. That said, skip the stretch if you like a glove that feels roomy inside.

On the other hand, I recommend avoiding heavy gloves made from nylon or polyurethane. These materials are often thicker, warmer and weatherproof, so they’re more likely to make you overheat. (Depending on the design, they may also make it hard to use your phone or check your smartwatch.)

Everyone has their own Goldilocks spot for how much warmth they need from their gloves. The important thing to keep in mind is that your body feels warmer while you’re running–speaking broadly, we recommend dressing for a run as if it's 10- to 20 degrees warmer than the temperature outside (including the wind chill.) That’s a good rubric for determining both when to start wearing gloves in the winter, and the level of protection you want against the cold.

Thinking about gloves specifically, your running gloves probably shouldn’t be as warm as your everyday winter gloves. A warmer glove will keep you going in colder temperatures but will cause you to sweat more, so it may not feel comfortable for long.

Winter nights come early, so visibility is an essential concern for all cold-weather running gear. If you frequently run near a road, or in areas with little street lighting, every item of clothing you wear, head to toe, should feature a reflective or high-visibility element.

In fact, gloves are among the most important pieces of reflective running gear you can wear. They catch drivers’ eyes especially well because your hands move as you run, creating a more noticeable effect.

When should I start wearing running gloves in the winter?

Every person feels differently about gloves, but as I said earlier in the piece, experts recommend dressing for a run as if it’s 10 degrees warmer than the effective temperature with the wind chill. If you normally wear gloves on a 50-degree day, start putting on gloves when it’s 40 degrees.

A good running glove should fit snug around your hand. If there’s room for your hand to move inside the glove, your skin may rub against the fabric and start to chafe. At the same time, it’s important to make sure they aren’t too tight, which might reduce circulation.

One way to check if you have the right fit is by doing a pinch test. Put on one glove, then pinch the fabric at the tip of a finger with your other hand. Ideally, you should have about a quarter-inch of extra room.

Most glove brands use one of two measurements to determine sizing: The circumference of your fingers at the knuckles (without the thumb), and full hand length from the base of the hand to the tip of the middle finger. Check the product listing on the glove to see how the brand measures.

To measure the knuckle circumference, hold your fingers together, then wrap a measuring tape around your knuckles. Don’t squeeze your fingers too tight, though.

When measuring your full hand, make sure your middle finger is fully extended to ensure a proper measurement.

#294. Flying With Your Bike? These Editor-Tested Travel Cases Make Packing Easier and Help Prevent Damage

After 100-plus flights with bikes, these cases offer the best mix of protection and ease.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Do you ever fly with your bike for events, vacation, or training? A dedicated bag or case is a great investment that makes traveling with your road, gravel, or mountain bike easier than using a cardboard box. Plus, these cases help ensure your bicycle arrives at its destination without damage.

I’ve traveled with a bicycle several times a year for cycling events, bike races, business, and riding vacations for almost three decades. I’ve taken bikes on trips around the country and across the globe. I estimate I’ve made at least a hundred round-trip flights with a bike. On these trips, I’ve used everything from old bike boxes to hard-plastic travel cases to transport my bicycles—ranging from lightweight race bikes to heavy-duty downhill machines—to and from my destination.

In my travels, I’ve found that certain cases and bags work best for different bikes and different riders. Depending on your bicycle, its accessories, and your comfort level with tools, some choices may be better than others. Even your bike’s physical size can affect your travel case choice.

Bike travel cases come in two primary styles: hardshell and softshell. Hard cases feature a tough plastic outer shell with foam internal padding. Most soft cases are constructed from durable nylon and rely on padding to protect your bike. Many soft-sided cases use a rigid internal frame. This provides structure and protects the bike from crushing forces, and some feature plastic sheets for improved puncture protection. Most hard and soft cases include extra padding for the frame and straps to hold the frame and wheels in place.

Hardshell Cases provide the highest level of impact protection. However, these cases also weigh more, which can lead to even higher luggage fees. Hard cases also don’t fold down (which means they take up more space in a hotel room or rental car when not in use). Plus, they’re harder to store at home or in your garage when you’re not traveling.

Softshell Bags offer nearly the same level of protection as hard-shell models. Soft-sided bags are typically lighter than hard-case models, and most fold or roll down for easier storage. Many newer models have fixed attachment points, roll cages, or reinforcement that add protection. Since switching to a softshell bag more than fifteen years ago, I haven’t looked back.

Pro Tips: Before flying with a bike, I always do a few things upfront to ensure a smooth trip. In my travels, I’ve never had a bicycle go missing, and it was only delayed twice (once at London Heathrow and another at Paris Charles de Gaulle). ——————🎟️ Know the airline's bike policy before buying tickets: It’s often worth paying a slightly higher price for an airline with a lower bike fee or a more generous size limit.——🛫 Limit or avoid connections: This helps avoid bikes getting lost in transit or missing loading onto a flight.——💳 Get a membership or an airline card: Having status with an airline or an airline credit card can help reduce or eliminate baggage fees. (They also help when trying to check in a bike with confused airline staff.)——📱 Prebook your bike: Some international carriers require you to reserve space for your bike 48 hours in advance. Also, screenshot or save your confirmations and the airline’s bike policy on your phone before you go to the airport; it can be handy at bag drop.——🚕 Rentals and taxis: Before you reserve a rental car, check that your bike bag fits inside. Bike bags usually fit in wagons or small SUVs, but do your research before you arrive. When ordering an Uber or Lyft, you usually need to book an XL (and even then, some drivers may be grumpy about your bike).

A 2026 Bicycling Gear of the Year selection, the Orucase Sentinel is the best bike case I’ve used in over twenty-five years of traveling with a bicycle. While heavier and larger than the brand’s B2 and old-school Airport Ninja cases, it is easy to use, offers solid protection, and packs down small for storage.

What sets the Sentinel apart from other travel bags is its aluminum rollcage and expandable wings. The cage and the bag’s hard plastic bottom help prevent baggage handlers from crushing or damaging your bike if they throw or drop it. Plus, the expandable sides (combined with an aluminum crossbar) allow many road and gravel bikes to fit without removing the handlebar. This really simplifies travel—and the time it takes to pack or reassemble your bike when you reach your destination—for bikes with integrated cables or a one-piece cockpit.

I used this case for a two-week trip to the Tour de France and brought along a nearly $16,000 Cannondale SuperSix Evo Lab71. The case fit the 58cm bike without removing the bike’s one-piece bar or my pedals. Plus, I easily packed a spare set of wheels, tools, helmet, and shoes while staying under the airline’s 70-pound weight limit.

Do you travel with different bikes for different trips? Some bags are optimized for carrying road bikes, while others are best for mountain bikes. The Evoc Bike Bag Pro is ideal if you need one case for various bike types or riding destinations. The brand’s bike bags are among the most popular soft-sided options for road, gravel, and mountain bikes (it also makes a version for BMX), and I’ve used at least three generations of Evoc bike bags for over fifteen years.

The Bike Bag Pro is a premium version of the company’s standard Bike Bag. It features an integrated aluminum chassis that holds your bike’s frame and fork in place by its axles. Evoc lengthened the Travel Bag Pro (compared to previous versions of its bags) to accommodate bikes with long wheelbases. The bag’s wheel pockets will swallow 29-inch wheels wrapped in 2.6-inch tires. When not in use, the Bike Travel Bag Pro folds down tidy enough to fit under a bed.

Traveling with a time trial or triathlon bike can be a challenge due to the bike’s aerobars and integrated cables. Scicon’s AeroComfort 3.0 Triathlon blends the low weight of a soft-sided bike bag with a rigid frame to protect your prized ride when in transit to your next even or training camp. This travel bag is designed specifically for aerobikes and requires minimal disassembly—You don’t even need to remove your bike’s aerobar or seatpost.

An aluminum adjustable chassis holds the frame in place by the axles—either quick-release or 12mm thru-axles and the wheels stow in dedicated pockets on the sides. The four-wheeled design makes it easy to maneuver through crowded airports, and the compact design keeps it within many airlines’ standard luggage dimensions, which may help you skip oversize baggage fees.

Don’t have a tri-bike? Scicon also offers versions of the bag for road, gravel, and mountain bikes.

Pro is cycling component behemoth Shimano’s accessory brand, and its Bike Travel Case is one of the best deals available for a soft-sided travel case. I’ve used this affordable bag to carry gravel, road, and mountain bikes on trips across the U.S. and to Europe.

Compared to many bags, one upside of Pro’s Bike Bag is its ability to carry large and XL-sized bikes. The Pro Bike Bag features an adjustable alloy base that holds your bike’s axles, while padded wheel pockets and foam blocks help protect your bike. Integrated pockets allow riders to stash pedals, tools, a mini-pump, and other essential riding gear.

B&W’s International Bike Box II is a simple, effective, and affordable hard-shell case. The clamshell design is easy to use, and the interlocking halves fasten with six buckles to keep everything secure. This budget-minded case includes wheel bags and multiple layers of foam to protect the frame from the wheels. Two fixed wheels and a pair of rotating castors make the International Bike Box II as easy to maneuver as a shopping cart.

Pro Tip: If you’re uncomfortable packing or building your bike, most shops will pack your bike in a case for a fee. Be sure to call ahead to a shop in the place you’re visiting to schedule assembly and repacking your bike before you depart. Bikeflights.com is a great option to ship your bike to a shop or hotel. Bikeflights’ labels now use RFID tags, so you know its location as it travels to your destination.

Many travel cases are optimized for road and gravel bikes. This makes fitting a mountain bike in them a tight squeeze, or requires lots of disassembly of your bike. Dakine’s Bike Roller Bag has enough space to fit bikes with 29-inch wheels, downhill bikes, and even 29er downhill bikes. Unlike many other soft-sided bags, the Bike Roller Bag has wheel sleeves inside the main compartment, which reduces the number of external zippers that could fail. Heavy-duty padding helps protect the frame, fork, and wheels, and the included accessory bags secure your pedals and tools.

Thule’s Round Trip Transition fits most road and mountain bikes within its tough, ABS plastic shell. Nylon wheel bags prevent frame and wheel rub during transport. The two-piece, hard-shell design cradles the frame in a lightweight aluminum stand that doubles as a work stand, simplifying reassembly and maintenance once you arrive at your destination.

A hundred bucks for a cardboard box? This isn’t your average cardboard big box fished out of the dumpster behind your local bike show. Bikeflights specifically designed this box to withstand the rigours of round-trip airline travel.

Cardboard is lightweight, inexpensive, and (when the bike is packed properly) a surprisingly safe way to ship a bike. However, bike breakdown and packing difficulty will vary depending on the bike you’re bringing on your trip. Keep in mind that cardboard boxes offer no puncture or impact protection and can fall apart if they get too wet (such as when left on the tarmac in the rain waiting to be loaded onto a flight). The Bikeflights Bike Box comes in four sizes: small, medium, large, and extra large.

Pay attention to the size and weight of a bike case, particularly as it relates to the weight of the bike you plan to transport. Many airlines have a 50-pound weight limit before incurring an overweight fee, or a 70-pound limit for bicycles and sports equipment. You need to factor in the weight of the case, the bike, and other items you’ll carry in your bag before selecting a case.

While hard-shell cases offer additional protection, they weigh more. This leaves less for packing materials, bike, and gear. Softshell cases are lighter, which means you can pack a heavier bike without exceeding the limit, but they may provide less protection for your bicycle. The weight difference can be extreme: Thule’s Roundtrip Transition is made of ABS plastic and very rugged, but it weighs 39 pounds. Dakine’s soft-sided Bike Roller Bag weighs just 17.75 pounds.

Most airlines have a dimensional limit of 62 linear inches—calculated by adding together the total length, width, and height—for checked baggage. If an item of luggage is larger, it can incur an oversize or bicycle bag fee. Almost all bike bags will fall outside this limit, so be prepared in advance.

If you’re hellbent on beating the bike bag or oversize baggage fee, Orucase’s old Airport Ninja/Sub62 bag comes in smaller than 62 linear inches. However, it requires a lot of disassembly.

Before choosing a case, it’s good to know how much bike disassembly and assembly you’re comfortable and confident in performing.

Cases like the Orucase Sentinel and Scicon’s AeroComfort require very little wrenching to pack and unpack a bike. However, these cases are larger and likely to incur a bike or oversize fee. Hard-shell cases and lighterweight soft-sided bags require removal of both wheels, the bar and stem, pedals, and seatpost. Sometimes you may even need to remove the rear derailleur and fork to fit a bike in a case.

Several brands offer additional protection to supplement the stock padding that comes with most cases. You can also use pipe insulation, which is inexpensive and can be purchased at your local home-supply store. Always ensure you have all the necessary tools to get your bike back up and running at your destination.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#295. Are GLP-1 Drugs Quietly Changing Our Sex Lives?

By now you’ve probably heard about GLP-1s, sold under brand names such as Ozempic and Wegovy. This class of medications mimics naturally occurring hormones involved in appetite control and blood sugar regulation to treat type 2 diabetes and aid weight-loss efforts. It should be no surprise, then, that conversations around these popular drugs have largely centered on the scale. However, some scientists are starting to look more closely into how they may impact something perhaps even more personal: our sex lives.

At present roughly one in five Americans reports taking or having taken a GLP-1, according to a recent poll. As the number of people using these medications has soared, so have anecdotal reports about how they’re impacting users’ day-to-day—and yes, this includes things like pleasure and sex drive. Though there hasn’t been a ton of research into the relationship between sexual health and GLP-1s yet, more scientists are starting to investigate potential impacts.

In a review published in Obesity Pillars in March 2026, for example, researchers propose that GLP-1s may influence desire by impacting brain chemistry. But how exactly might these drugs impact sex drive? And is there a way to remain engaged in your sex life while on a GLP-1? We tapped experts to find out.

To understand how GLP-1s might influence libido, it helps to walk through how they work more broadly.

Some options, like Wegovy and Ozempic, contain semaglutide, which is a synthetic version of a naturally occurring hormone, glucagon-like peptide-1, or GLP-1. Semaglutide binds to GLP-1 receptors throughout the brain and body, helping regulate appetite, blood sugar, and feelings of satiety, James Simon, MD, an ob-gyn and reproductive endocrinologist and one of the researchers behind the Obesity Pillars study, tells SELF.

Other options, like Zepbound and Mounjaro, contain a different active ingredient called tirzepatide, which mimics both GLP-1 and a related hormone, and thus impacts the body in similar ways to semaglutide.

On top of reporting reduced appetite and increased satiety, a number of patients have also found that these weight-loss medications quiet what they call “food noise.” But as it turns out, the same parts of the brain that control appetite are also responsible for other reward-seeking behaviors, according to Dr. Simon. He says this could help explain why taking GLP-1s may have the auxiliary impact of decreasing appetite for another pleasurable activity: sex.

On top of that, early research suggests that GLP-1s may affect certain serotonin receptors, including one called 5-HT2C. This is thought to be a key player in the sexual side effects often experienced by those taking selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), such as reduced libido and delayed orgasm.

“We know that, while SSRIs are fantastic options for anxiety and depression, they can have a significant impact on sexual desire and orgasmic function in both men and women,” says Dr. Simon. “It makes sense that other medications that also impact serotonin pathways might have similar impacts on sexual desire in some individuals.”

Sexual function isn’t just about hormones and brain chemistry. It also depends on the pelvic floor, a group of muscles that support the bladder and bowel, among other organs, and play an active role in arousal and orgasm, explains pelvic-health physical therapist Iris Xu, PT, DPT, of Fusion Wellness & Femina Physical Therapy.

“During arousal the pelvic-floor muscles increase blood flow to the genitals,” Dr. Xu says. During penetration the muscles lengthen and relax to allow for comfortable insertion and boost sensation. And during orgasm they contract rhythmically, creating the pulsing feeling associated with climax, she says.

In general, weight loss—from GLP-1s or other methods—can improve pelvic-floor function because reduced abdominal pressure means the muscles don’t have to work as hard to support the pelvic organs, Dr. Xu says. A 2024 study published in Archives of Gynecology and Obstetrics found that women carrying more fat, particularly in the pelvic area, had weaker pelvic floor muscles than those with less.

But GLP-1s don’t just encourage fat loss. Because these medications can lead to relatively rapid weight loss, preserving lean muscle mass can be challenging—especially without adequate protein intake or resistance training, says Dr. Xu. “[GLP-1s] can also cause loss of lean body mass and strength, especially when used in isolation without exercise or diet modifications,” she adds. In extreme cases this can lead to a condition called sarcopenia, which some studies have linked to reduced pelvic floor function. (FWIW, muscle loss can occur no matter how you lose weight. But by accelerating the weight-loss process, GLP-1s may speed up muscle loss as well.)

At the time of writing, research specifically examining GLP-1 medications and pelvic-floor outcomes remains limited. There is also little data on these drugs’ impact on muscle loss. But the research we do have points to this being a likely outcome, and Dr. Xu says losing too much lean mass may weaken pelvic floor support. This, in turn, can affect arousal, orgasm intensity, or overall sexual function.

As mentioned earlier, part of the notoriety of these medications is the speed at which many patients lose weight. Research has shown that, on average, people who are overweight or living with obesity can lose anywhere from roughly 10% to 20% of their total body weight on a GLP-1, depending on factors like which drug they use, what dose they take, and how long they continue treatment.

However, despite cultural messages to the contrary, weight loss does not automatically translate to increased body confidence and desire, Joy Berkheimer, PhD, LMFT, a sex and relationship therapist, tells SELF.

“Particularly if you have a long history of having your body policed against external beauty standards—as most women and people assigned female at birth do—the rapidity of the physical changes can lead you to feel unfamiliar in your body,” she says. Sexual desire and pleasure are often closely tied to embodiment, so a lack of embodiment can impact intimacy, she says.

It’s not all bad news; for some people the broader health changes associated with these drugs may actually improve aspects of sexual well-being. People go on GLP-1s for help with a variety of health conditions, such as obesity, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, and polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), to name just a few. Addressing these sorts of underlying issues may benefit sexual health.

That means even if the medications dial down some of the brain signals tied to desire, other changes happening in the body (e.g., improved energy, hormone balance, and physical comfort) may help support a healthier sex life, Dr. Simon tells SELF.

“Fat cells are highly inflammatory and impede our well-being far beyond their impact on our weight, leading to things such as joint pain and muscle fatigue,” he says. Feeling weak and achy can reduce interest in any physical activity—sex included!—as well as decrease pleasure during them. But as fat mass decreases and inflammation drops, people may feel more comfortable, energetic, and ultimately sexier. Additionally, as body composition improves, hormone levels may shift in ways that boost sexual desire and function, particularly in those with dysfunction, Dr. Simon says. (Body fat contains enzymes that can convert testosterone into estrogen. When levels of these hormones are unbalanced, it can impact sexual health.)

GLP-1 medications have also been shown to improve markers associated with vascular health, including blood pressure. Healthy blood flow is essential to arousal in people of all genders, says Dr. Simon. For those with vaginas it supports clitoral engorgement, lubrication, and vaginal expansion.

Finally, as metabolic health improves some people will see an increase in their energy levels and feel more comfortable in their bodies, says board-certified bariatric surgeon and obesity medicine specialist Betsy Dovec, MD, FACS, DBOM. For some—particularly those navigating postpartum body changes or the menopause transition—that renewed energy and groundedness can translate into increased confidence and desire, she says.

Taken altogether these physiological shifts can enhance sexual function for some people, even as the medications potentially continue to lower the volume on certain reward pathways.

Of course, our sex lives aren’t driven by biology alone. They are mediated by culture and society, the relationships we’re in, our sense of self and self-confidence, and more. The broader life changes that can accompany weight loss may shift libido north or south.

In a society that often equates thinness with desirability, people who don’t fall into the narrow confines of “thin” may feel undesirable, unsexy, or even undeserving of pleasure. For some individuals changes in body composition toward that supposed ideal may lead to increased confidence.

A 2025 survey from the Kinsey Institute and DatingAdvice.com found that 59% of GLP-1 agonist users said the medication had an impact on their dating life, with a number saying it boosted their confidence. Justin Lehmiller, PhD, a social psychologist, research fellow at the Kinsey Institute, and host of the Sex and Psychology podcast, tells SELF that confidence can have huge impacts on our sexual satisfaction.

“Feeling confident makes it easier to surrender to pleasure and facilitates communicating about our sexual needs and desires, which helps to ensure that we’re getting more of what we want in bed,” he says. “By contrast, when we aren’t feeling confident, it’s easy to get stuck in our heads during intimacy and start worrying about things like how we look.”

For those who are single, increased self-confidence may inspire someone who previously didn’t use dating apps or go out to bars because of body image hang-ups to start putting themselves in situations where connection feels more possible, Dr. Simon says. Meanwhile, in long-term relationships that confidence could translate into greater willingness to initiate sex or say yes to a partner’s advances, he adds. It may also mean someone feels more comfortable experimenting with positions they once shied away from—potentially even discovering ones that bring them more pleasure.

In these cases the reward pathways are still muted. However, because other things that shape sexual desire and enjoyment (like confidence) have increased, patients on these drugs may be experiencing better and/or more sex overall.

“Changes in libido are among the most common concerns people bring into sex therapy,” Dr. Berkheimer says. “But often they are a completely normal response to life transitions or physiological shifts, rather than a sign that something is wrong.”

Desire isn’t static, she explains. Rather, it fluctuates across the lifespan in response to factors like stress, sleep quality, exercise routine, medication, illness, hormones, relationship dynamics, and more. That means any shifts you notice after starting a GLP-1 medication aren’t necessarily a sign that something is off—your body might just need time to adjust, Dr. Berkheimer says. Still, if the change feels distressing or different enough to affect your well-being or relationships, it’s worth bringing up with your doctor.

Sexual health, Dr. Dovec says, isn’t a frivolous concern. “Pleasure matters. Intimacy matters. Feeling sexy matters. These are at the core of quality of life,” she says. Shifts in sexual desire and function can offer useful information about what’s happening in your body more broadly. So if sexual changes happen, talk to your provider. As frustrating or unwelcome as these shifts can be, they’re often temporary or solvable with a provider’s help, according to Dr. Dovec.

Sometimes the solution is as simple as adjusting GLP-1 dosage or timing; other times a clinician may suggest lifestyle changes, like adjusting your diet or exercise routine, or additional treatments that support hormone balance.

Not sure how to start the conversation? Dr. Dovec suggests keeping it simple: “You can just say, ‘Something feels different,’ or ‘I don’t feel like myself sexually.’ You’re not going to shock or embarrass your doctor.”

If you find yourself missing pleasure during this season of libidinal lull, Dr. Berkheimer encourages approaching your body with curiosity rather than pressure and expanding intimacy beyond intercourse. “That can look like slowing down and focusing on sensation instead of performance, exploring non-goal-oriented touch like massage or extended skin-to-skin contact, [or experimenting with] sex toys or pleasure aids,” she tells SELF.

Working with a body-neutral or Health at Every Size (HAES) sex therapist can also help you navigate medication effects, physical changes, identity, cultural conditioning, and more so you can erect an updated pleasure practice that honors the body you’re in now, Dr. Berkheimer adds.

#296. Are Tangerines Good for You? 5 Health Benefits You Might Love

Tangerines are not just tasty — they’re a powerhouse of nutrients. Packed with tangy flavor and vibrant orange color, these citrus delights offer a host of health benefits. From boosting your immune system to rejuvenating your skin, tangerines are nutrient-rich allies for your well-being. Let’s delve into their nutritional profile and discover why they’re a smart addition to your diet.

Tangerines are nutritional powerhouses. Here’s what each of these little champs pack under their orange belts:

Tangerines are teeny cousins of the orange but with a thinner, easier-to-peel skin. They boast a sweet and juicy flavor and pack a ton of vitamins, particularly vitamin C, as well as minerals like potassium, antioxidants, and dietary fiber.

These tiny bursts of sunshine have many benefits that can significantly enhance your health. Here’s why you might want to make tangerines a regular part of your diet:

Tangerines are loaded with vitamin C, turning them into tiny, tasty guardians for your health. This crucial vitamin supercharges your immune system by enhancing the function and effectiveness of white blood cells, which are essential for fighting off pathogens and infections. By improving the activity and response of these cells, vitamin C helps your body combat a wide range of infections more effectively.

Therefore, regular consumption of these mini-oranges satisfies your taste buds and boosts your body’s defense mechanisms — a win-win!

Want that glow? Tangerines have got you covered. They’re high in potassium, a real game-changer for regulating hydration and balancing fluid levels in your skin cells. This essential mineral keeps your skin cells plump and hydrated, warding off pesky, dry, dull patches.

Plus, potassium supports the removal of toxins and wastes, which means clearer, more radiant skin.

Tangerines are also a fantastic source of vitamin A, which strengthens the outer layer of your skin, smoothing out wrinkles and reducing fine lines. Along with vitamin C, it’s a potent antioxidant, protecting your skin from the damaging and aging effects of free radicals.

Are you having tummy troubles? Tangerines can help with a fiber boost that keeps things moving smoothly along your digestive tract.

These zesty little superheroes are your gut’s new best friends. They’re loaded with fiber that bulks up and softens things down there, making your bathroom visits smooth and speedy. This fruity fix helps manage everything from irregular pit stops to those bloated bleurgh days.

Fiber also balances your gut flora, promoting a healthy microbial environment in your intestines. This balance is crucial for optimal digestion, nutrient absorption, and immune function.

So, grab a tangerine to remedy your belly blues next time your gut feels out of whack.

Tangerines are a dynamo when it comes to battling serious health baddies like cancer and heart disease. These little orange wonders are loaded with flavonoids, natural compounds that help with heart health and cancer prevention.

Flavonoids help relax the blood vessels, lowering blood pressure levels and reducing the strain on your heart. This helps keep your ticker ticking smoothly and reduces the risk of cardiovascular diseases like heart attacks and strokes.

But wait, there’s more! When it comes to cancer, flavonoids mess with the bad guys — cancer cells — stopping them from multiplying and spreading their nonsense around your body.

Keep your peepers sharp with a dose of vitamin A from tangerines. This essential nutrient and compounds like beta-carotene shield your eyes from age-related issues and support healthy vision. It plays a key role in creating rhodopsin, a protein in your eyes that allows you to see in low-light conditions.

Munching on tangerines helps keep your night vision in superhero shape and supports overall eye function, keeping your peepers sharp and responsive.

Furthermore, tangerines contain other essential eye health nutrients, like lutein and zeaxanthin. These antioxidants are found in high concentrations in the retina, where they help filter blue light and prevent oxidative damage, further protecting the eyes from conditions like cataracts.

Sure, tangerines are delish and make your taste buds do a happy dance, but they’re also packed with nutrients that can seriously amp up your well-being.

From giving your immune system a high-five to keeping your heart beating like a healthy drum, tangerines are basically wellness wrapped in a bright orange peel. So, go grab one and make it your main squeeze!

#297. How Taylor Knibb’s Kona Win United the Endurance Community

An emotional Taylor Knibb looks out at the crowd after winning the 2026 Ironman World Championship in Kona. (Photo: Brad Kaminski/Triathlete)

In this job, I’m not supposed to have favorites. I’m supposed to be an impartial reporter of events, especially when it comes to a race like the Ironman World Championship.

But I really, really wanted American Taylor Knibb to win this year – not because we share the same nationality, but because we share the same philosophy. I think you, as a triathlete, share that philosophy, too.

At the pre-race press conference this year, Knibb made a surprisingly tender observation, at least in contrast to the usual bluster we see from pro triathletes ahead of a title race.

“I think it’s a shared experience,” Knibb said of Kona. “I feel like as humans, we connect through shared experiences, because it’s hard to connect with someone if you have no idea what they like. It’s a bridge between people: I see something the same way, I’ve experienced something the same way. For a race like Kona, people who were racing it 40 years ago had very probably similar thoughts and experiences. The island hasn’t changed that much, I don’t think…for a race to have been here for this long and have so many people race it…that’s a really big connection.”

Triathlon, as an organized sport, is only 52 years old. Most of the original legends have just barely aged up and aged out – Gordon Haller, the first Ironman champion, famously raced his final Ironman in 2023. But there’s a thread that runs directly from Haller to Knibb, and it’s not because they’ve both won the race – it’s because they even did it in the first place.

Very few people are brave enough (or dumb enough, depending on your perspective) to do an Ironman triathlon. When I finished my first, my mentor, Carlos, told me less than one-tenth of one percent of the global population will ever finish an Ironman. I don’t know if he made up that fact, but I do know that when he told me, I stood up a little bit straighter. I wanted to breathe in that rare air.

Even fewer people have qualified for and raced the Ironman World Championship in Kona. It’s a grueling race, with a swelling swim, windy bike, and humid run. Those who spend years building up to it can still be humbled by the challenge. In this job, I’ve come to understand that those athletes spend even more years telling tales of the race, each time with a new, progressively more exaggerated description of suffering. We give them a pass, because honestly, anyone who voluntarily put themselves in those conditions earned that right.

That’s why whenever we spot another triathlete out there, “in the wild,” we gravitate towards each other. I rarely wear shirts from races these days, but when I do, it’s almost guaranteed that someone will stop me in the gym or grocery store to swap race stories. I repay the favor when I’m out and about. My husband, who served in the Marines, jokes that triathletes are worse than veterans when it comes to battle stories.

There’s a shorthand that comes with encountering another triathlete, especially one that does Ironman. We know the lived experience of early-morning workouts, endless poring over websites and books for training secrets, the stiff walk the day after a century ride, the ravenous hunger that never seems to be satiated. We know what it’s like to doubt whether or not we can do something, and to go for it anyway. We know the horrible space between wanting to be a role model for our kids to work hard and dream big, and the constant worry over whether triathlon is a selfish pursuit.

In the words of Knibb: “It’s a bridge between people: I see something the same way, I’ve experienced something the same way.”

In a time when polarization runs rampant and loneliness is a public health crisis, a lot of us are looking for that bridge between people. And this weekend, we found it in the middle of the Pacific Ocean. Thousands of people cheered for Knibb along the course, but they also cheered for the 2,500 other athletes covering the same ground. Millions more took to the livestream, social media, and comment sections, because they wanted to be a part of it, too. They stood outside through alternating periods of sticky rain and blistering sun, laggy feeds and dropped connections, to pull for people they didn’t even know. And they did it until the very final finisher crossed the line to deafening midnight cheers.

Knibb was there until midnight, too. Because clearly, she gets it: This sport turns complete strangers into a supportive community, bound by mutual respect and a deep understanding of what it takes to endure.

Knibb is now an Ironman World Champion, but she’s also one of us. You are, too. And this year’s race was a celebration of exactly that.

#298. Elliptical vs. Rower: Which Is the Better Cross-Training Machine for Runners?

Does it really matter which option you choose at the gym? A certified personal trainer weighs in.

On the days when your training plan calls for a cross-training session, you may consider two classic cross-training machines: the rower and the elliptical.

Both machines are great for low-impact aerobic conditioning—a necessary break for your body from the repetitive motion of running while still building cardio endurance—but they deliver it in completely different ways.

🏃🏻‍♀️ Learn how to balance running with complementary workouts that build strength and help prevent injuries in the Runner’s World Guide to Cross-Training.

So, which option should actually earn a spot in your cross-training routine? We break down the pros and cons of each to help you decide.

This machine is low-impact, easy on the joints, and the motion is closest to running without the ground reaction forces, explains Lindsey Bomgren, CPT, founder of Nourish, Move, Love. When you’re running, your body absorbs 1.5 to 3 times your bodyweight during each step. The elliptical, on the other hand, places about 70 to 80 percent of your bodyweight on your feet.

On the elliptical, you can vary resistance and incline, get a steady aerobic session, and it’s a good option for maintaining fitness when you are dealing with injuries like shin splints or plantar fasciitis, Bomgren adds.

Indeed, a small 2021 study in the International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism found that the elliptical is a good substitute for running “during periods when a reduced running load is required, such as during rehabilitation from running-induced injury” when it comes to factors like VO2 max, heart rate, and energy expenditure. Even pro runners like Parker Valby love to use the machines similar to the elliptical.

“The elliptical is still a fairly repetitive, machine-guided motion, so it doesn’t do much for lateral stability, core rotation, or posterior chain strength,” Bomgren says. She also notes that the elliptical can feel mentally monotonous.

The rowing machine is a full-body workout, according to Bomgren. It targets your legs, core, back, and arms in one continuous motion, and it demands good posture and breathing control. “For runners, the posterior chain [muscles on the back of your body] and core engagement are big wins, and the low-impact nature makes it joint-friendly,” she says.

This matters because running is repetitive, Bomgren says—it requires the same motion, the same muscles, and the same impact over and over, which is a recipe for injury. Rowing engages different muscle groups and involves an entirely different range of motion.

The rowing motion is not very running-specific, Bomgren says. Because you’re seated, it doesn’t load your lower body in the same way running does. It also requires proper technique—if your form breaks down, your lower back may compensate, increasing the risk of strain.

Anyone with lower back issues should be cautious on the rower until they have the technique dialed in. For those dealing with foot, ankle, or shin issues, the elliptical may be a gentler option. Work with your care team to decide on a cross-training plan that’s right for you if you do have any existing injuries.

Bomgren recommends the rowing machine as the better cross-training option. “The full-body conditioning, core and back strength, and posterior chain work make it a better complement to running than the elliptical, which is basically a lower-impact version of more of the same,” she says.

Aim for one or two rower sessions per week, either on a nonrunning day or as an add-on after an easy run, Bomgren suggests. She recommends the following interval workout:

●Warmup (3 minutes): Row at a conversational pace. Use this time to dial in your form: Drive through the legs, keep the back flat, and let the arms finish the stroke. Your strokes should be long and smooth rather than short and fast.

●Intervals (12 to 15 minutes): Row 2 minutes at a moderate pace, then 1 minute at a push pace. Repeat for 4 to 5 rounds.

●Cooldown (3 minutes): Row at a conversational pace to bring your heart rate down. You can follow this up with a few minutes of stretching for your hips, hamstrings, and upper back.

Danielle Zickl is a freelance writer who has 10 years of experience covering fitness, health, and nutrition. She's a graduate of Ithaca College. #299. The Ari Shafer Shows How to Balance Speed and Adventure

The Shafer balances performance gravel with 57mm tire clearance, mounts, storage, and suspension.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

ACTUAL WEIGHT 22.2 lb (size small, as tested)USE Gravel, gravel racing, touring, bikepacking, rough roads, singletrackPRICE AS TESTED $6,812MODEL PRICE RANGE $2,549–$8,499FRAME ONLY PURCHASE OPTION Yes, $1,999CUSTOMIZABLE BUILDS YesSIZES OFFERED XS, S, M, L, XLTIRE CLEARANCE 57mmBB STANDARD BSA 68mmDERAILLEUR HANGER UDHSUSPENSION FORK COMPATIBILITY Yes, 60mmWARRANTY Lifetime frame warrantyCRASH REPLACEMENT Yes, at Ari's discretion

Close your eyes and picture a gravel bike. You’ll probably imagine something reasonably light, reasonably fast, with enough tire clearance for rough roads and enough mounts for a few bottles and bags.

Ari hasn’t pushed the Shafer to one extreme. It isn’t a dedicated aero gravel racer, and it isn’t an epic adventure bike. It’s a balanced all-arounder: fast and light enough for performance riding, but with the tire clearance, mounts, storage, geometry, and other features that make it useful when the route gets rougher, longer, or less predictable.

The frame clears 57mm tires and has integrated downtube storage, fender mounts, rear rack mounts, and a third bottle mount beneath the downtube. The rigid fork has three-pack mounts and dynamo routing. The Shafer’s geometry is also suspension-corrected for a 60mm-travel gravel fork.

The claimed frame weight is 928 grams for a medium, and its carbon fork is claimed at 491 grams. Ari says the current generation is more than 200 grams lighter than the previous Shafer while adding features such as the downtube storage.

And then Ari does something I haven’t seen another gravel-bike brand do: You can buy the Shafer with both the rigid fork and a RockShox Rudy suspension fork. So long as you run the brake hose externally on the rigid fork, swapping between a rigid and suspended front end is relatively easy. You don’t even need to mess with the crown race: The rigid fork’s is molded into the steerer.

The Shafer belongs to a category I think of as big-tire, adventure-capable performance gravel bikes.

These aren't dedicated gravel race bikes, and they aren't epic bikepacking rigs. They're balanced all-arounders: fast and light enough for performance riding, but with the tire clearance, mounts, storage, geometry, and other features that make them useful when the route gets rougher, longer, or less predictable.

The bikes I'd cross-shop with the Shafer include:

Ari’s buying experience is one of the bike’s strongest selling points.

The company offers a complimentary custom setup based on your measurements, riding position, and riding style. Ari can customize things such as handlebar width, stem length, crank length, and seatpost or dropper length, as well as set up and tune the bike before it ships

And the customization doesn’t stop at the online configurator.

I asked Tyler Cloward, Ari’s director of product development, whether a customer could order a Shafer with something completely outside the menu—for example, Light Bicycle wheels or a Polymer Workshop Rover integrated cockpit.

There are practical limitations: Ari may have better relationships with some brands, and unusual parts can mean additional lead time or different pricing. But the online configurator isn’t a hard boundary. So feel free to ask for a different chainring size, bar tape, or any other little detail that you want.

That’s the kind of flexibility I am always looking for when I buy bikes, and it’s something many brands don’t offer, or reserve only for their most expensive models. Ari offers it starting at $2,549.

Ari also gives buyers a 30-day return guarantee, allowing you to ride the bike on your own roads and trails before deciding whether to keep it.

The original owner gets a lifetime frame warranty, and Ari’s warranty can transfer once to a second owner under its terms. Crash damage isn’t covered by the warranty, but Ari says it may offer discounted replacement parts for non-warranty situations such as a crash, at its discretion.

My biggest complaint is the FSA SRS headset cover on my review bike. The cover has a port for routing the internal routing of brake hoses, but the opening isn’t sealed. It’s a forward-facing hole that’s basically primed to suck in grit and water as you ride—or when you wash the bike—which will then bathe the headset bearings.

That’s not great considering what it takes to replace the headset bearings on the Shafer. Because of the internal brake routing, servicing the bearings requires disconnecting the hydraulic brake hoses from the levers.

A little seal around that opening would go a long way.

I tested a size-small Shafer Elite with SRAM Rival XPLR AXS E1. I upgraded it with Zipp 303 XPLR S carbon wheels, a tubeless conversion, a RockShox Reverb XPLR AXS dropper, and the dual-fork option: Ari’s standard rigid fork and a RockShox Rudy XL Ultimate.

As configured, my bike costs $6,812 and weighs 22.2 pounds with the Rudy and Reverb installed.

That isn’t representative of the lightest possible Shafer.

The rigid fork on my bike weighs 536 grams. The cut Rudy weighs 1,371 grams, an 835-gram difference. And the Reverb is roughly 400 grams heavier than a good carbon seatpost.

So simply switching to the rigid fork and a conventional seatpost removes about 2.7 pounds (1.2 kg) from the configuration I tested.

For unknown reasons, my bike was delivered without a power meter, although the standard Rival build includes one.

It’s smooth, well balanced, and has a touch of mountain-bike-like composure. It feels stable rather than twitchy or edgy, but it is absolutely lively and tossable. It’s responsive on the climbs, and feels more efficient than you might expect from an all-arounder gravel bike.

The comfort is good, too. It doesn’t feel overbuilt, and there is enough compliance for long rides without making the bike feel soft or vague. The huge tire clearance gives you another effective way to tune the ride, too. Go bigger for more control and comfort, go narrower to make it snappier.

I tend to ride gravel bikes on a lot of singletrack and other terrain where a drop-bar bike probably shouldn’t be. That’s part of why I configured the Shafer with 2.25-inch tires, a dropper, and suspension. I was asking more of this bike than most gravel riders probably will.

Even there, the handling was really good.

It’s agile and nimble, but predictably so. No surprises. It consistently felt well sorted and dialed.

The geometry makes sense for that character. A 69-degree head angle, 83 mm of trail, and 78 mm of BB drop give the bike a stable foundation, while the size-specific chainstays—from 425mm on the XS to 440mm on the XL—are intended to keep the rider centered across the size range.

The Shafer never felt slow or reluctant to change direction. It just didn’t have that nervous quality some performance gravel bikes use to create a sense of speed.

With the rigid fork, the Shafer is a lightweight performance gravel bike. You lose 835 grams compared with the Rudy, and the bike naturally becomes better suited to smoother surfaces and more performance-focused riding.

With the Rudy, it moves toward drop-bar mountain-bike territory. That’s the configuration I used for a lot of my more questionable rides, and the extra control and capability make sense when the route includes rough fire roads and singletrack.

The weight penalty is substantial, but you’re adding suspension to a gravel bike because suspension can absolutely be an advantage on some terrain. But it also can be overkill for some riding.

That’s why I like Ari’s two-fork option. I don’t have to decide which version I want forever. I can have both.

The Shafer’s feature set works similarly. Fender mounts, rear rack mounts, the third bottle mount beneath the downtube, and frame storage give you many ways to carry gear. The rigid fork has three-pack mountsm which let you mount a variety of cargo carrier options.

Yet the bike never feels like it was designed around carrying a giant expedition load. It’s still a performance gravel bike. That’s the balance Ari got right.

The Shafer doesn’t try to be the fastest gravel bike, the lightest gravel bike, or the most capable bikepacking bike. Instead, it does a lot of things well enough that I rarely found myself wishing I was riding something else. For me, that’s the appeal.

The weight is competitive. The ride is excellent. The tire clearance is what it should be. The handling works well on gravel and remains consistent when the trail gets rough. You can configure it to fit your needs and priorities, and change its personality with a different fork.

And you can do all of that starting at $2,549, with customization options included.

I’ve ridden plenty of bikes that promise to do everything. Usually, that means they do everything adequately. The Shafer is different. It’s a very good all-around gravel bike, and one that gives you a surprising amount of freedom to decide what “all-around” means.

A gear editor for his entire career, Matt’s journey to becoming a leading cycling tech journalist started in 1995, and he’s been at it ever since; likely riding more cycling equipment than anyone on the planet along the way. Previous to his time with Bicycling, Matt worked in bike shops as a service manager, mechanic, and sales person. Based in Durango, Colorado, he enjoys riding and testing any and all kinds of bikes, so you’re just as likely to see him on a road bike dressed in Lycra at a Tuesday night worlds ride as you are to find him dressed in a full face helmet and pads riding a bike park on an enduro bike. #300. Say What? 7 Tips to Unclog Your Blocked Ears

Earwax buildup, allergies, infections, or changes in air pressure might be behind your clogged ears. There are many easy ways to get relief at home.

Whether it’s from a cold, allergies, or changes in air pressure, blocked ears can disrupt your day-to-day activities and even cause discomfort. Thankfully, there are several effective methods to help unclog your ears and restore your hearing. Listen up!

Why are my ears clogged?

Clogging can happen either on the inside or the outside of your eardrum. Here are the most common ways your ears can get blocked:

  • Earwax in the outer ear helps prevent particles and excess water from entering the middle ear. However, if earwax builds up too much outside the eardrum, it can cause a blockage.
  • If you’ve been swimming recently, some water might be stuck in your ear canal, pushing against your eardrum. When that water hangs around too long, it can lead to a swimmer’s ear, an outer ear infection.
  • Sinus infections, ear infections, and Eustachian tube dysfunction can pressure your eardrum’s inner side.
  • Allergies can cause uncomfortable inflammation and congestion in your ears. Your sinuses, throat, and ears are connected, so when you feel stuffed up and sniffly, your inner ear feels the pain too.
  • Changes in air pressure, like when you fly, can cause uncomfortable ear pressure.

Best clogged ear remedies

1. Pop and unclog

The easiest way to unclog your ears is by “popping” them. Just pinch your nose shut, seal your lips, and gently blow. This simple technique, known as the Valsalva maneuver, won’t clear earwax or fluid but is a common trick people use on planes.

2. Swallow, yawn, or chew

The Eustachian tubes connect your middle ear to the back of your throat. They briefly open when you swallow, yawn, or chew. Altitude changes can cause these tubes to close, but chewing gum or yawning can help reopen them. Alternatively, you can try the Toynbee maneuver, where you hold your nose and swallow.

3. Ear drops

Over-the-counter (OTC) ear drops can soften and dissolve excess earwax. If you prefer a DIY approach, warm a small amount of mineral oil and use an eye dropper to apply a few drops into your ear for a few minutes.

Pro tip: Baby oil or olive oil can also be used, but make sure it’s not too hot. Additionally, diluted hydrogen peroxide drops can be helpful.

4. Warmth and gravity

To loosen up clogged earwax, use a warm, damp washcloth as a compress. Lie down with the clogged ear facing down against the heated washcloth. Gravity and heat will help the earwax move along more easily.

5. Hit the steam room

Steam can help drain sinuses and alleviate pressure in your inner ear. Close the bathroom door, let the hot shower run for a while, and then luxuriate with deep, cleansing breaths. 

6. Take allergy medication

Because your throat, sinuses, and ears are interconnected, any sickness affecting your sinuses or throat can also impact your ears.

Over-the-counter antihistamines, decongestants, or nasal sprays can relieve sniffles, coughs, and ear discomfort.

7. Rinse away the gunk

Rinsing your nasal passages with a medication-free saline solution can help reduce congestion and clear out mucus that might be causing ear blockage. You can also consider investing in a nasal irrigation system for more thorough mucus clearing.

When to see your doctor

Have you been unable to unclog your ears for a few days, or are you experiencing severe pain, fever, dizziness, hearing loss, fluid discharge, or unusual odor? If so, it’s crucial to contact your healthcare provider promptly. These symptoms may indicate an infection that needs medical attention.

What not to do when you have clogged ears

  • Cotton swabs: Q-tips and other cotton swabs to remove earwax can push it further into your ear canal, so don’t do it. 
  • Candling: Ear candles might seem like a fun party trick, but there’s no science to prove they work, and they’ve been shown to cause injuries.
  • Sprays: Decongestant nasal sprays can be helpful, but using them too long can lead to rebound congestion.
  • Drying solutions: A few drops of rubbing alcohol or a mixture of one part vinegar and one part alcohol can help dry out the ears when you have a swimmer’s ear. However, doing this regularly can lead to irritation.

Takeaway

Clogged ears are often caused by earwax buildup, allergies, infections, or changes in air pressure. You can use over-the-counter or DIY ear drops, irrigation kits, or warm compresses to unblock your ears. Antihistamines or nasal sprays can also help relieve clogs caused by allergies.

PSA: Consult a healthcare provider if your blocked ears are painful or at-home remedies don’t work.

#302. The Things I Missed When Switching Between Shimano and SRAM According to Our Members

Bicycling members explain how parts, travel, and wrenching time shape their groupset choices.

When I wrote about why I switched from Shimano Dura-Ace to SRAM RED AXS, I knew riders would have opinions. SRAM versus Shimano is one of those arguments cyclists can have forever, usually while insisting they are being completely objective. Plenty of readers agreed with my decision. Plenty of others thought I had missed some important things.

So I invited four Bicycling members to join me for a video call: Alex Landt in San Diego, Earl Peterson in Alaska, Nick Malaspina in New Jersey, and Bryan Davis in Vermont. We spent an hour talking about what they ride, what they work on themselves, and what they are thinking about when choosing between groupsets.

I still think SRAM is the better choice, especially when someone is starting from scratch. But their answers sent me back to a part of the decision I had treated too casually: very few riders are actually starting from scratch.

My argument for SRAM included the convenience of a fully wireless system. No wire to deal with when I travel. Removable batteries. Easy firmware updates. Alex did not disagree with any of that. He just did not see one Di2 wire as a major problem for every rider.

“With the age of fully integrated bikes, I don’t think a cable running from a central battery to a derailleur is making the biggest difference for folks that are buying these bikes brand new, having somebody else build it for them, and they’re never going to service it. A lot of this comes down to how much you actually work on your bike.”

Alex works on his own bikes. He also travels with a bike box that lets him leave the saddle and seatpost in place, which means he never has to unplug a Di2 wire from the battery. I have to remove my seatpost whenever I pack my road bike. That wire has disappeared into the frame once or twice, making bike reassembly unpleasant.

Alex also brought up older bikes, wheelsets, and parts that already work for him. Alex was not arguing that modern Shimano restores old-style backward compatibility. It does not. Neither Shimano nor SRAM gives riders the mix-and-match freedom common in the 11-speed era. But it’s true that a rider with a bike they like, spare wheels, and a few usable parts in the garage is making a different calculation from someone ordering a new frameset and a complete drivetrain at the same time.

Earl lives in Alaska, where access to replacement parts shapes his choices long before he gets to hood ergonomics or shift speed.

“My metro area is 100,000. You’d think there'd be plenty of biking, but that's not true. I have four bike shops, and nobody stocks anything that I can work on. I like to service my own bikes. If I’ve got a problem with anything, even my SRAM bikes, they have to order parts. That element of it, for me, I would have liked to have seen addressed, because Alaska isn’t the only remote place in the country.”

That was a fair criticism of my original story. I am in Philadelphia, with more bike shops than I can reasonably visit in a week, and I can get current SRAM or Shimano wear parts without much trouble. During a normal week, availability barely registers in my decision. Earl does not have that luxury. A rider with fewer shops, a relatively speaking less common brand in local stock, or a bike that needs to work next weekend has to put spare-part availability much higher on the list.

Nick probably gave the clearest explanation of why SRAM worked for him. He enjoys working on bikes, but he does not have an endless Saturday to strip one down and rebuild it. He bought an S-Works Roubaix without a firm plan for the rest of the build, then slowly acquired the components through friends who were changing their own bikes.

“With two little girls running around, and a wife out there hustling as well, the windows during which I actually had enough time to make the changeover were an hour here, maybe a Saturday here, then probably the next Saturday after that. I could do the cranks, get the derailleurs on, change the cassette, put the chain on, pair it with my existing Rival levers, and leave all the hydro alone. I could ride it through the rest of the week until the next window of opportunity came in and say, ‘Okay, today’s brake-bleed day.’”

For Nick, the system let the project happen between the rest of his life. He did not need one uninterrupted day. He got the bike riding, then finished it in pieces when he had time. SRAM’s compatibility within its current AXS system and not needing to fish for wires inside the frame made it simple.

Bryan had a similar reaction to SRAM’s setup process, even though it ran against the instincts he built while working in a bike shop as a teenager.

“When I set up my Force eTap, I thought it was weird that I had to use my phone and the whole app thing. But I admit, it works really well. There’s the first setup, and then I rode it for a little bit and things broke in. Then I pulled the phone out again and fine-tuned it, and I haven’t touched it. It seems weird to me, but it works.”

While my groupset preference has swung strongly toward the latest generation of SRAM, I wouldn't tell somebody with a working Shimano groupset, a preferred mechanic, easy access to spare parts, and no interest in a full rebuild to throw it out. A rider’s local shop, existing wheels, travel habits, comfort with maintenance, and the time they have to work on a bike all change the answer. Plus, modern 12- and 13-speed road systems from both companies have made it harder to keep old parts in play, not easier.

I am not going back to Shimano at the moment. I am going to be more careful about how I answer the question. Before telling someone to buy SRAM or Shimano, I would ask what bike they have, what they need to keep running, where they buy parts, and how they actually spend their time with the bike. The brand debate can wait until after that.

A few readers asked why Campagnolo did not make it into this conversation. Not because I ignored it. I have tested Super Record 13 for about a year, and the current group is good. The problem is keeping it serviced and running.

I am in Philadelphia, where two high-end bike shops are within a mile's walk of my home. Neither stocks Campagnolo quick links, brake pads, chains, or rotors.

That is why I didn't list Campagnolo alongside SRAM and Shimano as a general recommendation. Those current Campy parts are good, great even. But I cannot recommend a group to most riders when they cannot walk into a shop, see the parts, buy the parts, or easily find someone who has worked on the current system.

Test Editor Dan Chabanov got his start in cycling as a New York City bike messenger but quickly found his way into road and cyclocross racing, competing in professional cyclocross races from 2009 to 2019 and winning a Master’s National Championship title in 2018. Prior to joining Bicycling in 2021, Dan worked as part of the race organization for the Red Hook Crit, as a coach with EnduranceWERX, as well as a freelance writer and photographer.

#303. 10 Signs You Might Not Really Be in Love: How to Tell the Difference

Love can feel like navigating a choose-your-own-adventure book with half the pages missing. Are you truly in love or just caught in a wave of infatuation? Sometimes, what seems like a heart-thumping romance may be a fleeting crush.

Wondering how to tell the difference? We’ve got you! Here’s a rundown of the 10 signs you’re not really in love.

Feeling a bit puzzled about your feelings for boo? That’s pretty normal. But before you start planning your future or picking out matching Halloween costumes, you may wanna make sure it’s real love and not a case of a serious crush.

Here are some signs that you may not really be in love:

Caught up in the romance novel vibe? If you’re all about the feelings of being in love rather than who’s sharing your popcorn, it might just be that you’re smitten with the idea of love itself.

Time to check if your relationship is more about the fairy tale than the real person.

Chatting with your partner shouldn’t feel as shallow as a kiddie pool. If deep talks are tougher than pulling teeth and rarer than a unicorn, it’s a red flag.

Sticking to small talk about the weather and dinner plans suggests the emotional depth for a lasting bond might be missing.

When discussions about future plans feel as far-fetched as sci-fi adventures, they may reveal underlying doubts about the relationship’s viability.

If imagining a future together feels unrealistic or undesirable, it’s time to ask yourself why. Real love plans a future; infatuation lives for the weekend.

Remember when their sock on the floor was cute? If little quirks now make you more cranky than charmed, it might mean the love goggles are off, your feelings have shifted from affection to annoyance, and the reality check has bounced.

Love is seeing imperfections and adoring them anyway.

Feeling more at ease or more ‘yourself’ when your partner isn’t around is a telling sign. If you’re secretly throwing mini-parties when they leave the room, you need to stop and think. Real-deal love means missing their chaos when they’re gone, not celebrating the silence.

Shared values are the anchor of deep, lasting relationships. If your core values clash more than a polka dot and stripes ensemble, you’re in for a rough ride, as finding common ground could be challenging!

Lasting love grows from shared beliefs and mutual respect, not from opposing battle lines.

No respect? No future. Respect is as critical to love as air is to breathing. Without mutual respect, you might just be coexisting rather than genuinely connecting.

If you no longer admire or respect each other’s opinions and choices, sustaining a healthy relationship will be difficult.

If they’re out of sight and totally out of mind, that’s not just independence — it might be indifference. When love is real, you should long for their laugh or lame jokes when they’re away. Could it be that your emotional attachment isn’t as strong as it should be for a lasting relationship?

If your best moments are consistently away from your partner, your heart might not be in it to win it. Perhaps your relationship isn’t providing enough support or happiness.

True love enriches your life and doesn’t play second fiddle to your social circle. It’s time to evaluate where your emotional energy is invested.

Still window shopping while you’re supposedly locked down? It’s a sign you might not be all in. A love that lasts doesn’t keep a backup catalog — it’s too busy loving what it already has.

Knowing why you’re still scanning for alternatives can help you address what might be missing or unfulfilled in your relationship.

Are you genuinely in love or just in love with being in love? If you’re secretly thrilled when they’re not around, stuck in surface-level chit-chat, or dreading deep-future talks, these are cosmic signs that it’s rethink o’clock.

Don’t ignore the signals — tuning in now can save you heartache later and lead you toward a love that genuinely fulfills you.
