#304. The 5 Best Rain Jackets That’ll Keep You Dry and on Pace

From waterproof and windproof jackets to weather-resistant packable shells, this outerwear will keep you running all year long.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

“Rain or sweat, you’re gonna get wet,” is the adage we use before heading out for a run in the rain at Runner’s World HQ. But that doesn’t mean you should shirk coverage or give up entirely on keeping dry during a workout. A good running jacket should keep out moisture, protect you from wind gusts, and allow airflow while pushing the pace.

There are materials to consider, along with weather ratings, that depend on your needs and personal preference. Jacket features like zippers and toggles shouldn’t be overlooked when shopping for a protective shell, either. You don’t have to prove anything to us, but if you wish to brave the elements—or just act like a kid and jump in puddles—here’s our guide on how to pick the best rain jacket based on the jackets our testers loved the most.

Water-resistant: Breathable shells or lightweight windbreakers are usually made of nylon and polyester, which keeps out moisture better than cotton. These jackets will sometimes have a DWR (durable water repellent) finish, but they won’t keep you dry during long runs in rainy conditions or downpours.

Waterproof: Jackets that are waterproof include laminates or coatings. These waterproof jackets will keep you dry but also feel like you stepped into a sauna as you accumulate sweat on your run. To help alleviate this, brands like Gore-Tex have created a permeable membrane, allowing airflow and preventing water from passing through.

Number rating: Some manufacturers share a rating on their product page, like 10K/10K or 20K/20K. The first number refers to water-resistance. It represents the height of a water column (in millimeters) that 1 square inch of a jacket’s fabric can withstand before it starts to leak. The higher the number, the better the resistance. The second number refers to the grams of water vapor per square meter that can pass through the jacket’s fabric. A higher number, like 20K, indicates better breathability. It should be noted, however, that there is no industry standard for “waterproof” or “breathability.”

Brands will sometimes list 2L, 2.5L, and 3L under jacket specs. These stats give you more insight into how the jacket is constructed.

Two-layer (2L) jackets feature a waterproof membrane bonded to the inside of a durable outer fabric, with an interior liner to protect the waterproof membrane. The interior liner keeps the jacket from sticking to your skin, but also adds weight.

2.5L jackets have a waterproof coating applied to the inside of a durable outer fabric and a protective film–the “half layer”–over the waterproof coating to protect it from contact with your body. The typical 2.5L jacket is lightweight and more affordable, but is often not as durable as a 2L or 3L design.

3L jackets have a waterproof membrane sandwiched between two other layers of fabric—an outer layer and an inner layer. It’s thicker than the 2.5L design, so it offers maximum protection for the waterproof membrane, allowing for the most robust waterproofing and breathability. This is what you want if you’re going out in a storm.

Waterproof jackets are either like a plastic bag or have a permeable membrane. The latter will provide some breathability, but you can still overheat depending on effort and duration of your run. Look for jackets with mesh panels and vents that allow air circulation so you can stay dry and keep cool.

All of the jackets on this list were tested by Runner’s World staff. We logged miles on humid, overcast days and rainy runs, noting the jackets’ breathability, range of motion, and if they made that distracting swish-swish noise. Our testers even subjected themselves to shower-testing when we had dry spells in the Lehigh Valley, here in eastern Pennsylvania. They noted how long it took for water to soak through and if any controlled droplets seeped in.

Our editors will continue jacket testing throughout the season, reporting on which are the best lightweight shells and which keep the water out best. We’ve included a range from waterproof jackets to lightweight, weather-resistant jackets, and noted their weatherproofing and layers ratings to help you shop smarter.

Besides the rotating color palette and patterns to look forward to every season (Janji chooses locations the world over, collaborating with local artists on its apparel’s graphics), there are so many functional features we love about the Rainrunner. For one thing, it’s waterproof and breathable. The back has layered slits for ventilation, promoting airflow so you won’t get too swampy in warmer weather or when building up a sweat.

The Rainrunner’s lightweight ripstop fabric is treated with C0-DWR water repellency and has fully taped seams for water resistance. Two zippered pockets have nylon pulls for easy closure, and an inset mesh sleeve in the left pocket is wide enough to store your phone so it doesn’t bounce. You can pack down the jacket into one of the pockets for easy storage.

Senior Art Director Colin McSherry liked the sleek fit of the jacket, saying it didn’t flap on runs. While the vents provided air circulation around his core, he did wish there were vents along the sleeves.

“While temp regulation is decent in the midsection of the jacket, it does get a bit moist in elbows and pit areas of the jacket,” he said. “Could benefit from micro perforations or venting in those areas.”

On the other hand, Senior Reviews Editor Cat Bowen said, “I’ve run ultras in sideways Scottish rain in this jacket. It’s perfect. No notes. 10/10.”

The jacket features a 2.75-layer Pertex Shield membrane that serves as a one-way valve for liquid: it completely blocks out precipitation while venting sweat vapors.

Our testers liked its slim fit. “One of my favorite things about the jacket was how light it was,” said hype editor and tester Ashley Tysiac. “I hate when running jackets are too bulky and distracting; instead, the Patagonia Houdini was so light that at times I forgot it was there. “Having even one extra pocket would make it more feasible to stick your phone, gels, etc. in there and not have to utilize a running belt or pocketed shorts while wearing the jacket,” said Tysiac. “The one, tiny pocket on the chest could only fit my keys, which was disappointing.”

The Canopy is a part of marathon history. Brooks-sponsored athlete and Olympian Des Linden crossed the finish line wearing the jacket at the 2018 Boston Marathon, becoming the first American woman to win the race in 33 years.

It’s more of a windbreaker than rain jacket, but we love it for its semi-fitted silhouette, lightweight material, and packability. “I wore it on a gusty hike up Whiteface Mountain in the Adirondacks and I thought the wind resistance was amazing,” said jacket tester and Senior Features Editor Pavlína Černá.

“Because it is lightweight, you don't overheat too much, even when running in warmer conditions,” said tester and News Editor Theo Kahler. “I wore it for an hour-long run in a downpour where the temperature was in the 60s. I didn't feel like I was overheating.”

However, Kahler noted that he became saturated during that hour-long run in the rain, proving this jacket’s limitations in wetter conditions. (That didn’t deter Linden from taking home the gold.)

Shop Men’s at brooksrunning.com Shop Women’s at brooksrunning.com

Jackets will come with instructions on how to wash. You can wash your jacket in the machine on a gentle cycle set to cold using a mild detergent. Make sure all pockets are empty, zipped closed, and drawcord toggles on their loosest setting so they don’t tangle or snag in the wash. Air dry the jacket or put it in the dryer using the lowest heat setting.

The coating will fade eventually with normal use or if it’s splashed with oils, like sunscreen. This is why you should clean your jacket regularly to remove dirt and oils so the laminate works properly. You can tell when the coating needs a refresh with the splash test. If the water beads and rolls off the coating is still working. If it soaks into the fabric, that means the DWR needs a refresh. Some DWR coatings can be reactivated with heat. You can put the jacket in a dryer on a warm, gentle cycle.

How do I make non-waterproof jackets waterproof?

Sprays like Nikwax TX.Direct can be used on jackets and other gear to make it waterproof. Follow the directions on the spray before using. And do it outdoors.

#305. Think Your Saddle Is Too High? The Signs Every Cyclist Should Know Before Their Next Ride

A quick check can reveal whether your saddle height is working against you.

A too-high saddle can feel fast for 10 minutes and terrible for the next two hours. It can show up as pain behind the knee, pressure in the saddle, numbness, or that familiar feeling that you’re reaching for the pedal instead of driving through it.

And because saddle height is the foundation of bike fit, getting it wrong can send you chasing the wrong fix. Riders often blame the saddle itself, their bib shorts, or even their flexibility when the issue is simply that the seat is a little too high.

To get the most out of your ride, consider a full bike fit—not just a saddle height change. Check out Bicycling’s Guide to the Perfect Bike Fit.

That said, saddle height is also where fit advice gets messy. There isn’t one perfect number that works for everyone, and the usual rules of thumb are only starting points. Your ideal height depends on your body, your mobility, your injury history, your cleat setup, and more.

Quick Signs Your Saddle May Be Too High• Pain behind the knee • Saddle sores or numbness • Discomfort where your hamstrings meet your glutes • Rocking hips while pedaling • Reaching for the pedal at the bottom of the stroke Quick Fix• Lower the saddle a few millimeters, do a real ride, and reassess.

Here’s how to tell whether your saddle may be too high and a simple at-home check you can do before your next ride.

Saddle height is one of the first things riders adjust, and for good reason. When it’s close, you feel smoother and more comfortable. When it’s off, the problems can spread everywhere.

But this is where people get tripped up: saddle height is important, but it is only one element in an interconnected system. If your cleats are in the wrong place, your saddle is too far forward or back, or your crankarms don’t suit you, changing saddle height alone may not solve much. It’s the beginning of fit, not the whole thing.

A common starting point is a height that provides around 30 degrees of knee bend at the bottom of the pedal stroke (6 o’clock position). But that is a starting point only, not gospel. Two riders with the same height and inseam may still end up at different saddle heights because bodies aren’t identical and neither are pedaling styles.

Pain is the clearest warning that something in your position needs attention. Riding is hard. Suffering through an interval is one thing. Pain caused by pressure, strain, or repeated irritation from a bad setup is another.

A saddle that’s too high often shows up in a few predictable ways:

This is the classic one. If you feel pain at the back of the knee, especially after longer rides or harder efforts, a too-high saddle is one possible cause.

But not the only one. Fit problems tend to overlap. So treat this as a clue, not a verdict.

If the back of your pedal stroke feels strained, tight, or tuggy, especially when you’re trying to make power, your saddle may be a little high.+.

A high saddle can make you unstable on the bike. Instead of sitting planted, you start shifting and searching. That extra motion can increase friction and pressure, which can mean hot spots, sores, and numbness.

If your hips are dropping side to side at the bottom of the pedal stroke, there’s a decent chance you’re compensating for too much saddle height.

Some riders point their toes naturally. But if you’re really reaching at the bottom of the stroke and compensating by going toes-down, that can be another sign the saddle is too high.

Rocking hips can also happen with a saddle that’s too low. So can a toes-down pedaling style. Tight hamstrings, limited mobility, weak core stability, and other fit issues can all muddy the picture. Back-of-knee pain can come from saddle height, but it can also come from saddle fore-aft, cleat setup, or a combination of things.

That doesn’t make the signs worthless. It just means you should think in patterns, not absolutes.

If you have knee pain plus hip rocking plus pressure and instability in the saddle, now the case gets stronger.

Todd Carver, Specialized’s human performance manager, shared a simple check that can help flag a saddle that may be too high.

If the distance from heel to pedal is more than about one centimeter, your saddle could be too high.

The result is a prompt to look closer, not a green light to make significant changes without further investigation.

Don’t make a giant change. That’s how you turn one problem into several problems.

Start small. Lower the saddle a few millimeters at a time, then ride it long enough to notice whether the change actually helps. One short spin around the block is not enough. You want enough ride time to see whether the pain eases, whether your pedaling feels smoother, and whether you stop shifting around on the saddle.

If you’re dealing with persistent pain, don’t keep self-diagnosing forever.

A good fit pro can sort out whether saddle height is the actual problem or just the most obvious symptom.

Riders fixate on saddle height because it feels fundamental. And it is. But it’s also just one part of a system.

A high saddle can absolutely cause trouble. So can cleat position. So can saddle setback. So can crank length. So can your mobility. The goal is not to chase some magic formula you found online. It’s to get to a position that lets you pedal smoothly, make power comfortably, and finish rides feeling worked, not damaged.

That’s why the best takeaway is a modest one: use the common signs, do a quick check, make small changes, and listen to what your body tells you.

Previous to his time with Bicycling, Matt worked in bike shops as a service manager, mechanic, and sales person. Based in Durango, Colorado, he enjoys riding and testing any and all kinds of bikes, so you’re just as likely to see him on a road bike dressed in Lycra at a Tuesday night worlds ride as you are to find him dressed in a full face helmet and pads riding a bike park on an enduro bike. He doesn’t race often, but he’s game for anything; having entered road races, criteriums, trials competitions, dual slalom, downhill races, enduros, stage races, short track, time trials, and gran fondos. Next up on his to-do list: a multi day bikepacking trip, and an e-bike race.

#306. Does Creatine Increase DHT? What You Need to Know

Ah, creatine! It’s a popular supplement promising muscle gains and enhanced performance. But as you’re hitting the gym harder and seeing results, there are some potential side effects to be aware of. Here’s the lowdown.

Creatine monohydrate is a naturally occurring substance found in muscle cells. It helps to produce adenosine triphosphate (ATP) — your muscles’ go-to fuel when working hard.

Although you can find creatine in foods like red meat and seafood, many gym enthusiasts and athletes boost their stores with supplements. Why? Because more creatine equals more ATP, which means more energy for high-intensity activities. More fuel means more mileage!

Now, here’s where things get hairy. You might dial up your body’s DHT (dihydrotestosterone) production when you uplevel creatine. DHT is a derivative of testosterone and plays a big-league role in developing male characteristics. But here’s the catch: while DHT might beef up your alpha vibe, it’s also notorious for thinning out hairlines in peeps predisposed to male pattern baldness.

So, do creatine supplements cause baldness? Maybe! The buzz mainly stems from a small 2009 study where college-aged rugby players loaded up on creatine and saw their DHT levels increase significantly.

Because DHT can shrink hair follicles and shorten the hair growth cycle, it may seem logical to blame creatine for contributing to hair thinning. However, it’s important to remember that these findings are a one-hit wonder — they haven’t been seen again in other studies. Plus, let’s not forget that intense workouts alone can pump up these hormones, too.

As a result, the jury’s still out, making the creatine-and-baldness saga a hot topic for gym gossip and scientists alike.

The same 2009 study found that after a week of taking high-dose creatinine at 25 grams per day, DHT levels rose by 56%. When the researchers dropped the dose to 5g daily for two more weeks, levels remained 40% higher than baseline. These findings contrasted with the control group participants who took a placebo.

Does this mean creatine could spell disaster for your do? Well, creatine boosts DHT, the usual suspect in male pattern baldness, also called androgenic alopecia. However, your disposition to hair loss and the effects of DHT is genetic, meaning that it’s inherited.

Some folks are more prone to DHT’s hair-ruffling effects because of how their androgen receptor gene is wired. Hormones like testosterone and DHT bind to androgen receptors, typically triggering normal hair growth. However, variations in the AR gene make the androgens extra effective, making you more likely to experience hair loss.

So, while there isn’t much evidence to say that creatine supplements cause hair loss, the connection to increased DHT levels is worth considering if your family reunions look like a convention for bald eagles.

Beyond the potential for a breezy scalp, creatine is actually solid in the safety department, with long-term studies giving it a thumbs up. However, although creatinine doesn’t pose a risk to healthy individuals, it might not be your best move if you have kidney, high blood pressure, or liver disease.

Another thing to keep in mind is that creatinine loves to hang onto water, so expect some extra bloat and weigh-in surprises as your body adjusts.

Thinking of starting a creatine kick? Chatting with your doctor first is always wise, especially if you have other health conditions or take medications. They can advise you and rule out any potential interactions.

If you’re taking creatinine and notice changes to your hair, a check-up is a good idea. Shedding a few strands is normal, but it’s a red flag if you start losing clumps of hair. Rapid hair loss can indicate underlying health issues that go beyond your hairstyle.

Furthermore, consult a doctor if hair loss is weighing on your mind. They can offer solutions or treatments to manage your hair loss and stress.

Creatine is celebrated for its muscle-building prowess, but rumors of a link with hair loss exist. The good news is there’s little conclusive evidence directly connecting creatine supplementation to permanent hair loss.

However, creatine loading may boost DHT levels, a hormone linked to male pattern baldness, especially in people genetically predisposed to hair thinning.

So, if you’re concerned about hair loss, it might be wise to talk with a doctor before adding creatine supplements to your muscle-building routine.

#307. Should I Exercise with a Phlegmy Cough? What You Need to Know

You’re feeling a bit under the weather, but you don’t want to lose the momentum of your fitness routine. So, should you push through and hit the gym, or is it better to rest and let your body heal? Let’s break it down!

Sleep is the best way to help your body recover quickly when you’re sick. But if you’re determined to rise and grind, you could use the “neck check” to decide whether to lace up those sneakers or stay in bed.

Many sports doctors use this theory to say that if your symptoms are above the neck — sniffles, sore throat, or a mild headache — you’re generally good to go for a light workout. But if you’re dealing with chest congestion, a hacking or juicy cough, diarrhea, a fever, or an upset stomach, it’s better to take some time to catch up on your Netflix watchlist.

Big disclaimer: there’s little scientific evidence behind the “neck check,” so use your best judgment.

If you’re going with the above-the-neck rule, exercising with the following symptoms is probably okay.

Going super hard if you have a mild cold is not a good idea. But a light workout, like a walk or a chill Peloton sesh, can be a great way to stay active without overdoing it. Stretching or light yoga might also do the trick.

Stick to light activities like walking for most earaches. Avoid intense workouts like weightlifting, yoga, or pilates, as they can throw off your balance and put pressure on your sinuses, exacerbating the pain.

Light and short workouts are likely fine if your sore throat is mild and lacks fever, cough, or swallowing issues. Remember to stay hydrated — it can ease your sore throat and is beneficial during exercise.

Light activities like brisk walks or gentle bike rides can help for allergy-related stuffy noses. If your nose is blocked, stick to very light activities, focusing on breathing. Skip workouts if you have a fever, chest congestion, or a productive cough with phlegm until you’re symptom-free.

If you’re experiencing the following symptoms, the workout can wait.

Working out with a fever increases dehydration risk and can worsen the fever. Plus, fever saps your muscle strength and coordination, making you more prone to injuries. So, do yourself a favor and skip the workout until you’re back to normal.

An occasional cough is your body’s way of clearing out irritants, but a frequent or phlegmy cough could signal a respiratory infection like a cold, flu, or even pneumonia or asthma. While a tickle-induced cough isn’t a gym deal-breaker, a persistent one is.

Diarrhea and vomiting can dehydrate you, and physical activity only makes that dehydration worse. Feeling weak? That’s a recipe for injury. Plus, stomach bugs are highly contagious. If you feel antsy, stick to light stretching or yoga at home.

The flu hits your respiratory system hard, with symptoms like fever, chills, sore throat, body aches, fatigue, headache, cough, and congestion. If you’ve got the flu, take it easy and give your body some well-earned R&R.

Once symptom-free, ease back into exercise gradually. Start with less intense workouts to avoid overdoing it. As your symptoms fade, you can gradually return to normal activity.

Regular exercise may shorten recovery time, particularly for acute respiratory infections. Listen to your body’s signals to gauge your strength. If you’re still contagious, opt for home or outdoor workouts, so you don’t spread those germs to fellow gym-goers.

#308. The Indoor Training Upgrade That Could Keep You From Bailing Mid-Workout

If you have a good trainer but still struggle to finish intervals, overheating may be part of the problem.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Most indoor training setups already have a fan. The problem is that many riders underestimate how strong that fan needs to be. A typical house fan just won't move enough air to cool you down during any interval workout you might do indoors.

On a hard or even moderate indoor ride, keeping cool and comfortable can make the difference between doing the intervals you planned and spending the session feeling like you are fighting the room. So yes, I'm going to argue that if you train indoors regularly, you should spend some money on a good fan (or three).

Riding outdoors creates its own airflow. Plus, your body cools itself partly by sweating. Sweat has to evaporate to carry heat away, and moving air helps it do that. Without much airflow, you will sweat a lot and still overheat.

That discomfort is easy to dismiss as part of indoor training. But the reality is that it adds physiological stress you don't need. As you heat up, your heart rate can climb even while your power stays the same, and the effort can start to feel harder than the workout calls for. Holding a power target is already difficult, and if the workout wasn't designed with heat training or adaptation in mind, then you are simply making it harder than it should be.

A really strong fan will not make threshold intervals pleasant. But it can be critical to completing a difficult workout inside.

Some fans are marketed specifically for indoor training; these are quite good but also quite expensive. I generally recommend something marketed more as a utility blower or air mover. In general, more fans are better because each one can add airflow from another direction and cover parts of your body a single fan misses. My own setup has three: two facing me and one blowing on my back. The two in front keep air moving across my chest, arms, legs, and face while the third keeps air circulating across my back, helping with evaporative cooling there. It may sound like a lot, but as I've upgraded my cooling setup, I've definitely noticed my ability to handle intense indoor sessions improve.

Remote fan control is nice, but it is not a huge dealbreaker for me. If you want the most streamlined experience, the small price premium for the Vornado FLY MAX is worth it. It comes with a remote that can strap to your handlebars, so you can adjust the speed without getting off the bike. If you do not need that convenience, my no-remote recommendation is the Lasko U15617, a high-velocity utility blower with three speeds and a pivoting head that lets you aim the air where you need it.

Also, if your trainer setup is in a place like a basement or garage where there isn't an easy way to open a window or vent to the outside, a dehumidifier can help make your training space more comfortable and conducive to longer sessions. My setup is in the basement, and I monitor both humidity and temperature down there. During a typical 60- to 90-minute trainer session, the humidity in the space can easily climb 25%.

All the marketing around indoor training tends to focus on the fun big-ticket items like trainers and bikes. Sure, there are plenty of reasons to upgrade a trainer or add another screen. But if your setup already lets you ride and follow a workout, consider investing in airflow. So you can push harder and unlock all the benefits of indoor training without unnecessarily overheating.

Test Editor Dan Chabanov got his start in cycling as a New York City bike messenger but quickly found his way into road and cyclocross racing, competing in professional cyclocross races from 2009 to 2019 and winning a Master’s National Championship title in 2018. Prior to joining Bicycling in 2021, Dan worked as part of the race organization for the Red Hook Crit, as a coach with EnduranceWERX, as well as a freelance writer and photographer.

#310. Firefly Built a Rim-Brake Road Bike Nobody Asked For. So Why Does Everybody Want One?

There are plenty of reasons to design a new bicycle in 2026. More tire clearance. Better aerodynamics. Lower weight. More integrated everything.

“Because nobody was asking for it” is not usually among them.

But here we are. Firefly has built the bike it says nobody asked for: a titanium road bike with 40mm tire clearance and caliper rim brakes.

Because a great rim-brake road bike offers ride feel and sensations that, in my considerable testing experience, disc-brake road bikes still haven’t quite unlocked. At least not yet. And those qualities are worth considering because they point to something that can get lost when we talk about the evolution of road bikes strictly in terms of what newer technology makes possible.

I keep my Mosaic RS-1, a steel bike with rim brakes, tuned up and ready to ride, and I try to ride it regularly. While it has electronic shifting, SRAM Force eTap 12-speed, it’s otherwise about as analog as it gets. Hell, it rolls with tubes.

I keep riding it because there is still something special about the way a great rim-brake bike rides. It’s not weight; the Mosaic isn’t especially light. It’s some combination of weight distribution, stiffness, frame and fork, wheels, and tires that gives the bike a particular liveliness and set of sensory inputs that just feel right.

Whatever the cause, I don’t think the sensation should be dismissed simply because the technology has fallen out of favor.

Kevin Wolfson, Firefly’s cofounder and lead frame designer, sees a more practical reason for the format’s appeal. A good rim-brake bike can still make a lot of sense for riders who value “the simplicity, and the ease of ownership, and, if you are inclined to agree with us, the elegance of a good rim brake [bike].”

The catch is that disc brakes also brought a major advantage: big slick road tires. If there’s one thing I wish my Mosaic could do that it can’t, it’s fit a tire wider than 29mm. Rim brakes still offer qualities I value in the way a bike rides and looks, while disc brakes opened the door to the big-tire road bikes that have become so compelling.

Which raises an interesting question: Do you really have to choose between the two?

Firefly isn’t the first to ask it. Rivendell has been making bikes along these lines for years, and English has built a few bikes around the direct-mount “gravel” version of Cane Creek’s eeBrake, which, sadly, never saw widespread adoption. There have also long been long-reach caliper rim brakes from companies including Velo Orange, Tektro, and Yokozuna, along with Paul’s center-pull Racer, that can provide clearance for much larger tires than a traditional short-reach rim caliper. The idea isn’t new.

What wasn’t right, at least for Firefly, was the particular combination of parts available.

The key was the fork. Firefly had already developed a titanium, 3D-printed disc brake fork with Josh Ogle for its other bikes. Wolfson told me the company began seriously developing its own titanium fork during the COVID-19-era supply-chain problems, when buying carbon forks became increasingly difficult. Once Firefly and Ogle had a working concept, they realized how much freedom it provided to design complete custom bikes.

Most carbon forks are available in only one length and a couple of offsets, so a frame designer has to make the geometry work with what’s available. But Firefly can specify its titanium fork’s offset and axle-to-crown length “to the millimeter,” Wolfson said. That gives it more freedom to refine trail, front center, tire clearance, and other aspects of the bike around the rider and intended use.

For this project, that was the enabler. Ogle could modify the existing disc-brake fork design to accommodate a center-mount caliper rim brake and the 40mm-plus clearance Firefly wanted. In 2026, no mainstream fork company is going to tool up a carbon fork with that combination of clearance, geometry, and a center-mount rim-brake crown.

That changed everything. Once the guys had seen the limited edition Mavic Ksyrium SL Heritage rim-brake wheels that helped spark the idea, and once they figured out that Cane Creek’s Brompton eeBrake could be modified to work with cable-pull road brake levers, the project went from a fun thought experiment to something they could actually build. As Firefly co-founder Tyler Evans put it, “it kind of spread like a contagion.”

And then came the details: 3D-printed titanium dropouts, seatstays that echo the fork, and a stainless-steel bolt running through a conventional quick-release hub and threading into brass inserts. Of the wheel-clamping system, Firefly says, “This is a tiny f***ing thru-axle. Stop making a big deal about it.”

The bike you see here is Firefly’s shop bike, built in a size that Evans, Wolfson, and cofounder Jamie Medeiros can all ride with small adjustments. Evans was the first to ride it, taking it on a mixed-terrain group ride and coming away fully chuffed. “It was pretty darn amazing,” he told me. “I was actually blown away.” He described the bike as light and snappy, with more “oomph” in acceleration than he expected. Not noodly, but responsive. He also said it felt unusually connected to the ground.

He kept returning to the relationship between the frame and fork.

“There’s something about when you make the frame and the fork together, you’re making one thing,” Evans said.

That’s one of the consequences of Firefly making its own fork. Rather than designing a frame around an existing fork with a couple of offsets and a single length, it can treat the fork as part of the bike’s geometry and tune it accordingly. Wolfson said that gives Firefly a “more complete custom frame set overall” than it could produce before.

And that matters because Firefly only builds custom bikes. Every one is a one-off for its customer, with fit, handling, and ride feel built into the design from the start. The fork isn’t just what makes the 40mm tire and rim brake fit; it’s part of how Firefly shapes the whole bike around the rider.

That makes the Firefly more than a rim-brake bike with 40mm tires. It’s a chance to see what a big-tire rim-brake bike can become when the frame, fork, geometry, and ride feel are designed together for one rider, using modern tools and materials.

While bikes like the All Road Rim Brake have existed in various forms for years, one likely reason this bike has resonated is that it’s a Firefly. The company has built its reputation on attractive, thoughtfully considered, beautifully executed bikes, and it obsesses over details you probably don't consciously notice but that make the whole thing look right.

The seatstays are a good example. Firefly made them a scaled version of the same oval profile as the titanium fork blades, allowing Ogle to carry the fork’s shapes and surfaces into the rear of the bike. “I thought it would be a nice way to carry the theme further through the bike,” he told me. And it wasn't just visual: The design also let Firefly narrow the dropouts a few millimeters for heel clearance without interfering with the cassette, hub, and other hardware inside the rear triangle.

And then there is the timing. Just as the industry is talking about bigger and bigger tires, 32-inch wheels, and increasingly elaborate bicycles, Firefly made something comparatively stripped down.

“I think there was something that was like really fresh about it,” Wolfson said. And, he added, “we really tried to make it a beautiful bike.”

I don’t think the argument is that rim brakes are better than disc brakes. They’re not. Disc brakes offer real advantages, and the ability to run big tires is just one of them.

But “better” doesn’t necessarily mean “nothing was lost.”

Maybe what I like about rim-brake bikes comes from their brake architecture. Maybe it’s the frame and fork. Maybe it’s the weight distribution, stiffness, wheels, tires, or the interaction of all those things. Maybe it’s simply the product of decades of development around one particular style of bicycle.

But that uncertainty is part of why I find the Firefly so compelling.

There’s one more question, and this one is easier to understand: Will people actually buy it?

Firefly says the response has been much stronger than it expected.

The frameset is $7,200, including the titanium fork, and complete bikes start at $10,000. That is a significant investment for a bike that, at least in part, runs against the overwhelming direction of the mainstream bike industry.

A few years ago I wrote about the “brown diesel manual station wagon” problem: enthusiasts say they want the thing, but the real test comes when it’s time to spend money. Wanting something and buying it are different things.

Maybe hundreds of people want a bike like this. Maybe 50. Maybe five.

Honestly, even if only five or 10 riders ever buy this bike, it would make me happy.

Because those would be five or 10 people who, thanks to Firefly and Josh Ogle having a silly idea and then being unable to leave it alone, get to ride a bicycle that wouldn’t exist otherwise.

Whether anyone asked for it or not, that’s reason enough to build a bike.

#311. Gravel Bikes Are Changing. Finally.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

This new trend is the best thing that could have happened.

I’ve previously argued that there are too many gravel bikes with little distinction among them.

Have you ever wondered why so many are out there? I believe I know the answer. I’ve ridden on roads in several countries around the world. A paved road is a paved road. I can take my road bike anywhere, and I’m confident I’ll have the right gear for the ride.

The same can’t be said for gravel roads. Their roughness and composition vary hugely. The champagne gravel of Steamboat Springs, Colorado, for example, is much different from the punishing rocks on the roads around Emporia, Kansas, that make up the Unbound Gravel race route.

But even saying gravel is different by region or geographic zone isn’t adequate: Gravel is so variable that nearly every gravel road is unique, and they often change by the mile. My local gravel roads in Durango, Colorado, are so diverse that on some a 30mm tire is sufficient, while on others a 45mm tire is preferable.

This is why, when you enter any bike shop in any location and ask to see a road bike, the salesperson will likely guide you to the same equipment. But if you ask to see a gravel bike, the salesperson is likely to respond: “What kind?”

In this way, gravel bikes are like mountain bikes. It’s not a monolithic category; many brands have numerous gravel bike families in their portfolio. Specialized, for example, has three families: Crux, Diverge, and Diverge STR. And when each brand has several gravel bike families, the result is a lot of gravel bikes.

The problem lies in how brands have created various gravel bike categories that ultimately aren’t very different. Much of the supposed differentiation among gravel bikes is superficial.

But a recent development has introduced more purposeful differences that will end up helping more riders find models with features to suit their needs. And it’s beginning to shake up the category.

The trend is toward increasing use of 53–57mm wide cross-country mountain bike tires, which began when some racers realized that for certain types of gravel, a tire that wide offered an advantage over the standard 42–45mm. The reasons: If the surface is very rough, a wider tire rolls faster. If sharp rocks abound, a wider tire is more resistant to flats. It’s hard to see obstacles when riding in a fast-moving group, and wider tires are more forgiving if a rider is surprised by an unseen bump or hole. But because many riders’ gravel bikes were designed when 45mm-ish clearance was all that was required, they were jamming in the biggest tire their bikes could (barely) fit, often causing damage from the tire or mud scraping away frame material.

The demand for such high tire clearance quickly outpaced development, leading to very few performance-oriented gravel bikes safely fitting such wide tires. Even as recently as earlier this year, new race-oriented gravel bikes were still debuting with less-than-50mm clearance, while racers wanted bikes that could accommodate 57mm tires.

That’s changing, though, and we’re beginning to see more high-performance gravel bikes with room for large tires.

I’ve tested this trend by outfitting a 3T Extrema Italia—for a long time, one of the only high-performance gravel bikes with 57mm tire clearance—with various mountain bike tires, most notably the 57mm (2.25-inch) Maxxis Aspen ST 170 TPI tires. And I can attest to mountain bike tires on a gravel bike being a real game changer—much faster, smoother, more forgiving—and providing much more confident handling.

Recently introduced bikes, such as the second-generation Allied Able, Argon 18 Dark Matter, and Fara Gr4, officially fit 57mm tires, joining the likes of 3T’s Extrema Italia and the Storm Makai in the big-clearance club. Many more gravel bikes with enhanced tire clearance (that I’ve tested but are still under embargo for now) are on the horizon. Not all of them will fit 57mm tires, but increasingly, 50mm and above will be the norm.

Here’s the thing, though: Not all gravel rides and gravel riders need 57mm tires every day. Despite the trend’s popularity, I believe things will settle down, and monster gravel tires will be something pulled out of the quiver as conditions require.

Tire selection is the foundation of gravel racing. If I wanted to compete in as many events as possible, I’d—with 100 percent certainty—get a gravel bike with aerodynamic frame shaping that fits 57mm tires, likely the Allied Able, so I could use them when needed. Because when the big tires are an advantage, they’re a huge advantage. (I’d still ride 45–50mm tires in most events, though.)

But I’m not racing, nor am I planning to. And for my daily gravel riding, a quick, agile, tight gravel bike like Cervélo’s new Aspero 5 is better than one with huge tire clearance.

What’s important is that the Cervélo and the Allied are more than superficially different.

The Allied has 57mm tire clearance and geometry designed to accommodate a suspension fork without any fit or handling compromises. It’s ready to take the best tire for any racecourse and has gobs of clearance for muddy races when fitted with narrower tires. It also has geometry that offers mountain bike–adjacent stability on rougher terrain.

The Aspero 5 has only 45mm tire clearance, but it’s more aerodynamic and has road-adjacent mannerisms—in my size, its wheelbase is nearly 40 mm shorter than the Able’s. That makes it feel sportier on less severe terrain than the Allied.

The takeaway here is that brands are finally starting to take risks in the gravel category, finding ways to improve their products and meet riders’ needs instead of rushing to join a trendy category with another similar bike just to claim a spot.

I still think we have too many gravel bikes that are too alike. But this tire trend has, finally, created some real choice in the gravel category.

A gear editor for his entire career, Matt’s journey to becoming a leading cycling tech journalist started in 1995, and he’s been at it ever since; likely riding more cycling equipment than anyone on the planet along the way. Previous to his time with Bicycling, Matt worked in bike shops as a service manager, mechanic, and sales person. Based in Durango, Colorado, he enjoys riding and testing any and all kinds of bikes, so you’re just as likely to see him on a road bike dressed in Lycra at a Tuesday night worlds ride as you are to find him dressed in a full face helmet and pads riding a bike park on an enduro bike. He doesn’t race often, but he’s game for anything; having entered road races, criteriums, trials competitions, dual slalom, downhill races, enduros, stage races, short track, time trials, and gran fondos. Next up on his to-do list: a multi day bikepacking trip, and an e-bike race.

#312. European Beauty Standards: Impact on Self-Image and Diversity

Though we see flickers of progress come and go, European beauty standards — which essentially worship white physical features as the best — are still prevailing across popular culture.

Keep reading to learn more about the damaging beauty ideal. Plus, hear from Siena Liggins, an independent artist and songwriter, about how it affects the music industry and what’s necessary for change.

European beauty standards focus on specific physical features, including light skin and eyes, thin bodies and noses, and poker-straight hair, to name a few.

“It’s honestly just a trickle effect of something that just exists in our culture on a very wide scale,” Liggins says about European beauty standards.

The Western ideal defines beauty through thinness and whiteness, something American culture was all about for, you know, ever.

But beauty standards often shift in America, moving from one extreme like the rail-thin “heroin chic” look in the 90s to today’s adoration of big butts and busts, with a focus on exercise.

Still, whiteness remains the most represented ideal, and we still obsess over thin bodies, regularly debating which celebrities may or may not be on weight loss medication.

The impression the European beauty standards leave us with is that those who most closely match the call for light skin and eyes, thin noses, etc., are the best or most attractive people — leaving some people of color to internalize the messaging, resulting in feelings of self-hate.

This Western beauty ideal is not only exclusionary — shutting out Black, Indigenous, Arab, and Asian, Pacific Islander people — but it’s also deeply harmful.

The standard is unmistakably splashed across the entertainment and beauty industries, from not finding your makeup shade to not seeing your features represented in media.

It also penetrates our daily work and play, creating societal issues and difficulty with self-esteem that impacts everything from securing and keeping a job to socializing and education, starting as young as nursery school.

For one workplace example, a 2020 study found that white women or Black women with straightened hair are more likely to land job interviews than Black women wearing natural hairstyles like afros, twists, curls, or braids.

Some of the first research on skin color and self-perception among Black children included “the doll test.” Researchers presented Black children, aged 3–7, with four dolls that all looked the same — except for their skin color — and asked them a series of questions about which dolls were nicest or prettiest and which they liked best.

Two-thirds of the Black children chose the white doll. The test was repeated in a similar way in 2005, with 16 of the 21 preschool-aged Black children selecting the white doll.

Needless to say, the beauty standard also negatively impacts the educational system, romantic relationships, and a slew of other dynamics and environments.

“The reality is that you need people to challenge them if you’re ever going to see anything change,” Liggins says about beauty standards.

She points to “AMERICAN REQUIEM,” one song off Beyoncé’s country album Cowboy Carter.

“She talks about how for things to stay the same, they have to change again,” Liggins explains. Though she believes Beyoncé refers to a hope for peace and healing in the United States, Liggins says this concept can lend to beauty standards.

When it comes to the idealistic view that we put on celebrities and pop culture, Liggins says you have to reimagine what it looks like over and over again. “And what that requires is letting in new people, and it can’t just be from a vanity’s perspective,” Liggins says.

Coupled with who is represented in music videos, Liggins says change is also needed at a gatekeeper level. “It has to be the people who are coming up with the ideas and bringing them into fruition who also have to have diversity, not just a thought but of background, culture, and ethnicity,” she says.

Otherwise, Liggins says, we’ll only continue to see spikes in diversity, making inclusion more of a fad than a serious change.

#313. Anxiety Tattoos: How Ink Therapy Can Help Ease Mental Health Struggles

Tattoos have long been a flex in personal expression and artistry. For some peeps, they’re the go-to for commemorating life wins or solidifying deep-seated beliefs — from quotes that got you through dark times or portraits of your fave pets.

The act of getting inked can also be a profoundly therapeutic experience. The machine’s buzz and the needle’s sharp sting are part of a ritual that may help bring internal battles to the surface. But is there a link between anxiety and the decision to get tatted? Could framing your fears and anxieties in gorgeous designs help you cope? Continue reading to find out.

For many, tattoos are much more than art. Peeps who have anxiety may get tattoos as a way of taking control over their narrative, including their mental health struggles.

Anxiety disorder makes life challenging, and you may feel you’re stuck in a rip tide of continual worry, fear, and dread. Even if you know it’s the anxiety talking, you can still struggle to contain these overwhelming feelings, and it’s exhausting. Anxiety can trick your mind, tell you you’re unworthy, and there’s no way out.

But here’s where tattoos come into play — they create a visual shoutout to your strength and resilience. Imagine marking your skin with reminders of the battles you’ve won and what you’ve overcome.

Getting inked can feel like grabbing the reins back from anxiety and stress. A tattoo is an affirmation. It can turn your invisible battle scars into something tangible and beautiful, giving a sense of ownership over your body and experiences. This is huge when anxiety tries to convince you that you don’t have a say in your own story.

Whether it’s a poignant quote, a symbolic image, or just a badass design, a tattoo packs a punch of personal significance and your enduring strength. You’ve taken a deliberate, proactive step to help you take greater control over your life, and that should be celebrated.

Psychologically, tattoos are visual high-fives to yourself. For the anxious folks, tats are a way to take those messy, abstract feelings and pin them down in something real and tangible.

There’s also some evidence to suggest that the pain involved in tattooing can be cathartic, offering a physical release for emotional pain. This could explain why people who self-harm or live with substance misuse or eating disorders might be drawn to the tattoo chair — it’s a place where psychological pain is acknowledged and artistically transformed.

Research suggests there may be correlations between tattoos and mental health.

One 2013 study involving 65 female participants living with anorexia, bulimia, and binge eating disorder explored the relationship between eating disorders, self-injury, and tattoos. Around 51% of the participants reported a history of self-injury, and 27% had at least one tattoo. Those with tattoos were more likely to have a history of self-harm, so the authors suggested that tats could be a form of self-punishment.

However, in an interesting twist, 27% of those with tattoos showed no history of self-injury. These peeps reported more positive body image, higher self-esteem, and fewer mental health struggles.

The relationship between tats and mental health is complex and still being decoded. Further research would help confirm the link between the two.

Tattoos can swing either way on the mental health seesaw. For some folks, getting tattooed is symbolic of their healing process. It says, “Hey, I’ve been through some stuff, but look how I’ve grown!” These tattoos often become symbols of a deeply personal journey, spotlighting moments of triumph over anxiety and depression.

But here’s the flip side: if someone gets inked on a whim or during a rough patch without much thought, that tattoo could be a permanent reminder of a not-so-great time.

In a 2011 study of 82 peeps getting their first tattoo, researchers measured their feelings about their appearance and body both before they got the tattoo and then again immediately and three weeks after the tattooing. The findings showed that right after getting their tattoos, folks of all genders experienced a decrease in appearance anxiety and dissatisfaction. Three weeks later, they reported increased body appreciation, a stronger sense of having a distinctive appearance, heightened feelings of uniqueness, and improved self-esteem. However, female folks experienced increased anxiety related to how others viewed their physique 3 weeks post-tattoo, while males reported a decrease in this type of anxiety.

These results suggest that getting a tattoo can positively affect mental health, but of course, the impact varies among individuals.

Tattoos can be an artistic strategy to enhance your mental health game, but it’s crucial to take a beat and really think it through before you get inked.

Whether you’re looking to mark a milestone, manage the mayhem of anxiety, or remind yourself that everything will be okay, a carefully considered tattoo can be a meaningful addition to your narrative, helping you manage anxiety and positively shaping your story.

#314. 20 Cycling Gifts Under $50 That Riders Will Actually Use, According to Our Editors

Useful, tested gear picks under $50 for riders who are notoriously hard to shop for.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

STOP: Read this story before you buy a gift for a bike rider in your life.

When shopping for a present for a cyclist in your life, you want to get them something they will appreciate and use, not junk that will get returned or sit unused in their closet. Resist the temptation to buy a bicycle-themed necktie, t-shirt with a poorly drawn bike, or a novelty cycling jersey, and instead, choose something they will love.

Admittedly, cyclists aren’t always the easiest people to shop for during the holidays, birthdays, or as a small gift to show appreciation. Cycling can be an expensive, gear-heavy activity with many niches and sub-categories, each with particular equipment needs. Yet you can still find great gifts for riders that won’t break your budget and will get used on rides.

Here’s a list of 20 of the most helpful, beautiful, fun, and affordable gifts for cyclists under $50; items we’ve tested, loved, and still rely on. Want even more great deals on cycling gear and accessories? Bookmark our Best Bike Gear Deals page for sales and discounts from top cycling retailers.

Bells are handy on the bike path, around town, and on the trail. Aussie brand Knog’s Oi bell is discreet, looks good on everything from a commuter to a race bike, and weighs only about 25 grams. Pick up the Oi Classic with a glass-fiber lever or step up to the Oi Luxe with a metal hammer for about $20 more.

Want to save weight in your tires or space in your seat bag? TPU tubes are lighter than traditional butyl rubber tubes and roll faster. They also pack down to about half the size of traditional inner tubes, so they’re the perfect spare tube for your flat kit. They’re available in sizes that fit most road, gravel, and mountain bikes.

Electric mini inflators have taken the cycling world by storm. These devices let you quickly and precisely air up any bike tire. However, most inflators are a bit too large and heavy to carry in a jersey pocket or seat bag. Although the Pocket SE doesn’t have a pressure gauge, this pint-sized inflator weighs only 90 grams and fills up to four tires per charge.

We were skeptical that $40 shorts could be this good. However, the Black Bibs consistently outperform shorts that cost six times as much. They’re very simple—no fancy fabrics or creative cuts—and that’s why we love them. Made entirely of plain black Lycra with mesh straps and large leg grippers at the cuffs, they don’t look like anything special. However, even after logging over a year in the Black Bibs, one tester consistently reaches for them first.

Toe covers are perfect for days when it’s not quite cold enough for full booties, but you want to keep your toes warm on the ride. Pearl Izumi’s Amfib model is a solid pick; plus, they are reflective for rides after dark. They provide enough stretch to fit over most road shoes (with cleats) and are easy to put on and take off.

The Duraglove ETs from Defeet are an awesome addition to any rider’s fall and winter cycling wardrobe. They’re perfect for rides where temperatures are still above freezing but not warm enough to go without gloves. These gloves have rubber grippers (for holding your handlebar in wet conditions) and are touchscreen-compatible with your smartphone or head unit. They’re an excellent value for under $25.

Lezyne makes some of our favorite cycling lights for commuting, road, gravel, and mountain biking. However, while super bright and durable, the brand’s lights can be a bit costly. The KTV Drive combo is a lightweight set of front and rear lights to keep riders visible on commutes and in urban environments. They’re rechargeable, have up to 40 hours of runtime, and fit most bikes.

Sometimes the best gifts are high-end versions of normal things you wouldn’t buy for yourself. While only 33 grams and the size of an Allen key, Daysaver’s Essential8 has the same wrenches as your regular multitool. The design uses nested and flippable magnetic bits made from high-quality stainless steel. As a bonus gift, the Essential8 pairs perfectly with the Coworking5 extension.

The small but mighty Mattone is a great choice for sleek, waterproof, and secure storage. Thanks to its elastic material, you can pack it to the gills or keep a minimal setup and cinch it tight with the Boa dial.

We look for two traits in a good seat bag: Carrying essentials securely without rattling, and mounting under the saddle without moving around. The Speedsleev Ranger 2.0 Small checks those boxes admirably. It has slots for repair items including CO2 and tire plugs, and a larger compartment for spare tubes and multitools. We’ve loaded it with two TPU tubes, a full-size multitool, CO2, and a plug kit, and still have room to spare.

The Wolf Tooth 6-bit hex wrench multitool is a great gift for any maintenance-minded cyclist. With an optional key ring and a sleek profile, the tool is easy to carry on rides (or when asked to fix your nephew’s bike after holiday dinner). It has everything you need for most basic repairs. Plus, it’s made in America, with replacement parts available.

Dynaplug makes the best (and lightest) tubeless tire plugging tools on the market. The Carbon Racer comes pre-loaded with plugs and takes the guesswork out of fixing a tubeless puncture when sealant isn’t working. The Carbon Racer works like the brand's aluminum Racer Pro plug tool but uses lighter (and more cost-effective) nylon and glass-fiber construction.

Stan’s NoTubes is the original tubeless sealant brand and still one of our top overall picks. Most tubeless sealant was designed for mountain bike and gravel tires that run lower pressures. However, road tires typically need more air pressure, which makes punctures and cuts harder to seal. Stan’s latest introduction is optimized for road bikes with 50+ psi and claims to repair holes up to 7.8mm in size.

A foam roller is a must-have accessory for recovery, preventing injury, and staying fresh. “I’ve been using this foam roller for years, and it's still going strong,” said Senior Health & Fitness Editor Jason Griffin. You can use it to work out tension throughout your body, especially on the glutes, quads, and IT band. Griffin also describes a dual purpose for this foam roller: “I even use this as a balance-board base with an old skateboard deck for cross-training days.”

Multitools are incredibly convenient, but can be hard to manipulate in tight spaces or when you need extra torque to loosen a stubborn fastener. This micro ratchet is a smart alternative that can speed up repairs and adjustments. It includes hex sizes: 2-, 2.5-, 3-, 4-, 5-, 6-, and 8mm, plus T10 and T25 Torx bits, a Phillips screwdriver, and two tire levers. Plus, it’s still small enough to stash in a hip pack or hydration pack.

The machined aluminum Sport Mount is a great gift because it has everything we love about K-Edge’s products—it’s functional, looks great, and is priced right. The Sport Mount fits 31.8mm round bars and holds your head unit sleekly out front and aligned with the stem. Unlike cheap mounts, the Sport’s insert is replaceable if damaged.

Socks are always a go-to gift choice when you don’t know what to give someone. Luckily, almost every cyclist needs more riding socks—and Swiftwick makes some of our favorites. The Merino wool Pursuit crew socks keep your feet dry and warm in winter while providing cushioning and compression.

If your giftee doesn’t already have a Buff in their closet to wear as a scarf, headband, or helmet liner, now is a great time to get one—it also works as a face covering when the temperature dips. The stretchy polyester microfiber is easy to pull up over the mouth and nose as needed, and it wicks moisture to keep them dry.

What started as a homemade, low-sugar, all-natural sports drink is now a player in cycling nutrition. Skratch Labs offers a palatable solution that keeps you hydrated and energized without causing tummy aches. The brand’s formula is designed to replace exactly what you lose through heavy sweating, whether riding outdoors or on the indoor trainer. Skratch offers several flavors (like lemon-lime, orange, pineapple, and more) and seasonal ones (like apple cider).

Do you have a young reader in your life who likes bikes? “The Ragtag Best Friends Bicycle Club” by Marley Blonsky, a cycling advocate and co-founder of All Bodies on Bikes, tells children about Maisel, her sister Zoe, and new friends as she learns that riding her own way makes cycling great.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.
